Ten code letters of the French ambassador to Rouillé and Bernis in the Dutch royal archives, listed on DECODE as not decrypted. The Dutch codebreaker Lyonet’s decipherments of eight sibling letters are among the images; aligning them with their cipher recovered 651 groups of the code, which decrypt nine of the letters (89.0% of the groups in this code measured as sense). A letter to Vienna filed with them is in another code, with its own page. 878 · 1117 813 · 1138 · 583 · 578 · 888 · 878 · 945 864 le danger de la religion, mais le peuple de = 219 1018 1138 · la = 583 382 · que = 197 194 · M. = 196 · vous = 569 · 13 = full stop The Hague → Versailles · numerical word-and-syllable code of about 1,200 groups · January 1757 – January 1758 The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters, 1757–58 to Cardinal de Bernis Go to the full text ↓ Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V, inv. 192: code letters of the French ambassador to the foreign secretaries Rouillé and Bernis, opened by the Dutch post and copied for the stadholder’s cabinet. DECODE lists ten of them, all in one code, as not decrypted: no decipherment was imaged with them. Clear copies of all ten turned out to be in the Fagel registers of the Nationaal Archief (found by WAINUT after the decryption). Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 192. DECODE lists them as not decrypted, saying the solutions were on separate sheets. The cipher One numerical code for the whole year; the key voted from Lyonet’s letters had 651 groups (extended later with register values); group numbers run up to about 1,200. How it was read Eight clear pages that look like d’Affry’s own letters are Lyonet’s decipherments of the cipher beside them. Aligned group by group (7 letters, about 3,300 groups) they give the key; ten letters then decrypt at 60–95% each from the key alone. Checked against Bussemaker (1906) and Coquelle (1904). What it says The navy and the convoys, the Gouvernante’s tears, Ostend and Nieuport, spies sent to England, a French loan tried in London. Still open The letter to Stainville in Vienna (R1071) is in another code and has its own page. Of this code, 94.2% of the groups read as sense (8,787 of 9,327); the lowest letters are R1068 (60 groups, 75%), R1074 and R1076 (about 89%). Lyonet’s own copies are in the Nationaal Archief, not digitised. No. 171, 26 April 1757 (DECODE R1069): the intercept copy in figures (left, 865 1028 875 1018 569 …) and Lyonet’s clear copy of the same letter, filed with it (right): J’ai l’honneur de vous addresser la copie d’une lettre que Mr de la Salle m’a écrite de Hambourg . Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 192, no. 171 (26 April 1757), via DECODE R1069.

Louis-Auguste d’Affry (1713–1793), a Swiss officer in French service, was Louis XV’s envoy and then ambassador at The Hague from 1755 to 1762 (the dates 1755–1762 match the title of Bussemaker’s extracts; the biographical details are not from the sources and were not checked here). His despatches went by the Dutch post, and the stadholder’s cabinet had them opened, copied and given to Pierre Lyonet (1706–1789), the naturalist who was also the Republic’s cipher secretary. Karl de Leeuw’s history of the Dutch black chamber (2000) records that Lyonet broke d’Affry’s first code in June 1756 and then “two more French ones”. The decipherments were copied for the Princess Governess and the regents. One set is in the Nationaal Archief (Stadhouderlijke Secretarie, 1.01.50 inv. 221 and 223, “grouped by the cipher used”, not digitised). Robert Fruin excerpted it in the 1850s, and Bussemaker printed his excerpts in 1906, as Dutch summaries with some verbatim French sentences. Another set is inv. 192 of the Prins Willem V archive in the Koninklijk Huisarchief, catalogued on DECODE as nineteen records, R1052–R1076 and R2067. Each record is one letter: the intercept copy of the cipher, with the clear passages of d’Affry’s original written in. Seven are marked “solved by Dutch codebreakers, the solution written on separate sheets”, and eleven as not decrypted. Ten of the eleven are this target; the eleventh, R1071, is in another code and has its own page ( d’Affry to Stainville, August 1757 ): DECODE Date, number To Groups R1072 6 Jan 1757, no. 123 Rouillé 556 R1076 7 Jan 1757, no. 124 Rouillé 424 R1073 25 Jan 1757, no. 133 Rouillé 315 R1064 1 Feb 1757, no. 136 Rouillé 1,249 R1065 3 Feb 1757, no. 137 Rouillé 1,082 (has a decipherment; see below) R1067 1 Apr 1757, no. 161 Rouillé 1,481 R1068 26 Apr 1757, no. 172 Rouillé 60 R1054 19 Jul 1757 “B.” (Bernis; DECODE reads Bonnac) 369 R1070 22 Jul 1757, no. 210 “B.” 400 R1074, R2067 17 Jan 1758, no. 283 “B.” / d’Usson 538 + two pages

A first pass took the DECODE note literally and treated the siblings’ solutions as lost. The attack started from cribs: Bussemaker’s verbatim sentence of 19 July placed “des précautions” (800 698) in R1054 by its repeat twelve words apart, and “le danger de la religion” turned up in the 22 July letter. That showed a word-and-syllable nomenclator, but cribs and a language-model solver got no further than a few dozen groups. The clear pages among the images are Lyonet’s decipherments. On R1066 (17 February) the clear page 5578, headed “N° 142 … D’A. à R.” with a clerk’s mark, begins with the same sentence as the intercept (“Mon courrier n’est arrivé que le 15 au soir”). It then goes on, where the intercept switches to figures, with “J’ai vu Mr de Slingerland chez moi ce matin”. It is Lyonet’s decipherment of the whole letter. The same mark heads clear copies in R1052, R1053, R1062, R1063, R1065, R1069 and R1075. Their openings fit their ciphers group for group: J’ai l’honneur de vous… = 865 1028 875 1018 569. R1066, page 5578: Lyonet’s copy of no. 142 (17 February 1757). Slingerland dictated to d’Affry the substance of Holdernesse’s letter to Yorke: Sa Majesté Britannique a évité la guerre autant que la prudence et les intérêts de sa part l’ont permis … Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 192, page 5578, via DECODE R1066. R1065, listed as not decrypted, is one of them. Its cipher is cut into thirteen numbered paragraphs that alternate between two sets of pages, and its clear copy is on four others. DECODE had noted a clear letter “whose relation to the ciphered periods is unclear”.

The clear copies were transcribed from the scans and aligned with their ciphers one group at a time, each group graded H (forced by the text on both sides or repeated) or M. The seven letters were R1052, R1053, R1062, R1063, R1065, R1066 and R1069, plus the ciphered parts of R1075, about 3,300 groups. The alignments were made letter by letter and cross-checked; a vote over all of them gives the key. It is a two-part code: the numbers are not in alphabetical order. Its group numbers run up to about 1,200 (the voted key has 651 groups, more after the register values were folded in), for letters, syllables, words and names, with homophones for the common ones ( de 219, 1018, 1138; la 583, 382, 10; que 197, 194, 31). Some examples: 13 is a full stop, and 105, 107 and 797 are usually nulls. Leurs Hautes Puissances is 399 627 261. Le Roi de Prusse is 16, Hollande 294, Reischach 488, Sa Majesté 22, religion 578. The Jan–Feb and Apr–Jul letters differ in their habits (which homophones the clerk favoured) but not in the code. The DECODE transcriptions needed correcting on the way. Two copyists wrote 8 as a looped figure that the transcribers read as 0, so 056 is really 856 and 099 is 899. This affects R1064, R1067, R1072 and R1075. Elsewhere groups are run together (58291 = 582 91) or lines dropped or repeated.

Each letter was decrypted with the key, and the few groups missing from the key were inferred from context and recorded with their evidence. Inferred values are in braces in the working files. The full French decryptions are in the repository; extracts follow. 6 January 1757 (R1072, no. 123): the Italian The whole letter concerns “the Italian”, a spy who wants to be paid for earlier warnings of English designs on the French possessions in the two Indies. For a hundred louis and a pension he offers to leave at once for England and report on the English forces by land and sea, the secrets of the London cabinet, their intrigues in foreign courts, the plans for the 1757 campaign, and England’s correspondents in France. D’Affry thinks the money well spent if the man is sound. The key alone gave about two thirds in sense here (89% after the image re-transcription, 96% after the register values were folded in), and Bussemaker has no entry for this date. The Italian reappears on 3 February, when d’Affry pays him the hundred louis and he leaves for Helvoet. 7 January 1757 (R1076, no. 124): convoys and herring A convoy the Dutch feared for had arrived: four ships were to escort it, and the storm kept two of them in port. D’Affry expects the navy to be enlarged sans augmentation dans les troupes de terre , and he expects the case to be pressed harder now that people see the English respect Dutch shipping only as far as it is protected. So every convoy through the Channel must be strongly escorted. In Amsterdam he talked with a regent about the herring. Bussemaker’s summary (no. 56): enlarge the navy without the army, protect trade, herring privileges for the republicans. 25 January 1757 (R1073, no. 133): a false rumour It was said that d’Affry had given the States-General a memorial calling any increase of the land forces a breach of neutrality. The rumour was quashed, but he went to see the Grand Pensionary. He told him the King neither wished to meddle nor ever had, but as a friend would regret seeing the Republic take on heavy expenses. Steyn answered that the increase would meet many difficulties. If its opponents could not stop it, he said, they could at least get a declaration made first to Versailles, Vienna and London, by which the Republic would confirm its resolution to stay strictly neutral; nothing would come of it before about the twentieth of next month. The register copy (scan 42R) gives these words exactly, and corrects the key-only reading in about ten places: à cette occasion for à cet égard , avec le même froid for avec le même succès , vers le vingt du Mois , Il faudroit voir si celà ne va pas mieux . 1 February 1757 (R1064, no. 136): taxes and herring The States of Holland had adjourned until the 20th, when the augmentation comes up. The war funds were no larger than usual, and the means proposed (a sixth added to the house tax, a general rise in excises, interest on public funds cut to 2%) were so heavy that the augmentation looked unlikely. D’Affry then argues for a temporary favour to the Dutch herring fishery while France lacks sailors. It could be revoked when no longer deserved, and it would widen the quarrel between the Republic and England. He asks for it only if Holland blocks the augmentation. Then comes intelligence on suspects travelling through Antwerp, Breda and Liège. Bussemaker’s no. 59 gives the first part point by point and leaves out the agents, as Fruin said he did. 1 April 1757 (R1067, no. 161): the Gouvernante The Maastricht convoy crisis. D’Affry found the Pensionary “fort embarrassé”: ce qui se passe ici aujourd’hui n’est […] que pour le perdre . The same afternoon he read the King’s declaration to the Princess Governess: «… tu n’es pas ministre; faut-il que ce soit moi qui favorise les moyens de faire du mal à mon père?» Je lui ai répondu que S.A.R. savoit jusqu’à quel point le Roi mon maître a cherché à éviter la guerre … Je demande à S.A.R. d’employer non seulement ses bons offices, mais son crédit et son pouvoir pour déterminer une réponse prompte et telle que le Roi a droit de l’espérer. Coquelle quoted the Governess’s words (NOTES.md says 1904; the Sources list gives the book as Paris, 1902) from the Paris original, with the day given as 5 April. The piece that Bussemaker’s no. 67 quotes about Wassenaer (“son fils cadet a actuellement un employ en Frise, dont la nomination dépend de Mme la Gouvernante”) is piece no. 7 of this letter. The numbered pieces follow the page order, not the number order. 26 April 1757 (R1068, no. 172) Il a passé Vendredi au soir un courrier de Vienne à Londres. Vous savez mieux que moi ce dont il est chargé. M. de Colloredo doit faire passer à M. Starrenberg ce qu’on lui aura répondu. The key alone gave hier and read the name as d’Aremberg ; the Fagel register copy (below) has Vendredi and Starrenberg , Starhemberg, the imperial ambassador at Versailles. The DECODE note asked whether this note was left undecrypted because a different code was used. It was not: it is the same code as no. 171, which Lyonet deciphered. 19 July 1757 (R1054, to Bernis) Nobody knows the purpose of the Gouvernante’s journey to The Hague. If it is to push an augmentation of the land forces, d’Affry asks for orders at once: … il me paroit qu’il seroit essentiel aux intérêts du Roi de m’envoyer des ordres sur le champ [de demander] une confirmation de tout ce que les Etats-Généraux ont promis à Sa Majesté, et en même tems une déclaration de leur part qu’ils ne feront camper aucun corps sur leurs frontières. Je sens la dureté de cette proposition … The passage runs from group 145 to group 351, and Bussemaker’s French agrees with it word for word except in four places. The cipher has “M. le maréchal d’Estrées” where Fruin wrote “M. le Cte”. It has “de sa communication” for “de la communication du Royaume”. It spells out Leurs Hautes Puissances , and it has “des ordres” for “ordre de demander”. The page ends with an attack of gout. 22 July 1757 (R1070, no. 210, to Bernis): Ostend The Gouvernante is said to be going to the States of Holland to speak for her father George II, pointing to the danger to the Protestant religion. D’Affry doubts she will: if she proposes land troops, the other side will propose ships. Her party protested at the French occupation of Ostend and Nieuport. D’Affry notes that sensible people see the other side of it: with Ostend closed to the English, Amsterdam and Rotterdam will take over the trade England did with the Low Countries. Then Bussemaker’s sentence, group for group: Il y a quelques villes où quelques ministres hollandois ont prêché sur le danger de la religion, mais le peuple n’en paroit pas animé . If the Princess takes the Ostend affair as a pretext, he will ask her for an audience without waiting for orders. 17 January 1758 (R1074, no. 283, and R2067) The first part is an extract from a correspondent’s letter. A French loan of two millions had been tried in England by “des gens si maladroits” that the ministry heard of it and a new law followed. It could still be got round: four millions at four or four and a half per cent at most, given “un profond secret, une parfaite connoissance du pays”. D’Affry adds that a Sieur Mac[donald] of the Bulkeley regiment has passed through on his way from France to England, and he suspects him of carrying commissions for the enemy. Some Scots and Irish in French service are spies, he writes, but to act would throw suspicion on the rest. The companion letter of the same day to d’Usson (R2067) has no DECODE transcription. It was transcribed from the images and decrypted at about 91%. It is d’Affry’s own letter of the same number, covering the extract. He thinks money operations in England useless: if found out, they would make France’s needs look greater than they are and put the English on their guard. Englishmen will still lend in France when the interest is right, and some already hold French life annuities. He adds that two or three Englishmen are at The Hague, one of them Mac…, and that two Spaniards from Paris, one a secretary of the Spanish embassy, are on their way to London.

Re-measured 5 October 2026. The 21 September figure (86%) counted every group that had a value. A sense measure ( measure_sense.py ) now counts a group only if its nine-group window reads as French: 89.0% of the 9,306 groups in this code (Lyonet’s eight letters counted as read; rerun 14 October 2026 without R1071, which is in another code and was counted unread until then, giving 82.3%). Four letters were re-transcribed from the images, which recovered the copyist’s looped 8 that DECODE reads as 0 and 135 groups the earlier parse had lost: R1072 0.66 → 0.89, R1067 0.66 → 0.79, R1074 0.70 → 0.75, R1064 0.77 → 0.81. Pooling every occurrence fixed eighteen more code values ( lui , dit , faire , Écosse , la Gouvernante …). R1071 (4 August 1757, to Stainville in Vienna) is in a different code: its own page . Per letter, between about 4% (R1073) and 25% (R1068, a 60-group note) of groups were still open in the last measurement of 27 October (listed as [n] in the older decryption files). R1072 gave only about two thirds in sense from the key alone, because its DECODE copy was the worst transcribed; after re-transcription and the register values it measures 96%. Grades: values forced by a decipherment are H; values inferred from context in the letters without a decipherment are M or ? and listed with their evidence in read/R*_new.tsv . 56 groups of the key are ambiguous between two values ( amb_M.json ). The eight decipherments themselves are Lyonet’s. The contribution here is the key and the decryption of the ten letters (R2067, the cover letter to R1074, counted separately) that have none on DECODE. Contributed, 21 October 2026. WAINUT , a Dutch AI company, found that the clear text of all ten letters without a Lyonet sheet is digitised after all: clerks’ copies in the Fagel registers, Nationaal Archief 1.10.29 inv. 5186 (1757) and 5187 (1758), in date order with number and addressee ( pull request #65 ). Aligned against them, this key gives the register’s word for 4,333 of 5,554 keyed groups (78%), against at most 21% for shuffled keys; the per-letter figures were re-run here and reproduce. The registers were found after the decryption and were not used for it: the 89% is a reading from the key alone. They settle open groups ( projets , lundi , mardi , là dessus …), contradict some key values (675 is vingt , not deux ; 1106 froid , not succès ; 992 is -er , not des , at all eleven places) and correct the 25 January letter in about ten places. Folded into the key, 21 October 2026. The proposals were checked on sixteen register scans read here, and each candidate was set against Lyonet’s own decipherments. 58 values were adopted: 21 groups that had no value and 37 values replaced (from the key or inferred earlier). Seven were dropped because Lyonet reads them otherwise as often or more: some groups really take two values ( moi and mois , le roi de Prusse and prussien , utile and utilité ). Re-measured, the ten letters with no contemporary decipherment on DECODE go from 82.4% to 86.0% of their groups read as sense, and the whole code from 89.0% to 91.3% (8,492 of 9,306); R1073 reaches 94%, R1072 93.5%, R1074 77.5%. Against the register text the key now matches 81% of keyed groups (was 78%); that figure is partly circular, since the new values come from the same registers. Second pass, the same day. 131 groups still had no value. For 86 of them the register gives a clean word, seen on its scan (two more scans read, 63R and 248R) and not contradicted by Lyonet: Allemagne , Berlin , Wassenaer , question , six , toutes , possible , huit … The other 45 stay open: the register piece is a single letter or a syllable cut at the edge of the alignment, or the occurrences disagree. The code now reads at 94.1% (8,761 of 9,306 groups), and the ten letters with no decipherment on DECODE at 90.6%; R1067 went from 79% to 92%, R1074 from 75% to 89%. Still open: those 45 groups and the groups that take two values. Checked on the images, 27 October 2026. The last five letters still measured on the DECODE transcription (R1054, R1068, R1070, R1073, R1076) were checked line by line on the scans. DECODE had dropped two whole lines of R1076 (the first lines of its paragraphs 4 and 8) and two groups of R1070, split three groups of R1054 at a superscript correction, and run groups together in R1073; R1070 and R1076 have their two pages in reverse order on DECODE. Measured on the new transcriptions the code reads at 94.2% (8,787 of 9,327 groups); R1073 rises from 93.9% to 96.2% and R1076 from 87.3% to 88.7%. A few groups lie in the binding or under ink.

Decryption R1053.txt Il est arrivé hier ici un courrier de Mr de Haren, Ministre de la Republique à Bruxelles, par lequel ce Ministre donne avis de la marche de l'Armée du Roi, composée de Nonante Mille hommes. Cette nouvelle a dabord allarmé, et quelques Republicains sont venus me demander si je le savois. Je les ai assuré que non; et je leur ai dit que vous ne manqueriez pas de me mettre en état de notifier aux Ministres de la Republique la marche de cette armée, et de témoigner en même tems à Leurs Hautes Puissances la droiture des intentions de Sa Majesté à leur égard. J'ai ajouté que si le courrier que j'attendois m'en aportoit la nouvelle, j'en ferois part sur le champ, et que si vous ne me le marquiez pas on pouvoit compter que cette nouvelle n'étoit qu'un panneau du parti anglois pour alterer notre confiance mutuelle, mais j'esperois que l'on n'en seroit la duppe. Vous jugez, Mr, combien il est important que je sois instruit de bonne heure de tout ce que Sa Majesté jugera devoir être communiqué ici. Mr Burdin, qui m'a porté une lettre de vous de recommandation, s'est informé depuis Anvers jusqu'ici et dans les differentes routes qu'il a fait en Hollande d'un officier Suisse au service des Etats Generaux, nommé Ficher. Cet officier est parti il y a quelques jours pour Paris accompagné d'un François arrivant d'Angleterre, qui doit avoir emprunté beaucoup d'argent à Amsterdam de la part de l'Angleterre pour faire à Paris et dans le Royaume le metier d'espion. Ce François s'appelle Meunier; mais il a traduit son nom en Anglois, et doit porter celui de Muller ou de Miller. Il y a aparence que Ficher cherchera à voir Mr Burdin par lequel on pourroit decouvrir la verité de ce que j'ai eu l'honneur de vous marquer. Translation R1053_en.md <!-- English translation of plain/R1053.txt (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): Lyonet's contemporary clear decipherment, imaged on the DECODE record R1053 and transcribed here. --> # R1053, d'Affry, The Hague, 1757: English translation of the contemporary decipherment A courier arrived here yesterday from Mr de Haren, the Republic's Minister at Brussels, by which this Minister gives notice of the march of the King's army, made up of ninety thousand men. This news at first caused alarm, and some Republicans came to ask me whether I knew of it. I assured them that I did not; and I told them that you would not fail to put me in a position to notify the Ministers of the Republic of the march of this army, and at the same time to assure Their High Mightinesses of the uprightness of His Majesty's intentions towards them. I added that if the courier I was expecting brought me the news, I would communicate it at once, and that if you did not tell me of it, they could count on this news being nothing but a trap of the English party to undermine our mutual confidence; but I hoped no one would be its dupe. You can judge, Sir, how important it is that I be informed early of everything His Majesty sees fit to have communicated here. Mr Burdin, who brought me a letter of recommendation from you, has made enquiries from Antwerp to here, and along the various routes he has travelled in Holland, about a Swiss officer in the service of the States General named Ficher. This officer left a few days ago for Paris, accompanied by a Frenchman arriving from England, who is said to have borrowed a great deal of money in Amsterdam on England's behalf in order to ply the trade of spy in Paris and in the kingdom. This Frenchman is called Meunier; but he has translated his name into English, and is said to go by that of Muller or Miller. It seems likely that Ficher will try to see Mr Burdin, through whom one might discover the truth of what I have had the honour to tell you. This man gave the merchant addresses in his own hand, which you will find in this packet, and an itinerary for the merchant in case he wished to go to Brittany, which the merchant gave to me. He added that this man was at Cologne and might perhaps come to Amsterdam. Their conversation took place on the twenty-eighth of ____ last, on the road and at Breda. This man called himself Mr Delf at Brussels, and is said to have taken back his name of Comte d'Urvoy. In the distress I am in, I did not think to have a copy made of Baron von Hatzel's letter; but as you have it, you will be able to see whether, despite the difference of condition, this man is the same, or whether they are two monsters. Decryption R1063.txt N° [134] D'A. à R. Du 27 Janvier 1757 J'écris aujourd'hui à Mr de Hatzel comme vous me l'ordonnez; mais je crois qu'il n'aura rien à nous reveler que de vague. Je suis persuadé que l'homme dont il nous parle n'est autre chose que le Comte d'Urvoy. On n'a point encore entendu parler de lui dans ce Païs. Les bruits de l'augmentation de Terre prennent vivement depuis avanthier au soir; à en croire le public elle va être determinée. J'ai lieu (de croire) qu'Elle ne le sera pas si tôt. Comme Mr de Reischach a la permission de sa Cour de presser plus ou moins la demande du secours, j'ai cru devoir Lui conseiller de voir les Ministres pour leur demander à quoi cette affaire en étoit. Cela a produit ce que j'en esperois; c'est à dire de l'embarras, et tout embarras est un moyen leur de retarder, et quelque fois même d'anéantir les Projets qui pourroient nous gêner. La Cour de Vienne a en main de quoi les retenir, par les questions qu'Elle peut agiter sur les Places de la Barriere, et sur tout sur l'occupation de Namur. Daignez vous rapeller ce que j'ai eu l'honneur de vous en dire; mais comme ce moyen est très delicat, je crois qu'il faut pour l'employer de concert avec Vienne, attendre que la delicatesse du moment nous y conduise; car il pourroit arriver l'evenement le plus singulier qui seroit que l'Imperatrice auroit malgré Elle une Guarnizon dans une de ces Places les plus fortes, que ces étrangers approvisionnent amplement de tout. Comme je ne suis instruit de rien, je ne puis que vous mettre sous les yeux une idée de ce qui (peut) arriver. Je ne puis croire que ce Païs manque de raison au point de vouloir s'engager et augmenter les troubles qui agitent l'Europe; mais si cela est, une explication prompte sur Namur seroit plus essentielle que je ne peux l'exprimer. I am writing today to Mr de Hatzel as you order me; but I believe he will have nothing but vague things to reveal to us. I am persuaded that the man he speaks of to us is none other than the Comte d'Urvoy. Nothing has yet been heard of him in this country. The rumours of the augmentation of the land forces have been gaining ground strongly since the evening before yesterday; to believe the public, it is about to be decided. I have reason (to believe) that it will not be so soon. As Mr von Reischach has his court's permission to press the request for help more or less, I thought I should advise him to see the Ministers and ask them how matters stood. This produced what I hoped for, that is, embarrassment; and every embarrassment is a means for them to delay, and sometimes even to destroy, the projects that might hamper us. The court of Vienna has in hand the means of holding them back, through the questions it can raise about the Barrier towns, and above all about the occupation of Namur. Be pleased to recall what I had the honour of telling you about it; but as this means is very delicate, I believe that to use it in concert with Vienna we must wait until the delicacy of the moment leads us to it; for the most singular thing might happen, namely that the Empress would have, against her will, a garrison in one of the strongest of those towns, which these foreigners supply amply with everything. As I am informed of nothing, I can only put before you an idea of what (may) happen. I cannot believe that this country is so lacking in reason as to wish to commit itself and increase the troubles that agitate Europe; but if it is so, a prompt explanation about Namur would be more essential than I can express. [107] ## English summary The States of Holland have adjourned and reassemble on the 20th to deal with the army augmentation, which d'Affry hopes will fail. The war funds for this year are no larger than last year's, and the proposed means (a sixth added to the house tax, a general rise in the excises, and cutting interest on public funds to 2%) are so burdensome that the States are unlikely to adopt them. On herring: he has learnt how important it is to reduce the Dutch fishery's profit and encourage the French one, but with French sailors short in wartime he thinks a temporary favour to the Dutch fishery would cost little, would be revocable if the Republic misbehaved, would please nearly all the Dutch, and would widen the Anglo-Dutch quarrel over the fishery; he would ask for it only on condition that Holland resists the augmentation. The rest is intelligence: a suspect (Charles de Quintin, travelling from Antwerp to Breda with a Lyon merchant, flagged by M. de Hatzel) will be arrested if he comes to Holland; a captain of the Löwendal regiment has arrived; "the Italian" reports that one La Combe (translator of the Lettres philosophiques) and an old man from Liège have left England for France to report on the French navy; and a Paris article in the Amsterdam gazette supplement about two ship captains is answered with an extract of d'Affry's passport register (captains of the Comte de Maurepas and another Bordeaux ship, and a surgeon from Coutras). ## Comparison with Bussemaker no. 59 (1 Février 1757) Bussemaker: States of Holland adjourned until the 20th, then the augmentation comes up; war funds no more than usual and the means so oppressive that the augmentation becomes unlikely: a sixth surcharge on the house tax, a general increase of the excises, reduction of interest on public funds to 2%; France should protect its own herring fishery against Dutch competition, but not at present, with French sailors lacking, so favouring the Dutch would do no harm; the favour is temporary and can stop once the Republic no longer deserves it; it would please the Dutch most and, herring being a bone of contention with England, estrange the two countries; he asks for it only if Holland blocks the troop augmentation. This matches §§1-8 point by point and fixes 674 = 20, 981 = x (sixième), 42 = générale. Bussemaker (Fruin) omits the intelligence paragraphs §§3-4 and §§9-13, as his preface says he did for agents and intriguers. J'espere que ce sera sans succés pour ceux qui la desirent. Les fonds pour l'Etat de Guerre de cette année ne sont pas plus forts que ceux de l'année precedente, et les moyens qu'on se propose pour employer pour en trouver paroitront si onereux, qu'il est aparent que cette seule proposition arretera tout: Ils doivent porter une Augmentation d'une sixieme sur la Taxe des Maisons, une augmentation generale sur les accises, et une Reduction des Interêts sur les fonds publics à 2. pour Cent. Il est à presumer que les Etats ne consentiront point à une Operation qui fouleroit le Peuple, revolteroit les riches, et decrediteroit totalement les fonds publics chez l'Etranger. J'aurai l'honneur de vous rendre compte de l'Etat de cette affaire dans le tems méme de l'assemblée si je le peux. Je verrai aujourd'huy l'Italien. J'executerai ce que vous m'ordonnez, et les arrangements que je prendrai avec lui, seront le sujet de ma premiere Depêche. Il est indubitable que Mr D'Urvoy, qui écrivoit de Londres au Senechal de Quintin, qui a voyagé D'Anvers à Breda avec le Negociant de Lyon, et dont Mr de Hatzel m'avoit écrit, ne soit le même homme. Je suis assuré que s'il vient en Hollande, il sera arrêté, et si cela arrive, je ne perdrai pas un moment à vous en donner avis, et à vous demander les Ordres de Sa Majesté à cet égard. J'attends sur ce qui le regarde une Reponse de Mr de Hatzel. Par les Lumieres que j'ai cherché à acquerir, Monsr; sur nôtre Commerce, j'ai vû combien il étoit important de diminuer le benefice de la Pêche Hollandoise du Harang, et d'encourager la nôtre; mais cet encouragement ne m'a pas paru essentiel dans un tems, ou nous n'avons que trop d'occasion d'employer nos Matelots. J'ai crû qu'il ne seroit pas d'un grand préjudice aux Sujets de Sa Majesté de voir faciliter une importante Pêche à la quelle ils ne peuvent fournir tant que la Guerre durera D'ailleurs cette Grace n'est point un Traité, et n'est que momentanée. Elle auroit encore été le prix de la bonne Conduite, et aroit pu cesser au moment ou le Roy l'auroit crû convenable au bien de ses Sujets, ou dans l'instant ou Sa Maj: auroit cessé d'être satisfaite de la Republique. Cette Grace est de toutes celles que le Roy peut accorder à ce Païs la plus desirée, parce qu'elle interesse presque tous les habitans de la Province de Hollande, et comme cette Pêche est le point de jalousie le plus vif entre l'Angleterre et la Republique; cette faveur les éloigneroit encore l'une de l'autre. Je ne vous la demanderois cependant Mr. que conditionellement, et en me mettant à portée de la communiquer si la Hollande resiste à l'Augmentation, et si Elle se conduit bien, ou de la taire si Elle se laissoit entrainer Je vous prie de vouloir bien dire à Mr. le Marechal de Belle Isle que Mr. de Nispen, Capitaine dans Lowendal est venú ici, et que je compte vous envoyer Jeudi ou Vendredi un detail Chiffré de ses observations. L'Italien m'a dit aujourdhuy, qu'un nommé La Combe, qui doit être Commis chez un Fermier General, étoit parti d'Angleterre il y a deux Ans, qu'il avoit emprunté à son depart de l'Argent de Pichon, et qu'il en empruntoit encore pour entretenir Correspondance avec lui. Ce Lacombe est le même qui a traduit les Lettres Philosophiques et Politiques de Mr le Comte d'Orreri. Il m'a dit de plus qu'un nommé Mr Lanzi de Liège, agé d'à peu près 50. ans, parlant fort bien Italien, François, Anglois, et Latin, est parti d'Anglet: il y a trois Semaines pour la France, qu'il est chargé de rendre compte de l'etat present de nôtre Marine, et de s'introduire chez quelque Commis Subalterne de nos Bureaux. Vous verrez Mr dans la fin du Suplement de la Gazette d'Amsterdam d'aujourdhuy un Article de Paris du 24. . . . Il est vrai que les deux Capitaines, dont il y est parlé, ont passé ici. Voici l'Extrait de mon Registre des Passeports du 18. Janvier du dit jour. "Les Srs Joseph du Perieux, Capitaine du Navire le Comte de Maurepas, de Bourdeaux, natif de Libourne, Bernard Clement Omeri, Chirurgien, natif de Coutrai, et Perot Imbert, Capitaine du Navire la Subtile de Bourdeaux, natif de la dite Ville, allant à Paris, et de là à Bourdeaux, pour un Mois." Vous remarquerez que le Passeport regardoit les deux Capitaines et le Chirurgien, et que la Gazette ne parle que des deux Premiers. Je joins ici deux Lettres une pour Mr de Montaran et l'autre pour Mr de Cremille. Vous trouverez Mr dans ce Paquet trois Exemplaires d'un Ouvrage auquel Mr Rouillé d'Orfeüil a fourni la forme et la Diction. J'espere que vous en Serez content. Translation R1064_en.md <!-- English translation of read/R1064_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): the reading follows the contemporary clear copy in the Fagel register, aligned with the keyed decode; where the figures give another word they are followed. --> # R1064, d'Affry to Rouillé, The Hague, 1 February 1757 (no. 136): English translation The States of Holland have separated and are to reassemble on the 20th of this month to deal with the matter of the augmentation. I hope it will be without success for those who want it. The funds for the war establishment this year are no larger than last year's, and the means that are proposed for finding them will appear so burdensome that it is likely this proposal alone will stop everything: they are to consist of an increase of one sixth on the house tax, a general increase of the excises, and a reduction of the interest on the public funds to 2 per cent. It is to be presumed that the States will not consent to an operation that would crush the people, revolt the rich and wholly discredit the public funds abroad. I shall have the honour to report to you on the state of this affair during the assembly itself, if I can. I shall see the Italian today. I shall carry out what you order me, and the arrangements I make with him will be the subject of my first despatch. There is no doubt that M. d'Urvoy, who was writing from London to the Seneschal of Quintin, who travelled from Antwerp to Breda with the merchant from Lyon, and about whom M. de Hatzel had written to me, is the same man. I am sure that if he comes to Holland he will be arrested, and if that happens I shall not lose a moment in informing you and in asking for His Majesty's orders in the matter. I am waiting for a reply from M. de Hatzel about what concerns him. From the knowledge I have tried to acquire, Sir, about our trade, I have seen how important it was to reduce the profit of the Dutch herring fishery and to encourage our own; but this encouragement did not seem to me essential at a time when we have only too much occasion to employ our sailors. I thought it would not be a great prejudice to His Majesty's subjects to see an important fishery made easier, to which they cannot contribute as long as the war lasts. Besides, this favour is not a treaty, and it is only temporary. It would also have been the price of good conduct, and could have ceased at the moment the King thought it fitting for the good of his subjects, or at the instant His Majesty ceased to be satisfied with the Republic. Of all those the King can grant to this country, this favour is the most desired, because it concerns nearly all the inhabitants of the province of Holland; and as this fishery is the sharpest point of jealousy between England and the Republic, this favour would set them further apart. I would nevertheless ask you for it, Sir, only on conditions, and putting myself in a position to communicate it if Holland resists the augmentation and behaves well, or to keep it quiet if she let herself be carried along. I beg you to be so good as to tell Marshal de Belle-Isle that M. de Nispen, a captain in Löwendal's regiment, has come here, and that I expect to send you on Thursday or Friday a ciphered account of his observations. The Italian told me today that one La Combe, who must be a clerk with a farmer-general, left England two years ago, that on leaving he had borrowed money from Pichon, and that he was borrowing more of it to keep up a correspondence with him. This Lacombe is the same who translated the Philosophical and Political Letters of the Earl of Orrery. He also told me that one M. Lanzi of Liège, about 50 years old, who speaks Italian, French, English and Latin very well, left England three weeks ago for France, that he is charged with reporting on the present state of our navy and with getting himself in with some junior clerk of our offices. You will see, Sir, at the end of the supplement of today's Amsterdam Gazette, an article from Paris of the 24th. It is true that the two captains it speaks of passed through here. Here is the extract from my register of passports of 18 January, of that day: "Messrs Joseph du Perieux, captain of the ship Comte de Maurepas of Bordeaux, native of Libourne; Bernard Clement Omeri, surgeon, native of Coutras (written Coutrai); and Perot Imbert, captain of the ship la Subtile of Bordeaux, native of that town; going to Paris, and from there to Bordeaux, for one month." You will notice that the passport concerned the two captains and the surgeon, and that the Gazette speaks only of the first two. I enclose two letters, one for M. de Montaran and the other for M. de Crémille. You will find in this packet, Sir, three copies of a work to which M. Rouillé d'Orfeuil gave the form and the wording. I hope you will be pleased with it. [Notes in the register:] The letter of N. to his uncle van Oller was enclosed in an envelope addressed to M. de Montaran. [The work:] La Vérité des Faits. This seemed so odd to me that I wished to clear it up, and I went straight to the Grand Pensionary's yesterday evening. He told me that the Assembly might indeed resume at that time, P2: and that he nevertheless expected to be able to delay it until the fast day. I repeated to him, regarding the augmentation, what I had told him before. He does not seem to me far from making an issue of it. In truth this sentiment comes from his real fear of losing his post; but as all the P3: Republicans want him to keep it, I would not be surprised to see him work feebly for the augmentation, certain of seeing it thwarted by them. He also told me that if they decided on it, it would not be without taking the precaution of declaring to the other neighbouring powers what the purpose of P4: this step is. I answered him: you must surely judge, Sir, that the King my master would not learn the news of a step that might be contrary to the neutrality you have promised without ordering me to put very positive questions to you about the Republic's intentions. I hope to know more before the end of this month. I shall have the honour to P5: report to you on it. Mr de Nispen, who came here, left this morning to carry out what Mr de Crémille ordered him. He will be at Maaseik in 6 or 7 days, and I am certain that he will carry out well everything prescribed to him; but I beg you to be so good as to represent to Marshal de Belle- P6: Isle how inconvenient it is, in entering enemy country, to be reduced to roads so out of the way that one can only advance in divisions of two or four battalions. I agree that Guelders is so bare of troops that one need not fear to find any in the field or on one's P7: way; but this manner of arriving piecemeal has the drawback of announcing an army from very far off; by which means the provisions that this country could furnish us will be partly shut up in Wesel and in Guelders, and the rest will be saved into Dutch Guelders, all the more easily since the P8: Rhine and the Meuse lead there. I would therefore think it very useful to send ahead of the army's advance guard a considerable corps of light troops, and to give this corps a few of the lightest field pieces: this corps could then move briskly towards Cleves and onto the Rhine P9: and would thereby prevent the export of a great part of the provisions. Mr de Nispen has undertaken to explain to Mr de Crémille the usefulness and even the necessity of this arrangement, so that I shall not make a separate memorandum of it. Mr von Reischach's courier took advantage of a moment when the wind was favourable on the 26th of last month, and although the P10: wind has varied, I hope he will have arrived in England and that you will soon have news of him. I have given the Italian the hundred louis according to His Majesty's orders. This man left this morning for Helvoet and from there for England. He assures me that he would manage to bring Pichon to Liège. He will use the pretext of watching our moves and of reporting P11: to Hanover everything we do. As it often happens that one cannot cross here with east and north-east winds, and these winds do not prevent arriving at Ostend, he will write to me directly by that route. I shall inform Mr d'Aubigni [the cipher adds: at Liège] at the same time as I have the honour to pass on to you the news of P12: the Italian, if you approve. The day before yesterday I sent you a note on a certain Lacombe. I think no action should be taken concerning him before we have Pichon, because the latter might take fright if he learned that Lacombe had disappeared, and it is to be presumed that Pichon has more than one correspondent. The Spanish ambassador despatched P13: a courier to Paris yesterday. I do not know on what business. R1066 Lyonet's contemporary clear decipherment, imaged on the DECODE record and transcribed here. Translation R1066_en.md <!-- English translation of plain/R1066.txt (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): Lyonet's contemporary clear decipherment, imaged on the DECODE record R1066 and transcribed here. --> # R1066, d'Affry, The Hague, 1757: English translation of the contemporary decipherment I saw Mr van Slingelandt at my house this morning. I told him what you prescribe to me in your despatch of the 11th regarding the negotiation with England. He answered that he thought he should communicate to me the substance of Lord Holderness's letter to Mr Yorke. Here it is as he dictated it to me. His Britannic Majesty has avoided war as far as prudence and the interests on his side allowed. His Majesty sincerely desires peace, provided that its conditions are equitable enough to make it lasting, that it includes all the respective allies, and that it preserves the rights and possessions of the subjects of Great Britain. In that case the King of England will be pleased to see this negotiation opened between Mr Yorke and Mr d'Affry, without the mediation of a third party. You see, Sir, that this language has nothing excessive in it; but neither has it anything acceptable, since it is right that England should take the first steps. Besides, the reservation of all its allies, and the vague condition of rights and possessions, do not offer easy terms. R1067, 1 Apr 1757, no. 161 D'Affry reports his interview with Pensionary Steyn on the King's orders (the demand for an answer on the passage of French troops by Maastricht/Namur): Steyn, embarrassed and under attack by enemies trying to bring him down, could not answer before the week-end. D'Affry then saw the Gouvernante (Anne of Hanover), gave her the King's declaration; she answered "must it be I who favour the means of doing harm to my father?" (George II); he asked her to use her credit to obtain the answer the King had a right to expect. Transcription R1067.txt # R1067 re-transcribed from the images 5 Oct 2026 (IMG_R1067_I5579_P1 ... The register's blank "( )" is kept. --> # R1067, d'Affry to Rouillé, The Hague, 1 April 1757 (no. 161): English translation Yesterday I went to the Grand Pensionary's to give him an account of the orders with which His Majesty has honoured me, and which you were so kind as to send me in your despatch of the 28th. I found the Pensionary very cold and embarrassed. It is certain that everything going on here today is set in motion only to ruin him. He told me that it was impossible to answer me on the matter today, and that in the ferment in which minds are, he did not think he could convene an extraordinary assembly for tomorrow; but that he expected to be able to obtain my answer for me on Monday or Tuesday at the latest. I told him that I would have the honour of informing you of this today, and in the rest of the conversation I tried not to depart from what you prescribe to me. As the Grand Pensionary spoke to me a good deal about Madame the Governess, I asked him whether it suited him that I should see her. This question relieved him and pleased him. On leaving him I went to Her Royal Highness, to whom I read the Declaration I enclose. After this reading I spoke to her much as to the Grand Pensionary, but with all the reserve of which I am capable in the terms I had to use. When I had finished, and saw that she did not answer me, I looked at her, and I saw her eyes in tears, and she said these very words to me: "Mr d'Affry, I beg your pardon; but for a moment do not be a minister. Must it be I who make easier the means of doing harm to my father?" I answered her: "Your Royal Highness knows how far the King my master has sought to avoid and to shorten the war. Besides, I do not know the destination of his forces in Germany; but I beg you, Madam, as a man very touched by and very grateful for the kindness with which Your Royal Highness honours him, to be pleased to think only of the extreme importance for the Republic of winning the King's friendship and keeping it. I ask Your Royal Highness to employ not only your good offices but your credit and your power to bring about a prompt answer, such as the King has the right to hope for." I left her on that. This morning I went to the President of the week, who happens to be Mr van Borssele; he told me, like the Grand Pensionary, that it would not be possible to answer me before Monday or Tuesday. Accordingly I am writing to Mr Lesseps so that he may warn Mr Cobenzl and our commissaries who are at Brussels, because if the navigation of our convoys were far enough advanced to be stopped at Maastricht, a courier could be sent to me, on whose arrival I would press harder. From what I have reported to you of my conversation with Madame the Governess, you see that it is to her that we owe the difficulty being made for us. The Stadholderians are taking advantage of it to ruin the Grand Pensionary and to destroy, if possible, the Republican party. That party is neither as firm nor as united as could be wished. Count Wassenaer has not yet been willing to come back here, and his younger son at present has a post in Friesland whose appointment depends on Madame the Governess. The passport granted to Mr von Reischach is the argument I use most. It is unanswerable, and I hope that at the beginning of next week I may be able to send your courier back to you with an answer such as we must demand, and to which Their High Mightinesses, or at least part of those who represent them, will have had the skill to add ill grace, revealing a fund of ill will. At four in the afternoon I was in conference, and I handed over the ( ). It was taken at once to the States General. I know that it was not badly received, and I have reason to believe that Holland will give an opinion such as it should be. I believe that this very evening I shall even have Mr de Byemont, who is to bring me the consent of Their High Mightinesses for the passage of Namur. As there is as yet no news that our boats have arrived there, I do not doubt that we shall have time to get our answer about Maastricht before our boats are under the walls of that place. I am all the more pleased to have sent the warning that had been communicated to me, as it appears that the disguised Prussian party has completely failed in its enterprise. I would even believe that some of these gentlemen have been arrested, who will probably be hanged, and who well deserve it. I have just received a report, and from a good source, which says that the town and citadel of Wesel have been entirely abandoned by the Prussians, and that they have even begun to demolish the fortifications. This morning there was a conference at Mr Yorke's, attended by the commissioners of the posts, to establish the correspondence from here to Hanover and to Berlin, since they can no longer let it go by Emmerich; but if we wish, the East Frisian route will not withdraw the correspondence from our inspections. I enclose a recommendation of the States General on behalf of some of those interested in the prize taken by the privateer Lalley. I am persuaded that this recommendation will not be heeded, and I believe that never was a prize more legitimate. I shall send to Mr de Moras in the next few days a memorandum that I believe no better founded than this one. It concerns some Englishmen established at Rotterdam who carry on an immense trade in our produce, and above all our wines, with England. If their ships meet some French privateer, they show them certificates of domicile in Holland. If they meet English privateers, they produce baptismal certificates of that nation and letters that open the ports of England to them, in accordance with the Treaty of 1652; which is truly an intolerable abuse. Mr de Saltikof a écrit à Mr de Golofkin qui m'a envoyé cette lettre ce matin. Vous verrez, Mr, que Mr de la Salle croit sa justification remplie, et je le desire; mais Mr de Golofkin le fils, m'a dit avoir parlé de Mr de la Salle à Mr de Laurenzi qui lui a dit qu'il savoit bien qu'il y avoit un projet de proposé à Mr Yorke; mais chimerique, et auquel ce ministre ne s'étoit point arrêté. Quoi qu'il en soit, je crois qu'il n'y aura nul inconvenient à parler de Mr de la Salle à Mr de St Sauveur à son passage ici, pour qu'en arrivant à Petersbourg il puisse faire veiller à sa conduite. On a pris et conduit à Dunkerque un vaisseau hollandois, nommé les cinq freres, capitaine Jarighates. Les proprietaires et les interressés à ce vaisseau sont gens considerables. Un de ces derniers entr'autres, est un homme qui a une très grande influence en Frise, et qui en fait le meilleur usage. Permettez moi de vous prier d'en parler à Mr de Moras, et de lui dire que si, comme les proprietaires l'assurent, cette prise n'est pas validée, il seroit à desirer que le Conseil des Prises terminât promptement cette affaire, parce que dans ce cas la detention du vaisseau et de son equipage desobligeroit ceux qui s'y interressent, et feroit plaisir à nos adversaires. Translation R1069_en.md <!-- English translation of plain/R1069.txt (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): Lyonet's contemporary clear decipherment, imaged on the DECODE record R1069 and transcribed here. --> # R1069, d'Affry, The Hague, 1757: English translation of the contemporary decipherment I have the honour to send you the copy of a letter that Mr de la Salle wrote to me from Hamburg, which came with a letter from Mr Saltykov, of which I also enclose the copy. Mr Saltykov wrote to Mr Golovkin, who sent me this letter this morning. You will see, Sir, that Mr de la Salle believes his justification complete, and I wish it were; but Mr Golovkin the son told me that he had spoken of Mr de la Salle to Mr Laurenzi, who told him that he knew well that a project had been proposed to Mr Yorke, but a chimerical one, to which that minister had paid no attention. However that may be, I think there will be no harm in speaking of Mr de la Salle to Mr de St Sauveur when he passes through here, so that on arriving at Petersburg he can have his conduct watched. A Dutch ship called the Five Brothers, captain Jarighates, has been taken and brought into Dunkirk. The owners of this ship and those with a stake in it are considerable people. One of the latter in particular is a man who has very great influence in Friesland, and who makes the best use of it. Allow me to ask you to speak of it to Mr de Moras, and to tell him that if, as the owners assert, this prize is not validated, it would be desirable for the Prize Council to settle the matter promptly, because in that case the detention of the ship and its crew would offend those concerned in it and would please our adversaries. D'Affry doubts she will; if she does and proposes a land-forces augmentation, the other side will propose a naval augmentation instead. Translation R1070_en.md <!-- English translation of read/R1070_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): the reading follows the contemporary clear copy in the Fagel register, aligned with the keyed decode. --> # R1070, d'Affry to Bernis, The Hague, 22 July 1757 (no. 210): English translation It is said today that Her Royal Highness is to go to the States of Holland to harangue them in favour of her father, to represent forcefully the necessity of helping his Electoral States, and to set out the extreme danger to the Protestant religion. I do not believe she will bring herself to it; but in case she does, I am almost sure that if she proposes an augmentation of the land forces as the first means, they will on the contrary propose to her an augmentation of the navy, as an absolute remedy against the vexations and the robberies of the English. Their partisans are spreading the most odious rumours about the occupation of Ostend and Nieuport by our troops, but sensible people understand well that the port of Ostend is closed to the English. Amsterdam and Rotterdam will profit from a trade that England carried on with the Low Countries and Germany worth more than six hundred thousand pieces a year. There are some towns where some Dutch ministers have preached on the danger to religion, but the people do not seem roused by it. The event of Ostend will bring no change to the resolutions of the Republic, unless Her Royal Highness makes it serve as a pretext for steps dictated by her heart but surely disowned by reason. In that case I shall not hesitate a moment to inform you, and if it were pressing I would think I should, without waiting for His Majesty's orders and yours, ask this princess for a conference in which I would try to prove to her how essential it is for her, and for the interests of the Stadholder her son, to deserve His Majesty's goodwill. That will not be difficult for me. You will find enclosed, Sir, a letter, or a fragment of one, of the 15th from London, and a statement of the English navy. Il assure qu'il communiquera tout ce qui se traitera de secret dans le Cabinet de Londres, de tous les Projets proposés aux Ministres, de toutes ses intrigues dans les Cours étrangères, de tous les Plans de Campagne pour cette Année, et des Correspondances que les Anglois ont en France. Il m'a assuré qu'il connoissoit des Lettres trés interessantes, ecrites de Madrid par Mr Wal en Angleterre, et que si on veut y mettre le prix, il se faisoit fort d'enlever quelques unes, mais qu'en ce cas il faudroit lui assurer une Pension qui le met en état de vivre en France ou en Angleterre. Vous voyez Mr ce que cet homme propose. Ce qu'il demande est considerable, si c'est un Imposteur, mais s'il remplit ses engagemens, il semble qu'on ne pourroit mieux employer l'argent qu'on lui donnera. J'attendrai sur celà vos ordres avec impatience. Si vous agréez ses services, son retour à Londres ne sauroit étre assez prompt. Je suis convenu avec Mr Hensi, que je lui donnerois demain Vingt Cinq Guinées pour un quartier de son Correspondant. Nous verrons ce qu'il fera à l'avenir. He told me that he expected to be rewarded already for the service he claims to have rendered through the reports he gave on England's projects against our possessions in the two Indies, and namely through the report of a man named Maham, or Mahom, commandant or sub-commandant of the fort at Crown Point. After much debate we agreed that he would stay here at a ducat a day until you had given me new orders. He now asks for a gratuity of a hundred louis. At that price he will leave at once for England, from where he proposes to inform us of the state of that power's land and sea forces; of the true state of the kingdoms of England, Scotland and Ireland, of the troops maintained in those kingdoms, and a detail of the quarters they occupy; of the present state of English America, of the troops there, of the state of their forts, of the state of the inhabitants and their inclination, of the projects of the two proprietors of Pennsylvania, Mr Penn and Lord Baltimore, of the attacks that will be made there, and of the instructions that will be sent to Lord Loudoun. He assures me that he will communicate everything secret that is dealt with in the London Cabinet, all the projects proposed to the Ministers, all its intrigues in foreign courts, all the plans of campaign for this year, and the correspondence the English have in France. He assured me that he knew of very interesting letters written from Madrid by Mr Wall to England, and that if one is willing to pay the price, he would undertake to carry off some of them, but that in that case he would have to be assured a pension that would enable him to live in France or in England. You see, Sir, what this man proposes. What he asks is considerable if he is an impostor, but if he fulfils his engagements, it seems that the money given him could not be better employed. I shall await your orders on this with impatience. If you accept his services, his return to London cannot be too prompt. I have agreed with Mr Hensi that I would give him tomorrow twenty-five guineas for a quarter's pay of his correspondent. We shall see what he does in future. Translation R1073_en.md <!-- English translation of read/R1073_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): the reading follows the contemporary clear copy in the Fagel register, aligned with the keyed decode. --> # R1073, d'Affry, The Hague, 25 January 1757 (no. 133): English translation The rumour had been spread that I had given a memorandum to Their High Mightinesses in which I declared to them that His Majesty would regard an augmentation of the Republic's land forces as an infringement of neutrality. This rumour was destroyed at once; but I thought I should take this occasion to see the Grand Pensionary. I declared to him that the King did not intend, and had never intended, to meddle in the affairs of Their High Mightinesses; but that out of his affection for them, His Majesty would see with sorrow that they engaged in heavy expenses, whose consequences the Republic ought to fear and whose cost it ought to wish to be useless. I repeated to him what I had told him on this some time ago, and with the same coolness, because he answered me: "I am sure that this operation will meet many difficulties, and I firmly believe that if the Republicans cannot prevent it, they will at least be strong enough to have it preceded by a declaration to our court, to that of Vienna and to that of London, by which the Republic will confirm its resolution to remain strictly neutral; and none of this will be in question until about the twentieth of next month." It seems that the Abbé Senski, as you will see, no longer supplies very interesting news from London. We should see whether this does not improve. Nous manquons de Bled au Canada. On vient de me dire qu'une Flotte de Vingt Six Voiles étoit prêt de sortir de Portsmouth. Le Sr Macdonald est arrivé depuis peu de jours de France, et est parti d'ici pour se rendre en Angleterre: J'ai quelque Sujet de croire qu'il a été chargé de quelque Commission de la part de nos Ennemis: Je crois que cet homme a servi dans le Regiment de Bückley gt. On devroit faire quelque attention aux Ecossois et aux Irlandois qui sont dans nos Troupes, quelques uns sont des Espions, mais il seroit peut être imprudent et dangereux de marquer de la défiance aux autres. Je verrai s'il y a moyen d'être instruit des allures du Sr Macdonald, et de ses Correspondances. On what I had heard of a negotiation to be made in England for a loan of twenty millions, I wished to know whether it had really been in question, and whether it would have been possible for us to find such a resource in that country. All the information I could wish for has been gathered on this subject, and I have been assured from a good source that it would not have been extremely difficult to find this sum before the proclamation, but that the business was so badly conducted, and such clumsy persons were employed in it, that it was inevitable that the affair should come to the knowledge of the British Ministry, which gave rise to the new law. Nevertheless there still remain means of evading its execution, and if we wished, it rests only with us to borrow today four millions at four, or four and a half per cent at most. As to the funds we should assign to the payment of this interest, the way of making the payments, and of bringing the principal into France without danger to the lenders, it is a very delicate matter, which requires profound secrecy, a perfect knowledge of the country, and intelligence in the people who would be employed in it; and I believe it should remain between the Abbé, you and me. I shall await his orders and yours. We are short of wheat in Canada. I have just been told that a fleet of twenty-six sail was ready to leave Portsmouth. Mr Macdonald arrived from France a few days ago and has left here for England. I have some reason to believe that he has been charged with some commission on behalf of our enemies. I believe this man served in Bulkeley's regiment. Some attention should be paid to the Scots and Irish who are in our troops; some are spies, but it would perhaps be imprudent and dangerous to show distrust towards the others. I shall see whether there is a way of being informed of Mr Macdonald's movements and of his correspondence. Cette operation une fois resoluë sera poussée avec d'autant plus de Vivacité, que l'on commence à voir que les Anglois respecteront la Navigation Hollandoise à raison de la Protection qu'Elle aura, et qu'il est la dessus necessaire d'escorter fortement tous les Convoys qui auront à traverser la Manche. Dans les premiers jours de mon retour ici, on me marqua d'Amsterdam, que nous ou nos Entrepreneurs avions dans le Texel prés de soixante Batimens chargés pour la Marine du Roy, que les Capitaines et les Entrepreneurs ne vouloient pas risquer le Voyage pour aller en Angleterre sur la simple Sommation de quelques Capitaines de Vaisseaux de Guerre Anglois, et que les Proprietaires des Vaisseaux frettés pour nous ne vouloient pas les laisser passer l'hyver chargés dans le Texel. Mr. Borel fut consterné et me pria de ne faire aucune demarche. Il m'assura qu'il se chargeoit de tout. Effectivement, il n'a cessé de ce moment là de travailler, et a determiné le Convoy qui auroit êté de quatre Vaisseaux d'Escorte sans la Tempette qui en a mis deux hors d'êtat d'aller, je ne peux vous depeindre l'inquietude ou ils ont eté ici de ce Convoy. Nous aprenons enfin qu'il est arrivé, et on se loüe beaucoup ici du Secours qu'on a donné à Belle Isle, à un des deux Vaisseaux de Guerre, qui a êté fort mal traité d'un Coup de Vent. Une grande partie des Republicains desirent vivement quelque grace pour le harang. Si la Resolution de l'Armement passe sans augmentation de Terre, et il est certain que ce sera un moyen de plus de l'éloignement entre l'Angleterre et la Hollande. J'espere Mr que vous verrez encore combien je cherche à suivre mes Instructions. Je vous repête avec verité que je leur dois ma conduite, et les succés que vous avez bien voulu aprouver jusqu'apresent. Translation R1076_en.md <!-- English translation of read/R1076_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026). --> # R1076, d'Affry, The Hague, 7 January 1757 (no. 124): English translation I continue to believe that the arming of the eight ships will take place without the augmentation of the land forces, and we shall know it in a few days, for the resolution on this must have been taken the day before yesterday in Guelders. Once resolved, this operation will be pushed with all the more vigour as people are beginning to see that the English will respect Dutch navigation in proportion to the protection it has, and that it is therefore necessary to escort strongly all the convoys that have to cross the Channel. In the first days after my return here, I was told from Amsterdam that we or our contractors had in the Texel nearly sixty ships loaded for the King's navy; that the captains and the contractors would not risk the voyage on the mere summons of a few captains of English warships to go to England; and that the owners of the ships chartered for us would not let them spend the winter loaded in the Texel. I had a conversation on this subject with Mr Borel, clerk of the Admiralty of Amsterdam, in which I spoke to him with all the force of which I am capable, and I ended by telling him that, once the States were assembled, I would go to the lodging of Amsterdam to repeat what I had just told him, and declare there that since the navy's contractors had dealt in good faith and in confidence in the safety of the flag, the States, and above all the city of Amsterdam, would be guilty through their weakness of the failure to supply our navy. Mr Borel was dismayed and begged me to take no step. He assured me that he would take charge of everything. Indeed, from that moment he never stopped working, and he brought about the convoy, which would have had four escort ships but for the storm that put two of them out of action. I cannot describe to you the anxiety they have felt here over this convoy. We learn at last that it has arrived, and people here speak highly of the help given at Belle-Île to one of the two warships, which had been very badly handled by a gale. A great part of the Republicans keenly desire some favour for the herring. If the resolution on the arming passes without an augmentation of the land forces, it is certain that this will be one more means of estrangement between England and Holland. I hope, Sir, that you will see once more how much I seek to follow my instructions. I repeat to you in truth that I owe them my conduct, and the successes that you have been pleased to approve until now. It seemed to me useless to attempt any money operation in England itself, which, if it came to be discovered, would make our needs appear greater than they are and would cause the precautions to be increased. Despite these precautions the English will still invest with us when the interest can tempt them, and they still have at present, with bankers of this country and at Brussels, funds that could not find a place in our life annuities. I know that there are here two or three young Englishmen, one of whom is called Macdonald. The letters of the 10th from London have brought us nothing new. Yesterday I again had the Jew Boas. He told me that Mr de Beckerschee of the Pels counting-house was at The Hague about the money seized at Osnabrück, in which that house has an interest. He asked me whether he had come to see me; I told him no. He answered that he was surprised at it. I replied that I was not, since, as the Messrs Pels produce nothing to justify the use of the money, it was apparent that it concerned our enemies. Whereupon Boas told me that he did not believe it was intended directly for the payment of their troops, but that he believed it was intended for and ad[dre]ssed to subjects of His Prussian Majesty; and I do indeed believe that all the chests that are not [?specified] in the petition will end by being declared good prize. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 4 November 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter Alfonso II d’Este, duke of Ferrara, to his agent at Venice, 14 April 1576, on cc. 76–77. A later note on c. 77r reads “A Monsig.r Ariosti Ambasciatore / Venezia”, which agrees with the catalogue but is later testimony. Where Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Autografoteca Campori, Lettera E, Este (d’), Alfonso II d’Este, cc. 76–77. Catalogue item 1566 (it holds three letters in three systems; the 1559 letter has its own folder ). The cipher A simple substitution of Italian with 20 signs and nulls: x, y and k freely, and & and 3 once each. The digit 7 stands for itself once. There are no word breaks and no code groups. Two hands write it, the second with far fewer nulls. How it was deciphered A quadgram search on period Italian with no crib; 8 of 10 restarts reached the same solution. No decipherment stands on the leaves. What it says The duke tells his agent how to handle a man who fears stricter proceedings: he was never in Este pay, Ferrara cannot shelter him, and he is to get fifty scudi. A second hand turns to oils and almonds, a Roman complaint and the prisoners of Rovigo. Still open “Read” rests on three words of margin: 706 of 740 words (95.4%) have no restored or changed letter, against a bar of 703. No human palaeographer checked it: AI agents transcribed and read the letter from the images, and an independent AI verifier checked a sample of the signs (VERIFY.md). Credit WAINUT (an AI company) transcribed the signs, broke the key and read the letter with AI agents viewing the images.

The sign alphabet is Latin letter forms in a secretary hand, so the cipher looks like nonsense Latin script. The first hand runs to c. 77r line 6 with nulls on 8.4% of signs; the second takes over at line 7 and writes the postscript with nulls on 1.2%, dropping or shortening letters. The table runs in blocks: a–d map to z u t s, e–h to a b c d, and q–t to e f g h. The first version of the transcription wrote one shape for cipher q and cipher g . That was wrong: the hand writes two signs, a looped-tail g (= s ) and a straight-tailed q (= m ). All 339 such signs were re-read by tail on enlarged crops, in order, before any comparison with values given by sense, so no value in the decryption is chosen by sense.

Of 740 words, 737 (99.6%) read as sense, and 706 (95.4%) have no restored or changed letter. The first hand gives 535 of 557 (96.1%) and the second hand with the postscript 171 of 183 (93.4%). The contributor offers to call it a partial reading if more margin than three words is wanted. The key was tested on its own split, which was not set up in advance: −10.17 per letter against a best of −13.38 for 200 shuffled tables, reproduced at −10.18 against −13.56 for 500. The standard validator was not run. The Italian and an English translation are under Full texts.

“Read” has three words of margin over the bar, so a few changed words would make it a partial reading. Some signs in the second hand carry a stroke above them that was not recorded. An independent AI verifier checked the first version; its report is in the folder. No independent check has been run on the final version. Three gaps are recorded with blockers (too short, illegible, needs physical access). The transcription was made by AI agents from the images and checked only by an independent AI verifier; no person has compared it with the images.
