Vestre Excelencie Servulus Marcolinus. {Address:} Illustri domino Francisco Sfortie etc. ## f. 55r-v, 57r = decipherment of f. 56 (Rome, 3 Mar 1447) [canvases 53 right, 54 left, 55 right] Illustris ac excellens domine honorandissime. Sono stato da la Majestà del Re, et cum quelle rasone me sono acadute a la mente lo confortata et pregata a nome del mio Signore a prendere tanto majore cura et caricho de contribuire a la spesa vostra, quanto el bisogno è majore per la morte del Papa, dal quale non è più da expectare subventione alcuna. In effecto la soa Serenità è restata contenta non solamente de pagare quelo devia pagare el Papa, ma etiandio de contribuire de majore quantità non era stato rasonato da prima, cioè de ducati novantaquatro milia d'oro et in oro ogni anno et per dui anni come ha scripto el prefato Signore che'l restava contento de dui anni, et vole pagare li dicti dinari in questo modo, cioè vintimilia ducati nel mese presente, et altri xx m nel mese d'Aprile sequente al più tardi, et lo resto per la mità al fine de li sei mesi dal dì de la ferma vostra, et l'altra mità al fine del ano, et questo per lo primo anno: ma per respecto al secondo anno resta contento per tuto Martio del dicto anno de pagare quarantamilia ducati, et li altri LIIII m de sei mesi in sei mesi come è dicto de sopra, et cussì ha promesso la soa Serenità per capituli firmati et conclusi cum si et sigilati del suo sigillo, et ancora sotoscriti de soa propria mano: et debbe fare exbursare li dicti dinari a li tempi a qualuncha messo del prefato Signore, o vostro havendo expediente mandato a ciò. Per parte del Signore li è promesso, che non fareti contrasini contra li suoi, immo che bisognando mandarà el prefato Signore in suo aiuto, o tanti de li vostri, o de le altre gente ducale quante monta la spesa quale el fa per la conducta vostra, et ancora li è promesso, che quello pagherà el Papa serà electo debia pervenire in la soa Majestà. Per tanto de tuto aviso la Excelentia vostra acciò sapia quello è facto, et a bona fede doe cosse recordo. La prima che, o la Excelentia del Signore, o vui provediati de uno, quale habia mandato expediente a recevere el dinaro, et a confessare de haverlo recevuto, et ancora possa solicitarlo presso la Majestà del Re, perché sapeti bene, che dove va el dinaro non se po usare troppo diligentia. La secunda, che'l me pare necessario chiarire la prefata Majestà quanto più presto se po, come la conclusione è facta cum lui, aciò non se possa excusare, che per non essere chiarita non habia facta provisione al dinaro. Io li ho ben dato bona speranza de la conclusione secundo quello me dixe V.S., ma questo non credo che basti, et da mi non procederia a farli altra chiarezza, non havendo altro, o dal Signore, o da V.S., la quale me poterà scrivere la intentione soa circha de ciò {ciò written above a blotted word}, et io senza expectare altro la exequirò. Aviso ancora la excelentia vostra, che la Majestà del Re intende che in la dicta summa de novantaquatro milia ducati, quali debe pagare, se includano li xx m del [gap; the copyist drew the cipher sign ꝺ+÷ in the margin]: Ma lui prende el caricho de fare che li pagli, e presto. Se havesse possuto fare meglio, al che me sono sforzato quanto m'è stato possibile, lo haveria facto voluntera, ma non possendo ho acceptato quello ho possuto obtenere. Quanto a la elecione del Papa ve ho scripto per altre quello haveva inteso, adesso non me occorre altro, excepto che tutto se farà per haverne uno che sia amico, et non volendo esserlo se haverano de li modi da farlo pentire. Me recomando a V.S. et etiandio a la illustre Madona Bianca. Ex Roma tertio Marcij. Servitor devotus Marcolinus. {Address:} Illustri domino Francisco Sfortie etc. ## f. 61r = decipherment of f. 62 (Rome, 4 Mar 1447) [canvas 58 right] Illustris ac excelse domine honorandissime. Dico etiamdio che per tre meie {blot in the margin} ho avisato V.S. ____ de la morte dal Papa ____ {two underlined blanks} et de quanto me acadeva circha de ciò, ni da poy s'è innovato altro, excepto che li Cardinali questa sira sono intrati in conclave, et sperasse che assay tosto elezerano un altro Papa, et molto sono le opinione diverse a chi debia tocare la ellectione: Dio vegla che bona sia. Simelmente ho avisato per altre letre de la conclusione facta cum la Majestà dal Re. Adesso ve mando alligate a le presenti certe letre de la Majestà dal Re, per le quale intenderite la bona dispositione soa, avisando V.S. che la intesso molto voluntera quello li ho dicto per vostra parte, et maxime ha gustato quello dicesti de havere alienato l'animo da le cosse del reame, et demonstrato una bona voluntà de volerve havere per tuto suo. Me recommando a la S.V. Ex Roma die quarto Martii 1447. per V.S. servitorem devotum Marcolinum de Barbavariis. {Address:} Illustri domino Francisco Sfortie etc. ## f. 68 = decipherment of f. 69 (Rome, 6 Mar 1447) [canvas 65, upper leaf] Illustris ac excellens domine honorandissime. In questa hora decima septima, o circha, è publicato Papa Monsignore da Cologna {so in the copy: Tommaso Parentucelli, elected as Nicholas V on 6 March 1447, was cardinal-bishop of Bologna; the cipher was not checked at this word}. Credo firmamente che serà amico, e presto me sforzarò de vederne la experientia circa le cosse me sono comesse. Et de quello seguirà V.S. ne serà avisata, la quale me po avisare, se gli pare che sia da servare per mi più uno modo che un altro. Me ricommando a la Excelencia vostra. Ex Roma sexto Marcij 1447. Per Servitorem V.V. Marcolinum de Barbavariis. {Address:} Illustri domino Francischo Sfortie etc. ## f. 74r-v = decipherment of f. 75 (Rome, 8 Mar 1447) [canvases 71 right, 72 left] Illustris ac excelse domine honorandissime. Da poi ve scripsi la ellectione del novo Papa sono stato quello dì de la ellectione per non perdere tempo a li pedi de la soa Beatitudine, et da poy alchune parole generale dicte reallegrandome a nome del Duca de la ellectione soa toccai etiandio el facto del dinaro per V.S.; in effecto me pare che la Sanctità soa insieme cum li Cardinali habia presso deliberatione de procurare pace in Italia, et de mandare per questa caxone el Camerlengo et lo Vicecanciellero insieme da la Majestà del Re, quale sono partiti questo dì, ma no li reusirano li pensieri, perché lo Re, dal quale sono stato per questa casone un'altra volta, delibera de darli molto bene ad intendere, et specialmente al Camerlengo, perché l'altro è Veneciano, che queste parole de pace non gli piaceno, excepto se non fano prima la provisione del dinaro per V.S., et de le gente per mandare insieme cum la soa Majestà, a ciò che cum questa via sia proveduto a la securezza del stato del prefato Duca, et li inimici temendo le provisione se reducano a meglore condictione de pace, o non volendola per amore se gli possa redure cum la forcia. Delibera etiandio la soa Majestà, se questo parlare non moverà el Papa et li Cardinali a fare altra deliberatione meglore et più grata de aprirli come essa Majestà intende tore in si el carrego de pagare la spesa vostra, et dire che siano certi ge la farà pagare tuta a loro, et se anchora questo non aiutarà, mostra de volere usare altro che parole, cioè venire a li facti dicendo, che li preti sono homini da bastonate, non da pregare. Non so quello seguirà, pur non sono anchora sanza speranza, che'l Papa et li Cardinali intendando el malcontentamento del Re se debiano movere a piglare meglore deliberatione; de quello seguirà V.S. ne sarà avisata; et forse como per altre ho scripto non serà altro, che bene che V.S. facia de le demonstratione per timorezare anchora più la brigata et redurla a quello desideramo. Ho recordato anchora a la Majestà del Re el facto de li dinari per V.S., et me ha resposto che sanza fallo li meterà tale ordine non vi mancharano a li termini, et simelmente ha dicto che in questa septimana aviarà el suo, quale el manda dal Signore [gap; the copyist drew ꝺ+÷ in the margin] per quelli vinti millia ducati. Me ricommando a la Excellentia Vostra, et maraviglo che da si non habia mai havuto ni letra ni risposta. [gap] = a blank left by the copyist; [?] = uncertain. ## f. 39 = f. 40 (Rimini, 13 Feb 1447) If the courier has not kept the ways Your Lordship would have wished, it came about because, those of the [gap] being his, it did not seem to him that he needed to come with any other caution. Now I have warned him as much as is needed, and he will call at the house of Cecco, your chancellor, as you write. I send by him the safe-conduct requested for those two men of yours, and next Wednesday I shall go to [Atachio?] by way of San Giovanni in Marignano, according to your command, and I shall keep all the ways they give me for finding myself with Your Lordship. With Lord Sigismondo I have kept the manner Your Excellency advises me of; to whom I commend myself. Rimini, 13 February. Your Lordship's servant, Marcolino. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## f. 48r-v = f. 49 (Rome, 27 Feb 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. Having arrived here I found the Pope had passed from this life, as you will have heard, and he has indeed wished to do as Your Lordship used to say: to die so as to do harm not only living but also dying. I have been with the Camerlengo, who, having heard the reason for my coming, says that in effect it is necessary to wait for the election of another Pope and to treat the matter with His Holiness, and that meanwhile I can go to His Majesty the King to tighten the matter with him; and so I shall do, and Your Lordship will be told what follows. The said Camerlengo received very gratefully all I told him on your behalf, and from the words he used with me he seems to me very willing to have and keep good friendship with Your Lordship. He charged me to write to you to be of good heart, because whoever is elected to the papacy will gladly do things that please you. He says too that he will be a friend of the lord your father, or at least not his enemy, but rather believes he will be his friend and favourable, and God grant it be so. It is thought that the election must fall either to Monsignor of Capua or to Monsignor of Fermo; yet it could be that it falls to others, because it seems to me it always falls to the one no one has commonly thought of. If Your Excellency made some show and demonstration of wanting to advance into the Marche or elsewhere, so that news of it came here, I believe it would be very useful to warm the minds of these priests and make them hotter to contribute to your expenses; and I say this because they have built an almost certain foundation that Your Lordship will in any case go to the favour and help of the said lord your father. That opinion, however, I have striven to get out of their heads, and said that such a foundation is vain, and that, though you are well disposed, this good disposition must be helped otherwise than with words, that is with money. But to take it from them still [gap?]. Rome, 27 February. Your Excellency's little servant, Marcolino. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## ff. 55r-v, 57r = f. 56 (Rome, 3 Mar 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. I have been to His Majesty the King, and with such reasons as came to mind I urged and begged him, in the name of my lord, to take all the greater care and burden of contributing to your expenses as the need is greater through the death of the Pope, from whom no subsidy is to be expected any more. In effect His Serenity has been content not only to pay what the Pope was to pay, but also to contribute a greater sum than had first been discussed, namely ninety-four thousand ducats of gold, in gold, every year and for two years, as the said lord wrote that he was content with two years. He will pay the said money in this way: twenty thousand ducats this month, and another twenty thousand in the coming month of April at the latest, and the rest half at the end of six months from the day of your engagement and the other half at the end of the year, and this for the first year; but for the second year he is content to pay forty thousand ducats by the whole of March of that year, and the other 54 thousand from six months to six months as said above. And so His Serenity has promised, by articles signed and concluded with him, sealed with his seal and also signed in his own hand; and he is to have the said money paid out at the due times to whatever messenger of the said lord, or of yours, holds a sufficient mandate for it. On the lord's part he has been promised that you will make no attacks on his men; rather, if need be, the said lord will send to his aid either as many of your men, or of the other ducal troops, as amounts to the expense he bears for your condotta; and he has also been promised that what the Pope pays, once he is elected, shall come to His Majesty. Of all this I inform Your Excellency so that you know what has been done, and in good faith I recall two things. The first: that either His Excellency the lord or you provide someone with a sufficient mandate to receive the money and to acknowledge receiving it, and also to press for it with His Majesty the King, because you know well that where money is concerned one cannot use too much diligence. The second: it seems to me necessary to make clear to His Majesty as soon as possible that the conclusion has been made with him, so that he cannot excuse himself that, not having been made certain, he has not provided the money. I have indeed given him good hope of the conclusion according to what Your Lordship told me, but I do not think that is enough, and from my side I would not go on to give him any other assurance, having nothing else either from the lord or from Your Lordship, who may write to me your intention about this, and I shall carry it out without waiting for anything else. I inform Your Excellency also that His Majesty the King understands that in the said sum of ninety-four thousand ducats which he is to pay are included the 20 thousand of the [gap: the lord of Ferrara?]; but he takes on himself the burden of making him pay them, and soon. For this he will at once send one of his men, and when they are paid they will not be counted in the said 40 thousand ducats to be paid in March and April, but in the others to be paid from six months to six months; and even if the [gap: lord of Ferrara?] paid no part of them, His Majesty the King remains bound to pay the said sum of ninety-four thousand ducats every year. Had I been able to do better, which I strove for as far as was possible, I would gladly have done it; but not being able, I accepted what I could obtain. As for the election of the Pope, I wrote to you in other letters what I had heard; now I have nothing else to add, except that everything will be done to have one who is a friend, and if he will not be, they will have ways to make him repent. I commend myself to Your Lordship and also to the illustrious Madonna Bianca. Rome, 3 March. Devoted servant, Marcolino. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## f. 61r = f. 62 (Rome, 4 Mar 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. Replying briefly to what Your Excellency writes to me in letters of the twenty-seventh of last month, I say that the ducal courier whom you had escorted brought me no letter but yours; I hear indeed that he brought others to the Bishop of Novara and to Messer Pietro of Monferrato, and also to Simone Arrigoni, servant of the lord your father, who has stayed in this place many months for His Lordship. I say also that by three letters of mine I have informed Your Lordship of the death of the Pope and of what happened to me about it; nor has anything new happened since, except that the cardinals entered the conclave this evening, and it is hoped they will very soon elect another Pope, and opinions are very divided as to whom the election should fall to: God grant it be a good one. Likewise I informed you by other letters of the conclusion made with His Majesty the King. Both the first and the second letters I sent into the hands of the Magnificent Madonna Aura, as Your Lordship told me, and by sure messengers, and the said letters should have arrived safely. From now on I shall direct such letters to Messer Angelo in Urbino, as you write. And I shall continually inform Your Lordship of things as they happen. Now I send you, enclosed with these, certain letters of His Majesty the King, by which you will understand his good disposition; informing Your Lordship that he heard very gladly what I told him on your behalf, and above all he relished what you said of having turned your mind from the affairs of the Kingdom, and showed a good will to have you wholly his. I commend myself to Your Lordship. Rome, 4 March 1447, by Your Lordship's devoted servant Marcolino de Barbavara. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## f. 68 = f. 69 (Rome, 6 Mar 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. At this seventeenth hour or about, Monsignor of "Cologna" [so the copy; Tommaso Parentucelli, cardinal of Bologna] has been proclaimed Pope. I have seen what Your Lordship writes to me in yours dated the fourth of this month, and the explanations you give me about the enemies' offer to this Duke of Ferrara ꝺ. I have done everything to induce him to help the Most Illustrious our Lord in this need of his, but I suspect he will do nothing at all, although he speaks general words, and at other times has spoken to me of particular ones. I know well that he has taken suspicion of me, and certainly wrongly, but the simplicity of Giovanni del Maino was the cause of it, having had him told of the suspicion Your Lordship had, and of me for the warning I had given to [gap] ꝺ. Still I shall solicit and importune as much as I know and can to induce him to it, though I have little hope of it. Further, I am much astonished that, having informed Your Lordship from Reggio on the twenty-fourth of last month that I was coming here, begging you to send one of your men soon, to whom I would pay out twenty thousand ducats, and that the rest was still being got ready, I have never had a reply; and I also begged Your Lordship to write to me about the way and manner you thought I should take in coming to you, to tell you what the Duke has charged me with, and I have never had an answer. For which reason I have decided to write you this one, fearing that the other has gone astray, and so I pray that you will inform me at once, so that I may satisfy the commands of my Lord. I send enclosed to Your Lordship certain briefs, which my said Lord has sent after me, which he addresses to you [?]. Given at Ferrara, the 6th of March. C. S. ꝺ. V. Humble servant, Pietro da Pusterla. [Address:] To the Most Illustrious Lord Francesco Sforza, etc. ## f. 70r-v = clear copy of f. 71 (Ferrara, 7 Mar 1447) 1447, 7 March. [I have?] seen the Duke of Ferrara. Your Excellency writes to me in yours dated the third of this month, pressing me to make every effort to induce this Lord Duke of Ferrara to pay the expense of the Magnificent Lord Guidemo ꝺ. I have used every art and ingenuity possible, using even great liberality, that of the enemies, which, however, it has not been possible for me to make him do what I wished, because today he answered me that he had wanted to see his revenues, and has recognised that he cannot meet that expense; nevertheless he says he wants to be a good son of the Duke, and also to come into this enterprise against the Venetians, on condition that he is referred back to a proposal made at other times with His Lordship, in which he offered to give him forty thousand ducats a year, and besides, to be in that enterprise, so many and such things that with half of them, without him, the world would be won entirely. I have informed my Lord of it, and I shall also let Your Excellency hear everything by word of mouth. I am greatly astonished not to have had an answer from you to the letters I wrote on my arrival here, and about the money I had for you; I sent those letters four days before the one I wrote to the Lord of Faenza, and according to what Belino answered me, he wrote that he had sent them to you by a messenger of his own. I beg Your Excellency most urgently, if you have not answered me, to be pleased to answer me and to send for the said money, so that I may soon come to you to do what the Lord has charged me with; he, I suspect, will not send {"remeta", with "era" interlined to give "remetera"} more money here until he knows from me that I have counted out this, so as not to put so large a sum here at one stroke. If it were not for the money I would have set out towards Your Excellency, as the Lord commands me; for the proposal to which the Duke of Ferrara refers is a thing, first, not to be greatly esteemed, even if it was negotiated by others than me, who will have to pursue it most promptly [?]. I urge and pray Your Lordship to press warmly the negotiation begun with the Bolognese, because it will infallibly succeed for you, and the Lord is greatly pleased with it, and I have such knowledge of it that if you press it well it will be accomplished for you: by means of which there will also be occasion to do our will on this man, besides the other benefits that will follow from it ꝺ. I do not write in too much detail, because I still hope from hour to hour to set out towards Your Excellency, to whom I always commend myself. Given at Ferrara, the seventh day of March. E. S. ꝺ. V. Humble servant, Pietro da Pusterla. I send you enclosed three briefs which the Lord sent me today. [Address:] To the Most Illustrious Lord Francesco Sforza, etc. ## f. 76r-v = clear copy of f. 77 (Ferrara, 8 Mar 1447) 8 March [1447]. Today it is eleven days since I arrived here, and before and since I have written several times to Your Lordship to send one of your men here, to whom I would give twenty thousand ducats, and I have never had an answer, at which I am in very great distress. I suspect the messengers have gone astray. I have made this one in duplicate, and sent it by way of the [gap], the other by way of Epelino, so that one of them reaches Your Lordship, whom I inform, from what I hear from this Lord Duke of Ferrara, that on Sunday the [gap] came with the whole army of the Venetians to Cremona crying "Long live Saint Mark", and that at once the Ghibellines and the Maltraversi were together with Your Lordship's men-at-arms and showed such spirit and loyalty towards you that none of the Guelphs dared to stir {corrected from: to stay}, and the [gap], seeing that he was given no {corrected from: by} further hearing, has turned back. From what the Duke of Ferrara has, they have returned {corrected from: they have set out} towards Bordolano, and Giovanni Filippo seems to have gone to them. What I hear further I shall report to Your Lordship, whom I pray, if you have not sent to collect the money that I have here, to send for it, and also to inform me of the manner I am to take in coming to you, so that I may come to carry out what my Lord has charged me with. Further, as a true servant of Your Lordship, I urge you to make sure of and come to a clear understanding with the Count of Urbino; and I say this because I have it from a worthy person that he is in close negotiation with the Venetians, and disposed not to come into Lombardy with Your Lordship. Otherwise, I have written to you {corrected from: avio}, begging you warmly to press and pursue the negotiation of Bologna, because it will be accomplished for you, and so I repeat it to you anew; and at Lodi [?] such an egg is cooking for you, which comes to Your Lordship; keeping him well in hand [?], I am certain he will do what you wish. The day before yesterday I wrote to Your Lordship about the deed which they had done [gap] {6tr} at Cremona; since then I have word that they have gone to Soncino. The Duke writes you four briefs, enclosed, all of the same content, from which you will better understand the matter. Now I no longer know what to say to myself about so many letters that I have written to Your Lordship without ever having had an answer: it grieves me more that Giovanni Matteo writes to me that he has recovered [?] another good part of your dispatch, and that once these are paid out, he will inform you at once; which I am certain he says for no other reason than to send them here as soon as these are counted out; so for God's sake write me something. Further, I repeat to you the matter of the Count of Urbino, because I have fresh news that he is in close negotiation, still 6 [?] [gap], when this was written. The Duke of Ferrara has become somewhat bold, having heard that Master Tommaso has been made Pope, as one who has firm hope that he must be our friend. Messer Andrea Dandolo, on his way to [gap], happened to say to a trusted man of his that the hope the Signoria had of taking Cremona was given them by a squadron captain of the [gap], who is his kinsman; so I wished to inform Your Lordship of it, to whom I always commend myself. Uncertain renderings are in [square brackets with ?]. ## f. 66r-v = clear copy of f. 67 (Ferrara, 6 Mar 1447) 1447, 6 March. I have seen what Your Lordship writes to me in yours dated the fourth of this month, and the explanations you give me about the enemies' offer to this Duke of Ferrara ꝺ. I have done everything to induce him to help the Most Illustrious our Lord in this need of his, but I suspect he will do nothing at all, although he speaks general words, and at other times has spoken to me of particular ones. I know well that he has taken suspicion of me, and certainly wrongly, but the simplicity of Giovanni del Maino was the cause of it, having had him told of the suspicion Your Lordship had, and of me for the warning I had given to [gap] ꝺ. Still I shall solicit and importune as much as I know and can to induce him to it, though I have little hope of it. Further, I am much astonished that, having informed Your Lordship from Reggio on the twenty-fourth of last month that I was coming here, begging you to send one of your men soon, to whom I would pay out twenty thousand ducats, and that the rest was still being got ready, I have never had a reply; and I also begged Your Lordship to write to me about the way and manner you thought I should take in coming to you, to tell you what the Duke has charged me with, and I have never had an answer. For which reason I have decided to write you this one, fearing that the other has gone astray, and so I pray that you will inform me at once, so that I may satisfy the commands of my Lord. I send enclosed to Your Lordship certain briefs, which my said Lord has sent after me, which he addresses to you [?]. Given at Ferrara, the 6th of March. C. S. ꝺ. V. Humble servant, Pietro da Pusterla. [Address:] To the Most Illustrious Lord Francesco Sforza, etc. ## f. 70r-v = clear copy of f. 71 (Ferrara, 7 Mar 1447) 1447, 7 March. [I have?] seen the Duke of Ferrara. Your Excellency writes to me in yours dated the third of this month, pressing me to make every effort to induce this Lord Duke of Ferrara to pay the expense of the Magnificent Lord Guidemo ꝺ. I have used every art and ingenuity possible, using even great liberality, that of the enemies, which, however, it has not been possible for me to make him do what I wished, because today he answered me that he had wanted to see his revenues, and has recognised that he cannot meet that expense; nevertheless he says he wants to be a good son of the Duke, and also to come into this enterprise against the Venetians, on condition that he is referred back to a proposal made at other times with His Lordship, in which he offered to give him forty thousand ducats a year, and besides, to be in that enterprise, so many and such things that with half of them, without him, the world would be won entirely. I have informed my Lord of it, and I shall also let Your Excellency hear everything by word of mouth. I am greatly astonished not to have had an answer from you to the letters I wrote on my arrival here, and about the money I had for you; I sent those letters four days before the one I wrote to the Lord of Faenza, and according to what Belino answered me, he wrote that he had sent them to you by a messenger of his own. I beg Your Excellency most urgently, if you have not answered me, to be pleased to answer me and to send for the said money, so that I may soon come to you to do what the Lord has charged me with; he, I suspect, will not send {"remeta", with "era" interlined to give "remetera"} more money here until he knows from me that I have counted out this, so as not to put so large a sum here at one stroke. If it were not for the money I would have set out towards Your Excellency, as the Lord commands me; for the proposal to which the Duke of Ferrara refers is a thing, first, not to be greatly esteemed, even if it was negotiated by others than me, who will have to pursue it most promptly [?]. I urge and pray Your Lordship to press warmly the negotiation begun with the Bolognese, because it will infallibly succeed for you, and the Lord is greatly pleased with it, and I have such knowledge of it that if you press it well it will be accomplished for you: by means of which there will also be occasion to do our will on this man, besides the other benefits that will follow from it ꝺ. I do not write in too much detail, because I still hope from hour to hour to set out towards Your Excellency, to whom I always commend myself. Given at Ferrara, the seventh day of March. E. S. ꝺ. V. Humble servant, Pietro da Pusterla. I send you enclosed three briefs which the Lord sent me today. [Address:] To the Most Illustrious Lord Francesco Sforza, etc. ## f. 76r-v = clear copy of f. 77 (Ferrara, 8 Mar 1447) 8 March [1447]. Today it is eleven days since I arrived here, and before and since I have written several times to Your Lordship to send one of your men here, to whom I would give twenty thousand ducats, and I have never had an answer, at which I am in very great distress. I suspect the messengers have gone astray. I have made this one in duplicate, and sent it by way of the [gap], the other by way of Epelino, so that one of them reaches Your Lordship, whom I inform, from what I hear from this Lord Duke of Ferrara, that on Sunday the [gap] came with the whole army of the Venetians to Cremona crying "Long live Saint Mark", and that at once the Ghibellines and the Maltraversi were together with Your Lordship's men-at-arms and showed such spirit and loyalty towards you that none of the Guelphs dared to stir {corrected from: to stay}, and the [gap], seeing that he was given no {corrected from: by} further hearing, has turned back. From what the Duke of Ferrara has, they have returned {corrected from: they have set out} towards Bordolano, and Giovanni Filippo seems to have gone to them. What I hear further I shall report to Your Lordship, whom I pray, if you have not sent to collect the money that I have here, to send for it, and also to inform me of the manner I am to take in coming to you, so that I may come to carry out what my Lord has charged me with. Further, as a true servant of Your Lordship, I urge you to make sure of and come to a clear understanding with the Count of Urbino; and I say this because I have it from a worthy person that he is in close negotiation with the Venetians, and disposed not to come into Lombardy with Your Lordship. The day before yesterday I wrote to Your Lordship about the deed which they had done [gap] {6tr} at Cremona; since then I have word that they have gone to Soncino. The Duke writes you four briefs, enclosed, all of the same content, from which you will better understand the matter. Now I no longer know what to say to myself about so many letters that I have written to Your Lordship without ever having had an answer: it grieves me more that Giovanni Matteo writes to me that he has recovered [?] another good part of your dispatch, and that once these are paid out, he will inform you at once; which I am certain he says for no other reason than to send them here as soon as these are counted out; so for God's sake write me something. Sono stato da la Majestà del Re, et cum quelle rasone me sono acadute a la mente lo confortata et pregata a nome del mio Signore a prendere tanto majore cura et caricho de contribuire a la spesa vostra, quanto el bisogno è majore per la morte del Papa, dal quale non è più da expectare subventione alcuna. Da poi ve scripsi la ellectione del novo Papa sono stato quello dì de la ellectione per non perdere tempo a li pedi de la soa Beatitudine, et da poy alchune parole generale dicte reallegrandome a nome del Duca de la ellectione soa toccai etiandio el facto del dinaro per V.S.; in effecto me pare che la Sanctità soa insieme cum li Cardinali habia presso deliberatione de procurare pace in Italia, et de mandare per questa caxone el Camerlengo et lo Vicecanciellero insieme da la Majestà del Re, quale sono partiti questo dì, ma no li reusirano li pensieri, perché lo Re, dal quale sono stato per questa casone un'altra volta, delibera de darli molto bene ad intendere, et specialmente al Camerlengo, perché l'altro è Veneciano, che queste parole de pace non gli piaceno, excepto se non fano prima la provisione del dinaro per V.S., et de le gente per mandare insieme cum la soa Majestà, a ciò che cum questa via sia proveduto a la securezza del stato del prefato Duca, et li inimici temendo le provisione se reducano a meglore condictione de pace, o non volendola per amore se gli possa redure cum la forcia. Delibera etiandio la soa Majestà, se questo parlare non moverà el Papa et li Cardinali a fare altra deliberatione meglore et più grata de aprirli come essa Majestà intende tore in si el carrego de pagare la spesa vostra, et dire che siano certi ge la farà pagare tuta a loro, et se anchora questo non aiutarà, mostra de volere usare altro che parole, cioè venire a li facti dicendo, che li preti sono homini da bastonate, non da pregare. Non so quello seguirà, pur non sono anchora sanza speranza, che'l Papa et li Cardinali intendando el malcontentamento del Re se debiano movere a piglare meglore deliberatione; de quello seguirà V.S. ne sarà avisata; et forse como per altre ho scripto non serà altro, che bene che V.S. facia de le demonstratione per timorezare anchora più la brigata et redurla a quello desideramo. Ho recordato anchora a la Majestà del Re el facto de li dinari per V.S., et me ha resposto che sanza fallo li meterà tale ordine non vi mancharano a li termini, et simelmente ha dicto che in questa septimana aviarà el suo, quale el manda dal Signore [gap; the copyist drew ꝺ+÷ in the margin] per quelli vinti millia ducati. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## f. 48r-v = f. 49 (Rome, 27 Feb 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. Having arrived here I found the Pope had passed from this life, as you will have heard, and he has indeed wished to do as Your Lordship used to say: to die so as to do harm not only living but also dying. I have been with the Camerlengo, who, having heard the reason for my coming, says that in effect it is necessary to wait for the election of another Pope and to treat the matter with His Holiness, and that meanwhile I can go to His Majesty the King to tighten the matter with him; and so I shall do, and Your Lordship will be told what follows. The said Camerlengo received very gratefully all I told him on your behalf, and from the words he used with me he seems to me very willing to have and keep good friendship with Your Lordship. He charged me to write to you to be of good heart, because whoever is elected to the papacy will gladly do things that please you. He says too that he will be a friend of the lord your father, or at least not his enemy, but rather believes he will be his friend and favourable, and God grant it be so. It is thought that the election must fall either to Monsignor of Capua or to Monsignor of Fermo; yet it could be that it falls to others, because it seems to me it always falls to the one no one has commonly thought of. If Your Excellency made some show and demonstration of wanting to advance into the Marche or elsewhere, so that news of it came here, I believe it would be very useful to warm the minds of these priests and make them hotter to contribute to your expenses; and I say this because they have built an almost certain foundation that Your Lordship will in any case go to the favour and help of the said lord your father. That opinion, however, I have striven to get out of their heads, and said that such a foundation is vain, and that, though you are well disposed, this good disposition must be helped otherwise than with words, that is with money. But to take it from them still [gap?]. Rome, 27 February. Your Excellency's little servant, Marcolino. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## ff. 55r-v, 57r = f. 56 (Rome, 3 Mar 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. I have been to His Majesty the King, and with such reasons as came to mind I urged and begged him, in the name of my lord, to take all the greater care and burden of contributing to your expenses as the need is greater through the death of the Pope, from whom no subsidy is to be expected any more. In effect His Serenity has been content not only to pay what the Pope was to pay, but also to contribute a greater sum than had first been discussed, namely ninety-four thousand ducats of gold, in gold, every year and for two years, as the said lord wrote that he was content with two years. He will pay the said money in this way: twenty thousand ducats this month, and another twenty thousand in the coming month of April at the latest, and the rest half at the end of six months from the day of your engagement and the other half at the end of the year, and this for the first year; but for the second year he is content to pay forty thousand ducats by the whole of March of that year, and the other 54 thousand from six months to six months as said above. And so His Serenity has promised, by articles signed and concluded with him, sealed with his seal and also signed in his own hand; and he is to have the said money paid out at the due times to whatever messenger of the said lord, or of yours, holds a sufficient mandate for it. On the lord's part he has been promised that you will make no attacks on his men; rather, if need be, the said lord will send to his aid either as many of your men, or of the other ducal troops, as amounts to the expense he bears for your condotta; and he has also been promised that what the Pope pays, once he is elected, shall come to His Majesty. Of all this I inform Your Excellency so that you know what has been done, and in good faith I recall two things. The first: that either His Excellency the lord or you provide someone with a sufficient mandate to receive the money and to acknowledge receiving it, and also to press for it with His Majesty the King, because you know well that where money is concerned one cannot use too much diligence. The second: it seems to me necessary to make clear to His Majesty as soon as possible that the conclusion has been made with him, so that he cannot excuse himself that, not having been made certain, he has not provided the money. I have indeed given him good hope of the conclusion according to what Your Lordship told me, but I do not think that is enough, and from my side I would not go on to give him any other assurance, having nothing else either from the lord or from Your Lordship, who may write to me your intention about this, and I shall carry it out without waiting for anything else. I inform Your Excellency also that His Majesty the King understands that in the said sum of ninety-four thousand ducats which he is to pay are included the 20 thousand of the [gap: the lord of Ferrara?]; but he takes on himself the burden of making him pay them, and soon. For this he will at once send one of his men, and when they are paid they will not be counted in the said 40 thousand ducats to be paid in March and April, but in the others to be paid from six months to six months; and even if the [gap: lord of Ferrara?] paid no part of them, His Majesty the King remains bound to pay the said sum of ninety-four thousand ducats every year. Had I been able to do better, which I strove for as far as was possible, I would gladly have done it; but not being able, I accepted what I could obtain. As for the election of the Pope, I wrote to you in other letters what I had heard; now I have nothing else to add, except that everything will be done to have one who is a friend, and if he will not be, they will have ways to make him repent. I commend myself to Your Lordship and also to the illustrious Madonna Bianca. Rome, 3 March. Devoted servant, Marcolino. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## f. 61r = f. 62 (Rome, 4 Mar 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. Replying briefly to what Your Excellency writes to me in letters of the twenty-seventh of last month, I say that the ducal courier whom you had escorted brought me no letter but yours; I hear indeed that he brought others to the Bishop of Novara and to Messer Pietro of Monferrato, and also to Simone Arrigoni, servant of the lord your father, who has stayed in this place many months for His Lordship. I say also that by three letters of mine I have informed Your Lordship of the death of the Pope and of what happened to me about it; nor has anything new happened since, except that the cardinals entered the conclave this evening, and it is hoped they will very soon elect another Pope, and opinions are very divided as to whom the election should fall to: God grant it be a good one. Likewise I informed you by other letters of the conclusion made with His Majesty the King. Both the first and the second letters I sent into the hands of the Magnificent Madonna Aura, as Your Lordship told me, and by sure messengers, and the said letters should have arrived safely. From now on I shall direct such letters to Messer Angelo in Urbino, as you write. And I shall continually inform Your Lordship of things as they happen. Now I send you, enclosed with these, certain letters of His Majesty the King, by which you will understand his good disposition; informing Your Lordship that he heard very gladly what I told him on your behalf, and above all he relished what you said of having turned your mind from the affairs of the Kingdom, and showed a good will to have you wholly his. I commend myself to Your Lordship. Rome, 4 March 1447, by Your Lordship's devoted servant Marcolino de Barbavara. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## f. 68 = f. 69 (Rome, 6 Mar 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. At this seventeenth hour or about, Monsignor of "Cologna" [so the copy; Tommaso Parentucelli, cardinal of Bologna] has been proclaimed Pope. I firmly believe he will be a friend, and I shall soon strive to see proof of it in the matters entrusted to me. Of what follows Your Lordship will be informed; and you may tell me whether it seems to you that one way rather than another should be kept by me. I commend myself to Your Excellency. Rome, 6 March 1447, by Your Lordship's servant Marcolino de Barbavara. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. ## f. 74r-v = f. 75 (Rome, 8 Mar 1447) Illustrious and excellent, most honoured lord. Since I wrote to you of the election of the new Pope, I was, on the very day of the election, so as to lose no time, at the feet of His Holiness, and after some general words rejoicing in the name of the Duke at his election I touched also on the matter of money for Your Lordship. In effect it seems to me that His Holiness together with the cardinals has resolved to procure peace in Italy, and for this reason to send the Camerlengo and the Vice-Chancellor together to His Majesty the King; they left today, but their plans will not succeed, because the King, whom I have seen again for this reason, means to make them understand very well, and especially the Camerlengo (because the other is a Venetian), that these words of peace do not please him unless they first make provision of money for Your Lordship, and of troops to send together with His Majesty, so that by this way the security of the state of the said Duke is provided for, and the enemies, fearing the provisions, are brought to better terms of peace, or, not wanting it out of love, can be brought to it by force. His Majesty resolves also, if this speech does not move the Pope and the cardinals to some better and more agreeable resolution, to declare to them that His Majesty means to take on himself the burden of paying your expenses, and to tell them to be sure he will make them pay it all, and if even this does not help, he shows he will use other than words, that is, come to deeds, saying that priests are men to be beaten, not begged. I do not know what will follow; still I am not yet without hope that the Pope and the cardinals, understanding the King's discontent, may be moved to take a better resolution; of what follows Your Lordship will be informed. And perhaps, as I have written elsewhere, nothing else will do but that Your Lordship make some demonstrations, to frighten the company still more and bring it to what we desire. I reminded His Majesty the King again of the matter of the money for Your Lordship, and he answered that without fail he will give such orders that it will not fail you at the terms, and likewise he said that this week he will send his man, whom he is sending to the lord [gap: of Ferrara?] for those twenty thousand ducats. I commend myself to Your Excellency, and I marvel that I have never had from you either letter or answer. Rome, 8 March 1447, by your devoted servant Marcolino de Barbavara. To the illustrious lord Francesco Sforza. I have seen what Your Lordship writes to me in yours dated the fourth of this month, and the explanations you give me about the enemies' offer to this Duke of Ferrara ꝺ. I have done everything to induce him to help the Most Illustrious our Lord in this need of his, but I suspect he will do nothing at all, although he speaks general words, and at other times has spoken to me of particular ones. I know well that he has taken suspicion of me, and certainly wrongly, but the simplicity of Giovanni del Maino was the cause of it, having had him told of the suspicion Your Lordship had, and of me for the warning I had given to [gap] ꝺ. Still I shall solicit and importune as much as I know and can to induce him to it, though I have little hope of it. Further, I am much astonished that, having informed Your Lordship from Reggio on the twenty-fourth of last month that I was coming here, begging you to send one of your men soon, to whom I would pay out twenty thousand ducats, and that the rest was still being got ready, I have never had a reply; and I also begged Your Lordship to write to me about the way and manner you thought I should take in coming to you, to tell you what the Duke has charged me with, and I have never had an answer. For which reason I have decided to write you this one, fearing that the other has gone astray, and so I pray that you will inform me at once, so that I may satisfy the commands of my Lord. I send enclosed to Your Lordship certain briefs, which my said Lord has sent after me, which he addresses to you [?]. Given at Ferrara, the 6th of March. C. S. ꝺ. V. Humble servant, Pietro da Pusterla. [Address:] To the Most Illustrious Lord Francesco Sforza, etc. ## f. 70r-v = clear copy of f. 71 (Ferrara, 7 Mar 1447) 1447, 7 March. The ciphered middle ran 63 lines over five pages. Where British Library, Add MS 4200 f. 88 (a Birch volume of Thurloe’s state papers); DECODE R8390, with copies R8391 and R8393. The cipher The Brienne office design: consecutive numbers run through the syllables in alphabetical order. How it was read A solver recovered the keys of matched controls but not this key. The DECODE-listed Deciphering Branch key sheet, BL Add MS 32263 f. 1, proved to be this cipher’s key; applied to a transcription corrected against the images, it deciphers the letter. What it says The Council heard the deputies of rebel Bordeaux before Cromwell, le General , gave the envoy his audience. The treaty is unsigned and England is said to help Bordeaux indirectly, so Brienne should hold back French mediation. Still open About twenty of 813 tokens (the corrected transcription; Tomokiyo’s has 810): six nomenclature codes (names, probably including the Stuart king) and the rare syllable numbers listed in section 06 (nine are listed there, not a dozen).

Add MS 4200 is one of the Birch volumes of Thurloe’s state papers. Folio 88 is headed in an English hand A Letter from Bordeaux the French Amb.r in England . The letter opens in clear, Monsieur, Cellecy vous fera veoir, que la nouvelle de mon retour en France n’est pas vraye , and continues in cipher for 63 lines over five pages. It returns to clear with on n’a point icy aucune nouvelle de la flotte depuis qu’elle a paru à la hauteur d’Escosse and closes De Bordeaux, A Londres 30 May 1653 . The English made a second copy of the opening and a second copy of the ending, with a frequency count (DECODE R8393 and R8391), and started contact tables on the commonest signs (R8386, R8388, R8389). None of these reaches a decipherment. f. 88r, the head of the letter: the clear opening Cellecy vous fera veoir, que la nouvelle de mon retour en France n’est pas vraye , then the first five lines of cipher, which decipher as Ce n’est pas que si nos affaires estoyent plus florissantes… Image: British Library, Add MS 4200 f. 88r, via DECODE R8390. The plaintext is not in print. Birch printed twelve of Bordeaux’s despatches of 1653 in the Thurloe State Papers and Guizot sixty more from the French foreign ministry’s archive, but neither has this one. Satoshi Tomokiyo published a provisional transcription of the cipher on cryptiana . His list gives the companion letter, Mazarin to Bordeaux of 22 June 1654, as solved by George Lasry in February 2025.

Tomokiyo’s transcription has 810 tokens over 156 symbols. There are 24 graphic signs ( u , x , d , ll , m , …), plain numbers, and numbers carrying a prime, two dots or an overbar. Brienne’s office used one design for its ciphers of 1651–54, known from two recovered keys: his cipher to d’Estrades of 1651, and Lasry’s key for the 1654 letter. In both, letters are signs or low numbers, and the syllables ba be bi bo bu ca ce … take consecutive numbers in alphabetical order through marked series, with a few common words filed in their alphabetical place. On 16 September a simulated-annealing solver was built with that order as a hard constraint and tested on controls: a Bordeaux despatch of 1654 enciphered with a random key of the same design and the same size. It recovered the key to within 1% in three of six control runs. On the letter, 21 runs over three series orders stopped at the level of the control’s failed runs. A second control, with one diacritic in ten misread, fell to 52% and 9%, and the notes concluded that a provisional transcription could explain the failure on its own. It did. Checked against the page images, the transcription has three kinds of fault, and together they are enough to stop a ciphertext-only attack: Two signs written as one. The transcription’s d covers two different glyphs, a looped ꝺ that is u and a backward ∂ that is n ( conte·n·te·me·∂·t , Bordea·ꝺ·x ). The English frequency count on f. 92 lists them on separate lines, so the 1653 analysts saw two signs. Dropped tokens and marks. In line 2, plus florissantes needs 76¨ ( lo ) and 27 ( n ), which the transcription leaves out. Elsewhere 96¨ na appears as 96‾, 79′ vous as 74′, 64′ ti as b 4′ , and 97¨ ne as a plain 97. Twenty-one corrections in all. One of them, the 52′ of commissaires , was omitted by the clerk himself and is restored from the duplicate R8393. The clerk’s own omissions. He often writes a syllable number without its mark: 38 for et , 43 for 43′ re , 54 for si , 97 for ne . In this design the mark is what separates re from a letter. A solver that trusts the marks puts those tokens in the wrong series.

BL Add MS 32263 is the Willes family’s volume of cipher keys, 1653–1850, from the Deciphering Branch. Folio 1 is headed To M.r Bordeaux French M.r at London 1653 , Key & Calculation , and Discovered Aug. 20th 1832 . That is how the year reads, and the sheet is printed ledger paper numbered 2801 to 3000, so it is a later working, not a key of 1653. The left half is the calculation : for each number, the letters that contact counts allowed. The right half has the settled values in boxes, and a panel headed Principal gives the commonest signs: u = n , 32 = s , m = e , 33 = t , 34 = u , 20¨ = de , 63′ = te , a = r . The sheet is transcribed in targets/bordeaux/key7537.txt . It is the Brienne design exactly: Series Values on the sheet plain 15–37 the alphabet, a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x y z prime ′ pa 25, pe 26, po 28, pour 31, par 32, qui 38, que 39, ra re ri ro 42–45, se si so 53–55, te 63, to 65, ve vi vo 73–75, vous 79; also negociation 19 two dots ¨ de di do du 20–23, dans 24, et 28, estre 29, estat 32, fa fe fi fo fu 37–41, fort 42, ha he hi ho hu 60–64, il 72, la le li lo lu 73–77, les 78, leurs 83, ma me mi mo 84–87, na ne ni no nu 96–100 overbar ‾ ba be bi bo bu 83–87, bien 89, bon 90, ca ce ci co cu 93–97; also Angleterre (?) 75 The gaps fill by the same order and are confirmed in the text: 29′ pu ( deputez ), 64′ ti ( resolutions ), 19¨ da ( d’accord ), 49¨ ge ( obliger , purgée ), 66¨–70¨ ja je ji jo ju ( sujet , jours , jusque ). Three words are fixed by context and fit their alphabetical slots: 40′ quoy ( pourquoy , quoy que ), 41′ quand , 79¨ leur . So are 16¨ comme and 53¨, which is General , Cromwell, both times it occurs. The graphic signs beyond the Principal list come from the text: x = o , x p written together = a , ꝺ = u , ∂ = n , q = i , ll = r , the stroked 4 = s , ≠ = g , h = p , H = z , 9 = i , φ = y , λ = s , θ = i , ω = n , ff = t , 〃 = n . Every such value was taken only when it gave the same sense at each occurrence.

Bordeaux-Neufville had come to London at the end of 1652 to win recognition of the young Louis XIV’s government from the Commonwealth and to keep England out of the Fronde. The city of Bordeaux, held by the Ormée and Condé’s party against the King, had sent its own deputies to ask for English help. The letter is written four weeks after Cromwell dissolved the Rump (20 April 1653, old style). It opens by denying the rumour that he is to return to France. The reception of the Bordeaux deputies would give France cause to show displeasure if its affairs were more flourishing; weakened by the Fronde, it cannot afford to. Its complaint is about order and precedence. The Council heard the rebels’ deputies through two commissioners, and only then gave the King’s envoy his audience with le General . Bordeaux reads this as a sign that the treaty, settled except for the signing, is being weighed against the rebels’ proposals. His advice is tactical. Brienne should not offer French mediation until the English position is clear, because help for the city, even indirect, would show there is no trust on the English side. The English fear, as he reports it, is that a France at peace at home would back the Stuarts. In the event the city surrendered to the royal army at the end of July 1653, and the Anglo-French treaty was not signed until 1655. (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.)

Rare tokens. 6¨ ( ils [..]rent leurs propositions ), 98 and 10 (both once), 30′ ( traiter de [..]), 35′, 68′, 14′ (taken as s’y ), 5¨ (taken as li in delibere ), and 46¨ ( la [France] , which fits its alphabetical slot but nothing else confirms). The duplicate of the ending agrees with the original token for token, so 68′ and the 24 in quand mesmes il auroit are what the clerk wrote. 42¨. The sheet has fort ; the sense of capables de fort prendre would be better served by faire . The value is left as the sheet gives it. The key sheet’s date. Aug. 20th 1832 is how the heading reads. Whether it records a later re-solution or a copy of an older key was not investigated.

Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from the glosses of one letter and tested it once on another: 0.873 of characters against 0.170 for shuffled keys. Where Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich, Clm 10382 (Collectio Camerariana 32), digitised microfilm MDZ bsb00112117, scans 470 and 476–477. Not on DECODE. The cipher A German letter cipher of two-digit numbers written run together: each letter has three numbers in a block of consecutive values (14–16 a, 17–19 g, 20–22 n …), and 86 and up are nulls. Names are spelled; no nomenclator was seen. How it was rebuilt From the word-by-word decipherment written above the lines of scan 470, then frozen and measured once on scans 476–477, transcribed after the freeze: 0.873 of characters against 0.170 for the best of 200 shuffled keys. What it says Money, a sum in reichsthalers, a monthly payment, the King of Denmark, commerce, and later in the year freedom and a marriage. The content is the period decipherment’s, not new. Still open The other cipher scans of the series and the clear German text around the groups are not transcribed; numbers 1–13 and 56–58 were not seen. Credit WAINUT found the cipher while paging the volume (lead 2187). Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) transcribed the groups, rebuilt and tested the key, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The decipherment is the clerk’s of 1629.

Ludwig Camerarius, the Palatine councillor who served the exiled Frederick V and then Sweden, kept a large correspondence, now the Collectio Camerariana in Munich. Among it are letters of Pfalzgraf Johann Casimir of Zweibrücken-Kleeburg, brother-in-law of Gustavus Adolphus, written between 1624 and 1629 (within nos. 106–164 of Clm 10382). Several carry passages in numbers, and a clerk wrote the decipherment word by word above them. The two letters used here are n. 138 (February 1629, scan 470) and n. 140 (Calmar, 3 July 1629, scans 476–477). Other scans with cipher (418, 447–448, 469, 471, 475, 482, 486) were not transcribed. Halm’s catalogue of 1874 lists the letters without a cipher note; no edition was found.

The numbers on scan 470 were split at the word boundaries the glosses give, and each number was given the letter it stands for most often. The values fall into blocks of three consecutive numbers per letter, in the order a, g, n, t, b, h, o, u/v, c, i, p, w, d, k, x, e, l, r, y, f, m, s, z, so the table was extended by block. The key was frozen by SHA-256 together with the protocol and the transcription before scans 476–477 were transcribed. The measurement used the 33 glossed groups of the held-out letter whose gloss has as many letters as numbers (165 characters). The frozen key renders 0.873 of the characters and 0.667 of the whole words; the best of 200 keys with the letters permuted renders 0.170 and 0.030. The thresholds, fixed in advance, were 0.85 and a margin of 0.30. Afterwards two values were changed, outside the test: 71–73 = y rather than i (the held-out part has freyheit , meyne , heyrath ), and 44–46 = p from one word, party . This is not the cipher of the neighbouring pieces: Oxenstierna’s letter of 1625 in the same volume uses another letter cipher, in Latin, and Clm 10380 n. 60–61 (1636) a three- and four-digit nomenclator. The letter of Carl Pawel to Frederick V of 1624 in the same volume uses this alphabet shifted by three ( targets/pawel1624 ).

Of the 127 glossed groups not cut by the binding, 99 decode exactly as glossed. Most of the rest are the clerk’s spellings ( heuraht , bunt , nemmen ) or numbers hard to tell apart on the microfilm (69/64, 23/24, 3/5, 4/9). Unglossed groups on the two scans: 4 non-null groups, of which 1 certain ( wie ), 1 probable ( daler , the end of Reichsthaler cut at the binding) and 2 unresolved. Numbers 1–13 and 56–58 were not seen, and 44–46 = p rests on one word. One reader (an agent) transcribed from a 1,334-pixel microfilm; no human has checked the numbers against the images. The clear German text of the letters is not transcribed, so the groups are given as a word list with their glosses, not as letters.

Francia 283C holds the Secretariat’s original letters and ciphers to the nuncio for 1580: “Corrispondenza fra il Cardinale di Como (Gallio) e Monsignore Dandini Nunzio a Parigi”. R72 , f. 52, is a single page of figures filed with Como’s clear letter from the Villa, 16 May 1580 (ff. 50–53, attached to the record). The decipherment is written in clear below the figures. George Lasry reconstructed a key for the other enclosure on DECODE, R73 (attachment D3190, 24 October 2020). Letters are two digits with an even second digit, vowels have one or two homophones, and there are no nulls. Nomenclator groups are three digits followed by a special mark, for pronouns, titles and common words: 124^ S.S., 824^ N.S., 822^ V.S., 224^ S.M.tà, 266^ che, 200^ non, 800^ mente, 988^ essere. R72 fits the same frame. Parsed with a small dynamic program (two digits, or three digits plus the mark, which SofPe’s 2019 transcription gives as 7 or t/+ ), every group except 38 falls inside Lasry’s table. The nomenclator words come out right, but the letters between them are nonsense. The record was fetched from DECODE with a session cookie: the page image, the clear covering letter, SofPe’s transcription, and Lasry’s key, which is attached to R72 although it was made for R73. The letter values were annealed by swaps over a fixed letter multiset, scored with Italian 4-grams from a Renaissance corpus, with the nomenclator words kept as known plaintext. Five of six restarts agreed, apart from one or two codes. The clear block on f. 52 was transcribed and aligned with the output. Three codes were corrected (22 l, 62 e, 72 i), and the leading stray “1” was set aside.

Where Nationaal Archief, 3.01.25 inv. 610 (R1036, nine pages) and 1.01.02 inv. 7408 (R1040). DECODE lists no decipherment and says the codebook “could not be identified”. The cipher Three-digit groups for words, syllables and letters. A mark on one digit (strokes, underline, caret, circle) makes a different group, so 340 and 340 underlined are unrelated. How it was read R1036 uses the 1765 Croiset codebook for the Russia legation, whose key is DECODE R1038. Parsed with the marks kept it decodes 84.2%; 34 values checked in context and 41 entries transcribed from the scans bring it to 1,663 of 1,719 groups (96.7%); the 23 October context pass raised this to 1,681 (97.8%), leaving 38 groups without a value. What it says The French and Spanish answers to the Austro-Russian mediation, Catherine II’s “Greek project” for the young Grand Duke Constantine, and Prussia’s accession to the Armed Neutrality. Still open The 1787 letter changes codebook part-way (as Karl de Leeuw noted in 2000). Its second part decodes with the same 1765 key; the first 2,259 groups (the first 1,928 plus the 331 of image 5474) use a missing codebook and stay open.

R1036 has nine scans. Two leaves are duplicate copies of the same passages (images 5419/5421 and 5420/5422). DECODE’s transcriptions of each pair agree at 96.7% and 99.6%, and they were merged, keeping the group that exists in the key where they differ. After merging, the despatch has 1,719 groups and 596 distinct ones. R1036, first page: the clear salutation, then the code, beginning 15, 452, 730, 833 = waar bij ingesloten . Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.25 inv. 610, first page, via DECODE R1036. The key is the codebook that Croiset prepared in 1765 for the Russia legation (DECODE R1038). Its values are words, syllables and single letters, so many words are built from pieces: Spa·nje , Dene·mar·ken , Enge·land . DECODE’s authenticated transcription of the key is partial, which is why about a sixth of the groups have no value on the first pass. The marks are part of each group. If they are dropped and the groups reduced to their three digits, unrelated entries collide and the decoding fails.

The reading of 23 October 2026 ( R1036_reading.md ): the decode, with the corrections of 30 September and the context values, divided into words group by group, in the spelling the code gives ( antwoort , ontfangen , reekent ). [?word] is partly carried, [word] supplied, […] unread, and a bracketed number is a group with no value. The opening: Hoog Edele Gestrenge Heer! Ik gedraage my eerbiedigst aan myne onderdaenige laatste aan UW Hoog Edele Gestrenge van den 26 jongstleeden en 1 deezer loopende maand, waar by ingesloten waren de antwoort van de hof van Frankryk en Spanje op de propositie welke de byde oorlogende hof aan dezelve hebben laaten volgen op de bewuste preliminaires propositie, de courier welke de Oostenrijkse Minister Zondag van zyn Hof ontfangen heeft (“I respectfully refer to my humble last letters to Your Honour of the 26th ultimo and the 1st of this month, in which were enclosed the answers of the courts of France and Spain to the proposal which the two warring courts had sent them following the known preliminary proposal, the courier whom the Austrian minister received from his court on Sunday …”) The despatch covers three matters: The mediation. The French and Spanish answers are unwelcome to Russia. England insists on keeping the American colonies in some form, and Spain will not negotiate while the question of Gibraltar, or an equivalent for it, is unsettled. There is doubt whether the Emperor is dealing honestly with Russia (of nu den Keizer in dezen met haar oprecht handelt) or only means to amuse her. The Greek project. The Empress has not abandoned her project. For some time the young Grand Duke Constantine has been in the hands of a Greek woman and is being taught Greek, and she has lately sent orders for twelve Greek boys to be procured. She keeps silent about the project even towards her confidants, but de Swart does not conclude that she has dropped it. The Armed Neutrality. Prussia is acceding. The Vice-Chancellor has spoken with the Swedish and Danish ministers about the accession act. The Empress wants it signed pure et simpliciter , without the secret articles, and asks for a firm and unalterable law for the rights of neutrals. The despatch also discusses the Prussian minister’s report to Berlin and the King’s reply on the fourth and sixth articles (the reading marks “fourth” and “sixth” as uncertain). The passage on the Emperor and the Greek project: Of nu den Keizer in dezen met haar oprecht handelt, [?dan] of hy daardoor maar zoekt om haar te amuseeren en aan zyne lyn te houden, gelyk veele met [738] veronderstel[len], is niet wel zeker te ontdekken; maar het is zeker dat se tot nog toe van den Keizer zeer [592]ig ingenomen is, en dat se ontrent de [?bevordering] van dit haare favoriet project op zyne Majesteit veel reekent en staat maakt. En tot bewys dat se het project geheel niet [?geabandonneerd] heeft, zo dient dat, behalven dat se de jonge Grootvorst Constantyn, gelyk [ik] reeds de eere hebbe gehad in een myner voorgaande aan U HoogEdelGestrenge te melden, in hand van [een] griekse vrouw al sedert een geruymen tyd stellen heeft, en hem de griekse tael laat [?leeren], verder een griekse [922^"]ucatie [553], zy heeft ook onlangs aan den [644^_] Rumanzow ordre zenden om twaalf griekse jongens te bezorgen, en het […] te maaken. (“Whether the Emperor is dealing honestly with her in this, [?or] whether he only seeks to amuse her and keep her on his line, as many suppose with [738], cannot well be discovered for certain; but it is certain that she is so far very [592] disposed towards the Emperor, and that for the [?furtherance] of this favourite project of hers she counts and relies much on His Majesty. And as proof that she has by no means [?abandoned] the project: besides having for a considerable time placed the young Grand Duke Constantine in the hands of [a] Greek woman … and having him [?taught] the Greek language, further a Greek [?education] [553], she has also lately sent orders to [644^_] Rumanzow to procure twelve Greek boys …”) This passage needed corrections to the key and to the transcription of the despatch, checked on the scans on 30 September; they were applied to the decoder on 23 October 2026. In the codebook the word stands to the left of its code, so 54 with two strokes is alhoewel , 314 with two strokes behalven and 941 underlined observeeren ; the words to their right belong to the next column. 47 underlined is k , not l , which also gives Denemarken wherever the machine text has Denemarlen . The mark that DECODE’s transcription puts before 380 and 303 is a dash after the group before them, so they stand for van and die . The group after jong is 191, ens , written above the line with a caret. The group given as [dan] is 601 with a bar, komen ; elsewhere the writer spells dan as 601 and 368 with two strokes, so the bar is probably a slip. In the codebook 644 underlined begins Veld Ma… , the rest lost in the shadow of the binding, and 339 underlined is faint; the officer is probably Field Marshal P. A. Rumyantsev, which has not been checked. The first line of the next page is cut off in the photograph, so the end of the Greek sentence is lost. Three more groups were decoded from their place in the codebook on 30 September 2026. 738 stands between 736 graaf and 739 Gu… ; its word begins gro… , and met grond veronderstellen , “to suppose with reason”, is the idiom (M). 299 stands between 298 fau… and 300 femme , with a faint F…ri… ; favoriet gives “this favourite project of hers”, the usual name for Catherine’s Greek project (I; Februari , also possible from the scan, gives no sense). 231 with a circle stands between 230 verdedig… and 232 vereenigen , with verd… legible; verder , “further”, fits the list of things done for the Grand Duke (I). Still open: 77 with a circle, which the codebook spells Stans or Stanz (between 75 Staat and 78 Ster… ) and which does not yet give a word before diep stilzwijgen , and the line lost at the top of image 5417. The full token-by-token decoding is targets/deswart1782/R1036_machine_decipherment.txt , with every group beside its value in R1036_tokens.tsv . The reading of the whole despatch, with its English translation, is R1036_reading.md and R1036_en.md ; DECODE’s constant misreadings in its transcription of the key ( hot = hof , chi = che ) are listed in R1038_key_misreadings.tsv .

The key as transcribed decodes 1,448 groups. The rest were filled only where a value fits every occurrence of the group in the letter. Examples: 881 = nje , completing Spa·nje each time; 340 underlined = mar in Dene·mar·ken ; 311 underlined = land in Enge·land . 176 with a caret = mpli , found twice in pure et si·mpli·citer . 741 = haar , used twelve times for the Empress: met haar oprecht handelt , om haar te amuseeren , haare mediatie . 39 = hun , as in hun acte and hun onderdaan . 681 underlined = mogendheden ( de oorlogende mogendheden van Frankrijk, Spanje en Engeland ); 363 with a circle = tusschen in tusschen·komst ; 3 with a circle = stel in veronder·stel·d and vast te stel·len . Each inferred value is labelled “contextual inference” in R1038_key_parsed.tsv , apart from the entries transcribed from the manuscript key. decode_1765.py regenerates everything.

Karl de Leeuw noted that the letter of 29 November 1787 is coded, “presumably by accident”, with two codebooks, so this page treats it as two parts, one per key. The change comes at group 180 of image 5459, where the 1765 key begins to give dit alles . The segment runs to the end of image 5473 (5,625 groups); image 5474, with its own marks and nonsense under the 1765 key, belongs to the first, missing code (23 October 2026). A context pass on 23 October fixed 28 values, each fitting every occurrence in R1040 and R1036 (34 underlined in , w+78 Weenen , 922 Hertog , 617 courier ), and the segment was divided into Dutch words ( R1040_part2_reading.md , with English); the French quotations in it are deciphered only in part, and the segment builds coherent sentences but reads at 88.8%, under the 95% bar. The text reports signs of an alliance with France, close attention to it from the Prussian and British representatives, news from Berlin, Kaunitz and the Bavarian exchange, and the likely positions of the four powers: Dit alles, [?gepaard] met veele andere omstandigheden, schynen als indicien te zyn welke de hiervoor [?gedetailleerde] [917^^] wegens een effectief, zo niet reeds [?gesloten], ten minsten op het [?tapyt] zynde allientie tusschen de oorlogende hof en Vrankryk zeer [?waarschynlyk] maaken. (“All this, [?coupled] with many other circumstances, seems to be indications which make very [?probable] the [?above-detailed] [917^^] about an effective, if not already [?concluded], at least [?pending] alliance between the warring court and France.”)

The first 2,259 groups (images 5453–5458, the first 179 groups of image 5459, and image 5474) are in a different codebook, probably the one used under Rechteren, the code of Rechteren’s letter of 1785 . It does not survive online, though the Rechteren cipher filed as Nationaal Archief inventory 158 may be it. Three plain/cipher pairs from the same legation (R2032, R2051 and R2052, from 1784 and 1786) were aligned against it. Transfers from them cover only 2–3% of the segment and give no connected prose, so no decoding of it is claimed.

In R1036, 38 groups have no value after the 23 October pass (56 before), and the line cut off at the top of image 5417 is missing. A third pass transcribed the entries that DECODE’s transcription of the key left illegible, straight from the codebook scans. The word stands to the left of its code, and the parallel columns of homophones confirm faint words. It kept the 41 values that fit the letter, such as 781 = geheel (“het Griekse project geheel stil”), 748 with two strokes = commercie (“de vrijheid van de commercie der neutralen”), 488 underlined = Zijne Keizerlijke Majesteit , and 515 with a circle = twaalf , the twelve Greek boys. The groups still open are entries lost in the binding shadow of the scan, blank in the book, or too faint to use. Inflections are sometimes uncertain where the key gives a stem only, as in hot for hof/hoven . The first 2,259 groups of R1040 are not decoded, pending the Rechteren-family codebook, probably Nationaal Archief 1.02.13 inv. 158, which is not scanned online. R1040 second part: about 240 groups without a value, and the French quotations (about 8% of the segment) deciphered only in part; their cells in R1038 are lost in the binding shadow or too faint.

Edward Elgar’s 87-sign note to Dora Penny of 14 July 1897, known only from the plate in her 1937 memoir. Fifty calibrated rounds, each scored against shuffled copies and real text put through the same system: the 27 opposite-orientation flips force one fixed table if it is a message, and under one fixed table no language, plaintext form, misread allowance or homophone set gives a reading. The statistics fit a writer with strong pair habits as well as English; a second text or a better image is needed.
