Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 28 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The document A slip of 87 signs in three lines, dated 14 July 1897, sent by Edward Elgar to Dora Penny inside a letter from Alice Elgar to Dora’s stepmother after the Elgars’ visit to Wolverhampton. Where The original is lost. The source is the plate on p. 98 of Dora Powell’s Edward Elgar: Memories of a Variation (1937); the 1949 edition differs by a second dot. The cipher Each sign is one, two or three arcs facing one of eight directions: 24 possible signs, 20 of them used. Elgar’s notebook key of the 1920s is one ordered layout of these 24 signs. How it was tried Fifty rounds, every hypothesis scored on Dorabella, on shuffled copies of its signs, and on real English put through the same system; a reading has to reach the level the real text reaches. What it shows The signs flip to the opposite direction 27 times, against 12.6 by chance. Any key that changes as it goes would wash that out, so a message would use one fixed table; under one fixed table nothing reads. Still open Whether it is a message at all, or a sequence with strong writing habits; this cannot be decided from 87 signs. A second text in the same system or a cleaner plate would. Credit Transcription: Hauer, Choi, Hindle, Smallwood and Kondrak (2025). Independent tests: Cooper Jager (2026). Prior analysis: Wase (2023), Nick Pelling, Klaus Schmeh.

The cipher as printed in the first edition of Dora Penny’s memoir, the only source since the original was lost. Image: Dora M. Powell, Edward Elgar: Memories of a Variation (Oxford University Press, 1937), p. 98, via the Internet Archive (Digital Library of India, in.ernet.dli.2015.155431). Dora Penny printed the note as an appendix to her memoir of Elgar, saying it was “the third letter I had from him, if indeed it is one” and that it had come enclosed in a letter from Alice Elgar after the Elgars’ visit to Wolverhampton in July 1897. On the back was written “Miss Penny”. She never had an explanation of it. The mark under the third line is a date, 14 July ’97, not a signature. The transcription used throughout is the five-reader consensus of Hauer et al. (2025): each sign is written as its orientation, A to H going clockwise from “opens to the right”, and its number of arcs, 1 to 3. The three lines have 29, 31 and 27 signs. Twenty of the 24 possible signs occur; the commonest, F2, eleven times. Readers disagree on 11 positions; a measurement of the 1937 scan here reclassifies 17 signs, and Cooper Jager’s 2026 reading differs at five. All of these readings were tested.

Three facts hold whatever key is assumed. The order is not random. The note repeats 19 pairs of adjacent signs; shuffled copies of the same signs repeat 11.2 on average (P = 0.004). It behaves like English letters on every statistic no key can change. Number of distinct signs, index of coincidence (0.059), repeated pairs, doubled signs and singletons together are typical of 87 letters of English (P 0.84) and of Elgar’s own letters (P 0.89), and atypical of speech sounds (0.002), music (0.03) and Latin (0.04). Consecutive signs face opposite ways far too often. A 180° turn between neighbours occurs 27 times against 12.6 expected; none of 5,000 shuffles reached 27. English under a random key gives 11; under the best layout of letters on the dial, about 25. One caution, first made by Jager: shuffles that keep every adjacent pair of the note match it on all of these, and on repeats two to four signs apart. A writer who chooses each sign from the one before, with strong habits, fits the statistics as well as English does. At 87 signs the two cannot be told apart.

Every hypothesis was scored three ways: on the note; on copies with its signs shuffled, or shuffled keeping every adjacent pair; and on real text, usually windows of Elgar’s own letters to the Pennys, put through exactly the system being tested. A result counts as a reading only if the note reaches the range of the real text and its decode splits into real words of the language; scoring above the shuffles alone only reflects the note’s known structure. The solver’s power was measured, not assumed. With the fast settings used in the first rounds, 87 letters of Elgar’s letters were recovered only 42% of the time; the failures were search failures, and with sixty restarts eleven of twelve windows were recovered (93–100%). From round 31 on, the main branches were run again at that strength or more, up to 920 independent long runs on 23 processor cores.

The flips are a property of how letters sit on the dial, so they survive only if the dial stays the same. When English is enciphered with a fixed table that puts common neighbours on opposite sides, the flips come out at 24.5 on average and reach 27 a third of the time; when any changing key is added (a periodic dial turn, Vigenère, autokey, a running key, Nihilist), they drop to 8–12 and reach 27 in at most one sample in a thousand. If the note is a message, Elgar wrote it with one fixed table throughout. English under such a flip-heavy table reproduces all six measured statistics at once (P 0.71), which neither a simple pseudo-writer (0.008) nor English under a random key (0.013) does. That is what makes the failure informative. With the transcription as it stands, English under one fixed table would be found about nine times in ten; the long search instead returns a flat field of different gibberish texts, none recurring, all below the worst real Elgar window.

Under the consensus transcription, the note is not English, Elgar’s own register, any of eleven other languages or any of the plaintext forms tried, written with one fixed table, with up to six misreads or with homophones. Two explanations remain, and 87 signs cannot separate them: A message the tests cannot reach : more misreads than the plate allows to be modelled (ten or more), a key changing partway through, or a plaintext form not tried. No message : a deliberate sequence written with strong habits (the flips, the repeated pairs), which fits every statistic measured. Undecidable at this length: a writer’s pair habits against language, a key changing partway, ten or more misreads, sign pairs or word signs standing for letters.

A second text in the same system. Elgar’s Courage cards (the first carries about ten such signs) and the “Microcryptogram” sold at Sotheby’s (lot 92). Any surviving key could then be checked on two documents. The rest of the Schooling cards. Elgar documented his 1896 solution on a series of index cards at the Elgar Birthplace Museum; cards 1–4 are printed in Bauer’s Unsolved! and the “Cryptogram” card is an alphabet exercise. Photographs of the whole series would show whether any other card carries text in the signs. Better images. The 1947 printing is scanned in greyscale on the Internet Archive (lending only); the 1946 and 1949 printings of the memoir (the 1949 one has a second dot at line 2, sign 11 or 12) and the Elgar Birthplace Museum’s photograph, to settle the 23 doubtful signs. How people fake ciphers. Recordings of people inventing cipher-like squiggles would test the no-message explanation directly.

One closed gap is a contribution: a value for a code group with every place it occurs, a passage re-read at the image, a key or a clear copy found in another volume or in print, a photograph from the archive. A reading becomes complete when at least 95% of its cipher tokens give sense, measured from a reading file, no gap is left untried, every letter is covered, and what stays open is scattered code groups or pieces blocked from outside (README, Conventions). An Italian letter to the duc de Nevers with long runs of unseparated two-digit figures, catalogued on DECODE under the wrong sender. The key in Nevers’s papers (BnF fr. 3995 f. 64), which Tomokiyo lists as Mantua’s cipher of 1590, was applied unchanged; 95.1% of the tokens decrypt. Mantua reports the rumour that Sixtus V was poisoned by the Spaniards and assures Henri IV of his devotion; no earlier decipherment was found. 4037224023132338173125962831 → sia stata procurata con veleno da Spagnoli · 40 s · 37 i · 22 a · 96 Spagnoli Mantua → the duc de Nevers · homophonic cipher of two-digit figures with a nomenclator · 17 September 1590 Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, to the duc de Nevers from Vincenzo I Gonzaga → to Duke of Nevers Go to the full text ↓ BnF, Français 3979, ff. 92r–93r, DECODE R4176: an Italian letter of three pages, with about 930 cipher tokens written as unbroken runs of digits. DECODE has no decipherment and names the sender “duke of Nevers”. He is in fact Vincenzo I Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, writing to his uncle. The key survives in Nevers’s own papers; applied unchanged, it decrypts about 95% of the cipher tokens. No earlier decipherment was found. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 8 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter The Duke of Mantua to his uncle Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers, 17 September 1590 (catalogue item 188); the politics is in figures. Where BnF fr. 3979 f. 92r–93r; DECODE R4176. The cipher Two-digit figures written without breaks: 11–40 are letters with homophones, 41–99 words and names, plus signs for titles and common words. How it was read The key is BnF fr. 3995 f. 64, Per Cavare 1590 (no. 35 in Tomokiyo’s list), applied unchanged. An Italian language model chose between look-alike figures (3/9, 0/8, 7/8) when dividing the digits into pairs. What it says Many believe Sixtus V was poisoned by the Spaniards; Italian powers want nothing more than Henri IV’s conversion; Mantua assures Nevers of his devotion to the French crown. Still open Four short garbled stretches (writer’s slips and one looped code group), the same on both images. No earlier decipherment was found. BnF fr. 3979 f. 92r (DECODE R4176 image P2): the clear text runs to che la morte del Papa , then the figures 40 37 22 40 23 13 23 38 17 31 25 96 28 31 … = sia stata procurata con veleno da Spagnoli . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3979 f. 92r, via DECODE R4176 (image P2).

The letter is dated 17 de Sett.re 1590 and addressed Ill.mo et Ecc.mo Sig.r mio Zio Oss.mo . It answers four letters of Nevers (12, 27 and 20 July, 6 August) and runs from f. 92r to f. 93r. The clear passages deal with family and business: Giulio Capilupi chosen as the new agent in place of Malegnano, the citadel of Casale, the outlaw Piccolomini, the imprisonment of Nevers’s daughter by the League, and a lawsuit at Milan with the Duchess Dorothea of Brunswick. The politics is in figures. Near the end the writer comments on the ciphers themselves. The cipher Nevers sent is molto artificiosa but hard to use without errors, so Nevers should use “the last one I sent you, which is used in this letter too”. That last cipher is in Nevers’s key collection: BnF fr. 3995 f. 64, Per Cavare 1590 (Gallica btv1b525085665, view 131), no. 35 in Tomokiyo’s list. Its values are: Letters, with homophones: 11 m, 12 f, 13 a, 14 h, 15 e, 16 n, 17 p, 18 g, 19 b, 20 z, 21 d, 22 a, 23 t, 24 u, 25 o, 28 u, 30 l, 31 r, 32 i, 33 c, 34 t, 35 o, 36 e, 37 i, 38 a, 39 o, 40 s. An overbar on a letter figure doubles it. Words and names, 41–99: 42 Mons. di, 43 Gran Duca di, 45 Papa, 47 Re di, 55 Cardinale di, 58 Duca di, 60 Legato, 80 Francesi, 81 Spagna, 84 Francia, 96 Spagnoli, 97 Roma; 26 Inglesi, 27 Venetia and 29 Consiglio sit among the letters. Signs: ● che, a barred θ per, ⊔ et, ⊕ S. M.tà, ⊡ S. Ecc.za, a flagged Γ S. A., T mille, + conto, and others.

Deciphered passages in bold, clear text plain; [..] is a stretch not decrypted, [?] a doubtful word. The writer’s spelling is kept. f. 92r: the death of Sixtus V … non lasciando di dirle, che è opinione di molti, che la morte del Papa sia stata procurata con veleno da Spagnoli , non lo potendo far risolvere a favor loro contro cotesto Regno di Francia, la conservatione del quale è desiderata da tutti i buoni Italiani, conoscendosi P. che, anichilata cotesta potenza, li medesimi Spagnoli procureranno di sottoporsi a ognuno [..] S. Ecc.za, da che mi spiace per i molti buoni effetti che mi prometto che ne debbano seguire , et veram.te da tutti i Potentati Italiani non è cosa più desiderata della conversione del Rè al Catolicismo, il che seguendo, si vede chiaramente aperta alla via della grandezza [..] a questo Regno di Francia. “Many believe that the Pope’s death was procured with poison by the Spaniards, since they could not bring him to decide in their favour against this Kingdom of France, whose preservation all good Italians desire, knowing that once that power is destroyed the Spaniards will try to subject everyone …; nothing is more desired by all the Italian powers than the King’s conversion to Catholicism, if that follows, one sees the way clearly open to the greatness … of this Kingdom of France.” f. 92v: the King’s conscience … cose tutte [..] che per interesse di stato la devono far risolvere a correre la fortuna di [..] come fanno Venetia et sì tutti gli altri principi et nobiltà francese [..] dubitando stante la [..] la sua conscienza, che in così universal concorso se le possa opporre mancamento alcuno per conto della religione. Mi è piacciuto infinitam.te intender che quello che il Legato hà scritto in Italia nel partir di Monsignor [..] sia stato menzognero … Nevers, a Catholic who had joined Henri IV (this background is not from the sources and was not checked here), should “for reasons of state resolve to share the fortune of [..] (the sign is unread; [the King?] is only a guess from the context), as Venice and all the other princes and the French nobility do …, [no longer] fearing that in so universal a concurrence any fault could be laid against his conscience on account of religion.” What the Legate wrote to Italy has proved a lie. (The identification of the Legate as Caetani is not from the sources and was not checked here.) f. 93r: a message for the King BnF fr. 3979 f. 93r (DECODE R4176 image P10): 6 d’Agosto presupongo che questa mia la troverà , then eleven cipher lines addressed through Nevers to Henri IV. The signs are ⊕ S. M.tà, the barred θ per, ⊔ et and ● che. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3979 f. 93r, via DECODE R4176 (image P10). … presupongo che questa mia la troverà presso S. M.tà, alla quale la priego far riverenza per me, con certificarla della ottima mia volontà verso il suo Re, al servitio di che, sì come non hò mancato in quello che hò potuto sin hora di darne c[..] parte, e si stia sicura la S. M.tà per[?] oltre la mia particolar inclinatione, et verso cotesta corona, et parimente la con S. M.tà gli interessi contro il [..] comune nemico, me le renderà sempre devotissimo servitore, come a tempo et luogo conveniente conoscerà chiaramente da gli effetti. Nevers is to assure the King of Mantua’s goodwill. Mantua’s own inclination, and shared interests against the “common enemy” (Spain), will make him the King’s most devoted servant, as the King will see from the effects at the right time and place. For an Italian prince bordering Spanish Milan, this was a guarded pro-Bourbon declaration, sent under cipher in the month after Sixtus V’s death.

Prior work. DECODE (no decryption on the record, cipher type unknown) and Tomokiyo’s nevers.htm . Tomokiyo lists the key, not this letter. No earlier decipherment was found. Key. Tomokiyo’s description of no. 35 pointed to fr. 3995 f. 64, which was transcribed from the Gallica image. Transcription. The digit runs were transcribed from the DECODE high-resolution strips: f. 92r in the main session, ff. 92v and 93r by two sub-agents. Unseparated figures lose their pairing whenever a digit is misread. Decoding. A decoder ( beam.py ) divides the digits into pairs and scores the candidate texts with the project’s it-cinquecento language model. It tries the alternatives 3/9, 0/8, 7/8 and 27/28 where the hand makes them look alike. The values of the graphic signs were then taken from the key sheet. Retry. The doubtful lines were transcribed again at triple scale and decoded again. This recovered most of ff. 92v and 93r. Blind re-transcription. Every open stretch was then transcribed again at four times scale by a sub-agent that had not seen the earlier digits, and the two versions compared. This gave contro cotesto Regno di Francia , tutti i buoni Italiani , anichilata cotesta potenza , si vede chiaramente , far riverenza per me and in quello , and confirmed sottoporsi as written: 56 more tokens. Second image. The BnF microfilm of fr. 3979 on Gallica (btv1b9060544v, views 160–162) was used to check every open stretch. On f. 93r the q-like sign is the key’s ♀ non and the next ● che , and the microfilm gives 14 35 31 38 hora : sì come non hò mancato in quello che hò potuto sin hora , 15 more tokens.

45 of 923 tokens are open (measured from the transcriptions; reading.md ). Each stretch was transcribed again independently at four times scale twice, and again on the Gallica microfilm, without a fit: f. 92r, line 5: about 10 tokens ( la nda a a di ) before S. Ecc.za . f. 92r, line 8: about 27 tokens in the middle, including 26 Inglesi. Probably the writer’s own slips; a search allowing any one digit to be changed finds no Italian. f. 92v: about 6 tokens after dubitando stante la ( la mondezza a me as written). The three signs there are nulls on the key. f. 93r, line 8: a looped, dotted code group before comune nemico , perhaps [Re di] Spagna. No other letter in this cipher is on DECODE, and there is no clear copy. The key is complete. The digits there are the same on the DECODE scans and the microfilm, so these are the writer’s own enciphering slips; only a second copy of the letter would settle them.

Ecc.a, l'una del 12, l'altra del 27, la terza del 20 di Luglio, et l'ultima del 6 Agosto, alle quali andarò rispondendo per ordine, pregandola ad iscusarmi se hò tardato à farlo, perche la morte di N. S.re successa alli 27 del passato à 23 hore, n'è stata cagione, parendomi ispediente che l'E. V. sia de primi avisati del successore che piacerà à Dio darci, non lasciando di dirle, che è opinione di molti, che la morte del Papa **sia stata procurata con veleno da Spagnoli**, non lo potendo **far risolvere a favor loro contro cotesto Regno di Francia, la conservatione** del quale **e desiderata da tutti i buoni Italiani,** conoscendosi P.— **che, anichilata cotesta potenza, {M} li medesimi Spagnoli procureranno di sottoporsi a ognuno [..] S. Ecc.za da che mi spiace** per i molti buoni **effetti che mi prometto che ne debbano seguire**, et veram.te da tutti i Potentati Italiani non è cosa più desiderata della conversione del Rè al Catolicismo, **il che seguendo, si vede chiaramente aperta alla via della grandeza a di che [..] a questo Regno di Francia.** S'io non hò mandato sin hora altro huomo in iscambio del Malegnano, è proceduto dalla carestia de soggetti fedeli, sufficienti, et sbrigati, tuttavia hò finalm.te fatto elettione di Giulio Capilupi, il quale frà poco si porrà in camino per costà. Ringratio V. E. degli amorevoli avertimenti che l'è piacciuto darmi intorno alla fabrica della Cittadella di Casale, et ne farò quel capitale nell'essecutione che meritano la prudenza, intelligenza, et amorevolezza di lei. Farò pigliar informatione di quel Vincenzo Badalocchio proposto all'E. V. per sec.rio in Roma, et della relatione che ne haurò, ella ne sarà fedelm.te avisata. Fù vera la retentione in casa del ## f. 92v Patriarca Alessandrino, et la carceratione di due P.ri Giesuiti per haver questi à suggestione di quello nelle prediche moteggiato contro le attioni di S. S.tà in questi motivi di Francia, mà furono liberati poco dopo. Il Piccolomini è dichiarato ribelle del Gran Duca per molti suoi misfatti, mà non già perche l'havesse trattato in Siena, mà egli hà la testa che vale per le taglie poste da S. A. et da altri Potentati molte decene di migliaia di scudi, et è così perseguitato dal Gran Duca in tutti i modi che hà carestia di terreno, et è di già abbandonato da suoi seguaci, sì che non può tardare à dar nella rete, et tanto basti per risposta della sua del 27. Stata aperta à Lione da deputati della Città. Ringratio V. E. degli avisi quali le è piacciuto darmi, et mi spiace sommam.te il danno ch'ella patisce nel suo Palaggio di Parigi, mà molto più la prigionia della S.ra sua figlia, et mia cugina, et l'occupatione de suoi beni fattale da quelli della lega, cose tutte [{0Δ}] **che per interesse di stato la devono far risolvere a correre la fortuna di [{4-sign}] come fanno Venetia et sì tutti gli altri principi et nobiltà francese [{9}] dubitando stante la [..] la sua conscienza, che in così universal concorso se le possa opporre mancamento alcuno per conto della religione.** Mi è piacciuto infinitam.te intender che quello **che il Legato** hà scritto in Italia nel partir **di Monsignor** [..] sia stato menzognero, et prometto a V. E. che ne godo altretanto di presente, quanto grande fù il travaglio che m'apportò l'aviso in contrario che hebbi di buonissimo luogo. Stante quello che V. E. mi scrive colla sua del ## f. 93r 6 d'Agosto, presupongo che questa mia la troverà **presso S. M.tà, alla quale la priego far riverenza per me, con certificarla della ottima mia volontà verso il suo Re, al servitio di che, sì come **non hò mancato** in quello che hò potuto **sin hora** di darne c[..] parte, e si stia sicura la S. M.tà per[?] oltre la mia particolar inclinatione, et verso cotesta corona, et parimente la con S. M.tà gli interessi contro il [..] comune nemico, me le renderà sempre devotissimo servitore, come a tempo et luogo conveniente conoscerà chiaramente da gli effetti.** Hò una lite in Milano di molta importanza con la Duchessa Dorotea di Bransvich per servitù della quale mi bisognarebbe giustificare ch'ella goda in Francia la Contea di Clermont che era del marito, di che suppl.co V. E. a far pigliare quanto prima diligente informatione, et trovandosi che così sia, farne cavar fede autentica, et mandarmela subito, poiche giustificato questo punto la vittoria restarebbe sicura dal canto mio. Se bene la Zifra mandata da V. E. è molto artificiosa, nondimeno porta seco qualche difficoltà, massime quando si fà qualche errore nel zifrato, però le piacerà servirsi dell'ultima che le mandai, la quale s'è adoperata anco nella presente. A Firenze hò fatto inviare le lettere mandatemi dall'E. The close and signature were not read. ## f. 92r *17 September 1590.* Most Illustrious and Most Excellent Lord, my most honoured Uncle, I find myself owing an answer to four letters of Your Excellency, one of the 12th, another of the 27th, the third of the 20th of July, and the last of the 6th of August, which I shall answer in order, begging you to excuse me if I have been late in doing so; for the death of Our Lord [the Pope], which occurred on the 27th of last month at the 23rd hour, has been the cause of it, since it seemed expedient to me that Your Excellency should be among the first informed of the successor whom it will please God to give us. I do not omit to tell you that it is the opinion of many that the Pope's death **was procured with poison by the Spaniards**, since they could not **make him resolve in their favour against that Kingdom of France, the preservation** of which **is desired by all good Italians**, it being recognised P.— **that, once that power is annihilated, {M} the same Spaniards will try to subject everyone [..] His Excellency, at which I am sorry** for the many good **effects which I promise myself must follow from it**; and truly nothing is more desired by all the Italian Potentates than the King's conversion to Catholicism, **which following, one sees clearly open the way to greatness, at which [..] to this Kingdom of France.** If I have not up to now sent another man in exchange for Malegnano, it has come from the shortage of subjects who are faithful, sufficient and free; however, I have at last made choice of Giulio Capilupi, who will shortly set out for your parts. I thank Your Excellency for the kind warnings you have been pleased to give me about the building of the Citadel of Casale, and I shall make that use of them in the execution which your prudence, understanding and kindness deserve. I shall have information taken about that Vincenzo Badalocchio proposed to Your Excellency as secretary in Rome, and you will be faithfully advised of the report I shall have of him. The detention in the house of the ## f. 92v Patriarch of Alexandria was true, and the imprisonment of two Jesuit Fathers for having, at his suggestion, gibed in their sermons at the actions of His Holiness in these movements of France; but they were freed shortly after. Piccolomini has been declared a rebel by the Grand Duke for many misdeeds of his, but not because he had plotted in Siena; but his head is worth many tens of thousands of scudi for the prices set on it by His Highness and by other Potentates, and he is so pursued by the Grand Duke in every way that he is short of ground, and is already abandoned by his followers, so that he cannot be long in falling into the net; and let this suffice for an answer to yours of the 27th. [It was] opened at Lyon by deputies of the City. I thank Your Excellency for the news you have been pleased to give me, and I am extremely sorry for the damage you suffer in your Palace in Paris, but much more for the imprisonment of the Lady your daughter, and my cousin, and the seizure of your goods made by those of the League, all things [{0Δ}] **which for reasons of state must make you resolve to run the fortune of [{4-sign}], as Venice does, and so all the other princes and the French nobility [{9}], doubting, given the [..] your conscience, that in so universal a concurrence any failing on account of religion could be laid against you.** I was infinitely pleased to learn that what **the Legate** wrote into Italy at the departure **of Monseigneur** [..] was false, and I promise Your Excellency that I rejoice at it now as much as the distress was great which the contrary news I had from a very good quarter brought me. Given what Your Excellency writes me in yours of the ## f. 93r 6th of August, I presume that this letter of mine will find you **with His Majesty, to whom I beg you to make reverence for me, assuring him of my very good will towards his King, in whose service, as I **have not failed** up to **now**, in what I could, to give him c[..] part, and His Majesty may rest assured for[?] besides my particular inclination, both towards that crown and likewise the interests, with His Majesty, against the [..] common enemy, will always render me his most devoted servant, as at the fitting time and place he will clearly recognise from the effects.** I have a lawsuit in Milan of much importance with the Duchess Dorothea of Brunswick, for the service of which I would need to prove that she enjoys in France the County of Clermont, which was her husband's; for which I beg Your Excellency to have diligent information taken as soon as possible, and, if it is found to be so, to have an authentic attestation of it drawn up and send it to me at once, since, this point being proved, the victory would remain secure on my side. Although the Cipher sent by Your Excellency is very ingenious, it nonetheless brings some difficulty with it, especially when some error is made in the enciphering; so you will be pleased to use the last one I sent you, which has also been used in the present letter. I have had the letters sent me by Your Excellency forwarded to Florence; I kiss your hands, praying God for a long and happy course of life for you [..]

There are four despatches, of 5, 15, 19 and 26 December 1674 (DECODE R1012–R1015; the "1674–1677" in DECODE’s summary is a span, and the catalogue names give the dates). All are in the Brussels volume SEG 2559, Fuenmayor’s papers, which also holds the Carpio and Balbases letters of 1677. The cipher is the Balbases syllabic nomenclator: numbers for letters and consonant-vowel syllables (21 a, 28 s, 31 r, 46 de, 58 lo, 66 re, 70 ta), letter pairs with a disguised consonant ( xo co, xi ci, af sa, if si, uf su, ac ma), and word codes: struck d que, bef Francia, dan -mente. 13 is a null in the Balbases key but e in this hand (see Method). The key is set out in full on the Balbases page . That it served Hernán Núñez in Stockholm in 1674 and Balbases at Nijmegen in 1677 suggests that Fuenmayor held one cipher for his correspondents among the northern Spanish envoys.

These are the cipher passages, taken from the margins and checked group by group against the key. Spelling is normalised. 5 December 1674 (R1012) …asegurándole en primer lugar que el reparo que hace del proyecto del tratado deste [reino] con esse reino es muy propio de su gran juicio y prudencia, y que creo ser cierto que estos ministros han convenido con el de Dinamarca en todos los puntos del proyecto que envié a V.S.; pero si la Dinamarca añadiese el de no oponerse a las armas que la Suecia pretenderá ahora, todos los artículos anteriores que contradijesen a esto quedarán anulados… y que las más veces no vienen a ser sino un juego de palabras con que pretextar lo que hacen y lo que no quieren hacer los príncipes. Ya tengo asegurado a V.S. que he representado y representaré siempre lo que importa que la Suecia tenga el freno desse reino. A later passage concerns the Swedish envoy at Copenhagen. Núñez asks Fuenmayor, if he has occasion to speak to him, to let him understand that Núñez has written of his many obligations to the envoy’s father-in-law, the Constable. Fuenmayor should believe him only where other sources confirm it, "siendo hombre lleno de artificios, sin más fundamento a veces que su propia inquietud". 15 December (R1013) Con grandes promesas de la protección de la Suecia, que les ha costado buenos regalos, y deseando el enviado de Brandenburg enviar un gentilhombre suyo en su navío, estos diputados le respondieron no se atrevían por no dar celos a la Suecia… Hamburg, that is. The despatch goes on to hope that, frightened, the Hamburgers "quiten a los suecos mucha parte de la confianza", which would restrain Sweden and "alentará igualmente a los dinamarqueses". 19 December (R1014) …la mira principal que este reino lleva en haber enviado a esse su embajador, según tengo entendido, es el tomar tiempo con esto para satisfacer a las instancias que hace este embajador de Francia, y el de no asistirle por ahora con el socorro que pretende en virtud de su tratado último. The marriage of Charles XI to the Danish king’s sister will be raised. The Anglo-Swedish treaty is only a renewal of the one Coventry concluded. …no hay otro medio de retener a la Suecia, y si esa corona se ajustase a la neutralidad, le faltaría a esta el único pretexto con que se [excusa con] la Francia. 26 December (R1015) …antes de separarse este senado, que será dentro de muy pocos días, se tomará resolución en él sobre el asistir o no a la Francia a mano armada. Ha dos días que he cesado en el remedio de los baños… para salir cuanto antes a hacer las diligencias que me sean posibles para que dicha resolución nos sea favorable, prefiriendo la solicitud del real servicio al riesgo de la vida. Sweden invaded Brandenburg that same month, which began the Scanian War (the passage does not say how the senate decided; this background is not from the letter and was not checked here).

DECODE’s ciphertext transcriptions (by MEG, 2020) were parsed into cipher groups and margin text. DECODE reads the clerk’s "q." as "g.3", so it was normalised to que . The monotone aligner written for Balbases 1677, run image by image, failed: the margin glosses cross page breaks. Run letter by letter, with seven anchors from representado y representaré (66 re, 30 p, ef se, 24 n, 70 ta, 48 do, 22 y), it converged in four rounds. The converged values (58 lo, 28 s, y n, uf su, 21 a, 31 r, struck d que) were recognised as the Balbases key. Applied unchanged, it decrypted all four letters in agreement with their margins. Second pass (22 Sept 2026): the 118 groups the key left without a value were each located on the sixteen DECODE images and compared with the margin beside them. 62 were DECODE misreadings (this hand’s closed 4 transcribed as 9, so “96” is 46 de and “189” is 184 sobre ; g for y ; groups split or run together), 48 were code groups the Balbases table lacks, fixed by the margin ( bof guerra, cuf Inglaterra, 187 tiempo, 149 quanto, 111 comercio, C+ ll ), 7 were nulls and 1 is illegible. Two key corrections apply throughout: 13 is e in this hand (13 8 el , 13 ef esse ), and the underlined N is V.S. DECODE also omits two whole lines of R1012 (“…mas veces no vienen a ser sino un juego de pa-”).

Of 1,716 groups, one has no value (R1014, illegible). Eleven values from the second pass are graded M (uncertain): among them the triangle sign on R1012 ( a , or a null), the nulls 500 and E, and R1015’s 21‡. The first pass had left 118 without a value (R1012 62, R1013 20, R1014 29, R1015 7). Values added here: 167 Suecia (H: every context), 161 resolución (H), os para (C), 6+ o (C), 4 t (C). 30 = p is DECODE’s transcription of the Balbases 26 (C). Drunk envoys, royal gossip, catalogue clerks with the best of intentions, and one minister who could not quite work his own code. 01 1533 Hungary → the Dukes of Bavaria key from adjacent plaintext “To be spoken with in the morning, when he is sober” DECODE filed this letter under “Augurellio”, the name on its address leaf. At the foot of two leaves it is signed, in cipher, Iorg Weinmaister : Jörg Weinmeister, a Bavarian agent in Hungary. The key was rebuilt from contemporary glosses on sibling letters in the same volume and on this one. Most of the letter is grim news, including the siege of the castle of Palota and a report of fifty thousand Turks marching from Belgrade on Buda. Then the talks on relieving Palota run into a practical problem. The magnate Török Bálint was sent to discuss the relief one evening in Vienna while well drunk, and will have to be approached again the next morning. the reading, in English …one evening at Vienna well drunk, was sent to talk of the relief, and is to be spoken with in the morning when he is sober. Weinmeister 1533, 96.7% deciphered Iorg Weinmaister · signed in cipher · 02 1580 Rome → the nuncio in Paris existing decipherment The Pope, the King of France, and the nun This is a cipher enclosure from the papal Secretariat of State to the nuncio Dandini, with the clerk’s decipherment written under the figures. George Lasry decrypted its companion letter in 2020 with his reconstructed key. This one uses the same nomenclator with different letter values, which were rebuilt here with a solver (simulated annealing) and checked against the clerk’s text. The two agree word for word, except that the cipher has commercio where the clerk wrote concetto . What Rome wanted kept secret was the gossip about Henri III and a nun. Whether or not it was true, the scandal was so great that the King “should stop going to that monastery altogether”, and the nuncio is to press this on him hard. The companion letter adds that he is not to raise the matter of the nun with the Queen. Italian La voce et l’opinione della pratica del Re Chr.mo con la monaca è uscita tanto publica che se ne ragiona hormai per tutto The talk of the Most Christian King’s affair with the nun has become so public that it is discussed everywhere. Como to Dandini 1580 Francia 283C f. 52: the figures, and the clerk’s decipherment beneath. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Francia 283C f. 52, via DECODE R72. 03 17th c. Sloane MS 3188 not a cipher Twenty-five “secret letters” that are notes on John Dee’s conversations with angels DECODE lists Sloane MS 3188 ff. 109–169 as twenty-five ciphertexts with no decipherment, sender and recipient unknown. They are bound straight after Dee’s own diaries of his spirit “actions”. They are a later reader’s notes on those diaries, in seventeenth-century English stroke shorthand with the names written out in longhand. The leaves hold an index of the Actions, a list of Dee’s writings, and a note on Kelley and Prague dated 1595. There is no cipher, no letter and no correspondent in them. longhand inside the shorthand 1582 … E.T. … Uriel … Reuchlin · Reconciliatio Kelliana Shippen’s notes on Dee f. 109r: shorthand strokes, with names written out in longhand. Image: British Library, Sloane MS 3188 f. 109r, via DECODE R8506. 04 1702–23 Blenheim Papers, Add MS 61575 not a cipher A “numerical cipher” with no numbers, thanking someone for cipher lessons DECODE catalogues folio 95 as a numerical cipher with no decipherment, by “Frederic, Re di Prussia”. There are no numbers on the page. It is seven lines of plain French, spelled by ear and chopped into syllables, and the writer is thanking someone for showing him how to write in cipher. Judging by the spelling, the lessons went better than the dictation. French, as spelled moy en me mon trant d’es cria re …for the trouble you took with me in showing me how to write in cipher A lesson in cipher en me mon trant d’es cria re · no digits at all · 05 after 1688 The Wallachian court → a “Most Reverend Father” existing decipherment A cipher used for nothing but insults The Szembek papers at Kórnik hold an “encrypted letter” catalogued as an 18th-century letter to the Szembek family. It is the postscript of a letter from the Wallachian court, written after the death of Prince Şerban Cantacuzino in October 1688. The Latin is in clear, and only single words are put into two-digit numbers. A second hand wrote the plain word above every run, and the key rebuilt from those glosses (22 numbers, no conflicts) reproduces them. The words the writer chose to hide are mostly names and insults. The imperial Jesuit envoy Antide Dunod, he says, led the late prince astray, and he gets five enciphered words to himself. The postscript also reports that a certain Gegenbey was killed and his head sent as a gift. Latin, cipher runs as glossed impostor et Detractor ille et sine conscientia Burgundus Antidius Dunod that impostor and detractor, the Burgundian without a conscience, Antide Dunod The Szembek postscript The insult, with the glosses above the numbers. Image: PAN Biblioteka Kórnicka, BK 1560, image 066, via the Wielkopolska Digital Library. 06 1758 “Cypher from Mr Eichel”, Prussia nulls only A sheet of cipher figures that is nothing but padding This sheet of figures sits in the Prussian papers at Kew. The key the catalogue proposed does not fit it. The key filed in the same volume does, and it begins by declaring every number that contains a 7, plus four whole ranges, to be a null. On that rule 117 of the 139 groups are nulls, and 21 of the remaining 22 land on cells the key leaves blank. It is a dummy sheet, and there was never a message on it. the key’s first rule Tous les nro où je trouve un ou plusieurs 7 sont les nonvaleurs Every number in which I find one or more 7s is a null. Eichel 1758 The Eichel sheet: 139 groups, 117 of them declared nulls. Image: The National Archives, Kew, via DECODE R595. 07 1524 Rome → Charles V key from adjacent plaintext · partial The oldest long cipher on the list, off by exactly a hundred years DECODE dated two letters from Rome to “April 1424”. That would have made them the longest ciphertext before 1450, and they were picked as a flagship target on that basis. The letter gives its own date on f. 128v: De Roma xviij de Abril 1524 . The catalogue’s “Luis Fernández” is the Duke of Sessa, Charles V’s ambassador. Eight sibling letters carry the court’s own decipherments. The key was rebuilt from them, about 110 code groups and the alphabet, and it deciphers the passage word by word except four code groups and one clause. Spanish De Roma xviij de Abril 1524 From Rome, 18 April 1524, and not 1424. Sessa 1524 1424 ↓ 1524 08 1710 Torcy → the plenipotentiaries at Geertruidenberg not solved “Mr Blencowe cannot decypher them”, and neither can we In the spring of 1710 Louis XIV sent two plenipotentiaries to Geertruidenberg to talk peace with the Dutch. Two of the French letters were intercepted and passed to the English, and they are now in the Blenheim Papers. On the back of Torcy’s letter of 3 April, another hand wrote the verdict of William Blencowe, England’s official decipherer. Three centuries later it still stands. For ninety years nobody found a message in them. Their letter counts are the problem: against a flat distribution they give a chi-squared of 1.25, where honest random sampling gives about 25. No cipher can produce that. Substitution and transposition keep the skew of the plaintext, and a one-time pad lands near 25. No plaintext of the slip exists, and no decipherment was found. The alphabet was recovered from the ciphertext alone, starting from probable words such as convulsio and plena luna , and 96.5% of the words are deciphered. The weekdays checked (3 April, 23 April, 23 May) match the calendar. Of the moon phases checked, four match (23 April, 19 July, 2 August, 18 August) and two do not (25 May and 12 June, taken to be D’Ewes’s own slips or loose wording). Clopton died on 9 May 1636. Each of these keys was recovered from the ciphertext alone, without an earlier decipherment of the text; how much then reads varies (Malsburg and Kauderbach are partial, Harley 1582 is decoded, not read), and the Kauderbach break drew on the vocabulary of the same writer’s later key. They were chosen for difficulty, not for the story; how they were picked is below . Two more breaks of this kind are already among the thirty: Soglia 1848 and D’Ewes 1635 . 01 1637 Wesel → Landgrave Wilhelm V of Hesse-Kassel ciphertext-only break · partial Ten letters from a war in Westphalia, with no key among 176 key sheets Otto von der Malsburg, Hesse-Kassel’s general war commissary, reported to his landgrave in 1637, the year the landgrave died in exile. The archive’s portal lists all ten letters as not solved. None of the 176 Hesse-Kassel key sheets fits them. The cipher is German in two-digit groups, with two to seven groups for each letter, capital signs for pairs such as ch , st and sch , and no word division. Annealing one page alone failed. Three letters pooled, 1,575 groups, gave the same key from every start. About 9,700 groups were transcribed from 18 scans, and 236 doubtful ones were checked again on the images. The letters cover garrisons without pay, the siege of Ehrenbreitstein and the refusal of safe-conducts to the Cologne peace talks. No reading was found anywhere before this one. Four of the ten letters build coherent sentences (89–93% of their words, measured); the others are decoded, not read, and the write-up counts 53% of the cipher as read. German das ich auch noch nit weiss, wo hervor unsere garnisonen hiernechst der unterhalt genommen werden soll that I still do not know where the upkeep of our garrisons is to come from now on Malsburg 1637, partial (53% of the cipher) f. 3, 5/15 January 1637: after the clear “gemachet” the groups read “das ich auch noch nit weiss”. Everything else is a cursive pseudo-script, 1,715 words with no gloss, no key and no edition. The first solver, one sign to one letter, produced gibberish. The way in was a statistic: one sign was followed by the same second sign in 262 of 283 cases, so the pair had to be a single unit. Fitting the commonest word to que broke it open. A re-check against the images then found that about 300 signs first read as one letter were a smaller look-alike for another. The mémoire describes the Protestant rising in Guyenne in the first days of Catherine de’ Medici’s regency. George Lasry wrote that he had broken it independently in 2023; his solution has not been published. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3157 f. 152r, via Gallica btv1b90598645 view 153. 03 1585–86 Henry of Navarre → Ségur ciphertext-only break Henry of Navarre raises a German army, in a table found by counting in fives Three letters in figures to Ségur, the envoy raising a German army, were listed as letters of Henry III. That is the trace of an alphabetical syllable table, ba be bi bo bu, ca ce ci co cu . A solver built on that structure, with the letters’ clear French as context, converged on a key whose letter part came out in alphabetical order by itself. It scored 97% on a matched control. The letters are signed Henry at Montauban and are Henry of Navarre’s. Lasry wrote that he broke them independently in 2024; his solution is unpublished. The cabinet gave up on the figures because the groups “are not separated, by blanks or dots as is usually the case.” The first problem was where one group ends and the next begins. The digits 5 and 8 never occur inside a group, so they are nulls. Without them the stream falls into about sixty two-figure codes. A homophonic solver found nothing. The way in was Kauderbach’s own key of 1761, kept in Dresden. Its numbers are different, yet its list of letters and syllables fits, and an assignment search onto that list converged twice to the same key. In each of the ten letters, 65 to 97% of the cipher decrypts to sense, including the news of the Treaty of Versailles of May 1756. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Archief Prins Willem V inv. 201, via DECODE R2078. 05 1619 Bonn → Munich ciphertext-only break Ten pages of figures with no sender, no recipient and no language, and the letter names itself DECODE knew only the year of this record: no author, no recipient, no place, no language. The cipher is a homophonic substitution on the even numbers 10 to 78, with two word-end signs and a three-digit nomenclator. Its key was recovered by annealing 2,482 letters against a 16th-century German model, with about sixty single-digit transcription slips repaired. The same key reads the sibling letter in the file unchanged. The decipherment then names the writer: Ferdinand of Bavaria, Elector of Cologne, to his brother Duke Maximilian, six weeks after the Winter King’s coronation, on quartering and paying the Catholic League’s troops. Neither letter was found in print. Every earlier pass took one sign for punctuation: the letter m is written as a group of two, three or four dots. Even after that the key would not come. A control experiment, real French enciphered under a key of the same shape, located the fault: the solver, not the manuscript. With one wrong constraint removed and its temperature fixed, the control solved completely, and the real text broke at once. The thirty come from the three hundred or so write-ups on this site and the notes behind them. They were chosen for the story, and difficulty played no part; the full list sorts by outcome, and the hardest breaks are ranked in the repository’s solved ranking . Each badge names how the text was obtained, in the terms of the site’s glossary. Ciphertext-only break (two of the thirty: Soglia 1848 and D’Ewes 1635), key from adjacent plaintext (six) and key from external plaintext (two: Ghinucci 1527 and Erving 1807, matched against a decipherment or an edition printed elsewhere) mean the key was rebuilt here. Known key applied (ten), external key matched (one) and existing decipherment (three) mean that a key or a decipherment already existed, and the work was transcription and decipherment. Partial means some of the text is still open. Quotations keep the original spelling, and the translations follow the write-ups. Four of the thirty are not ciphers at all, or hold no message; one was deciphered in print long ago, and one, the Geertruidenberg letter of 1710, is still unread. The selection was redone on 25 October 2026 from the larger list: six cards gave way to finds made since 2 October. The six hardest breaks were chosen the other way round, by difficulty alone, from the targets whose key was recovered from the ciphertext alone. The tests: the key recovered from the ciphertext alone, with no earlier decipherment of the text and no sibling key (the exception is Kauderbach, whose way in was the vocabulary of the same writer’s own key of 1761, although its numbers did not fit); an unknown system; the cipher transcribed from the images here; and a control, a sibling letter or a re-check on the scans behind the key. The extent read was not a test, and it varies: 95% or more for Ségur and Ferdinand of Bavaria, 99% for the Mémoire of 1560, partial for Malsburg (53% of the cipher) and Kauderbach (81%, 65–97% per letter), and decoded, not read for Harley 1582 R8505. Breaks first made by someone else and checked here, such as the Mercy instruction of 1648 (NoAutopilot), are left out, as are four that turned out to be independent re-solutions of a cipher someone had already broken. Two of the six, the Mémoire of 1560 and the Ségur letters, had been solved privately by George Lasry, who never published them; the cards say so. Adams’s coded despatches to Washington are not in Armstrong’s code, as the Madison editors say, but in his own (the = 1385). Its key was recovered to 1,166 numbers from the State Department clerk’s interlinear decodes on NARA M35 reel 3 and Ford’s printed decipherments of other despatches. With it the passages of No. 88 that Ford printed as “not decyphered” decrypt, 380 of 390 groups: Rumyantsev’s strokes at Wilna and Kurakin’s note. 668 · 295 · 818 · 864 — 790 · 1385 · 1434 · 168 · 1440 · 1081 and ex-pect-ation. Where National Archives, RG 59, Despatches from U.S. Ministers to Russia, microfilm M35 reel 3, frames 0206–0207 (the triplicate). Ford’s Writings of John Quincy Adams 4:355–58 prints it with “[Nine lines of this paragraph not decyphered.]” and the remainder “undecyphered”. The cipher A numbered syllabary of about 1,600 numbers (syllables, word-parts, common words), in which the is 1385 and of 1576. It is not the Armstrong code ( the = 972), which the Madison editors name. How it was decrypted The key was recovered to 1,166 numbers: from the clerk’s pencil decodes on fourteen frames of the same reel, and by aligning coded blocks of 1811–1812 with the Department’s decipherments that Ford prints. What it says Chancellor Rumyantsev had opposed the Emperor’s journey to Wilna, had two apoplectic strokes there, and could not stay long in office; France called Kurakin’s note a proposal it “had never thought of making to Russia even after the battle of Friedland”. Still open Seven groups cut by the binding gutter on the film (need the original) and three single groups (1508, 1185, 570). Credit The State Department clerk’s interlinear decodes of 1811–12 and Worthington Chauncey Ford’s printed decipherments (1914) supplied the plaintext the key was rebuilt from. This page was split on 14 October 2026 from a combined page ( legation.html ) that also held George W. Erving’s Madrid letter of 1807, which is in Pinckney’s legation code, a different cipher with its own page: Erving to Madison, 24 March 1807 .

The starting point was a note the Madison editors attach to Armstrong’s letters (Founders Madison/02-10-02-0369 and 02-12-02-0197): the code was “also used by John Quincy Adams at St. Petersburg and by Jacob Lewis at Saint-Domingue; key not found but substantially reconstructed by the editors”. On Adams to Madison, 7 January 1811 (03-03-02-0121), the editors speak of “a code provided by the State Department to John Armstrong in France and to both William Short and Adams”, citing Ford 3:328. If that held, the 580-group Armstrong table already rebuilt on this site ( Armstrong’s postscript ) would decrypt Adams’s coded despatches. It does not. What Ford’s own text says. Secretary Smith’s instructions of 1809 (Ford 3:327–28) say that “the cypher with which you are furnished” is “the same with that of our minister at London” (William Pinkney), and tell Adams to “obtain at Paris, a copy of General Armstrong’s cypher also, for the like purpose”, that is, to correspond with Armstrong. In 1810 Adams acknowledges “the copy of General Armstrong’s cypher” (Ford 3:370). He held both. The despatches to Washington use the other one. What the microfilm shows. Every coded despatch checked on M35 reel 3 (1811 and 1812) uses a code in which 1385 = the , 1576 = of , 1384 = that , 668 = and , 1401 = I . In Armstrong’s code the is 972 and of is 1354 . Run through the Armstrong table (592 entries as it now stands), these pages come out as noise. Reel 2 frame 0155, of 1810, is in the same Adams code. So the table already held cannot decrypt Adams’s despatches. The editors’ note on the 7 January 1811 letter concerns a private letter to Madison, not a despatch, and was not checked against its manuscript, which is in the Forbes collection and not online; it may be right for that letter.

The method is the one used for Armstrong on M34 roll 13, with a second source added. On M35 reel 3 the Department clerk wrote the decode above the groups of several despatches; every pair on frames 0047, 0048 (1811), 0182 (No. 80, 29 February 1812), 0183, 0184, 0185, 0189, 0190, 0194, 0198, 0206 (No. 88), 0210–0211 and 0247 was recorded with frame, page side and line. For most pages there is no interlinear decode, but Ford printed the Department’s decipherments. Coded blocks were transcribed from the film and aligned with Ford’s plaintext, group against syllable, and checked by eye: 39 blocks of 1811, and then eight despatches of October 1811 to September 1812, No. 95 against the Department’s own clear copy on frames 0230–0232. All the pairs, 3,127 from the clerk (with the earlier pair list) and 2,785 from Ford, were merged into one table of 1,166 numbers, each with a grade: Grade Meaning Numbers H the clerk’s interlinear decode over the group 431 C fixed by Ford’s printed decipherment between known neighbours 393 M the split of the syllables or the digit is a judgement 324 I inferred from the alphabetical slot and the sense only 18 The code is a numbered syllabary of about 1,600 numbers: syllables, word-parts and common words, with 1–100 mostly whole words (13 observation , 16 Emperor , 29 United States , 44 negotiation , 78 President ). An earlier version of this page described it as alphabetical blocks of fifty; the larger table does not bear that out. Values climb alphabetically only inside short runs, such as 1384 that , 1385 the , 1387 them , 1388 then , 1391 there , 1392 these , 1393 they , 1394 think , 1399 this , or 1592 on , 1594 one , 1595 ong , 1597 only , and then the run breaks (1304 tain and 1312 form sit among 1305 Bal , 1310 be , 1317 been ). The alphabetical slot therefore brackets a value only where the neighbours on both sides are in order, and inference from it is kept to grade I. A superscript o after a group adds -s ; a mark under a group changes it (a doubled letter, -ed , or another word: 1107 paper , 1107 with the mark well ; 1457 last , with the mark ll ; 1535 al , with the mark all ). A few groups carry two values in the sources (508 rect and ear ; 1570 of and occurr ; 1173 when and would ). In this hand 5 and 6, 7 and 9, and 0, 6 and 8 are easily confused. Re-transcribing No. 88 from zoomed crops corrected seven groups over two passes (168, not 158; 1426, not 1425; 302, not 502; 792, not 492; 1061, not 1081; 588, not 888; 1384, not 1385), showed that two groups of the last line are digits Adams himself overwrote (1383 than and 1097 sho , each with its last digit written over another), and showed that the underlined 1102 at the foot of the left page of frame 0206 is a catchword repeating the first group of the next page, not a group of the text. The table, its sources and the conflicts are in the repository ( targets/jqa/code_table.tsv , targets/jqa/consolidate.py , targets/jqa/code_conflicts.txt , targets/jqa/overrides.tsv , where every hand decision carries its reason).

No. 88 was written at St Petersburg on 25 June 1812, the day after the Grande Armée crossed the Niemen, when that news had not yet reached the capital. Ford prints it at 4:355–58, addressed to James Monroe. After Adams’s account of Prince Kurakin’s passports and the French ambassador’s demand for his, the paragraph ends: “On the other side I have reported to you what Count Romanzoff said to me the day before his departure for Wilna. Certainly negotiation then was his wish and expectation. [Nine lines of this paragraph not decyphered.]” The microfilm has the triplicate (M35 reel 3, frame 0206), and on it the clerk’s pencil stops exactly where Ford’s gap begins. M35 reel 3, frame 0206, foot of the left page. The clerk’s faint pencil runs above the groups down to 668. 295. 818. 864 (“and expectation”); from the dash and 790. 1385. 1434. 168… (“But the …”) there is none. Ford’s “nine lines not decyphered” begin here and run to the top of the right page. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, M35 reel 3, frame 0206, via the National Archives Catalog (NAID 188725601). The block runs from the last four decoded groups to the end of the paragraph: 133 groups, 129 of them in Ford’s gap, with the clear words scarcely (twice), undoubtedly and In the German Gazettes written in the line. The rebuilt table gives every group a value ( python render.py gap88.txt ), and all 133 give sense in the running text ( python measure.py ): 106 on clerk-attested values, 10 on Ford-fixed, 13 on uncertain and 4 on inferred ones; without the inferred values, 129 (0.970). In the decryption below, words in square brackets rest on grade-I values; groups in braces have a value that does not make sense in the sentence. The opening words in brackets are the clerk-decoded close of the sentence that Ford prints. [Certainly negotiation then was his wish] and ex-pect-ation. But the [journ-ey] it-self of the Emperor Alex-an-der to Wil-na was in opposition to the Chan-ce-ll-or and adv-ice, and if his ac-tive in-flu-ence had not been im-pa-ir-ed before it, it can scarcely fa-il to have been af-fect-ed by his ill-ness im-medi-ate-ly after his ar-[riv]-al [thither], which was undoubtedly an a-po-ple-ct-ic str-oke. Since then he has had a second and a more sever-e one. In the German Gazettes even his de-a-[th] has been an-no-un-ced; but that was a mis-take. At all events it is scarcely pos-sible that he should rem-ain much long-er in the depart-ment of foreign affairs. im-pa-ir-ed : the groups on the page are 1424, then the catchword 1102 at the foot of the left leaf, then 1112 1433 520 at the top of the right leaf. The catchword is the group Adams meant to begin the page with, 1102 pa (Ford-fixed nine times), and in No. 83 (frame 0190) he codes un-im-pa-ir-ed as 1477 1424 1102 1435 520 (1435 ir , Ford-fixed three times). The 1112 1433 on the new page are his own copying slips, one digit each, for 1102 1435: taken as he intended, impaired . Chan-ce-ll-or is 1385 1025 1016 1457 908 with the doubling mark under 1457, the same five groups Adams wrote for “the Chancellor” in No. 73 (frame 0165, Ford 4:256). The group before his illness is 792 by : the earlier transcription 492 use took an open hook for this hand’s looped 4. Most of what the first pass of 18 September inferred is now attested: itself (1081 self , clerk 0184, 0185, 0190), advice (1575 adv , Ford 0132; 1405 ice , Ford 0036 and clerk 0190), apoplectic (1141 ple ; 1060 ct , clerk 0182), stroke (1586 oke ), second (1077), severe (1091 sever ), remain much longer (743 rem , 162 much , 888 long ), mistake (134 mis , clerk 0182), announced (479 un ), At all events (283 event , clerk 0048), foreign affairs (68, 1517), and 1186 is attested as will and Wil- (clerk 0182, 0184). Opposition (83), the key word of the first sentence, is now grade C from No. 73. Four groups of the passage remain inferred (grade I): 1434 journ and 168 ey , 1479 riv and 1382 th . 1398 thither is graded M (code_table.tsv: sthey , also thither ) and is not counted among them. 3.1 What it says “He” is Count Nikolai Rumyantsev (Adams’s Romanzoff), Chancellor and minister for foreign affairs, who had gone to Wilna with Alexander. Adams reports that the Emperor’s journey to Wilna itself went against the Chancellor’s advice; that whatever influence he still had would in any case have been affected by his illness, an apoplectic stroke soon after his arrival there; that since then he has had a second and worse one; that the German gazettes had reported him dead, wrongly; and that he can hardly remain much longer at the head of foreign affairs. This fits what is known: Rumyantsev had a stroke in 1812 that cost him his hearing, and he left office in 1814. Adams’s own diary for September 1812 records Romanzoff speaking of two strokes of apoplexy suffered with the Emperor at Wilna. It differs on the timing from standard accounts (Britannica, Wikipedia), which tie the stroke to the news of the crossing of the Niemen on 24 June. Adams, writing at St Petersburg on 25 June before that news could have reached him, places the first stroke soon after Rumyantsev reached Wilna and a second, worse one before the 25th. Ford printed none of this. Four letters of Hieronymus Łaski and King John Zápolya to the Bavarian court, bound in the Munich key volume, are in one graphic cipher with word signs for the two kings. Its key was recovered from glosses written at the time over two of them (adjacent plaintext) and deciphers all four, the 1531 letter with e and r exchanged: 1,184 of 1,243 words (95.3%); four faint lines of a short note stay open. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (100% of the cipher) The letters Hieronymus Łaski, King John Zápolya’s envoy, to a Bavarian duke (Buda, 24 November 1529), with a letter of King John to Duke Ludwig; Łaski to the dukes’ secretary (Kraków, 16 June 1530); a short note to the same secretary; and Łaski to a ducal councillor (Łask, 17 September 1531). Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 ff. 121–123, 226–228 and 264; DECODE R9322, R9323, R9417 (catalogue 161) and R9403 (catalogue 162), listed with no sender or recipient. The cipher One invented sign per letter, words separated, and a few signs for whole words: a large dagger for King John, a large X for Ferdinand. In the 1531 letter the signs for e and r are the other way round. How it was deciphered A clerk of the time wrote the plain text over parts of R9322 and R9417. The key was rebuilt from 153 of those word pairs and deciphers the unglossed lines and the other two letters. What it says The Sultan has left John the kingdom of Hungary without tribute and will return against Ferdinand unless there is a concord; Łaski asks the dukes to work for it in the Empire, and in 1531 reports the Sultan’s terms: no peace unless Hungary is left to King John. Still open The flower word sign, probably the king’s title; the owl word sign of R9417; two faint words of R9323; a few cramped signs. Until 15 October 2026 these letters were split between two pages, each grouping the records of a DECODE catalogue entry. The other letters of those entries are different ciphers, each with its own page: the System A′ reports of 1534–35 , the Wardein report of 1537 , the King John letters in system L (with R9415 of 1533), the Fulda protest of 1576 , R9367 , R9416 , R9424 and R9319 .

For R9322, R9417 and R9323 they are counted on the decodes made with the gloss key, where a recognisable word with a slipped letter counts as deciphered, so they are generous; R9403 was deciphered line by line. Measured on the words of the running readings (24 October 2026), R9403 reads at 99.1%; R9322 (87.7%), R9417 (92.8%) and R9323 (93.9%) build coherent sentences but stay under the 95% bar.

The glosses give 153 cipher words with their plain words. Aligned sign by sign they fix 21 letter signs: 3 = i, x = e, circled cross = s, a flattened 2 = u/v, dotted circle = a, and so on ( sysB/key_from_glosses.tsv ). One sign, a w-shape, serves both c and t. Three larger signs stand alone for words: the dagger DAG is King John (“non alio loco vult habere [DAG] quam loco fratris sui”, said of the Sultan), the big X is Ferdinand (“concordiam inter [D] et [BIGX]” in R9323), and a four-lobed flower is probably the king’s title. In R9403 the starred x is e and the plain x is r, the reverse of the glossed letters, and some shapes differ; the raw decode of R9417’s first page shows the same exchange, so it is taken as a variant of the one key. A statistical check on the glossed words alone (a Latin letter model) passes: the glosses read far better than random keys or keys fitted to shuffled text.

Łaski writes that King John followed the dukes’ counsel. The Sultan, forced home by plague in his army, left John the kingdom of Hungary without tribute, with fifty guns and a thousand hundredweight of powder, and will come back next summer against Ferdinand’s lands unless there is a concord. A copy of the same news went to Count Palatine Frederick, the imperial captain. On f. 122, “Joannes Dei gratia rex Ungarie” tells Duke Ludwig that he is sending Lazarus the Jew as his envoy.

Both letters were classed decoded, not read in the reading audit of 22 October 2026 and deciphered again on 23 October. R9417 was transcribed again sign by sign at the image: its transcription had stopped at line 21, leaving eight lines out, and had coded the two circle and two cross signs the other way round from the glossed lines. R9323 was re-read word by word (eleven transcription corrections; the first sign of line 3 is the Ferdinand sign). Both now give Latin sentences ( sysB/R9417_reading.md , sysB/R9323_reading.md , with English; [D] is the dagger for King John, [BIGX] Ferdinand, [FLW] the flower sign, italics in the files mark the glossed words). Łaski has the secretary’s letters of 12 June. The army had lain before Buda; a concord is best made through certain princes of the Empire; Nicolaus Min[?k]uics is being sent to the King of France. The Sultan has been persuaded, with great labour, to a truce for the year, and is ready to take into his friendship whomever King John names; unless there is a concord this year he will come out next summer with immense power by land and sea. Envoys should meet at Coburg in Saxony on 4 July. On the King of Poland’s daughter nothing is done, and through Sigismund Herberstein someone (the owl sign) is pressing for her to be given to the Count Palatine Frederick. The note R9323: Carissime domine secretarie, scitote integerrime [FLW] amare duce[m] Bauarie et omnia pro illis facere uelle; sed ego multum cupio concordiam inter [D] et [BIGX], nam certum est si non erit concordia quia peribit Boemia, quam Turce sicuti et Austriam consument.

… cum hac hieme Turca oratoribus regis Ferdinandi hoc dederit responsum: Item ad dominum uestrum dicite illi nunquam ipsum amiciciam nostram, numquam pacem [pacem] uel inducias consequuturum nisi cedat regno Hungarie amico nostro Ioanni regi serenissimo; quod nisi fecerit, ueniam ad querendum eum … Ruffus brought the dukes’ letters on the 15th, and Łaski thanks them. The Sultan told Ferdinand’s envoys this winter that there would be no friendship, peace or truce unless Hungary was given up to King John. Ships, guns and grain are being carried to the Danube and soldiers levied. The diet of Speyer will be short; Łaski is ill but will ride post to it, and the dukes and their friends should stop any decision against the king until he arrives. On the marriage he cannot yet write: within ten days he will settle it with the King of Poland, “for among the Poles, as among the French, the dowering of kings’ daughters is fixed by law.” Postscript: the councillor should put the king’s letters before the imperial estates. The docket says “anno 32”; the text is dated 1531.

The flower word sign (R9322, R9323): probably King John’s title, not fixed by its three contexts. R9403: two words on f. 228 (“[?]orator”, “[?]meus”) and a small insertion on the first page; ten more words are deciphered but doubtful (ergo, Ruffus, sequentes, contra, postas, constituar, nam, ubi, dotandis, meus). On this matter I have already written to [King John]; but because Lord Nicolaus Min[?k]uics is now being sent to the King of France and to others, it was necessary to send the bearer of the present letter, [?a Jew], to [?you]. First, [King John] wishes [...] the princes to be content to stay at peace when the Duke [?of Württemberg] [?strives] to recover his dominion, and he asks this earnestly. The Emperor of the Turks has been persuaded, by my great labours, to a truce of a year; he is ready [sic: "paratur"] to take into his friendship and alliance all whom [King John] names and commends to him; and unless there is concord this year, he will come out next summer with unspeakable power by land and sea, which [...] I will write at another time. Yet your princes need not fear, for we will take care in time. It would be most necessary that you be appointed to the fourth day of July at Coburg in Saxony, for Min[?k]uics will certainly be there. That he could not meet you earlier as he had written was not his fault: the roads were so beset that he could in no way get through. But it is necessary that he go. About the King of Poland's daughter, I wonder that nothing is being done, since the King of Poland had already declared he would give her, and I suspect some ill will, because this business begins so coldly. So [...] it must be: let something be done quickly, for [owl] too is now soliciting, through Sigismund Herberstein, who is here, that she be given to Frederick the Count Palatine. So quick action is needed, lest another snatch away the best and richest prize, etc. Your princes, together with others, ought to send to Charles [?the Emperor] so that he holds back his brother from attacking [King John], because the King of Poland, the King of France and the other Christian princes will send. Finally, I wish to be most warmly commended to your princes, to whom I offer myself and all I have, etc. Kraków, the sixteenth day of June. Łask[i]. Written in his own hand. Nobilis ac egregie domine, amice carissime, salutem et mei commendationem. Quindecima presentis obtulit mihi Ruffus illius literas; quam gratas habuit primum [DAG = rex Ioannes], tum deinde ergo et abunde intellecta sunt ea omnia que continebant in literis illius. Ubi quum uestra dominacio mihi gracias principum suorum pollicetur, illarumque illustrissimarum dominacionum erga me beneuolenciam declarat, magno me gaudio exhilarat atque letificat, ut pote qui ab ineunte etate mea nihil magis semper et optaui et quesiui quam principum et magnatum uirorum conciliare mihi et graciam et fauorem; idque ipsum sum omni studio facturus, et nunc et semper in posterum ac seruiturus sum illustrissimis principibus uestre dominacionis corpore et omnibus meis facultatibus. Ceterum ub[i] cupiunt principes illustrissimi intelligere quid habeat Turca in animo et quo suo exercitu se mouere intendat, de hoc facile sue illustrissime dominaciones possunt intelligere, cum hac hieme Turca oratoribus regis Ferdinandi hoc dederit responsum: Item ad dominum uestrum dicite illi nunquam ipsum amiciciam nostram, numquam pacem [pacem] uel inducias consequuturum nisi cedat regno Hungarie amico nostro Ioanni regi serenissimo; quod nisi fecerit, ueniam ad querendum eum, nec curabo expugnare ciuitates, quia Deus dedit nobis maximas et amplissimas in imperiis nostris urbes, sequentes ad faciendum imperialem et militarem pugnam et ad destruendas eius prouincias. Inde illustrissimi principes perpendere possunt nullo pacto Turcam hanc expedicionem relicturum si non erit concordia. Nunc autem apud ipsum bellicus apparatus cum indicibili furia conficitur: naues infinite, bombarde, annona et uictualia colliguntur et deportantur ad Danubium, ac delectus fit militum. Quod autem ista Spirensis dieta sit ita breuis futura multum doleo; tamen quam primum post hanc intensissimam egritudinem meam aliquid roboris contra habebo, per postas ad ipsam dietam curram. [?]orator ad Cesaream Maiestatem et imperii status, quare rogat principes [?]meus illustrissimos principes ut cum aliis amicis suis impediant ne aliquid decernatur contra ipsum donec ego uenero. Non habet enim [DAG = rex] in toto imperio inter omnes principes cui plus fidat et cui etiam plus studeat et cupiat ipso effectu gratificari quam principibus uestre dominacionis, quod indubie ita est, et pro quo ego ero fideiussor. De matrimonio nescio quid scribam; tamen intra decem dies constituar cum Polonie rege serenissimo, et quidquid perfecero Spire declarabo. Nam apud Polonos sicuti apud Gallos lege cautum habetur de ex dotandis regum filiabus. De his uero et aliis rebus latius quum Spire erimus tractabimus. Interea me ex animo commendo illustrissimis principibus, quorum seruitor sum et ero; uestra etiam dominacio habeat me commendatum. Date decima septima Septembris anno tricesimo primo, Lasci. Translation R9403_en.md # R9403 (BayHStA KAA 4591 ff. 226-228), Hieronymus Łaski to a councillor of the Bavarian dukes, Łask, 17 Sept 1531: English translation Translation (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026) of `r9403/R9403_reading.md`. Same marks: `[DAG = …]` the king word sign (by context King John Zápolya), `[?]orator`, `[?]…` a word whose first sign is unread (translated as far as it carries), `[word]` a supplied or repeated word. Latin. ## Translation Noble and excellent lord, dearest friend, greeting and my commendation. On the fifteenth of this month Ruffus brought me his letters; how welcome they were first to [DAG = King John], and then therefore all that they contained in his letters was understood, and abundantly. Whereas Your Lordship promises me the favour of your princes and declares the goodwill of Their Most Illustrious Lordships towards me, it cheers and gladdens me with great joy, as one who from my earliest age has always wished and sought nothing more than to win for myself the grace and favour of princes and great men; and that very thing I shall do with all zeal, now and always hereafter, and I shall serve the most illustrious princes of Your Lordship with my person and all my means. For the rest, where the most illustrious princes desire to understand what the Turk has in mind and whither he intends to move with his army, Their Most Illustrious Lordships can easily understand this, since this winter the Turk gave King Ferdinand's envoys this answer: "Item, say to your lord that he will never obtain our friendship, never peace [peace] or truce, unless he gives up the kingdom of Hungary to our friend the most serene King John; and if he does not do that, I shall come to seek him out, and I shall not trouble to storm cities, for God has given us very great and very ample cities in our empires, following to make imperial and military battle and to destroy his provinces." From this the most illustrious princes can judge that the Turk will by no means give up this expedition if there is no concord. But now with him warlike preparation is being made with unspeakable fury: ships without number, guns, grain and victuals are being gathered and carried to the Danube, and a levy of soldiers is being made. That this diet of Speyer is to be so short I much regret; yet as soon as, after this most severe illness of mine, I have some strength again, I shall hasten to the diet itself by post. [?]orator to His Imperial Majesty and the estates of the Empire; wherefore my [?]… asks the most illustrious princes, together with their other friends, to prevent anything being decreed against him until I come. For [DAG = the King] has in the whole Empire, among all the princes, none in whom he trusts more, and whom he is more eager and desirous to gratify in very deed, than the princes of Your Lordship; which is undoubtedly so, and for which I shall be surety. Of the marriage I do not know what to write; yet within ten days I shall be settled with the most serene King of Poland, and whatever I achieve I shall declare at Speyer. For among the Poles, as among the French, there is provision by law concerning the dowering of kings' daughters. Of these and other matters we shall treat more fully when we are at Speyer. Meanwhile I commend myself heartily to the most illustrious princes, whose servant I am and shall be; may Your Lordship too hold me commended. Given the seventeenth of September in the year [fifteen hundred and] thirty-one, Łaski. He wrote. I ask most earnestly that Your Lordship may in some way present these letters of [DAG = the King] to the estates of the Empire. Key: key_from_glosses.tsv
