Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · complete The mémoire Armand de Bourbon, prince de Conti, generalissimo of the Paris Fronde, to Geoffroy, marquis de Laigue, his envoy to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm: Paris, 5 March 1649, the day after the Rueil conference opened. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 3854 no. 43, ff. 117r–120r (Gallica btv1b52520094g). Catalogue item 26, with nos. 41–42. The cipher Numbers for letters and syllables: four interleaved alphabets, syllables in blocks of five, a stroke under a number reverses its syllable, numbers from about 99 to 250 are nulls. How it was deciphered A clerk wrote the plain text between the lines from the thirteenth line on. The key was rebuilt from 1,485 glossed groups (ff. 117v–118v) and applied to the twelve lines he left: 264 groups, the address and the purpose of the mémoire. What it says The conference with the court is only a way to buy time and corn for Paris; “dès le moment qu’il entrera en France, cette conférence se rompra”. Still open 67 groups whose gloss is faint, blotted or struck; ten syllable values in the opening fixed by sense alone. Until 14 October 2026 this mémoire shared a page with Conti’s mémoires of 26 and 27 March 1649 (nos. 41–42). Those are in a letter cipher that George Lasry solved, a different cipher, with their own page .

BnF Français 3854 is a recueil of Fronde papers from the prince de Conti’s side, January to April 1649. Omont lists no. 43 (ff. 117r–120r) as “Mémoire, avec chiffre et déchiffrement, du prince de Conti, pour un de ses envoyés auprès de l’archiduc”, undated. Its first words, once deciphered, name the envoy: Pour Monsieur de Legue , Geoffroy de Laigue. The last line of f. 120r is glossed à Paris le 5me mars 1649 . No. 43, f. 117r. Twelve lines of numbers and clear words with nothing written above them; the clerk’s interlinear decipherment starts only at the foot ( po ur p r o cu , “pour procu[rer]”). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3854 f. 117r, via Gallica (btv1b52520094g).

The clerk who deciphered no. 43 wrote a letter or syllable above almost every number from f. 117r line 13 to the end of f. 120r. He wrote nothing over the first twelve lines. Those 264 groups carry the address and the purpose of the mémoire. The key, rebuilt from his glosses. Number/gloss pairs were transcribed page by page (by model sub-agents), and the tallies ( key43.txt ) show a regular design: Four interleaved single-letter alphabets: 3–25 run a→z, 28–50 run z→a, 51–73 run a→z again, and about 80–98 run down. Syllables in blocks of five, in vowel order: ca ce ci co cu = 256–260, and so on through the consonants, with a second, homophonic series in the gaps. Underlining a number reverses its syllable: 385 = ra , underlined 385 = ar . Code words: 451 la Reyne , 457 le cardinal , 458 le parlement , 472 l’archiduc , 482 France . The 500s are dates. Nulls: the numbers from about 99 to 250, which are never glossed. The opening, deciphered. Of the 264 groups, 220 take the value the same number has in the glosses; 24 follow from the alphabets or are nulls; 20 are syllables of the second series, fixed from context. The first draft was checked against the rest of the mémoire. Nine of the context and structural values were later found glossed on ff. 117r–120r, all as predicted: 279 de , 364 la , 354 ne (underlined, en ), 443 te , 445 su , 37 o , 43 h , 86 n , and 36 p . None was contradicted. Pour Monsieur de Legue. Parce que nous ne doutons que le cardinal ne donne une mauvaise interprétation à toutes ses actions, et qu’il ne face principalement ses efforts pour mettre l’archiduc dans la défiance de nos bonnes intentions sur le sujet de la conférence que [le] parlement a accordée, j’ay jugé à propos de vous en faire instruire, afin que vous puissiés destourner les mauvais effets des artifices du cardinal, et faire comprendre à l’archiduc que ce pourparler n’a esté causé et résolu que par les retardemens que l’archiduc apporte à nous secourir, et que nous sommes tousiours dans nos mesmes desseins … No. 43, f. 117r, lines 1–12, not glossed by the clerk; deciphered here Measured. Counting the opening with these values and the body with the clerk’s glosses, the mémoire has 3,367 code groups: 3,300 have a value or are nulls (98.0%, 89 nulls). The 67 without a value are groups whose gloss cannot be read. The key passes the project’s statistical test against random and refitted keys on shuffled text.

Conti writes to Laigue, who is with Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, to keep the Spanish alliance alive while the Frondeurs negotiate with Mazarin’s side. Why the conference happened. The parlement laid the Archduke’s envoy’s proposals ( dom Joseph ) before the Queen. Mazarin, who saw that real peace would ruin him, proposed a conference to drag things out and to make the Archduke believe the Frondeurs were giving way. “À quoy l’on a employé Vautorte.” Conti would have refused it if the Archduke’s help had been ready and Paris not starving. What it bought. No suspension of arms. Saint-Germain lets in a hundred muids of corn a day from Corbeil for as long as the conference lasts, which buys time, “mais fort peu, en vous attendant”. Why it cannot succeed. The deputies are “tous gens de bien, dans le zèle de la paix générale et dans une haine irréconciliable pour le ministériat du cardinal”. They cannot give way on Mazarin, whom the parlement has condemned. The generals stayed away on purpose, so as to be free to break the talks at will. The promise. “Dès le moment qu’il entrera en France, cette conférence se rompra”, and a truer one will be opened with the Archduke’s own deputies. The plea. “Il n’y a plus un seul moment à perdre pour nous secourir.” Laigue is to press for help with all the Archduke’s forces. The complete edited text of the mémoire is in targets/laigue1649/READING43.md . The Peace of Rueil was signed six days later, on 11 March (this background is not from the sources and was not checked here); Conti’s mémoires of 26–27 March, on their own page, show the generals still pressing the Mazarin article after it.

The opening. Ten of its context values (277, 314, 321, 358, 390, 398, 400, 407, 439, 442) never occur in the glossed text, so they rest on sense alone. None of them changes a sentence. Four short places in the glosses are faint, blotted or struck, and are left as gaps in the edition: f. 117v l. 18, f. 118v ll. 5–8, f. 119v l. 14 and f. 120r l. 0. The clerk wrote something at f. 119v l. 14 and struck it through, apparently “duc de Lorraine”.

A contributor recovered a key from the ciphertext alone; a re-transcription against it showed a reciprocal letter-pair substitution in ordinary cursive letters, with doubling dots, a null and partly syllabic figures. 844 of 1,102 cipher tokens are deciphered (76.6%, partial); special signs and eleven figures are open. f x i n e t i g · a y i a s n c h a s t e a u · [v] i l a i n s a/i b/p c/f d/q e/t g/u l/y m/z n/s o/r h/x Nancy → the comte de Vaudémont · reciprocal letter-pair cipher with doubling dots, a null and syllable figures, inline with clear French · 18 June 1592 Charles III of Lorraine to Vaudémont, 18 June 1592 from Charles III of Lorraine → to Comte de Vaudémont Go to the transcriptions ↓ BnF Français 3621 no. 97, f. 109 · the Duke writes to his son in the field about promises not kept, pioneers and munitions, Chasteauvillain and the quarters of La Fauche · DECODE record 9449 lists it as Non-decrypted and no key has been published, but Satoshi Tomokiyo reported reading it in 2025 (opening line only published; this reading is therefore an independent re-solution, not a first break; found after this reading) Key recovered from the ciphertext alone on 18 September by a contributor · re-transcribed from the page against that key on 22 September: every letter stands for its partner in eleven fixed pairs · most cipher tokens get a value, but the running text has a gap in almost every line, so the letter is decoded, not read; special signs, ten figures and three runs still open Arya Sanketbhai Patel · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) With Arya Sanketbhai Patel (solution) · Also credited · Satoshi Tomokiyo (unpublished earlier solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Copy of a letter from Charles III, duke of Lorraine, to his son the comte de Vaudémont, Nancy, 18 June 1592. Where BnF Français 3621 no. 97 (f. 109); DECODE lists it as Non-decrypted . The cipher A reciprocal letter-pair substitution (a/i, b/p, c/f …) in cursive letterforms, doubling dots, a looped æ as null word-divider, and partly syllabic figures. How it was read A contributor recovered a 44-symbol key from the ciphertext alone on 18 September 2026; a line-by-line re-transcription on 22 September gave the simpler key. Credit The 18 September key recovery was contributed by aryasn2026 in pull request #4. Still open Most special signs, 10 of the 14 figures and three garbled runs; no second letter in this cipher is known.

No. 97 is at folio 109 (Gallica canvas 227): “Coppie d’une lettre … de Charles de Lorraine à monsieur de Vaudemont”, Nancy, 18 June 1592. The volume is the duc de Nevers’s intercept and correspondence file for 1591–92. The task came with an instruction to check first for the ciphered originals of the letters intercepted in January 1592. They are not in the volume. No. 22, at folio 31, is a plaintext decipherment only : a fair copy of the French of three intercepted Vaudémont letters, with no cipher anywhere on the sheet, headed “Dechiffrement des lettres de Monsieur de Vaudemont à Monsieur de Lorraine [son] pere, interceptees et apportees à Monsieur de Dinteville, le XX[e] Janvier 1592”. DECODE agrees: its record for no. 22 (9444) is marked Decrypted . The other ciphered pieces of the volume (Birago nos. 31 and 36, Potier no. 79, Dinteville nos. 114 and 116) are Nevers’s own correspondents and their keys, not Lorraine’s. So no. 97 is a single copy with no sibling. The letter mixes clear French and cipher inline on the same lines , and the postscript is clear. The clear text concerns the same business as the cipher: munitions promised and undelivered, Chaumont, the sieur de Buzonville, the attempt on Chasteauvillain.

DECODE record 9449 is this letter, by shelfmark, sender, receiver and date, and its status field reads Non-decrypted ; of the eight DECODE records for Français 3621 only this one and no. 116 have that status. No key record in DECODE is attributed to Charles III or to Vaudémont. Keys for other Lorraine ciphers are published and are not this system: Bréval to Henri II of about 1620, and Bassompierre to Charles III of 1 August 1593, both reconstructed by Satoshi Tomokiyo. Desenclos and Lasry’s 2024 paper on the Henri IV–Nevers ciphers of Français 3995 never mentions Français 3621, and Henri Lepage’s 1864 edition of Charles III’s League correspondence stops in 1591 and prints no cipher table. A prior reading did exist. The search above looked for a published key and missed a published claim. Satoshi Tomokiyo’s list of unsolved historical ciphers marks this letter (“Duke of Lorraine (1592)”, DECODE R9449) as solved by him in 2025, and quotes its opening: “J’ay este infiniment mal satisfait du peu d’execution …”. He published no key and no further text. The entry was already there on 6 September 2026, before this attempt; it was found on 24 September, after the reading, and was not used. The reading here opens with the same words, which independently confirms the first line. Four 1592 key sheets in the Nevers key book, Français 3995, whose DECODE profile matched this cipher, were fetched and examined. None of the four is this key. Sheet What it actually is fol. 32 A jargon dictionary of covert equivalents — Nouvelles = “Draps de soye”, Necessité = “Medecine” — in geometric signs and figures 2–40. Not a letter cipher. fol. 83–84 An all-digit cipher with a Nulles row. “Duc de Lorraine” appears in it as nomenclator entry 46, so it is somebody else’s key that mentions Lorraine. fol. 98 Endorsed in its own hand: “1592 / Chifre d’entre le Duc de Parme et le Roy Cath[olique] en l’an 1592 / lequel sert aussi p[our] le Duc de Sessa et don Diego de Ybarra”. fol. 103 A Nevers-circle nomenclator, its flap listing Gondi, Nemours, Guise and Montpensier, with three homophones for every letter — not a one-for-one pair cipher. It shows what a full key of this milieu holds: syllable figures 1–72, double-letter figures 73–98, word figures 99–353, and lists of places in which Lorraine is 30 and Metz 68.

An earlier attempt had treated the page as a cipher of invented symbols: segment the glyphs, cluster them by shape, solve the cluster sequence. The segmentation worked (the baselines slope, and a shear of −0.031 resolves the block into 21 line bands), but the clustering was unnecessary. The glyphs are ordinary cursive minuscules , the same letters as the clear text, some with dots or a bar, with a handful of special signs, and at one and a half times native size they can be transcribed directly from the page. The contributor’s transcription recorded 1,109 tokens: 1,071 letter symbols in 44 distinct forms, and 38 nomenclator figures. Its letter frequencies match French rank for rank through fourteen places, and its index of coincidence lies between those of a monoalphabetic and a fully homophonic system. BnF Français 3621 f. 109, the opening of the fifteenth line (L14 in the re-read). The first eight forms, f x i n e t i g , spell chasteau . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3621 f. 109, via Gallica btv1b52524472n view 227. On a control with a known key of the same size, the random-move annealer of the earlier attempt recovered only 37–56% of letters at −2.64 per character while the true key scored −1.62: the failure was in the search. A steepest-ascent search with restarts from local optima recovers known keys at 98.7–99.6%. Two traps were closed on the way (free nulls that delete every hard position, and a degenerate etenete… key). The key it found was checked against the manuscript, not only the model: the eight-form group it deciphers as chasteau occurs twice in the cipher, and Chasteauvillain stands in the clear on the same page , in the body and in the postscript. The same page, in clear: “aussi si dieu nous fault la grace de prendre Chasteau[villain]”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3621 f. 109, via Gallica btv1b52524472n view 227. A 4-gram search over 44 free parameters can produce French-looking text from random input, so the pipeline was also run unchanged on shuffled nulls of the same symbols and frequencies, and scored blind: 4-gram score Dictionary coverage Distinct words of 6+ letters The manuscript −2.10 83.0% 33 Five nulls, mean (range) −2.73 74.6% 1.2 (0–3) Thirty-three long words against none to three: there was French under the transcription. From controls with deliberately merged glyphs, the contributor estimated that about a quarter of the glyph transcriptions were still wrong, and proposed re-transcribing the page with the key in hand. The 18 September decryption gave, for example, chasteauilainss [145] nntaises deramenermonarme dooites esquartiers de- , with whole words correct and the joins between them wrong.

The re-transcription was done as proposed: the native IIIF image of canvas 227 (4046 × 5762), sheared −0.031 and cut into 21 line bands, each viewed in five crops at 2.3×, every word checked against the 18 September decryption. Laid out as pairs, the 18 September values already showed the system: glyph a gave i and glyph i gave a, o gave r and r gave o, q gave d and d gave q, n gave s and s gave n. Every letter of the hand stands for its partner in eleven fixed pairs , the whole 22-letter alphabet of the period: Pair a / i b / p c / f d / q e / t g / u l / y m / z n / s o / r h / x Written a reads i , and so on both ways ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ ↔ Sign Value Examples Grade two dots under a letter the letter doubled: ṇ = ss, c̤ = ff, c̈ = tt promesses, assister, passer, affin, remettre H looped æ null, a word divider peu · d’execution , belles · promesses H Θ s chemins , audits H 31 ma (syllable) com-31-nder , de-31-nde , 31 resolution C 139 vous chemins, 139 tiendrés ; et 139 ne manquiés C 145 me affin que 141 ne 145 delaissent C λ, m̄, U, E, π, γ, ꜗ, low-barred t, figure-4 form open about 60 tokens I 13, 57, 88, 98, 103, 121, 122, 123, 137, 141, 146 open 17 tokens I At least part of the nomenclator is therefore syllabic, like the syllable figures of the fr. 3995 keys, and not only a list of persons and places. The 18 September key had 44 symbols instead of eleven pairs mainly because of two transcription merges . The transcription’s c was two glyphs, the secretary e (which stands for t) and c (which stands for f). The search had to send the merged form to t, so every f in the letter was lost ( intiniment , satistait ). This is why the old key had no value at all for b, f, g, x and z, a gap the earlier page had already flagged as the place where mis-transcribed glyphs had gone. Its B was likewise two glyphs, the beta-like b (p) and the looped secretary h (x, hence h): du peu but ceulx and d’execution . The dotted and barred variants that the search had spread over extra homophones are doublings. Correcting those turned most of the short connecting words of the old decryption into plain French with no further guessing. What changed in the decipherment: prisonniers is pionniers : the Duke complains of pioneers and munitions promised, not of prisoners. 139 and 145 are not names. The earlier page guessed, from the clear text, that they might be Chasteauvillain and Chaulmont; in context they decode as vous and me (grade C). The f words come back: infiniment , satisfait , fait , affin , faire , fauldra , la Faulche . The chasteauilains slip that the null test exposed is confirmed at both places (L14, L18): the scribe left out the v twice, so it is an emendation, not a fault of the key. The measure: the old claim that about three quarters of the letters were right was an estimate from controls. Counted word by word against the new decipherment, the 18 September key and tokens give the same words for 449 of 1,105 tokens, 40.6% ; the re-transcription gives 790, 71.5% (section 06).

The rule, stated in measure_reread.py : the unit is the cipher token (one letter sign, a dotted double counting once; one special sign; one null; one figure). Each word of the decipherment is graded H secure, C probable, M doubtful or I not deciphered, and a token counts as deciphered if its word is H or C. Every word is also decrypted mechanically with the pair key, so a decipherment that departs from the key shows up as an emendation. 258 tokens (1,102 less the 844 deciphered after the 5 October pass; 315 of 1,105 on the 22 September count) are not deciphered. Each open piece, with the reason it is open: Re-measured 5 October 2026. After a further pass on 5 October 2026, 844 of 1,102 tokens (76.6%) are deciphered ( measure_reread.py ); 787 (71.4%) also pass a lexicon check ( measure_sense.py ). These count tokens in recognised words, not sentences: read as a text, the decode has a gap in almost every line, and the letter is decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026). Settled: λ, γ, U, π and m̄ are nulls, and L18’s run reads l’effect du dict ; quelq , auld…is and promes were downgraded to M because they fail the lexicon check. Open: the special signs ŧ (12 tokens), ⊙ where it is not s, α, ꜗ, E, the figure-4, a Z and V (about 60 tokens with their words); ten single figures (14 tokens; 98 = ville fits but so do other nouns); the garbled runs of L12, L13 and L20 (about 35 tokens), legible at full IIIF resolution but not decodable under the pair key. Re-read 23 October 2026. The graded re-read of 5 October was written out as running text with the clear lines ( ct/no97_partial_reading.md , with English), the standalone crossed t taken as a null (eight of eight places between complete words). One sign in five is still open, and only about one sentence in seven holds: the letter stays decoded, not read. DECODE R9449 and R9444 were opened again (one image, no attachment), and the DECODE record list and the BnF keys of 1580–1600 were searched for a key in this pair system; none was found (fr. 3623 no. 23, R9453, is the Bienvenut–Nevers key of 1590). A key or duplicate may survive in the Lorraine ducal archive (Archives départementales de Meurthe-et-Moselle), not consulted. Special signs with no settled value: λ (11 times), m̄ (9), U (8), γ (5), E (4), π (4), ꜗ, t with a low bar, the figure-4 form, and the reversed 3 in some places: about 60 tokens, and most of the words not deciphered contain one. m̄ and λ stand between whole words and may be nulls, but that is not proved. Grade I. Open because no key survives and each sign occurs one to eleven times, too few for context to fix most of them. Ten figures : 57 (3), 88 (2), 98 (2), 13, 103, 121, 122, 123, 137, 146; 14 tokens, grade I (141, three tokens, was settled on 5 October as qu’il by pooling its occurrences: affin que 141 ne me delaissent ). 57 and 98 are persons or bodies ( ceulx de la 98 , les deputés de … 98 ). One letter, no key, no sibling in the same cipher. Three garbled runs , about 35 tokens, grade I: L12 after passer ; L13 between des and apres ; L20 around m’a d…te . At IIIF 1:1 the glyph sequence does not decode to French under the pair key even with the specials set aside; the original or a higher-resolution scan is needed to tell e from c, b from h and the dotted forms apart there. Doubtful readings (grade M) : dressera (L02), …ien (L03, L13, L17), manquiés and demander (L04), et re-/-solument (L12–13), ne fais , es and droites (L14), pour (L15), one vous (L16), asseurté (L20). Not counted as deciphered. Probable readings (grade C) , counted as deciphered: the figures 31, 139 and 145; pionniers , belles , ont , avoient , l’entendre , ausdits , conno-issent , mescontentement , prudence , affin , delaissent , remettre , commandement , quelq[u’un] , induiront , l’effect , vilain(s) , préadvertir , jour , ainsy , l’on avoit , oultre and a few short words. Every other deciphered word is H. Not consulted : the Archives départementales de Meurthe-et-Moselle, where a duplicate or a key would most plausibly survive; the remaining key sheets of Français 3995 one by one. Both need physical access or a catalogue not online.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. fr. 3621 no. 97, Nancy, 18 June 1592 decoded, not read A contemporary copy of Charles III of Lorraine's letter to his son the comte de Vaudémont, with clear French and cipher alternating on the same lines. The Duke is infinitely ill satisfied with the little execution of the promises of pioneers and munitions made to him, urges his son to press the attempt on Chasteauvillain, and writes of putting someone there to command and hold the plain and of bringing his army back to quarters. The volume is the duc de Nevers's intercept and correspondence file for 1591-92. A mechanical decode with holes in most sentences: shown so that the transcription and the key can be checked and improved, not as a reading. What the re-read changed: the system is a reciprocal pair cipher Going back to the page with the 18 Sept decode beside it showed that the key was not 44 free symbols at all. Laid out as pairs, the 18 Sept values already said so: glyph *a* = i and glyph *i* = a, *o* = r and *r* = o, *q* = d and *d* = q, *n* = s and *s* = n. Every letter of the hand stands for its partner in eleven fixed pairs: a<->i b<->p c<->f d<->q e<->t g<->u l<->y m<->z n<->s o<->r h<->x (22 letters, the whole alphabet of the period). Plus: * **two dots under a letter double it**: ṇ = ss (*promesses*, *assister*, *passer*), c̤ = ff (*affin*), c̈ = tt (*remettre*); * the looped æ is a **null**, used as a word divider (*peu · d'execution*, *belles · promesses*); * a small set of **special signs** (λ, Θ, ꝗ, m̄, π, γ, capital E, t with a low bar, reversed 3, a figure-4 form); Θ = s is secure (*chemins*, *audits*); the rest are open; * **figures for syllables and words**, at least some syllabic: **31 = "ma"** (*com-31-nder*, *de-31-nde*, *me 31-nde*, *31 resolution*), **139 = "vous"** (*chemins, 139 tiendres*; *et 139 ne manquies*), **145 = "me"** (*affin que 141 ne 145 delaisent*). The two transcription merges that did most of the damage in the 18 Sept decode: * the transcription's **c** was two glyphs, the secretary **e** (→ t) and **c** (→ f). The old key had to send it to t, so every f in the letter was lost (*intiniment*, *satistait*); five plain letters (b f g x z) had no cipher value at all, as the page write-up noticed; * its **B** was two glyphs, the beta-like **b** (→ p) and the looped secretary **h** (→ x): *du peu* but *ceulx* and *d'execution*. Correcting those two, and reading the dotted and doubled forms as doublings, turns most of the 18 Sept "connective tissue" into plain French with no further guessing. ## 2. Spelling as written. ## No. 97 (fol. 109, canvas 227) — Charles III of Lorraine to the comte de Vaudémont, Nancy, 18 June 1592 Headed, in the copyist's hand: **"Coppie d'une lettre de Monsieur de Lorraine à Monsieur de Vaudemont"**, with the older inventory number 125 at the head. > "Mon filz, J'ay ce jourd'huy au soir receu celles que vous m'aves escriptes du ⟨?⟩ > **[about twenty lines in cipher]** > … et de la, s'ilz pourront tascher de remedier, ou bien juger le peu d'effect qui peut ⟨?⟩ ou la somme > **[chiffre]** … et livrer bonne manquere ⟨?⟩. Je prie ⟨Dieu⟩ meilleurs moyens que vous envoyez brief des > biens expressement avec habitans de Chaulmont aussi bien. Et les fera entendre les promesses qu'ilz vous > ont faictes, le manquement d'ses munitions, et ⟨?⟩ qu'ilz veuillent y pourvoir, de sorte que faulte de la > ⟨?⟩ … Je ⟨?⟩ qu'ilz y pourvoiront. Mandez moy soudain de les nouvelles, de quoy attendant … priant Dieu > qu'il vous donne, Mon filz, ⟨ce que vous desirez⟩. Escript à Nancy, ce XVIII[me] jour de Juin 1592. > **Vostre bien bon amy, Charles**" Postscript, in clear: > "Depuis ceste escripte j'ay advisé de vous envoyer ⟨?⟩ et avez encor quelque manquement de la ⟨?⟩ vous a > promis vous la munition au S[ieu]r de Buzonville et autre de Chaulmont. Si vous faictes ⟨?⟩ à la dozime > apporte quelque advancement … soit de munitions promises et aultres choses, remettant le tout à vous. > **Mais pour cela, si vous pouvez venir à bout de Chasteauvillain, ne perdez pour ceste occasion les > ⟨jours⟩ en temps** … Puis si vous prenez Chasteauvillain, donnez ordre que vous en faictes quelque chose > pour secourir voz soldatz." So the ciphered middle is flanked by clear passages on the same business: munitions promised and not delivered, the inhabitants of Chaumont, the sieur de Buzonville, and above all the attempt on **Chasteauvillain** — the Champagne place whose capture the duke is urging on his son. ## No. 22 (fol. 31, canvas 71) — the January intercepts, deciphered by the other side Headed: **"Dechiffrement des lettres de Monsieur de Vaudemont à Monsieur de Lorraine [son] pere, interceptées et apportées à Monsieur de Dinteville, le XX[e] Janvier 1592"** (older number 138). It is a fair copy of the *plaintext* of three letters, with no cipher on the sheet: * **"Premiere lettre datée de La Fere du ⟨XVII⟩ Decembre 1591"** * **"Seconde lettre datée de Marcheonne ⟨?⟩ du ⟨VI⟩e Janvier 1592"** * **"Troisieme lettre datée du ⟨May…onne⟩ du ⟨XI⟩e Janvier 1592"** The substance is the relief of Rouen and the League's dealings with Parma's Spaniards, reported by the son to his father: > "… avec ⟨?⟩ canons, et douze cens picques de partie des Bourguignons … deux heures de marche … et > prenons le chemin droict à Rouen. Monsieur le duc du Mayne, se trouvant les Espagnols si resolus à une > bataille, s'en a approché ⟨du⟩ Roy … Mais lors qu'il s'en veut asseurer, le duc de Parme juge qu'il > ⟨fauldra⟩ … de ceste cavallerie, si difficile aux Espagnols …" and, further down the same sheet, the political matter: the cardinal légat and the Pope's charge, the Spanish pretensions, Villeroy at Pontoise, the house of Bourbon, the resolution of the duc de Mayenne, the sieur de Bellievre, and "la paix" — the peace nobody could any longer support the length of the war without. That is the double game the catalogue points at: the Duke of Lorraine's son inside the League army, writing home about Parma and about feelers toward Henri IV, and the King's side reading it. How it was deciphered George Lasry reconstructed about seventy elements of the key in 2020. With his values alone the decode gave only fragments (decoded, not read, 22 October 2026). On 23 October 2026 the decipherment made in 1589, on ff. 500r–500v, was found among DECODE R54’s attachments filed as “cleartext” and never opened. It was transcribed and aligned element by element with the figures under Lasry’s key, which confirmed one new value (4 = c, at all 17 places). What it says Navarre has come to Tours, lodged at Plessis, and waited on Henri III, giving him his shirt at his rising and his napkin at table; the King had him dine with him, “a mixing at court of heretics and Catholics”. Navarre’s troops are to be turned against Mayenne. In R54 the legate expects the Pope to recall him. Still open 29 single elements whose value only the decipherment gives (one place each, not adopted as key values), and a few words where the figures as transcribed give no word and the decipherment carries the reading. Until 14 October 2026 these two enclosures shared a page with Morosini’s other thirty-four cipher sheets of Francia 22, which use Meister’s key no. 40: a different key, with its own page . Francia 22, image 499v (DECODE R53): the clear passage in which Morosini waits for leave from Rome, and the first lines of the cipher in the second key. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 22 image 499v, via DECODE R53.

R53 , Francia 22/32, image 499v. A short clear passage (the legate is waiting “con quella sollecitudine” for letters from Rome granting his leave) and 785 cipher figures, transcribed for DECODE by the volunteer Midas on 31 March 2017. It was placed at Tours from the series; the clear letter it went with (f. 499r, docket f. 498v “4 di maggio”) puts it at Moulins in early May 1589. R54 , Francia 22/33, image 502r. 663 cipher figures (DECODE transcription by NiLan, 6 April 2017) and the clear dating line Di Molins à gli xi di Maggio 1589 . DECODE files a key for these two records under the name “ASV – F22b”: George Lasry’s reconstruction of 24 October 2020. He notes that it is variable in length and not deterministic. Its elements are one or two figures for syllables and letters (a 3 or 7, ba 86, ca 73, di 93, e 5 or 8, la 60, re 43, si 83, 85, 89 or 95, u 21 or 54), and three figures for a few syllables and words (102 mpo, 116 or 216 me, 495 or 498 chi, 496 che). Names carry a dot on the first figure: 1̇24 Umena (Mayenne), 1̇85 Navarro . There are no nulls. The other enclosures of Morosini’s legation use a different system, Meister’s key no. 40, with the dot on the middle figure and nulls.

The 1589 decipherment on f. 500r, aligned with the figures, gives the whole cipher. Of its 693 letters, 603 are the figures’ own value under Lasry’s key; the rest are the decipherer’s doubled consonants and words where the figures slip or a code has no value. Where the figures give another word than the decipherer wrote (six words), the figures are followed. The reading begins: Il Navarro, per quello che mi disse domenica il secretario del Vicelegato di Avignone, arrivò giovedì à Tours, et alloggiò à Plesi con grosa compagnie di signori et gentil’huomini francesi, che alloggiano nel Borgo verso detto Plesi; et il medesimo giorno andò à vederlo il Re; al quale la matina seguente esso Navarro diede la camisa al letto, et la salvietta alla tavola; ma Sua Maestà la fece desinare seco. Onde si è fatta una mescolanza alla Corte di heretici et di Catholici, che è odiosa à tutti li huomini dabene. (Navarre, from what the secretary of the Vice-legate of Avignon told me on Sunday, arrived at Tours on Thursday and lodged at Plessis …; the same day the King went to see him, and the next morning Navarre himself handed him his shirt at his rising and his napkin at table; but His Majesty had him dine with him. So a mixing of heretics and Catholics has come about at court, hateful to all good men.) Until the decipherment was found, the decode had made the vice-legate the visitor. The letter goes on: Navarre is to pass his troops in review before the King and, once more of the Vicomte de Turenne’s have joined, to send them against Mayenne ( Umena ), who is between Le Mans and Vendôme.

R54 continues R53’s last clause (the decipherment runs on from f. 500r to f. 500v). With Navarre beside the King, the legate expects the Pope to recall him, and asks that anyone at court who wants him back be told it is impossible “se non pensano di mandarmi un grosso essercito che mi accompagni et difenda dagli heretici”. Of 622 letters, 468 are the figures’ own value and 61 stand on digits that DECODE’s transcription marks illegible, supplied by the decipherment; one non is the decipherer’s insertion in the margin, with no figures under it.

The figures run on without separators, so the key cannot be applied group by group. The decoder of the sibling entry ( targets/morosini1588/decrypt.py , run with --f22b ) tries every way of dividing the figures into Lasry’s one-, two- and three-figure elements and keeps the division that a five-gram model of sixteenth-century Italian scores best. Where the key has a gap, the model fills it with the nearest Italian it can make from the elements it knows, so a stretch that looks like Italian is not proof that the values are right. The figures follow DECODE’s volunteer transcriptions; the scans were not checked figure by figure. The decipherment of 1589 (23 October 2026). DECODE R54 carries, as png attachments filed “[cleartext]”, the decipherment written in 1589 for both cipher passages, on f. 500r (R53) and f. 500v (R54). It was transcribed ( texts/R53_decifrato_f500r.txt , R54_decifrato_f500v.txt ) and aligned element by element with the figures under Lasry’s key ( research/reading_audit/b21_moro_align.py , texts/*_align.tsv ). The alignment confirmed one value, 4 = c, at all 17 places, and no letter rests on a look-alike sign. The readings, texts/R53_reading.md and R54_reading.md , with English beside them, follow the figures where they give another word than the decipherer wrote.

29 single elements whose value only the decipherment gives (57 q, 117, 637, 42, 53/0, 81, 38, 27 lu, 75, 11 and others; texts/f22b_values_b21.tsv ). Each occurs once in 1,448 figures, so they are not adopted as key values; the reading rests on the decipherment there. Words where the figures as transcribed give no Italian word (in R53 mi disse domenica , francesi , seco , al quale si tiene ; in R54 di qui , fin hora , perche , distrutti i primi ): lone figures or digits DECODE marks illegible, carried by the decipherment. Before the decipherment was found, a decode with Lasry’s values gave 75% of letters in Italian word forms but no sentences, and rebuilding the missing values from the cipher alone (14 October 2026) gave fits on R53 and R54 that agreed on one code in ten; none was adopted. Meister (1906) prints no second key for Morosini.

Spelling is the decipherer's (1589), except in the words taken from the figures, which keep the cipher's spelling. The clear text before the cipher (f. 499r-v, Morosini's illness and leave) is not part of this reading. R53 and R54 are two cipher passages of one dispatch's matter, deciphered on one leaf (f. 500r-v). - 'Umena' is Mayenne (code 1̇24); 'il Navarro' Henri of Navarre (1̇85, written over the word by the decipherer); 'Plesi' Plessis-lès-Tours; the Visconte di Turena is Henri de La Tour, vicomte de Turenne. - 'la camisa al letto ... la salvietta alla tavola': Navarre served the King at his lever and at table (the meeting of the two kings at Plessis, 30 April 1589). Carried by the decipherment only: 'non' in 'per mia disgratia non fosse' (added in the margin, '1 non'; no figures), 'di qui' (2 6 7 38), 'fin hora' (figures 95 23, 'sin'), 'perche' (9 1), 'distrutti i primi' (75, 11 and illegible digits), 'Nostro Signore' (code 1̇51, after figures that may give 'il'). ## Reading Se gli andavano ingrossando ogni giorno. L'essere dunque il Navarro col Re, et mescolati gli heretici con i Catholici alla Corte, penso che sarà maggiormente risoluto Nostro Signore à levarmi di qui, quando fin hora non lo habbia fatto; il che si per mia disgratia non fosse, et che voi sentiste anco alcuno di quei signori che havesse animo che io me ne tornassi alla Corte, non mancate vi prego di fargli conoscere che si tratta delli impossibili, se non pensano di mandarmi un grosso essercito che mi accompagni et difenda dagli heretici. Oltre che questa unione taglia la testa à tutto quello che habbiamo discorso insieme à la partita vostra; perche non è più in potere di alcuno di praticare et concludere cosa che vaglia, essendo distrutti i primi fondamenti. ## Notes - 'Se gli andavano ingrossando' continues R53's last clause ('Umena, al quale si tiene se gli andavano ingrossando ogni giorno': whose forces, it is believed, were growing every day). - 'Nostro Signore' (N.S.re, code 1̇51, which Lasry read 'h.s.re'; the decipherer's capital N looks like H) is the Pope. - 'questa unione': the union of Henri III with Navarre (truce of 3 April 1589). Navarre being, then, with the King, and the heretics mixed with the Catholics at the court, I think that Our Lord [the Pope] will be all the more resolved to recall me from here, if he has not done so already; and if by my misfortune that should not be, and you hear of any of those lords having a mind that I should go back to the court, do not fail, I beg you, to make them understand that it is a matter of the impossible, unless they mean to send me a large army to accompany me and defend me from the heretics. Besides, this union cuts the head off all that we discussed together at your departure, for it is no longer in anyone's power to negotiate and conclude anything worthwhile, the first foundations being destroyed.

Murray, in Paris to exchange the ratifications of the Convention of 1800, ended his despatch No. 5 with six code groups that the Madison Papers left undecoded (“key not found”). Every group is decoded between the lines in Murray’s own 1797–98 despatches from The Hague in the same code: 406 as arm in armies , alarmed and arming , 264 as neutral , 1004 as -ed . Where National Archives, RG 59, Diplomatic Despatches, Netherlands, vol. 4, on microfilm M42 reel 5, frames 0397–0398 (catalog NAID 188770447). Abstract in The Papers of James Madison, Secretary of State Series 1:353 (Founders Online 02-01-02-0456), where no decipherment is given. Catalogue no. 481. The cipher Murray’s legation code of 1797–1801: numbers up to about 1,600 for words and syllables, joined by dots inside the clear text. The postscript has six groups. How it was deciphered No key sheet survives. Murray’s 1797–98 despatches to Pickering in the same volume series carry a clerk’s decode between the lines, and every one of the six groups is decoded there, 406 as arm three times ( armies , alarmed , arming ). What it says “P.S. As to the armed neutrality not a Word has yet been said”: in the Paris conferences the French had not raised the League of Armed Neutrality of the northern powers. Still open Nothing in the postscript. The original copy, sent via Le Havre, was not found.

Murray had been minister at The Hague since 1797 and one of the three American envoys who signed the Convention of Mortefontaine with France on 30 September 1800. The Senate ratified it in February 1801 on condition that Article 2, which put off the old treaties and the indemnities for spoliations, be struck out, and Murray went to Paris in May 1801 to exchange the ratifications. His despatch No. 5 of 26 June reports a conference with Fleurieu and Rœderer the day before: the French ministers are “unanimous in refusing to accede to the Suppression of the Second Article”, and Talleyrand has asked whether Murray could exchange ratifications if theirs were conditional. The body is in a clerk’s hand. Below his signature Murray added a three-line postscript in his own hand, partly in code. The Madison editors abstract the letter (PJM-SS 1:353) and say of it: “Partially encoded postscript…not deciphered (key not found)”. The copy on the film is the duplicate, marked “Via Bordeaux / Sent 27 june 1801”. The original went via Le Havre in the hope of reaching Captain Rodgers before he sailed; it is not in the France despatches for 1800–01 (M34 reel 9) and was not found. Frame 0398, left page: the postscript under the subscription and Murray’s signature. “P.S. As to 536. 406. 1004. / 264. 1136. 1175. not a Word / has yet been said—”. No decode was written over it. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to the Netherlands, vol. 4, microfilm M42 reel 5, frame 0398 (left page), via catalog.archives.gov NAID 188770447.

The six groups are 536, 406, 1004, 264, 1136, 1175. The last was transcribed 1075 at first; at four times enlargement it is 1175, with the same narrow “11” that opens 1136 on the same line. The code is not one of the State Department codes already rebuilt in this project: the Pinckney code at Madrid has the = 1651, Armstrong’s Paris code 972, John Quincy Adams’s 1810 code 1385. Here the is 536. No key sheet is known, but Murray wrote many coded passages from The Hague, and in the Department someone wrote the meaning over the numbers: The sibling named in the catalogue. The postscript of 18 May 1801 to his No. 132 (same volume, frame 0372), decoded between the lines by Jacob Wagner: 1285.1181 Gaudin , 712.621.1161 Tribunate , 536 the , 247 Consuls . The group 536 shows the 1801 postscripts use the code of the 1790s. The 1797–98 despatches to Pickering. Diplomatic Despatches, Netherlands, vol. 3 (M42 reel 4, NAID 188770022) holds Murray’s despatches from his arrival at The Hague, with long coded passages on the Batavian revolution and the Directory, most of them decoded by a clerk. About 150 word and syllable pairs were taken from them. Every group of the postscript is decoded somewhere in those letters. Murray also wrote 406.1004 for armed himself in his No. 44 of 28 May 1798 (frame 0365, right page), “those ships to be armed”, where no decode was written but the clear text around it is about arming merchant ships. Cipher 536 406 1004 264 1136 1175 Value the arm -ed neutral -i- -ty P.S. As to the armed neutrality not a Word has yet been said— The armed neutrality is the League of Armed Neutrality the northern powers (Russia, Sweden, Denmark and Prussia) formed in December 1800 against British search of neutral ships. By June 1801 it was coming apart: Paul I was murdered in March, the Danish fleet was beaten at Copenhagen in April, and Murray’s own despatch of 7 May describes the coalition’s weaknesses. Murray tells Madison, in code, that the French had said nothing about it in the conferences on the Convention.

The Founders abstract and the 26 Murray–Madison letters of 1801 were checked: only the 7 May despatch (with its 18 May postscript) is coded and decoded. The letter is dated Paris, not The Hague as the catalogue entry had it. Vol. 4 of the Netherlands despatches was located on the National Archives catalogue (NAID 188770447) and its 433 frames downloaded. The 26 June letter is frames 0397–0398; there is no second copy in the volume. The postscript was transcribed and the 18 May decode read: 536 is the in both. Vol. 3 (M42 reel 4) was scanned frame by frame for coded passages, with subagents transcribing the groups and the clerk’s decodes. The pairs gave 1004 = -ed , 264 = neutral , 1136 = -i- , 1175 = -ty : “the [406]-ed neutrality”. That predicted 406 = arm . A search of the rest of vol. 3 for the group 406 found it decoded as armies , alarmed and arming . The attestations for 264, 1136, 1175, 1004 and 406 were checked on the frames. The method is a key recovered from adjacent plaintext: the contemporary decodes of other letters in the same file series, not a key sheet or a decoded copy of this letter. The statistical test is not applicable to six groups (verdict “too short”); the check is that every value is decoded in the siblings.

Nothing in the postscript: all six groups are graded C, read from contemporary decodes of the same code. The original of No. 5, sent via Le Havre, was not found, so there is no second copy to compare. Murray’s whole code was not rebuilt. The ~150 sibling pairs are kept as working notes in the folder; only the six used here were checked on the images.

A letter of the Count-Duke of Olivares, wholly in cipher, to the Duke of Alba, viceroy of Naples, on the deaths in his family and the future of his son-in-law. Brice Dudout read it with Philip IV’s cipher A plus 20 values learnt on its first part: 95.2% of 1,001 words, with the key only partly confirmed. lon D Q he tir for 2 q ho v fir 10 q fan 16 v 1 pen T 10 fro flu xer … BIENHETENIDOESTOSDIASQUEOSECERADIOS … Madrid → Naples · royal cipher A of Philip IV · 22 August 1626 Olivares to the Duke of Alba, 22 August 1626 Go to the full text ↓ The all-powerful minister of Philip IV tells the viceroy of Naples of the deaths in his family and names his son-in-law heir of his house, in a cipher the key for which was rebuilt six years later. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: complete · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · DECODE database (unpublished earlier solution) key matched At a glance External key matched · complete The letter Gaspar de Guzmán, Count-Duke of Olivares, to Antonio Álvarez de Toledo, 5th Duke of Alba, then viceroy of Naples; Madrid, 22 August 1626. Wholly in cipher except the closing, the dateline and the signature. A covering letter in clear of the same day (f. 11r) refers to it. Where Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/10249 (“Papeles varios”, Osuna; BDH bdh0000042230), ff. 13r–15r. DECODE R1190 lists the letter as “Decrypted”, but no decipherment or key is attached there. The cipher Philip IV’s general cipher A: a homophonic syllabary of letter groups, numbers for letters and syllables, special signs and a nomenclator (fro = Dios, 199 = hija). How it was deciphered The key K6A, rebuilt from the Santa Cruz pairs of 1630–32 ( Santa Cruz 1630 ), reads the first part. Twenty values learnt there only were added, the key was frozen, and then it was measured once on the held-out part. What it says The deaths of a young Guzmán nephew and of his daughter María after a stillbirth; he keeps her widower Ramiro Núñez de Guzmán, Marquis of Toral, as son and heir, with the dukedom of Medina de las Torres and the office of sumiller de corps. Still open The key is partial by the project’s protocol (0.506 against 0.144, under the 0.60 threshold). Thirteen codes have no value, and about 54 line ends are lost in the gutter. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée), with Claude Opus 5.5 agents, dated and identified the letter, extended the key, transcribed and read it. DECODE R1190 is credited as prior work, without a decipherment.

The letter belongs to the summer of 1626, when Olivares lost a nephew meant for the Church and then his only daughter, María, who died after a stillbirth. He writes to the Duke of Alba that he keeps her widower, Ramiro Núñez de Guzmán, Marquis of Toral, as son and heir of his house: the dukedom of Medina de las Torres on the commandery of Caravaca, granted by the King at the marriage, and the office of sumiller de corps, which the King gave Ramiro of his own motion in Barcelona. He offers his life to the King’s service and hopes the Duke his son will behave wisely. The facts agree with the known chronology. The lead (no. 1273) was catalogued as undated; the covering letter in clear fixes it at 22 August 1626. DECODE R1190 has the same letter with the status “Decrypted”. We checked the record: it holds three images, an empty documents list, no transcription, no key and no decipherer. Where the status comes from is unknown. If an earlier reading turns up, the credit here becomes verification rather than solution.

K6A is a homophonic syllabary (fer = de, xer = me, fan = que, pon = co) with numbers and a nomenclator. The first part of the letter (ff. 13r–14v, line 17) was transcribed and read, 20 values were added from it alone (for example hija for 199, ll for c‡), and the key was frozen by SHA-256 before the rest was transcribed. The held-out part (f. 14v.21–27 and f. 15r, 542 tokens, 20.7%) was measured once. With no contemporary decipherment, the measure is the share of decoded letters covered by Spanish words of five letters or more: 0.506, against 0.144 for the best of 200 keys shuffled within length classes. The criterion fixed in advance was at least 0.60 and a margin of 0.30. The margin is met (0.362), the threshold is not, so the key is partial. The ceiling is about 0.64: a perfect contemporary plaintext of the same series scores 0.636. Nine code tokens of the held-out part have no value and each cuts a segment.

The reading was made after the measurement and counted by script on the marked text. Of 1,001 words, 906 are certain, 47 probable, 13 restored and 35 unresolved: 953 read without restorations, 95.2%. A blind proof-reading of 13 sign forms, answered by Brice Dudout and fixed in advance, settled hol = Su Majestad, gli = buena, pr = for and the two forms of “t”. The three “hol” of the held-out part were then read “Su Majestad” by the value established outside it; this is a reading decision only, and without them the count is 94.9%. The Spanish and an English translation are under Full texts.

About 54 line ends are lost in the gutter of ff. 13v and 14v and are not counted. Codes with no value: 22‡, 197, bir, B_, dol, yil, 229, 102, Qar, per, hen, pes; bil is probably “V.E.”. Each occurs once, so a value from the sense would be a guess. The square sign is “mi” in the key and “merced” by the sense on f. 14r.26; the conflict is left open. The two forms of “t” (p and g) cannot be told apart at 120 dpi except where the proof-reading settled them. No edition was found: Elliott and de la Peña, Memoriales y cartas del Conde Duque de Olivares , has no letter to the Duke of Alba in 1626 by its table of contents (the text was not seen).

"His Majesty" stands for the code "hol" (probable). The translation follows the reading page by page; where the gutter cuts a line, the sentence is given in fragments. **f. 13r.** I have had much to offer to God these days, almost all the causes of grief that I can fear as a father and as master of my house having come upon me together. ‹…› de Guzmán, my nephew, died, a youth of ‹…› years [who] ‹…› in his gifts and in the promise he showed, and the one I had chosen to serve the King and the Church in that dignity. In my grief at this blow, which was in my ‹…› ‹…› the cause and the qualities, God prepared me, not without particular providence, for another, incomparably greater, with which He was to try me. A few days later my daughter María had a bad delivery, in which she lost a granddaughter who would have been a comfort to me for the continuation of my posterity, and ‹…›. The tears for this mishap were dried by the recovery of her mother: she having [come through] ‹…› dangers, the pleasure of seeing her well was enough to console me. But as María's virtue and her good inclination drew her towards what she now enjoys, and since she had the use of reason she strove to deserve it, and in the married state she excelled in love for her husband and in the ‹…› of all her qualities, God chose **f. 13v.** to give her the reward in advance ‹…› … when we imagined her in better health … my spirit gave way to grief, and the strength of the … could suspend the feeling and … new light to reason, to consider that … such [blows], if they come as punishment, are deserved …, and if by a higher providence, they must be venerated. And so, when there came before me my … the grief of the countess, the loss …, the forlorn state of the Marquis, and the grief of everyone, which even among … strangers has been great, I sought to offer to God what came from His hand, and to give … my part; and I judged as the first … for the Marquis, who, having been my daughter's husband, … his fortune so changed, moved … the most pitiless to compassion … that I had chosen this Ramiro … his blood and his person, which … is lovable, to make him master of my house … of all that they have deserved and are … my ‹…› and cares, I have found him … in the King's service most loyal and intelligent … as far as I have tried him, and of capacity … [with] greater signs he loved my daughter and respected the … heart, and he knew how to win her so much that, having … ordered the viaticum to be given her in the [extremity] … from which she was recovering, she said afterwards … **f. 14r.** with anguish, goes to see ‹…› that this poor Ramiro gave. The countess and I owe him love and respect, [he having treated us] with the humility and submission of a son, … who has put our reputation and our advice before the ‹…› licence that prosperity tends to allow. It is clear to me that if María, as God took her, forgetting all things here below (a reward that ‹…› her virtue, and how little it had turned her head), had remembered anything or had had time to dispose of it, it would have been her husband to whom she left all she could, and in whom she would have wished all I have, and that in ‹…› that moment she would have asked it of me tenderly. I saw the Marquis reduced to a state that imagination could not foresee, and his fortune so undone in an instant that little would not suffice to repair it, and great demonstrations were needed, since even the greatest did not match that for which I chose him; and afterwards the love grew, and the qualities by which he knew how to deserve us. The impossibility grieved me; the countess felt the same; my own spirit urged me; such reasonable tokens of devotion approved ‹…› ‹…› of fitting ‹…› ‹…› that they had to be great. The clemency of His Majesty (God keep him) encouraged it: he had granted me the favour, when I arranged María's marriage, ‹…› of the dukedom of Medina de las Torres on the commandery of **f. 14v.** Caravaca, so that with the revenues of some … of survivorship he might found a house in which … his children might succeed ‹…›, having with … if God gave me male sons, that I … his own should not be left without a house in which to succeed … that to such a daughter, who from her birth was … and company, no less was owed, I having succeeded, by her death, to the house which in the … of His Majesty and at my disposal had … for her, and which was already made mine, I begged … to give me ‹…› to pass it to the Marquis with some … fitting to the memory of my house and of … in which only the … holder now changed; and as it seemed to me that this ‹…› … compassionate and little cast down at goods … was completed by leaving … to the Marquis the office of his sumiller de corps, whose duties he performed in my absences … which His Majesty gave him of his own motion in [Barcelona] … I tried it, and I would not have resolved to [accept] the ‹…› that His Majesty did me, had he not shown so much … pleasure in it, or had it not been a means to … the Marquis to greater attention and care to … wishing that the one I esteemed as a son … always to such ‹…›, and that he should see that if … once I chose him as a son for his blood and for his … and [now] I seek him for his forlorn state, and because … **f. 15r.** the world ‹…› enhanced in it, the clemency of His Majesty, and his greatness merciful, and in me the reverence and care with which I serve him the more accredited; and to the ‹…› I have been so grieved by this ‹…› that, were I not bound to offer my life to the last spiritual service of His Majesty, I would cease to ‹…› ‹…› ‹…› ‹…› ‹…› near him, undeceived as to how little everything lasts, and intent on my salvation. I have given account to ‹…› of the state in which I find myself, so that he may see that in everything I live most confident in the [favour] he does me, and wishing to ‹…›. And I trust in God that, as the action was done in good spirit, and the King the ‹…› master of it, with a pious and compassionate end, it may serve so that, well judged, it deserves greater approval each day, and that the Duke my son may behave so wisely as to oblige everyone and grow in merit. So I wish it, and (in clear) may God keep Your Excellency as I desire. Madrid, 22 August 1626. Don Gaspar de Guzmán. Key: key.tsv

Fr. 3413 is a Nevers-collection volume of League papers, on Gallica as btv1b52510705j . No. 62 is ff. 126r–127r (views 259–261), and the address is on f. 127v: A Monsieur, Monsieur l’Abbé d’Orbais, Con er au Conseil estably a Paris pour la S te Union, A Paris . The abbé d’Orbais is Jean de Piles. He was the League’s envoy to Rome earlier in 1589 (targets/orbais/NOTES.md). (That he was later a deputy of the clergy at the Estates of 1593 is not from the sources and was not checked here.) The letter is dated only “du lieu que vous sçavez ce xxiij e d’Aoust”, but its content fixes the year. It reports how the news of the King’s death came to Rome. A courier from Spain had passed through Lyon on the 12th. The Grand Duke of Tuscany sent an express, which reached Rome on the 20th. The Grand Duke’s ambassador showed the Pope the original letter that the Duke of Lorraine had received, dated 8 August, from his agent in Paris, the s r Bardin: le Roy a esté tué, et c’est le Roy de Navarre qui l’a faict faire; l’on a proclamé Roy à Paris Monsieur le Cardinal de Borbon, et au mesme temps le Roy de Navarre s’est aussi faict appeller Roy par ceux de sa secte The writer apologises that his senior colleague, “son aisné de mesme charge”, has been kept from writing by a fever for a fortnight. He asks Piles to keep him in mind, and he signs in cipher.

Each key was photographed from the Gallica scan and tested against the ciphered groups: No. Folio (view) What it is On no. 62 53 f. 109 (227) A French key of letters to two-digit figures, with a nomenclator 1–99. Tomokiyo identifies it as Nevers collection no. 42. Does not apply: the letter has no figures. 61 f. 125 (257) An Italian key for the Savoy–Piedmont theatre (Birago, Saluzzo, Carmagnola…): a symbol alphabet, doubles, nulls, word signs, and a nomenclator 80–204. Different signs. It cannot give Cassin or protection . 69 ff. 137–138 (281–284) A French League key: a place-name nomenclator, boxed numbers, and a symbol alphabet written sideways on f. 138. Here the square is e and there is no W, so Cassin does not come out. Key no. 69, f. 138, the alphabet turned upright. It is a League key of the same period, but its square is e and its signs are not the letter’s. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3413 f. 138, via Gallica (btv1b52510705j).

Tomokiyo, cataloguing the Nevers ciphers, noted that no. 62 “appears to employ the Nevers–Piles Cipher” and deciphered Monsieur Cassin in it. Cassin appears as Pellevé’s secretary in the proceedings of the Estates of 1593. (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.) His table for that cipher was rebuilt from Piles’s own letters to Nevers of 1586 in BnF fr. 3612. That volume is not on Gallica, and the table has gaps. It does list word signs, among them ⌘ for Mr and n for et . The same cipher is used in BnF fr. 4715 f. 2 ( btv1b52509819x , view 17), the Cardinal de Guise to Nevers from Soissons, 6 October 1586. That letter is a full page of cipher, 29 lines, and the decipherer wrote the plaintext loosely above each line. Fr. 4715 f. 2r. Over the second cipher line the decipherer wrote encores … nouvelles de … qui s’est . Over the third, … vous aurez subiect d’estre satisfaict de nous … Je loue Dieu … aultant de content[ement] . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4715 f. 2r, via Gallica (btv1b52509819x, view 17). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3413 f. 127r, via Gallica (btv1b52510705j, view 261). The passage on f. 127r decrypts to “Depuis que Mr le […] mon maistre a esté retiré, j’ay veu ung advis qui confirme plus particulierement que nul aultre”: since his master withdrew, the writer has seen a notice that confirms the news of the King’s death more precisely than any other. ⌘ is Mr in Tomokiyo’s list of word signs and Ƒ is le , as the barred ʃ is in fr. 4715 ( pour le bien , le monde ). The sign between them, τ, has no entry anywhere; “Cardinal”, for Pellevé, is the likely sense, but it is not counted. The run begins with ʃ, which fr. 4715 gives as jay (“ʃ receu”, Jay receu ), and the next three signs give ung as in the 1586 letter. A constrained word search over a period French lexicon ranked confirme first among the candidates that make sense. After dedans deux jours , Ƒ = le and ħ = i (Tomokiyo’s second form of i) give le doien , the dean. The signature is the writer’s own name. In the key, 2 is b , and protection fixes the tailed m as o . The last sign is the H-form that is n in fr. 4715, so the name is Baron , not Barot. A “S r Baron” writes in the same League dossier of 1593 as Piles (Gallica btv1b9059406b , piece u, “Du S r Baron, du 7 aoust”). That identification is circumstantial. The run after vostre is not regne or Champaigne , as was guessed earlier. Fr. 4715 gives n = et and a = f , which make it et f e g n e , not sense. It stays open.

Measured over the fourteen runs: 91 cipher signs, 75 give sense, 82.4% (before the second pass with fr. 4715, the same count gave 47 of 91, 51.6%). Grades as in the table above: H for la protection , Cassin , vostre , maistre and Baron , C for the rest. Open, 16 signs: Re-measured 5 October 2026. The count stands at 75 of 91 signs (82.4%), now checked by a language-model score as well as by hand. On the native-resolution canvases the fifth sign of V2 carries an inner dot, so it is ⊡ = r and V2 decodes et-f-e-g-r-e ; in C the sixth sign is the hooked ʃ = y of fr. 4715 and C decodes v-o-p-a-e-y-s . Neither makes a word ( vos pays needs a missing letter), so neither is counted. The missing values would come from fr. 3612 f. 9, which is not digitised. Ƃ , the first sign of the depeschera run: the subject of the verb ( Sa Sainteté ? il ?). A single code sign with no entry in Tomokiyo’s table and none on the aligned part of fr. 4715. ʃ , the last sign of the same run. It is jay elsewhere, which does not fit here. τ , after Mr le : probably “Cardinal”, with no key entry. “pour ce qui touche φ tt o V æ ʃ° ÷ ”: the known values give v o p a e ? s , not sense. Vos amis and vos gens each need a value to break. “a vostre n a æ η ◻ θ ”: et f e g n e with the fr. 4715 values, not sense. Some values differ between the two letters. In fr. 4715, 8 is c and the plain m is r ; in no. 62, protection needs 8 = t , and the tailed m is o in both. Two squares ( n and u ) are told apart only by small differences of form. The rest of fr. 4715 f. 2 (lines 7, 9–11, 13, 16, 18 and 21–29) is not aligned sign by sign and might still give τ, ʃ°, Ƃ or the n–a pair. The real key source is Tomokiyo’s, BnF fr. 3612, six letters of Piles with interlinear decipherments. A new search of Gallica confirms it is not digitised; it has to be seen at the BnF.

Letter to the abbé d'Orbais, Rome, 23 Aug [1589], BnF fr. 3413 no. 62 A secretary of Cardinal Pellevé, signing Baron, writes from Rome to Jean de Piles, abbé d'Orbais, the League's envoy, with the news of Henri III's death: couriers from Spain, Genoa and Tuscany, and the Duke of Lorraine's letter from his agent Bardin in Paris, 8 August ('le Roy a esté tué, et c'est le Roy de Navarre qui l'a faict faire'; the Cardinal de Bourbon proclaimed King in Paris). In cipher: '[Ƃ] depeschera [ʃ] dedans deux jours le doien', 'la protection que vous sçavez', Mons. Cassin (his senior, ill with fever), 'Mr le [τ] mon maistre', 'j'ay veu ung advis qui confirme', the signature Baron. Cipher runs are marked in the Notes, not in the text. ## Reading Monsieur, nous ne cessons d'escrire pardeça et n'avons aucunes nouvelles de vostre part; nous en aurons pour l'advenir souvent et seurement, come je croy. Nous eusmes icy advis le xvij. de ce moys par un courrier extraordinaire qui venoit d'Espaigne, qui estoit passé à Lyon le xij., de l'accident qu'on disoit estre survenu à la personne du Roy, à quoy l'on ne faisoit fondement; les lettres de l'ordinaire du ix.e en faisoient aussi mention, et ung courrier de Gennes qui portoit lettres du xvij. dudict lieu en disoit beaucoup de particularités, et pour tout cela l'on n'y a pas donné grande creance jusques à dimanche qu'il en arriva un au soir, despeché exprès du Grand Duc de Toscane à sa Sainteté, accusant en avoir eu ung aussi exprès de Monsieur de Lorraine avec lettres escrittes à Nancy de l'xj.e d'Aoust, lequel courrier arriva à Florence le xix. mais si [?lassé] que le Grand Duc se resolut en despescher ung frais, qui arriva icy le xx.e sur le soir et s'adressa à l'ambassadeur dudict Grand Duc, lequel aussi tost s'en alla trouver sa Sainteté pour luy en donner l'advis, et luy monstra la lettre originale que Monsieur de Lorraine avoit receue du s.r Bardin, qui est son agent à Paris, en datte du viij. d'Aoust, laquelle lettre portoit ces motz: le Roy a esté tué, et c'est le Roy de Navarre qui l'a faict faire; l'on a proclamé Roy à Paris Monsieur le Cardinal de Borbon, et au mesme temps le Roy de Navarre s'est aussi faict appeller Roy par ceux de sa secte. L'on dict aussi que la grande Duchesse de Florence a eue lettres du mesme jour viij.e d'Aoust d'un sien qui demeure à Paris, qu'accusent semblablement la mort du Roy. Si ainsi est, je prie Dieu de bon coeur qu'il luy face pardon, et qu'il veuille avoir pitié de son ame. Les jugemens de Dieu sont fort profons et inscrutables. [Ƃ] depeschera [ʃ] dedans deux jours le doien. Devant cette nouvelle l'on n'eust sceu [?desirer] les choses mieux qu'elles estoient; pensés maintenant le reste. Dieu veuille que tout soit à sa gloire. Il ne vous fault rien dire pour ce qui touche […]. Il ne fault oublier la protection que vous sçavez pour beaucoup de raisons, qui est tout ce que je vous diray pour ceste heure. Me recommandant. Du lieu que vous sçavez ce xxiij.e d'Aoust. Avec vostre permission vostre treshumble serviteur Baron presente ses treshumbles recommandations à vostre bonne grace, et vous supplie l'excuser s'il ne s'acquitte mieux de son debvoir à vous escrire, estant si accablé d'affaires pour estre son aisné, de mesme charge, Monsieur Cassin, detenu d'une fiebvre dès il y a quinze jours. Maintenant que vous serez à vostre […] si l'histoire est vraye, il vous plaira, Monsieur, n'esloigner de vostre souvenance le moindre de vos serviteurs, mais le plus fidel et devot que pourrés jamais avoir, dont il vous fera à toutes heures bonne preuve quand il vous plaira, et sera tousiours prompt à aller executer vos commandemens sur les lieux, si vous luy faictes cest honneur de luy departir, et qu'il vous plaise l'avoir en vostre protection, de quoy il vous supplie treshumblement, et ne l'oublier aux occasions. Depuis que Monsieur le [τ] mon maistre a esté retiré, j'ay veu ung advis qui confirme plus particulierement que nul aultre. [?P.] A bien viene touts. ## Notes - **Cipher runs** (labels of `no62_cipher.txt`), in order: *[Ƃ] depeschera [ʃ]* (S1a+S1b, f. 126v l. 10-11); *le doien* (S2); *[…]* after *ce qui touche* (C, unread: v-o-p-a-e-y-s); *la protection* (P1+P2); *Cassin* (f. 127r l. 4); *vostre* (V1) and *[…]* (V2, unread: et-f-e-g-r-e) after *vous serez à*; *Monsieur le [τ] mon maistre* (G1+G2); *j'ay veu ung advis* (H); *confirme* (I); *Baron* (signature, f. 126v last line). - *[?P.] A bien viene touts* (f. 127r last line, in the same hand): a closing tag, half Spanish (*a bien viene*); not explained. - *Me recommandant* (f. 126v l. 17) runs into the dating line; nothing follows it. - *[?desirer]* (f. 126v l. 13, written *d?s?rir*) and *[?lassé]* (f. 126r, *laissé* in the hand) are read with doubt. Translation no62_en.md # BnF fr. 3413 no. 62: "Baron" to the abbé d'Orbais, Rome, 23 August [1589], English Translation of `no62_reading.md` (23 Oct 2026, Claude Opus 5.5, batch b31). Same holes. ## Translation Sir, we never stop writing from here and have no news from you; I believe we shall have it often and safely from now on. We had word here on the 17th of this month, by an extraordinary courier coming from Spain who had passed through Lyon on the 12th, of the accident said to have befallen the King's person, on which no one relied; the letters of the ordinary post of the 9th also mentioned it, and a courier from Genoa carrying letters of the 17th from there told many particulars of it, and for all that no great credit was given to it until Sunday, when one arrived in the evening, sent express by the Grand Duke of Tuscany to His Holiness, reporting that he had received one, also express, from the Duke of Lorraine, with letters written at Nancy on the 11th of August; that courier reached Florence on the 19th but [?so tired] that the Grand Duke decided to send on a fresh one, who arrived here on the 20th in the evening and went to the Grand Duke's ambassador, who at once went to find His Holiness to give him the news, and showed him the original letter that the Duke of Lorraine had received from the sieur Bardin, his agent in Paris, dated 8 August, which said in these words: the King has been killed, and it is the King of Navarre who had it done; the Cardinal de Bourbon has been proclaimed King in Paris, and at the same time the King of Navarre has also had himself called King by those of his sect. It is also said that the Grand Duchess of Florence has had letters of the same day, 8 August, from one of her people who lives in Paris, which likewise report the King's death. If it is so, I pray God with all my heart to pardon him and to have pity on his soul. The judgements of God are very deep and inscrutable. [Ƃ] will dispatch [ʃ] the dean within two days. Before this news one could not have [?wished] things better than they were; think now of the rest. God grant that all be to His glory. There is no need to tell you anything about what concerns […]. The protection you know of must not be forgotten, for many reasons; that is all I shall tell you for the present. Commending myself. From the place you know, this 23rd of August. With your permission your most humble servant Baron presents his most humble respects to your good grace, and begs you to excuse him if he does not do his duty of writing to you better, being so overwhelmed with business because his senior in the same office, Monsieur Cassin, has been laid up with a fever these fifteen days. Now that you will be at your […], if the story is true, may it please you, Sir, not to put out of your memory the least of your servants, but the most faithful and devoted you could ever have, of which he will give you good proof at any hour you please, and he will always be ready to go and carry out your commands on the spot, if you do him the honour of giving him them, and may it please you to keep him under your protection, which he most humbly begs of you, and not to forget him when occasions come. Since Monsieur the [τ] my master withdrew, I have seen a report that confirms it more precisely than any other. [?P.S.] Welcome to all. Key: key.md

Message A115 from the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre at Mogilev, in the double-box cipher under the daily key of 16 June 1942, published by Frode Weierud in 2020. Bletchley decrypted it at the time and Hanyok reproduced the decrypt: sixteen men of Police Battalion 51 killed, and the village of Borki razed and its inhabitants “liquidated”. The decrypt could not be aligned letter by letter with the 223 cipher letters, so the key was not recovered here. Where NARA, RG 457, Historic Cryptographic Collection, Boxes 202 and 1386, as published by Frode Weierud (CryptoCellar, 2020) and by Robert J. Hanyok, Eavesdropping on Hell (NSA, 2005). The cipher The double-box cipher: two 5×5 boxes, each letter pair enciphered twice through the same boxes, in the daily key of 16 June 1942 (discriminator ARTTN). 223 cipher letters. Where the text comes from Bletchley decrypted it at the time; Hanyok reproduces the typed decrypt. A key-free alignment of that text to the ciphertext, tried here, found no fit. What it says Sixteen men of Police Battalion 51 killed on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road; the village of Borki “dem Erdboden gleichgemacht” and its inhabitants liquidated. Still open A letter-by-letter check of the decrypt against the cipher, and the key, which need the exact enciphered wording. Credit Bletchley Park’s decrypt; Frode Weierud’s transcription of the intercepts; Ilya, a reader, located Borki. This page was split on 14 October 2026 from the page on the police radiograms of 1942. The five messages of 27 February 1942 are in another daily key, a different cipher with its own page: German police double-box radiograms of 27 February 1942 , which also describes the system and the failed ciphertext-only attacks.

A115 is Nr. 14 from Mogilev, callsign SQF, the station at the headquarters of the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre, handed in at 2325 on 16 June 1942 by its preamble and taken down at Beaumanor on 3742 kHz; stations 51 and 43 both copied it. Weierud’s paper, German Police Doppelkastenschlüssel Messages , transcribes it with the Red Forms of both stations. The first five-letter group, ARTTN , is the discriminator, which names the key and is not part of the text. The day’s key is not the key of the 27 February messages. The Red Form from intercept station No. 51: from SQF (Mogilev) to DQH (Berlin) on 3742 kHz, preamble NR 14 2325 228 ALQ , then the discriminator ARTTN and the text. Image: NARA, RG 457, HCC, Box 202, as reproduced by F. Weierud, CryptoCellar (2020). The cipher is the Army’s double box as the police used it from November 1941: two 5×5 boxes, the plaintext written in double lines (17 letters in the manuals, 21 in the Army’s NI variant), and each pair enciphered twice through the same boxes. The system, the manuals and the reference implementation are described on the 27 February page .

Hanyok’s Eavesdropping on Hell (NSA, 2005) follows this one message from intercept to decrypt, and reproduces Bletchley’s decrypt as entry 21 of that day’s German police decrypts: Bletchley’s decrypt of A115, entry 21. Image: NARA, RG 457, HCC, Box 1386, as reproduced in R. J. Hanyok, Eavesdropping on Hell (NSA, 2005). An Rf SS und Chef Orpo. An Strasse BOBRUISK–MOGILEW, Partisanenkampf: 16 Mann von Pol. Batl. 51 gefallen. Das Dorf BORKI, in dem Waffen und Munition gefunden wurden, wurde dem Erdboden gleichgemacht. Die Einwohnerschaft liquidiert. Von Höheren SS und Pol.führer Russland Mitte. To the Reichsführer SS and the Chief of the Order Police: in a fight with partisans on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road, sixteen men of Police Battalion 51 were killed; the village of Borki, where weapons and ammunition had been found, was levelled; the inhabitants were liquidated. From the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre. Hanyok notes that several villages named Borki exist in present-day Belarus and does not locate this one, but the place is well known: it is Borki in the Kirovsk district of Mogilev region, destroyed on 15 June 1942 together with the settlements around it (Zakrinichye, Krasny Pakhar, Dzerzhinsky, Proletary, Dolgoe Pole, Khvatovka). The operation was carried out by the Dirlewanger SS special battalion with Einsatzkommando 8 and police units after partisan attacks on the Mogilev–Bobruisk road; Dirlewanger’s own report counts 2,027 dead, and a memorial now stands on the site. Zhukov’s history of the Dirlewanger unit cites the same sixteen dead of Police Battalion 51 as the decrypt, so the message of 16 June is the Higher SS and Police Leader’s report of the Borki massacre. (Identification by Ilya, a reader, September 2026: Zhukov , Mogilev regional executive committee , partizany.by .) Because of this decrypt, Schmeh’s 2021 list of Second World War ciphers marks the group of messages “partially solved”.

The message is 228 letters in both intercepts and in the German preamble. Without the discriminator that leaves 223, but the cipher works on pairs and every enciphered text has an even length. The German clerk therefore added or dropped a letter, or a letter was lost in transmission. Where it went can be measured. A double-box cipher is deterministic on pairs, so a repeated plaintext pair in the same position of the layout gives a repeated cipher pair, and the pairs only show their repeats when they are counted from the right starting point. Counted from the end, A115 has 25 repeated digraphs of 19 types. Counted from the start it has 8, which is chance level. So the stray letter lies among the first nine or so, and the rest of the text pairs up normally.

A known-plaintext solver built for the February messages ( kpsolve.cs ) recovers the two boxes from about 80 plaintext–ciphertext pairs on synthetic controls (111 of 111 pairs consistent from random starts, 68 of 80 at 80 pairs). The decrypt of A115 should supply more than that, if the enciphered words can be placed under the cipher letters. Two aligners ( align115c.py , align115h.py ) tried to place them without any key: repeated cipher pairs must fall on repeated plaintext pairs, and the search backtracks exactly over spellings, X separators, numbers written out, address and signature placement, Borki / Mohilew / Bobruiisk variants, 222 or 224 letters, and line lengths 1–24. No combination gives a consistent alignment. The same search recovers a synthetic text spelled in one of the ways it tries in 35 seconds, and A115’s repeated cipher pairs are real (section 03). So either the words enciphered differ from Bletchley’s typed text, through abbreviation, order or extra matter such as a longer address, or the police layout differs from both manuals. The reading of the message therefore rests on the decrypt alone; it is not confirmed letter by letter here, and the key of 16 June was not recovered.

The letter-by-letter check and the key. They need the exact German wording that was enciphered, or about 80 pairs from another message of the same day. No other message of 16 June 1942 is in Weierud’s set. What an alignment would add. It would settle the police layout (lines of 17 or 21, left or right neighbour for same-row pairs) and show whether police boxes were random or built from a keyword; keyword-built boxes would open a keyword search on the 27 February key .
