As to the affairs of Italy I have nothing else to report, except that the same ideas and disposition towards peace are maintained, but no effort is spared to give every greater [443] […] to the provisions for war and to the advance of troops towards [?the frontiers]. The suspicions of the designs of France and of the [290] keep growing, that they are aimed at disturbing the affairs of the Empire. The [372], after obtaining the […] imperial sentence in his favour in the [?county] of Saarwerden, took possession of it by force of arms within a few days, and having sent a gentleman of his to inform His Majesty, he has had him ask for assistance for its defence, saying that five hundred [?horse] […] had come close to those [?frontiers] and that other troops were gathering there, insinuating that the French mean to [797] those passes for the design of making war in Germany; and from [?here] he has been promised assistance as he asked. [?But] greater commotion has been caused by the news brought by an express courier who came from [525] three days ago with letters of the twenty-sixth of last month: that the secretary, back from England, where […] went when called to negotiate peace [?with] that King, had reported that peace could not be concluded between the said crowns unless the Palatine is entirely restored to his state and to the electoral vote, and that this was the first article of the peace made with France, whose King has promised to help to this end with troops and money. All this the Lord [?Prince of Eggenberg] told me the day before yesterday, weighing the ill will of France and how badly the Elector of Bavaria would take it. It is many weeks since I saw in a letter written by the ambassador in England to this [649] that the said secretary had arrived there and was offering very rich terms, in particular to have restored to the Palatine not only the Lower Palatinate held by them but also the part held by Bavaria. To which he added afterwards, in further letters, that the Palatine, to whom this had been written, had not lent his ears, believing it all to be idle tales and that no reliance could be placed on the promises of the Spaniards. So one may suspect that the news now sent is a device to commit the Emperor further and force him to carry the war into Italy against France so as not to have it in Germany, and to divide Bavaria and make it suspicious and force it likewise to stay all the more closely united with the House of Austria. The ambassador of Savoy has also let it out that the [973] of the four cities of Languedoc have again begun to riot and that matters there are more broken than ever, though there is no confirmation of this from elsewhere, only of something at Montauban. Some take occasion to believe that these are [?mere] devices to give the imperials all the more courage to [?force] their entry into Italy, into the states of Montferrat and Mantua; and to the same end tends the saying that the French in Montferrat are reduced to seven or [?eight] hundred at most, which has likewise come from the said [ambassador] of Savoy. It is the opinion of a sensible person that, once the discontents of the Empire and the fears of a general rising cease with the dispatch of the troops to Poland and Flanders and with their march towards Italy, and the Empire being by the same means left as it were disarmed, and consequently in a state to hold the election of the King of the Romans - if it takes place, as is believed, at the beginning of winter - the settlement of the affairs of Italy will become much easier; which for the purposes mentioned must now be kept in suspense. The said election, however, is believed likely to suffer some delay from the accident of the new election of the Archbishop of Mainz, especially if he does not go about it with good legs; because with the pretext of the despatch he must await from Rome, of the regalia or investiture he must then obtain here, and of the need to settle the affairs of his church and gain enough knowledge and information of the affairs of the Empire before engaging in this very great function, he can put it off not only this coming winter but another one too; and even if he goes with very good legs, it remains very difficult for all this to be done by the beginning of winter. The Elector of Saxony is today much changed and estranged in will, not only over the church of Magdeburg taken from him and the others that it seems are to be taken from him under the imperial edict, but also over the suspicion he has formed that the aim is the destruction of the Lutheran religion and perhaps the humbling of all the princes of Germany and the removal of every counterweight to the House of Austria. He has declared himself much displeased with Count Trauttmansdorff and quite unwilling to come in person to the electoral diet, although they think he will not fail to send his ambassador. The Elector of Brandenburg shows himself just as well disposed, and from several sides there are excellent reports that he is about to declare himself a Catholic; and I am told as a thing almost certain, by a knight who has familiar correspondence with confidential ministers of His Highness, that when Saxony was speaking with Trauttmansdorff to the effect that he could not go to the diet because he would be alone, all the others being Roman Catholics, and Trauttmansdorff said that the Elector of Brandenburg would be there, Saxony replied in anger: I do not know; God grant he is not a Catholic too. Some are persuaded that he waits only for the return from Holland of Count Adam of Schwarzenberg, director of his council, a great favourite, who is a Catholic and a Knight of Malta, so that it may be seen to be his work, and also so that he may bring back the settlement for freeing his fortresses in the states of Jülich from the Dutch garrisons, since it would be impossible to recover them once he had declared himself a Catholic. May it please the divine goodness that it be true, and that this great increase be made to the Catholic religion and to the glory of Our Lord's pontificate. I do not fail, when the occasion offers, to encourage the said knight to further these inclinations, assuring him of His Holiness's fatherly disposition towards the person and house of that prince, and to make known with every fitting demonstration the esteem in which he would hold such a gain. Of the same Elector's sister, the wife of Gabor: some months ago (as I think I wrote) a very intimate servant of hers told Monsignor the Archbishop of Esztergom that she was much inclined to the Catholic religion. M.tà, e per li quali essa intercederà. S.re non sia ben affetto a S. M.tà, stante l'affetto e 'l credito che hanno gli Alemanni all'imperatore, massime in concorso del Papa e di Roma, e tanto maggiormente all'imperatore presente, in concorso de sensi et attioni del quale basterà per condennar quelle del Papa il credersi contrarie a' sensi dell'imperatore, io sarei di parere che per questa occasione non si disgustasse l'imperatore, né gli si desse materia di doglienze; ma che a' pretendenti si facesse insinuare che per facilitar le loro pretensioni procurassero una raccomandatione almeno generale da S. M.tà, o per lettere, o per mezzo dell'ambasciadore residente costà, o per mezzo del nuntio residente qua, il che ad ognuno sarà facilissimo ottenere e da loro non sarà giudicato difficile; o, quando in questo si trovasse inconveniente, stimarei che si potesse […] il segnar le suppliche tanto che si potesse far saper qua e sentir se S. M.tà havesse qualche senso particolare o circa la persona o circa la provisione che si domanda; il che procurarei far di modo che non restasse impegnato il nome de padroni, perché parlarei come se fussi ricercato qua da qualche amico di raccomandar quel tale costà, per haver informatione delle qualità di lui e del benefitio o dignità che ricerca; e quando li trovassi ben disposti, direi poi che fusse stato provisto per l'informatione data da me che 'l soggetto fusse grato a S. M.tà; e quando trovassi oppositione e difficoltà, avvisandone io costà, se paresse bene non provederlo, potrei pigliar occasione di rappresentar qua la stima che N. S.re fa del gusto di S. M.tà; e se non ostanti dette oppositioni paresse bene provederlo, potrei dire che con molto disgusto di S. B.ne e di V. S. Ill.ma l'avviso mio è stato più tardo che la diligenza di quell'huomo, il quale tanti giorni prima, havendo per altra via procurato detta provisione, ne haveva ottenuta la gratia. Quanto poi al modo o titolo delle provisioni, esprimer che li benefitii si provedono come vacanti propter haeresim, se bene si potesse sostenere anche secondo il tenor de compattati della pace di religione, nondimeno si potriano incontrar li pericoli e contingenze toccate da V. S. Ill.ma senza necessità; poiché crederei che senza specificar il titolo della vacatione bastasse il dire che il tal benefitio, dignità etc. si trovi al presente vacante, e secondo la dispositione de sacri canoni e de concordati con la natione Germanica la collatione e provisione di esso spetti di presente alla sede apostolica. M.tà e della religione cattolica, che l'intercessione di S. S. Ill.ma daria se[mpr]e […] di gran […], non sa per quello che farebbe S. M.tà; che egli, per la parte che [?gli toc]casse, serviria S. S. I did not think it right to speak of it with His Majesty before hearing the Prince; meanwhile His Majesty has gone out again to the hunt, where he will stay some weeks. Next week I shall go out to wait on His Majesty and shall speak to him [609] this business. As to the provisions of benefices and churches to be recovered, it is true that the Lord Prince declared to me that His Majesty did not claim, nor would let himself be drawn into claiming, what I was told, as I wrote on 7 April, namely the ius nominandi pro prima vice, so that he would not even be satisfied if Our Lord provided the persons His Majesty desired, unless the provisions were made as of persons nominated and presented by His Majesty; and this I think I wrote, or at least believed I wrote, in the plain letter of 9 June; but not that the Lord Prince and His Majesty give up the claim that, for His Majesty's merit, expense and zeal, for the service of God and the good provision of churches and bishoprics, it is not owed by the kindness and gratitude of the Apostolic See that the said churches be provided with suitable and deserving persons proposed by His Majesty and for whom he will intercede. I am persuaded nevertheless that they will come to see the fitness of the Apostolic See rewarding persons who have deserved well of the Catholic religion and of the Emperor himself, such as those Your Most Illustrious Lordship mentions in your letter, and I shall not fail to suggest it at suitable moments. As to the point Your Most Illustrious Lordship touched on in your letter of 28 April, I would not know what to say, except that - given the said claim, which is and will be fostered by those who hope to be provided through the Emperor; given the idea, which they have had and which cannot be uprooted, that Our Lord is not well disposed to His Majesty; given the affection and credit the Germans give to the Emperor, above all when set against the Pope and Rome, and all the more to the present Emperor, set against whose views and actions those of the Pope are condemned merely by being believed contrary to the Emperor's - I would be of the opinion that on this occasion the Emperor should not be displeased nor given cause for complaint; but that the claimants should be told that, to further their claims, they should obtain at least a general recommendation from His Majesty, either by letters, or through the ambassador resident there, or through the nuncio resident here, which anyone will find very easy to obtain and they will not think difficult; or, if this were found inconvenient, I would think the signing of the petitions could be […] long enough for word to be sent here and to hear whether His Majesty had any particular view about the person or about the provision requested. This I would try to do so that the name of the masters were not committed, for I would speak as if some friend here had asked me to recommend that person there, so as to have information on his qualities and on the benefice or dignity he seeks; and if I found them well disposed, I would then say that he had been provided on my information that the person was acceptable to His Majesty; and if I found opposition and difficulty, on my reporting it there, if it seemed best not to provide him, I could take occasion to represent here the regard Our Lord has for His Majesty's pleasure; and if, despite the opposition, it seemed best to provide him, I could say that, to the great displeasure of His Beatitude and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship, my report came later than the diligence of that man, who so many days before had obtained the provision by another way and had received the grace. As to the manner or title of the provisions, to state that the benefices are provided as vacant propter haeresim, although it could be upheld even under the terms of the compacts of the religious peace, one might nevertheless run into the dangers and contingencies Your Most Illustrious Lordship mentions, without need; for I would think it enough, without specifying the title of the vacancy, to say that such a benefice, dignity etc. is at present vacant and that under the provisions of the sacred canons and of the concordats with the German nation its collation and provision belongs at present to the Apostolic See. The [269] of Dohna, to whom I made known the order I had to recommend his person and house to His Majesty, has let me know that he would wish, in [?regard] of [his] great services in the past troubles, that [His Majesty] would grant him the favour of redeeming two estates [264] […] which the city of Breslau holds in pledge from His Majesty, and of giving him the title of prince over them. Before speaking of it to His Majesty I [?thought it best] […] to speak of it in confidence to the Lord Prince, as if for advice, saying that I would ask for it if he believed His Majesty could […] [?gratify] and oblige Our Lord and […] with that [702] token of His Majesty's love and goodwill towards Our Lord, and of seeing his intercession honoured; otherwise I would excuse myself […] with the Lord […] of Dohna, so as not to give occasion for cooling the new correspondence […] of affection which [337] we have tried to […] between His Majesty and [?Our Lord]. The Lord answered me that for a long time the […] of Dohna had been making this request, that Father La[…] had interceded very warmly for him, but fruitlessly, and that […] declared he would not make any more princes; but that notwithstanding […] I could make the representation, since [690] Dohna was a knight who had deserved very well of His Majesty and of the Catholic religion, and His Most Illustrious Lordship's intercession would always carry […] great […], though he did not know what His Majesty would do; and that he for his part would serve His Most Illustrious Lordship and help the Lord of [330] […]. So with this opening I shall resolve to speak of it […] at the first occasion. As to the matter of the baldachin, I shall await the orders Your Most Illustrious Lordship sees fit to give me; from here I have nothing to add to what I wrote in other letters, except that two days ago [540] told me [that] he has been written to from there, he does not know whether directly by the Sacred Congregation or by others, as [642] [992], of what great glory would […] to him if […] the satisfaction that is fitting in this with him. His Most Illustrious Lordship added: This glory I am content that the Congregation and Our Lord should gain, because I am in no position to break with the Emperor, and it is a good deal that he had the Prince of Eggenberg tell me that, although His Majesty does not wish cardinals to use the baldachin in his presence, since he knows that neither Spain nor France permits it, which are kings and not emperors, nevertheless it was neither his order nor his will that this be done in the way it was done; indeed he had been much displeased by it. That His Most Illustrious Lordship could not remedy it, but Our Lord could do so with two words, if, when the Emperor had a request made to him on the occasion of a promotion of cardinals, he answered that he wishes to please [His Majesty …] (continues on R294) R294, BAV, Barb.lat. 6960, pp. 75-76 (DigiVatLib pagination), 18 Aug 1629, Kiewning Nr. 160 (end) Cardinal Harrach, the Camaldolese foundation stone and the reform of the Augustinians. Ill.ma si è compiaciuta accennarmi circa la persona del padre Magno"). * **Paragraph 1 and the last paragraph**: Kiewning prints them in Italian. The page itself is largely in clear here; the clear words were re-read on the DECODE scans (DECODE's clear-text transcription of this record is mostly asterisks), the cipher runs checked against the decode. Valeriano hat ohne seine Teilnahme wegen der Carolina verhandelt ... ohne Befehl des Papstes und der Congregation ... Auch die Minister wundern sich darüber"). Read here from the figures (decode checked group by group on the scans, `R296_corrections.tsv`) and the clear words on the page. "Il p. Magno" / "detto p." is the Capuchin Valeriano Magni. `[?word]` partly carried, `[…]` unread, `[nnn]` a group not identified. --- Quel che V. S. Ill.ma si è compiaciuta accennarmi circa la persona del p. Magno mi è stato di non poco sollevamento in sopportar li suoi procedimenti, de quali fin hora ho solo scritto a V. S. Ill.ma quel che ho giudicato non poter tacere, senza mancar all'obligo preciso di suo servitore e di buon ministro di cotesta santa Sede; e V. S. Ill.ma si renda certa che, sicome l'ho sofferto fin hora, così lo farò per l'avvenire, ancorché con qualsisia repugnanza, col motivo di secondar li sensi di N. S.re e di V. S. Ill.ma. Io [?accertai] un pezzo fa V. S. Ill.ma che, havendo commesso il negotio de' beni ecclesiastici di Boemia, o almeno la divisione della rendita de' sali data in compensatione, al signor [275], al p. Valeriano et a me, li due unitissimi di volontà, sarebbe stata superflua la mia interventione. Hora conosco chiaramente non solo esser superflua, per le ragioni accennate, ma pericolosa, per la mira del padre che l'imperatore e tutti li altri conoscano che questo negotio così in Roma come qua è stato e deve esser guidato et eseguito secondo la sua direttione. Onde chiedevo per molto favore da V. S. Ill.ma, se si compiacerà, ch'io possa ritirarmi da questo negotio e lasciar che il p. Magno col signor cardinale facciano liberamente quel che il molto lor zelo gli detta, senza che altri entri a parte della gloria et honore di questo negotio, di che certo mi trovo senza alcuna ambitione. Il primo de li due [957] l'haveva [?accordato] senza nessuna difficoltà con li [?ministri] di S. M.tà; ma il p. Magno ha disegnato di farne tre, e […] m'ha dato parola, onde tien duro; e quante volte se n'è parlato, ancorché il signor cardinale mostri inclinar che siano per hora solo due, perché […] nella sua volontà, [?supponendo] che non sarà a quello discrepante la volontà del signor cardinale. Ma non ostante questo mi prometto di far che si stabilisca conforme al senso di V. S. Ill.ma prima che venga la risposta di […], senza che ella si resti punto impegnata o nominata. Potrei dir molto di questo buon padre, e particolarmente d'una mano d'impressioni con le quali haveva non poco alterato in questi giorni l'animo del signor cardinale; ma lo lascio così, per non tediarla, come perché non pensasse V. S. Ill.ma che io ne faccia più [593] di quel che conviene. Anzi in questo medesimo […] supplico V. S. Ill.ma a [?tener] in sé questo che le ho accennato, e non muover per ciò alla minima provisione o rimedio positivo, che non è punto […]; poiché per quel che tocca al signor [275] il tutto è aggiustato, perché [?S. S. Ill.ma] s'è chiarita che io non ho bisogno di legami o precetti [?sillogistici] per servir a [?S. S. Ill.ma], facendolo solennemente per mia volontà, et ha veduto e toccato con mani quello che passa, et è restato sincerato affatto, sì come anche il p. Magno è restato capace, e lo ha fatto anche, e se n'è confessato obligato, che io gli habbia dichiarata la mia natura e volontà altrettanto disposta et inclinata ad amarlo, […] e servirlo in tutto ciò che sinceramente mi rappresentarà di suo gusto e servitio, quanto d'offitii e servi[…], […] quando di vedersi tirar con industrie, artifitii e forza d'ingegno. Ma non devo lasciar d'accennarle che la scrittura data dal detto p. a S. M.tà e suoi ministri circa li beni di Boemia, prima che sia arrivata la minuta [?dell']instruttione di costà, è stata data senza mia participatione; e quando l'ho veduta non ho saputo finir [?d'approvarla], poiché, oltre a qualche parola della quale si poteva […], essendo la sostanza di essa più favorevole a S. M.tà di quella che sia la minuta venuta di costà, si dà occasione a questi d'[?impuntare] o di dire che costà si sia receduto, […] che, havendo il p. Magno avvantaggiato il partito di S. M.tà, sia stato abbassato da N. S.re o dalla sacra congregatione. Della scrittura non mando copia, supponendo che il p. l'habbia mandata a V. S. Ill.ma, secondo che le scritture date dal medesimo p. intorno alla Carolina, delle quali il p. mi dice [?haver] dato copia a V. S. Ill.ma, sono parimente state date senza mia participatione. E non so […] approvare che egli impegni il giuditio e volontà di N. S.re così francamente, e descendendo così a' particolari, contro una religione come quella de' [?Gesuiti], senza necessità, e, come io mi persuado, senza ordine preciso di N. S.re o della sacra congregatione; et ad alcuni ministri gravi, che me n'hanno parlato con maraviglia, ho detto non essere informato di questo negotio, ma non dubitar che quello che d'altri si potria offendere sia effetto del zelo del padre e non ordinatione di N. "Father Magno" is the Capuchin Valeriano Magni. --- What Your Most Illustrious Lordship was pleased to hint to me about the person of Father Magno has been no small relief to me in bearing his proceedings, of which until now I have written to Your Most Illustrious Lordship only what I judged I could not keep silent without failing in the precise obligation of your servant and of a good minister of that holy See; and Your Most Illustrious Lordship may be certain that, as I have borne it until now, so I shall do in future, however reluctantly, in order to second the wishes of Our Lord and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship. Some time ago I [?assured] Your Most Illustrious Lordship that, the business of the church property of Bohemia, or at least the division of the salt revenue given in compensation, having been entrusted to Signor [275], to Father Valeriano and to me, those two being entirely of one mind, my intervention would be superfluous. Now I see clearly that it is not only superfluous, for the reasons mentioned, but dangerous, because of the Father's aim that the Emperor and everyone else should know that this business, in Rome as well as here, has been and must be guided and carried out under his direction. I therefore asked Your Most Illustrious Lordship as a great favour, if you will be pleased, that I may withdraw from this business and let Father Magno and the Lord Cardinal freely do what their great zeal dictates to them, without anyone else sharing in the glory and honour of this business, for which I am certainly without any ambition. The first of the two [957] he had [?agreed] without any difficulty with His Majesty's [?ministers]; but Father Magno intends to make three of them, and […] gave me his word, so he holds firm; and every time it has been discussed, although the Lord Cardinal shows himself inclined that there should be only two for now, because […] in his will, [?supposing] that the Lord Cardinal's will will not be at variance with it. But in spite of this I promise myself to see that it is settled in accordance with Your Most Illustrious Lordship's view before the answer of […] arrives, without your being in the least committed or named. I could say much about this good Father, and especially about a handful of impressions with which he had in these days not a little upset the Lord Cardinal's mind; but I leave it at that, so as not to weary you, and also so that Your Most Illustrious Lordship should not think I make more [593] of it than is proper. Indeed in this same […] I beg Your Most Illustrious Lordship to [?keep] to yourself what I have hinted to you, and not to move on that account to the least provision or positive remedy, which is not at all […]; for as far as Signor [275] is concerned everything is settled, because [?His Most Illustrious Lordship] has satisfied himself that I need no bonds or [?syllogistic] precepts to serve [?His Most Illustrious Lordship], doing so solemnly of my own will, and he has seen and touched with his hands what is going on, and has been completely reassured; just as Father Magno too has been convinced, and has done so as well, and has confessed himself obliged, that I have declared to him my nature and will to be just as disposed and inclined to love him, […] and to serve him in everything that he sincerely represents to me as to his taste and service, as far as offices and serv[…], […] when he sees himself drawn by industry, artifice and force of wit. But I must not omit to point out to you that the paper given by the said Father to His Majesty and his ministers about the property of Bohemia, before the draft of the instruction from there arrived, was given without my participation; and when I saw it I could not bring myself to [?approve it], because, besides some word of which one could […], its substance being more favourable to His Majesty than the draft that came from there, it gives these people occasion to [?insist], or to say that there has been a retreat over there, […] that, Father Magno having advanced His Majesty's side, it has been lowered by Our Lord or by the Sacred Congregation. I do not send a copy of the paper, supposing that the Father has sent it to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, as with the papers given by the same Father about the Carolina, of which the Father tells me he has [?given] a copy to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, and which were likewise given without my participation. And I cannot […] approve that he commits the judgement and will of Our Lord so freely, and going so far into particulars, against a religious order such as that of the [?Jesuits], without necessity and, as I am persuaded, without a precise order of Our Lord or of the Sacred Congregation; and to some weighty ministers who have spoken to me of it with astonishment I have said that I am not informed of this business, but have no doubt that what others might take offence at is the effect of the Father's zeal and not an instruction of Our Lord or of the Sacred Congregation. I omitted to write to Your Most Illustrious Lordship with my last letters that, when His Majesty spoke to me of Father Magno, showing surprise that so much account had been made of him in Rome, I told him that the chief ground and motive of the marks of favour shown to Father Magno had been on His Majesty's account, because of the strong letters he wrote in his recommendation and because of the indications they had from his speech of the affection His Majesty bore him and of the confidence with which he dealt with the said Father; and that it was therefore right that His Majesty should keep a grateful recognition of all this, which I was telling him, and that His Majesty had believed that he would serve him well with his good offices, but that he had done the contrary. Dalla parte de' Spagnoli ho parimente nuovi rincontri, per quello che ha detto il marchese d'Aitona con suo confidente, che non vedano volentieri il duca di Fridland né altro capo grande passar in Italia con grande esercito; sì come che questi ministri si trovino anche essi in non picciola perplessità con la consideratione delle accennate difficoltà e delle maggiori che se gli sono per offerire nella prosecutione della guerra d'Italia; e con li avvisi che il Gabor o sia morto o non possa vivere, e che […] sia per sostituir altri non miglior di lui in quei stati, anche ne' comitati che devono dopo la sua morte tornar all'imperatore; e che il re di Francia, volto tuttavia a perturbar le cose di [?Germania], tenga tre gentilhuomini come incogniti per sollecitar gli animi de' malcontenti nell'Imperio, et unito con essi, e particolarmente con le [?città] libere, sia per entrar in persona con potentissimo esercito, facendo piazza d'armi in Argentina, col pretesto di procurar la restitutione del Palatino e la conservatione della libertà di Germania e dell'Imperio. Sento di buona parte che pensarono, con li apparati e con la presa de' [?passi] e con la fama del passaggio del generale con grande esercito, operare che Nivers si gettasse nelle braccia dell'imperatore, [?Venetiani] non ardissero dichiararsi, e Franzesi fussero anche essi per ritirarsi, così per rimaner soli come supponendo che si troveriano occupati con [665] [973]; e che con questo fusse per riuscir [?all']Imperio con facilità l'effettuar li altri gran disegni in Italia contro [?Venetiani] et altri. In che a questo [652] si crede che l'ordine dato ad Aitona di trattenersi sia proceduto perché di qua sia stato scritto in Spagna che il conte di Castro non sia bastante per portar il peso di questi gravissimi […]; e comunemente qua par che amino e stimino più il marchese d'Aitona che lui; et io non […] contento. On the Spanish side I likewise have fresh indications, from what the Marquis of Aytona has said to a confidant of his, that they do not like to see the Duke of Friedland or any other great commander enter Italy with a large army; and that these ministers too find themselves in no small perplexity, considering the difficulties mentioned and the greater ones that are bound to arise in pursuing the war in Italy; and with the news that Gabor is either dead or cannot live, and that […] is to put in his place others no better than he in those states, and also in the counties that after his death are to return to the Emperor; and that the King of France, still intent on disturbing the affairs of [?Germany], keeps three gentlemen here as if incognito to stir up the minds of the malcontents in the Empire, and, united with them and especially with the free [?cities], intends to enter in person with a very powerful army, making Strasbourg his place of arms, on the pretext of procuring the restitution of the Palatine and the preservation of the liberty of Germany and of the Empire. I hear from a good source that they thought, with the preparations, with the seizing of the [?passes] and with the report of the general's march with a large army, to bring it about that Nevers would throw himself into the Emperor's arms, the [?Venetians] would not dare declare themselves, and the French too would withdraw, both so as not to be left alone and supposing that they would be busy with [665] [973]; and that in this way the Empire would succeed in carrying out easily its other great designs in Italy against the [?Venetians] and others. And although so far they find their assumptions frustrated, nevertheless, finding themselves committed, and perhaps not entirely laying aside their hopes under the pretext and goading of the Spaniards, who would still like to regain some reputation and free themselves from the fear and jealousy of Casale; of Savoy, which aims to secure what it has gained in Monferrato and still to fish in troubled water; and of Guastalla, which seems to place in the rupture the increase and establishment of a great fortune, they do not cease to hurry their troops towards Italy. And I have it from a [?good] source that the general has been [?ordered] to come to terms, even at little advantage, and to disengage himself from Magdeburg and the other cities that might hold him back; so that the most sensible people think that only seeing […] resolved and ready to assist the allies in Italy powerfully can bring about peace, making the Spaniards persuaded that the [?league] could do them greater harm than leaving Nevers in the states of […] and Monferrato. Some days ago the [?secretary] of the Marquis of Aytona returned, who had been sent from here with money towards Nuremberg to pay the [?soldiery] that was afterwards made to pass into the Grisons, and military provisions for that enterprise; now the same Marquis is sending him to Spain. As far as the Count of Castro has told me, it is thought that he is to represent there the reasons why it is not fitting that a formed army of the Emperor should pass into Italy, and that in any case without sure and large assignments of money they will not march, and if they did march they would perhaps be more [939] [207] of harm; but so far I have not been able to find out with certainty what he is going for. The Marquis of Aytona has received orders to stay here until the affairs of Italy are concluded and [?settled]; the Count of Castro also said, until this business of [?England] is settled; which, since it can only be understood of the point of the restitution of the Palatinate, raised on the occasion of the peace with Spain, by which it is greatly desired, gives reason to believe that they have some intention of procuring it, in accordance with what I mentioned with my last letters had been written by the ambassador of [963]. In which, on this [652], it is believed that the order given to Aytona to stay has come about because it was written from here to Spain that the Count of Castro is not equal to bearing the weight of these very grave […]; and generally here they seem to like and esteem the Marquis of Aytona more than him; and I [do] not […] content. About the affairs of [?Flanders] marvels of success for us against the [?Dutch] are published every day; and lately they said that Count Henry had fought them for three days on end in the Veluwe, after which some six hundred of ours were found dead and over five thousand of the enemy; but from what I hear from the said ambassadors and their confidants, they think that Count Henry will be forced to withdraw for lack of victuals, and Bo[is-le-Duc?] […], impossible to relieve because of the impregnable [?fortifications] of the besiegers, will be forced to surrender to the enemy. Ho dato al signor Baron di Thun, maggiordomo del Re d'Ungheria, il breve che V. S. Ill.ma ha ottenuto in suo favore da N. S.re per il priorato di Ungheria in caso di vacanza; ne mostrò grandissimo gusto, e di restarne obligatissimo a N. S.re et a V. S. Ill.ma. Ma nel medesimo tempo ha dichiarato che il suo desiderio era col breve facultativo al gran mastro [?rilasciarsi] immediatamente per due fini: l'uno per assicurarsi di quelle difficoltà che li saranno suscitate in caso di vacanza, e l'altro per poter cominciar a ricuperar li beni che si trovano occupati di detto priorato; e che poi havrebbe desiderato restarne provisto ex nunc con titolo di coadiutore, il che però vorrebbe immediatamente dalla sede apostolica, mostrandosi molto sdegnato che il gran [?mastro] habbia fatto poco caso delle raccomandationi del Re d'Ungheria in suo favore, e che hora ad una semplice instanza del re di Francia habbia dato la gran croce ad un cavalier franzese che non è in conto alcuno da compararsi con lui né di servitii e meriti presso la Religione. Io gli rappresentai diverse difficoltà, e particolarmente che le coadiutorie non si concedono, o almeno senza che il titolare sia vecchio o infermo, il che non concorre nel prior d'Ungheria, e che egli non vi consenta; il che porterebbe difficoltà. Et il barone mi disse che non l'accettaria con queste conditioni, perché non ricercarebbe il consenso del priore né vorrebbe restargli obligato; ma che nondimeno sodisfarei al suo desiderio scrivendone a V. S. Ill.ma. Volsi prevenirlo con queste difficoltà, acciò o gli paresse men strana la negativa, o stimasse tanto più la gratia quando l'ottenga. Ne ha parlato poi col p. Magno, come suo amico e come quello il quale si tiene che possa tanto quanto vuole presso N. S.re e V. S. Ill.ma, e che habbia costà ottenuto cose non mai concesse et ad altri negate, in più [590], tra le quali si conta quella delle [?cappe] di Olmitz, dell'abbatia di Ber[…], le facultà, commissioni et esentioni concesse a lui e suoi compagni, la corrispondenza [620] e [226] che ha con V. S. Ill.ma, et altre simili prerogative e confidenze straordinarie. Per quel che intendo, il padre ha dato intentione del buon esito del negotio, per il quale si è offerto di scriverne a V. S. Ill.ma, a Paolucci et ad altri. Oltre alli motivi accennati di sopra, penso non ingannarmi in credere che il barone gusteria di poter portar la gran croce. V. S. Ill.ma considerarà se convenga consolarlo con un breve di [?coadiutoria], come egli domanda, o [?vero] un altro, dove, supponendo il breve di già mandato, si conceda che trattanto e fino che venga il caso pur di vacanza […] [?portar] della croce come priore, e procurar la ricuperatione […] del priorato, e di quelli che si ricupereranno da lui habbia l'administratione, e possa spender li frutti a suo arbitrio, purché sia in benefitio e servitio della medesima Religione. Il p. Valeriano mi ha detto haver significato a V. S. Ill.ma il discorso havuto col signor di Thun intorno al titolo di apostolico per il Re d'Ungheria, e che V. S. Ill.ma gli rispondeva che ne trattasse meco. Risposi esser negotio grave e da considerarlo, et informarsene bene per risponderne a V. S. Ill.ma, che io così havevo fatto, e desideravo lo facesse anche sua paternità per poter risponder di concerto; ma che a prima faccia mi pareva fuori di tempo il trattar questo punto, perché dar detto titolo come dovuto alli re d'Ungheria non stava bene alla sede apostolica, perché, quando pur li detti re havessero havuto ius per concessione apostolica al detto titolo, si era prescritto in contrario per il corso di centinara d'anni, e non n'havria riportato la sede apostolica merito né obligo alcuno dal re, perché l'havrebbe riputato dovuto, e per il medesimo capo non ne havrebbe fatto molta stima, come di cosa non conceduta in riguardo della persona e meriti di lui; e che il darlo come in riguardo del merito della sua persona l'impediva il trovarsi hoggi non solo delle dieci le otto parti de' regni d'Ungheria in mano d'heretici et infedeli, ma quella stessa piccola parte che si trova in nostra mano infetta per lo più d'heresia, anzi un asilo et una cloaca dell'immonditie di Boemia, Austria e Moravia, li cui predicanti et heretici discacciati tutti si ricovrano in Ungheria, dove si afferma che hoggi siano di tutte le sette d'heresia, e particolarmente d'Ariani, grandissimo numero; e che però si potria riservar il titolo di apostolico al moderno re, a similitudine di San Stefano, per quando Dio li havrà fatto gratia di ricuperar li suoi stati dalle mani d'infedeli et heretici e di piantarvi e stabilirvi la purità della religion cattolica. Che all'hora la sede apostolica con ragione l'honoraria di sì sublime titolo, e con altrettanta S. M.tà ne goderebbe e gioirebbe, come dovuto e proprio alla virtù e merito suo. The last paragraph from "because to give this title" follows the Roman decipherment printed by Kiewning (1897), Nr. 158; the rest is read from the clear words and the figures on the sheet. --- To Signor Baron von Thun, majordomo of the King of Hungary. I have given Signor Baron von Thun, majordomo of the King of Hungary, the brief that Your Most Illustrious Lordship obtained in his favour from Our Lord for the priory of Hungary in case of vacancy; he showed the greatest pleasure at it, and said he remained most obliged to Our Lord and to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. But at the same time he declared that his wish was, with the brief of faculty to the Grand Master, [?to be released] immediately, for two purposes: one, to secure himself against the difficulties that will be raised against him in case of vacancy; the other, to be able to begin recovering the occupied property of the said priory; and that he would then have liked to be provided now, ex nunc, with the title of coadjutor, which however he would want directly from the Apostolic See. He showed himself much offended that the Grand [?Master] has paid little attention to the recommendations of the King of Hungary in his favour, and that now, at a simple request of the King of France, he has given the grand cross to a French knight who is in no way to be compared with him, nor in services and merits to the Order. I put several difficulties to him, and especially that coadjutorships are not granted, or at least not unless the titular is old or infirm, which is not the case with the Prior of Hungary, and that he does not consent to it; which would cause difficulties. And the Baron told me that he would not accept it on these conditions, because he would not seek the Prior's consent nor want to remain obliged to him; but that I would nevertheless satisfy his wish by writing of it to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. I chose to forestall him with these difficulties, so that either a refusal would seem less strange to him, or he would value the favour all the more when he obtains it. He has then spoken of it with Father Magno, as his friend and as the man who is believed to be able to do as much as he likes with Our Lord and Your Most Illustrious Lordship, and to have obtained there things never granted and refused to others, in more [590], among which are counted that of the [?capes] of Olmütz, of the abbey of Ber[…], the faculties, commissions and exemptions granted to him and his companions, the correspondence [620] and [226] he has with Your Most Illustrious Lordship, and other such prerogatives and extraordinary confidences. From what I understand, the Father has given hope of a good outcome of the business, for which he has offered to write to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, to Paolucci and to others. Besides the motives mentioned above, I think I am not mistaken in believing that the Baron would like to be able to wear the grand cross. Your Most Illustrious Lordship will consider whether it is fitting to console him with a brief of [?coadjutorship], as he asks, or [?else] another one in which, supposing the brief already sent, it is granted that meanwhile, and until the case of vacancy comes, […] [?to wear] [the …] of the cross as prior, and to procure the recovery […] of the priory, and of what is recovered by him to have the administration, and to be able to spend the revenues at his discretion, provided it is for the benefit and service of the same Order. Father Valeriano has told me that he informed Your Most Illustrious Lordship of the conversation he had with Signor von Thun about the title of "Apostolic" for the King of Hungary, and that Your Most Illustrious Lordship answered him that he should deal with me about it. I answered that it was a grave matter, to be considered and well informed upon in order to reply to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, as I had done, and I wished His Paternity would do the same, so that we could reply in concert; but that at first sight it seemed to me untimely to raise this point, because to give the said title as due to the kings of Hungary did not befit the Apostolic See: for even if the said kings had had a right to the said title by apostolic concession, it had been prescribed against over the course of hundreds of years, and the Apostolic See would gain no merit or obligation from the King, because he would think it due, and for the same reason he would not much esteem it, as a thing not granted in regard of his person and merits; and that giving it in regard of the merit of his person was prevented by the fact that today not only eight parts out of ten of the kingdoms of Hungary are in the hands of heretics and infidels, but even the small part that is in our hands is for the most part infected with heresy, indeed an asylum and sink of the filth of Bohemia, Austria and Moravia, whose preachers and heretics, all driven out, take refuge in Hungary, where it is said that there are today a very great number of all the sects of heresy, and particularly of Arians; and that therefore the title of "Apostolic" could be reserved to the present King, after the example of Saint Stephen, for when God shall have granted him the grace to recover his states from the hands of infidels and heretics and to plant and establish there the purity of the Catholic religion. Then the Apostolic See would rightly honour him with so sublime a title, and His Majesty would enjoy it and rejoice in it with as much reason, as due and proper to his virtue and merit. Page 2 is read in part. --- After writing the [?cipher] I have learnt [that] these Spanish ambassadors are sending Bruneau to congratulate the new Elector of Mainz, but in fact so that under this pretext he may negotiate again with the [?said Elector] and with the other Electors, and particularly with that of [?Bavaria], to obtain the troops of the [?League] to relieve Bois-le-Duc, for which the Spaniards are greatly afraid. [?The one] whom the Marquis of Aytona is sending to Spain is not after all his secretary, but his equerry, [whom] he sent on other occasions, as I wrote, in the company of the secretary with the imperial troops to the Grisons. The said Bruneau told a person in his confidence that he thinks the Duke of Friedland will not go to Italy, because he has little wish to and goes there unwillingly, and that they too have little liking for his going, and that the same reasons would hold for anyone else; and that in fact they would be glad for the affairs of Italy to be settled, and that if something were proposed by way of compromise they themselves would help to make it take effect. And when this person asked him what compromise there could be, he let it be understood that if something were given to Guastalla and the French withdrew, matters would be settled, since they too would disarm and would see to it that the Emperor also withdrew from the Grisons (Rhaetia) and gave Nevers the [?investiture]. I have told this person to obtain leave to treat of it with me, and, to be sure that nothing has been said [or] understood wrongly, to bring it to me in writing, once he has first had it seen by Bruneau and by the Marquis of Aytona, with whom, this same person told me, the whole of this business rests. I do not doubt that it will meet with [546]-est reluctance in Nevers to give anything whatever to Guastalla; but I also hold it for certain that His Highness, and much less the Venetian lords, will not think it expedient, for an interest to the sum of a hundred thousand scudi, to [?expose] themselves to a most dangerous and very long war, which in a single month, in one week, costs it much […]. Nor am I at all sure, nor do I promise myself, that in the end the Spaniards or the Emperor will want it, above all if affairs in Italy or in Flanders go […] their [?dis]advantage. But without claiming that those who must be most watchful should [?remain] asleep on that account, and to prepare [?themselves] […] to promote [676] business, for […] and I […] within the terms prescribed [?to me] by [976], whom I beg to let me know, in case the treaty went [?forward], [?the] treaty, [?where] […] to govern myself on the point of the promotion of Don Cesare […] [?came] […] moved […]. Valeriano Magni's second writing on the Carolina. Kiewning gives a German regest with two Italian passages. * **The Italian passage** "quando l'efficacia ... e della sede apostolica" is Kiewning's print (OCR corrected); the figures and the clear words on the sheet agree with it (log). * **The rest**: the sheet mixes cipher with words in clear. The cipher is read from the figures (the decode with the 6956 key, `reread_b01/R301_dec.txt`, checked with its codes), the clear words from the DECODE scans (IMG_R301_I2533, I2534; DECODE's clear-text transcription is often wrong, `R301_corrections.tsv`). The right edge of p. 2 is cut off in the scan, so the last word or two of some lines there are missing. Kiewning's regest confirms each step (the writing shown to no one, more against the Jesuits than the first; Klesl and Pallotto with the Father; to the Emperor tomorrow and then to Nikolsburg; Bohemia; never to see the Emperor again; persuaded to show it to Pallotto tomorrow; the Jesuits "pupilla de gli occhi dell'imperatore"). * The sheet ends in the middle of a sentence ("la qu-"); the continuation (register p. 78) is not among the DECODE images: IMG 2534 is followed directly by 2535 (R302, "A 79", 28 August). I induced the Father to tell me the substance of the said writing, he saying that I would not on that account be prevented from [?affirming] that I had not seen [it]; and, seeing clearly that it would give grave offence, to the prejudice not only of his person but of the business itself and of the others who carry its weight with him, I tried to persuade him [to hold it back] at least eight or ten days, in which time I was sure no answer or order could come from there about anything written; and, after he had given the first writing to His Majesty, to see in the meantime what the said writing and his own spoken word could achieve with His Majesty and with those deputed [to] this business by His Majesty. This morning, when he was with me together with the Lord Cardinal, he told me he had put the last hand to the said writing, had added to it a most beautiful letter to His Majesty in the form of a [?fraternal] correction, that […], and that he was resolved to give [it] to His Majesty tomorrow, and then to go off at once to Nikolsburg; and if he did not hear from there that it had had the effect intended, he would go to Bohemia, to attend there to the business of the propagation of the faith […], and would never again see, let alone speak to, the Emperor, holding it a very great honour, indeed a glory, if in this way and for this cause he should leave not only the court but His Majesty's states as well; setting out other ideas which Your Most Illustrious Lordship can very well infer from the Father's vehemence. The Lord Cardinal had advised him against coming at present to this [662], and to defer it at least until the business of the church property was settled; but the Father would not bend. [762] seeing the very grave drawbacks that could be feared from such an action, not only on the part of [the] Emperor but for Father Valeriano too, if the force and skill of his mind, tongue and pen committed themselves so far and made this particular cause the universal cause of all the religious orders, of the Jesuits and of the Apostolic See, I showing myself to agree […], and without blaming or rejecting the Father's motives and reasons, […], he showed himself persuaded [532] give the said writing, but rather to let me see it and to [?amend it] according to my opinion. […] chiefly with the thought of being able to [?send] a copy this evening to Your Most Illustrious Lordship; but he had said that tomorrow […] he would come here to bring it to me; and so as not to disquiet him, make him suspicious or anger him, I have put no further pressure on him. In truth I know that the reasons put to him so far have made […] impression; they would have made a much greater one if he had refrained from touching […] on particular matters the Jesuit Fathers, who without doubt are the apple of the Emperor's eye. So I have wished to report all this to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, that you may know what is happening in so grave a business, [in which] that [920], the Sacred Congregation and the very person of […] are so much engaged; and that you may be forewarned in case some effort should be made there, on the part of the Jesuit Fathers or of His Majesty himself, to discredit the representation made by Father Magni; being sure that the singular prudence and […] of Your Most Illustrious Lordship, so that, even if it should please you to attribute some particularity or excess [?of pen] to the Father's vehemence, […] of the business remain confirmed in the ideas and sense of the Sacred Congregation and of […] in this matter; in which it will be of much […] if the occasion is taken away from whoever [it may be] to make himself there the interpreter of the will of Our Lord and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship, which ... The sentence on the intercepted Spanish letter follows Kiewning's print (Nr. 167); the rest is read from the figures and the clear words on the sheet. The despatch continues on R303. --- Bruneau has left on the journey I wrote of; and beyond the purposes reported, it is no great matter that he will have [to] diminish for him what the extraordinary courier from Spain [227]a[693] in the past days about the [?capitulations] of the [922] with the [?King of England] on the recovery of the […] and the electoral vote in favour of Frederick. When the accommodation of the affairs of Italy was raised with Bruneau again, he showed himself rather cold than otherwise; […] that person has told me that he wanted to speak of it to the Marquis of Aytona. But I place no reliance on it, because, although His Excellency shows himself desirous of peace, and says there will be time all this winter to negotiate […] that meanwhile the Queen will come and the wedding will be held, and the imperial troops will only hold the passes and not advance towards Italy, since the Duke of Friedland in Italy does not suit them, and that there is [652] little hope of holding Bois-le-Duc; nevertheless it is known on the other side that all their designs are [?turned] to the affairs of Italy, to driving out Nevers and with him every jealousy the French could cause, and to recovering […] all they have lost or are about to lose in Flanders, where they think of making a very long [?truce], whether Bois-le-Duc is kept or lost, and in every worse way. And the camp master Aldringen has left for Italy, and with him several [?colonels], among them Count Strozzi, as is written in letters of the twentieth from [?Halberstadt], where the General was still staying. And I am told that a letter of the Catholic King has been intercepted, addressed there to the Count of Monterrey, in which he wrote to him to sound out Our Lord about some settlement that had reason in it, so that if France did not accept it the Catholic King's cause would stand all the more justified, and if it accepted, he would have it rejected afterwards by the Emperor. [Which], if true, will show all the more clearly their aim of advancing their p[…], a tacit confession of what they intend, and of a want of justice on the part of the Apostolic See. In answer to Your Most Illustrious Lordship's [369] of the eleventh of this month, I will not fail to point out to Your Most Illustrious Lordship that in mine of the twenty-first of last month I reported [250] weighty reasons that had made me […] letter that […] to send the packet […] the Duke of Poli […] his [?son], of which there were two principal ones: the one, the opinion that […] that the aim was not only to keep […] but […] other people's states, and he did not doubt they would infer this as much from the summoning of the said Duke as from the [?conferring] of the title of lieutenant general once he had left the Catholic King's state; the [736] that […] the same [359] would not accept the post, being at present employed [555] in [405] with an immediate increase of post and emolument, and with […] and with […] so great and so great and so well founded that [537] it could be worth leaving them. But I wrote that [?for] the said reasons I had resolved [to] send the said packet by a discreet and confidential person; but it could happen that in the circumstances of the march […] the said Duke, and that therefore on the arrival [of] Your Most Illustrious Lordship's answer the packet [?might] be found in my hands. I have wished to report all this so as to be able to take new care [over] its delivery, with the certainty of meeting the will of Our Lord and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship. By other letters of mine Your Most Illustrious Lordship will have seen that, having learnt that the Duke had stopped ill at Hamburg, and therefore fearing that the report of his departure might have led the messenger astray, I resolved to write to Signor T[orquato] by the opportunity of a paymaster which I judged safe, on the thirtieth of last month; to which I have not yet had an answer. Read from the figures and the clear words on the sheet; Kiewning (1897) Nr. 167 gives a German regest that confirms the sense. --- … and if […] he has not had it, on [?Friday] I shall send again, [?this] time with every care. What I wrote in other letters of the haste with which Wallenstein was being pressed to cross into Italy I heard from the very mouths of the chief ministers of this court and of the Prince of Eggenberg, indeed from the [?Emperor] himself; but at the same time I believe I indicated […] difficult, chiefly because it was thought that the Spaniards could not consider it expedient to their interests. I shall make use, when the occasion offers, of the information Your Most Illustrious Lordship is pleased to give me about the indult that it has been resolved to grant to the [690] Leopold William; but […] [930] I shall make no move, since Your Most Illustrious Lordship gives me no hint of it, just as I have not done regarding what you wrote to me in your last letters about the letter written to you by Her/His Majesty [564], which I am glad to believe Your Most Illustrious Lordship will not have failed to answer, and will have sent the letter by another hand. I have received one by this ordinary addressed to the Emperor, and not knowing what it contains, I shall simply deliver it, without accompanying it with any other representation. I await with longing the decision on the matter of the visitor or vicar apostolic for the diocese of [?Aquileia], because the delay in this business, besides the grave spiritual harm, can bring in present circumstances other, not slight, temporal and political harm. As to the representations made by the imperial ambassador there on the matter of a promotion, I am sure Your Most Illustrious Lordship does not doubt that I had the least part in them; and I can further affirm to you with most sincere truth that I had not even the least knowledge of them, just as I can equally affirm that I have no such pretension nor such aim, but only to serve well […] Our Lord and that […]; and when God grants me the grace to do so, and Our Lord and Your Most Illustrious Lordship are persuaded that I have done my part as well as I can, if not as I ought, […] to have obtained [the] most sublime reward and recompense I could hope for; and with this, everywhere and in the hovel of my house, I shall acknowledge and profess myself obliged and grateful to the person and house of Your Most Illustrious Lordship equally with anyone else. And from what I indicated in my [326] of […] about Klesl's baldachin, you will have been able to see some proof of how detached I am from such a pretension, above all where the interests of that [920] are concerned […]. Read from the figures; Kiewning (1897) Nr. 168 gives only a three-line German regest, which confirms the first paragraph. --- Notwithstanding the arrangement made with Father Magni not to give the letter and writing mentioned in my letters of Saturday about the Carolina, he saw fit the following day, without telling me anything more, to send the letter to His Majesty and to give the writing to Count [?Slavata], one of the deputies; having learnt it from him, and spoken of it with the Father, he says […] sent a copy to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, [and] that he judged it necessary to give them because the business was asleep, […] and that he has grounds to think that an order is expected from there excluding him from this business, and that before such an order comes he wants to have given […] and perhaps to the Congregation […] writing, so that it cannot […] back […], and the Sacred Congregation stays committed in the name of the [667] and of Our Lord. He handles this [549] with letters of credence from the same Sacred Congregation; […] that, once the said writings are given, and if […] at once the effect he intends, he does not want to leave before the [566] […] comes from there, because […] and not to suffer a check nor be affronted by the business being put in other hands while he [690] has it […]. I have not thought fit to go to any other means with the Father than persuasion; not because I fear his force and […] [650] more than is proper, but because this business has been committed to the said Father and entrusted to his zeal and prudence without any subordination; and [966] in [?these] days I have seen the privileges granted to him there, by virtue of which he, with three companions, is exempted from every other superior of his and made subject immediately to the power, jurisdiction and direction of Our Lord or of the Sacred Congregation, solely in the business committed to them by them, to whom all his actions and negotiations can very easily be referred. So that […] it remains for me to wish that the writing now given by the Father, with the others given […], may be [?found] there to conform to the commissions and ideas communicated to him by Our Lord and the Sacred Congregation, and may produce good effects with the Emperor and [other] ministers, as the zeal of the Father himself […]. Had I known of his exemptions, I [?would] not have told the Emperor that the said Father [?would] in that be subordinate to me, and that I could have made provision when it was necessary; and I should be sorry if His Majesty took occasion to attribute to lack of sincerity what I said in good faith […] principle [326], because […] that exemptions from nuncios and ministers of the Apostolic See are never granted to any kind of person; and […] on the surer ground of what Your Most Illustrious Lordship was pleased to write to me […], and particularly in yours of 26 May and 2 June. And the truth is that in the patents granted to Father Magni for Upper Germany and for the kingdom of Bohemia he is not made subordinate to [?any] superior, but only that he proceed "requisito consensu" […], in the first […] of the Nuncio of Cologne and in the second of the Archbishop of Prague, without any [?mention] of the [552], although the countries spoken of are subject to this [559]. But since this is a point that depends on the will of our masters, it is not my part to do other than […]; I cannot allow it to be felt that in my time the dignity and reputation of this [550] should suffer so great a prejudice, which, as I know it was not [?given me] for my claiming or seeking it, knowing very well, indeed weighing, my small ability and merit [?before] I came here, so I should not wish to see it prejudiced by reason of my person, […] by the sole excess of kindness of Our Lord and [679] Your Most Illustrious Lordship [967] the Sacred Congregation […] has rested and still rests here […]. E. che, mentre il re di Francia scrivesse all'imperatore sincerando la buona intentione che S. M.tà ha havuta nella sua venuta in Italia, e di non pregiudicar alla dignità e giurisditione di S. M.tà Ces.a, e lo pregasse ad haver per raccomandato per amor suo la causa et interessi del signor duca di Nivers, e nel medesimo tempo ritirasse le sue truppe del Monferrato e di Susa, la Christianità e l'Italia incontinente haverebbe la pace, e 'l re Christ.mo conoscerebbe con effetti la stima che l'imperator fa di S. M.tà, e quanto la sua intercessione fusse di giovamento et utile al signor duca. Andai insinuando al signor principe le difficoltà e gelosie che si offeriscono a questo temperamento, e la moral sicurezza che sarebbe necessaria per levar il timore che si voglia appresso il deposito, che a Nivers gli habbia a pregiudicare la pretesa disobedienza e chiamata de' Franzesi, e che in vece di giovamento gli havesse portato la rovina co 'l perdimento delle sue ragioni, e che li passi de' Grigioni habbino sempre a restar chiusi a gli aiuti forastieri de' principi non confidenti a casa d'Austria. Insinuai parimente il temperamento per rimedio del primo senza intacco della reputatione imperiale: il concedersi l'investitura senza pregiuditio delle ragioni degli altri interessati, et in sostanza senza canonizatione delle ragioni del duca, fa solo che le cose rimanghino nello stato in che si trovano sino alla decisione. Del secondo, che si citassero le parti a dedur le ragioni che gli competono sopra li stati per la morte dell'ultimo duca Vincenzo. Del terzo, che ritirato primo il re di Francia del Monferrato, li passi di Susa e della Retia si lasciassero nel medesimo tempo. Mostrava il principe non far difficoltà nella sostanza, ma nella circostanza, che trovandosi le arme di Francia in Italia tutto ciò che l'imperatore facesse pareria fusse per timore di dette armi. Addussi diverse ragioni in contrario. Uscì il principe, quanto al primo punto, che ad instanza d'altro principe si potrebbe conceder l'investitura in quella forma; ma volendo stringer questo punto tornò pure a dire che non si poteva fare se prima Francia non si ritirava, perché pareria fatto per il medesimo timore. Non ostante che io replicassi che già si era fatto veder al mondo non si temer il re di Francia, né farsi caso di sue instanze accompagnate, come il principe diceva, dalle minaccie, con le risposte così chiare e risolute date a Sabran; et aggionsi poi che la detta investitura si potria dar in confidenza, che non si mostrasse se non dopo partito il re; che si potria far con data posteriore alla detta ritirata. Ma il signor principe persistè sempre saldo nell'accennata difficoltà, e che, mentre non si voglia ritirare, si farà entrar il duca di Fridland, et all'hora, dando S. M.tà la sentenza, si conoscerà che non la dà per timor del re, e se troverà difficoltà nell'esser eseguita, si farà eseguir con la spada. Ma dall'altro canto si sa ch'il mastro di campo Aldringher era avanzato verso li passi con grosso nervo di gente, e che ne' paesi di quei confini si davano piazze, mostre, et assegnavano tappe per ventiduemila [?huomini]. Paragraphs 1-3 follow the Roman decipherment printed by Kiewning (1897), Nr. 170; paragraphs 4-6 are read from the figures and the clear words on the sheet. --- In a long conversation I had the day before yesterday with Prince Eggenberg, while we spoke of current Italian affairs, His Excellency declared that if the King of France wrote to the Emperor to assure him of the good intention His Majesty had had in coming into Italy, and of not prejudicing the dignity and jurisdiction of His Imperial Majesty, and asked him to hold the cause and interests of the Duke of Nevers recommended for his sake, and at the same time withdrew his troops from Montferrat and Susa, Christendom and Italy would at once have peace, and the Most Christian King would see by deeds the esteem the Emperor has for His Majesty and how much his intercession had been of help and use to the Duke. I went on suggesting to the Prince the difficulties and suspicions that this arrangement raises, and the moral security that would be needed to remove the fear that, with the deposit, the alleged disobedience and the calling-in of the French might be held against Nevers, and that instead of help it might have brought him ruin with the loss of his rights; and that the passes of the Grisons might always remain closed to foreign help from princes not trusted by the House of Austria. I likewise suggested the remedy for the first without damage to imperial reputation: to grant the investiture without prejudice to the rights of the other parties, and in substance without sanctioning the Duke's rights, only that things should stay as they are until the decision. For the second, that the parties be summoned to set out the rights they hold over the states by the death of the last Duke, Vincenzo. For the third, that once the King of France had first withdrawn from Montferrat, the passes of Susa and of the Rhaetia should be given up at the same time. The Prince showed that he made no difficulty about the substance, but about the circumstance: that while the arms of France were in Italy, whatever the Emperor did would seem to be done for fear of those arms. I brought various reasons to the contrary. On the first point the Prince came out with the view that at the instance of another prince the investiture could be granted in that form; but when I wanted to press this point he again said that it could not be done unless France first withdrew, because it would seem done out of the same fear. Although I replied that it had already been shown to the world that the King of France was not feared, nor his demands heeded, accompanied as the Prince said by threats, with the very clear and resolute answers given to Sabran; and I added that the said investiture could be given in confidence, not to be shown until the King had left, and that it could be dated after the said withdrawal. But the Prince held firm throughout on that difficulty: if he will not withdraw, the Duke of Friedland will be sent in, and then, when His Majesty gives the sentence, it will be seen that he does not give it for fear of the King, and if there is difficulty in carrying it out, it will be carried out with the sword. The Duke of Friedland seems to be in no great hurry now; they say it is because they are waiting to hear the King of France's resolution [?after] Sabran's negotiation; but others put it down to the lack of provisions and money, to the obstacles and difficulties they find with the Spa[?niards], who aim meanwhile to wear out the Venetians and other princes of Italy with the expense until the new season; and finally that they fear to strip this country of men, things being troubled, and above all with the efforts of the French, of [?which] the Prince himself complained, exaggerating them sharply. But on the other hand it is known that the Maestro di campo Aldringen had advanced towards the passes with a large body of men, and that in the lands on those borders mustering places and musters were being given out and stages assigned for twenty-two thousand [?men]. Our Prince told me of the representation made by the imperial ambassador there on the matter of the promotion, and that he was answered with […], without specifying the particulars Your Most Illustrious Lordship mentioned to me. I do not know whether, so as not to consider himself [907] obliged to open himself further [?about] the [?affairs] of the peace, or because nothing else has been [?specified] to him by that ambassador. On the [?rank] of [?legate] he told me he had in answer that Our Lord would inform himself of the usual practice and would consider what [?he can] do; and he mentioned that at the wedding of Mat[?thias], when he was King of Hungary, Signor [277] was deputed as [?legate]; the King went out to meet him, but made the entry and gave him first place in his carriage; which carriage, however, I have heard at other times from Signor [207] was so made that it had neither first nor second place. I did not want to omit mentioning this to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. From another reliable quarter I have word that with Lorraine one must go very carefully in these affairs, and that France keeps its eyes well open with him. E. medesima per l'accomodamento delle cose d'Italia, come ho scritto con altre mie, insinuando come discorsi di speculativi e senza impegnar non solo i padroni, ma ne anche le parti, che non batteva la difficoltà nel punto di reputatione, come mostravano di pensare, poiché in questa parte si crede che si daria molto vantaggio a quella dell'imperatore, ma nelle gelosie e sospetti che dalli interessati si concepiscono, e per quanto essi pretendono non senza fondamento, circa la sostanza: cioè che, ritirati i Franzesi, si habbia la mira di voler di nuovo il deposito; che la decisione della causa non habbia da versar sopra 'l punto della successione, ma più tosto sopra la devolutione per la pretesa disubidienza e per la chiamata de' Franzesi, a fine di haver così la libera dispositione di detti stati, mentre Nivers non condescenda alla permuta, presidio o demolitione a sodisfatione de' Spagnuoli, et a rilasciar tanta parte de' stati a Savoia, Lorena e Guastalla quanta basti per contentarli e debilitar il duca e rendergli dannoso il soccorso de' Franzesi; e finalmente che si habbia la mira a non lasciar poi liberi li passi della Retia. E come questi professano sempre tutto il contrario de' sudetti concetti, hebbi campo di stringer che, stante questo, si renderia forse facile l'aggiustamento, del qual parimente si dichiarano desiderosi. Intanto sopragiunsero il palatino d'Ungheria e monsignor arcivescovo di Strigonia per trattar delle cose di quel regno, che trovavano in grandissimo pericolo ugualmente con la vita come con la morte di Gabor, e fecero l'uno e l'altro efficacissimi uffitii per l'aggiustamento delle cose d'Italia, come necessario per poter assistere alli bisogni et impedir le rovine di quel regno. Disse il signor principe d'Echembergh a monsignore haver lungamente discorso meco e di haver presi alcuni appuntamenti; ma dicendo io a monsignore ciò che era passato e quello che stimavo necessario per venir a qualche conclusione, tornò l'istesso giorno dal principe, et a me riportò immediatamente li sensi et appuntamenti presi con S. E., conforme a' quali havendo io formato la minuta di lettera per darne conto per corriero espresso a V. S. Ill.ma, e mostratala il giorno seguente a monsignor sudetto, e da questo essendo stata approvata dalla prima all'ultima parola, ma particolarmente quanto alli punti sostantiali come conformi all'appuntato da S. S. Ill.ma con S. E., quasi mi credetti haver concluso il negotio, poiché havendo destramente sentito monsignor vescovo di Mantova e questo residente di Venetia non li trovavo lontani. Ma andato poi dal signor principe e lettagli la detta scrittura, trovai li sensi di S. E. molto differenti, et in effetto che 'l re di Francia scriva a S. M.tà Ces.a e nel medesimo tempo ritiri le sue armi non solo dal Monferrato, ma da Susa ancora; e che 'l duca di Mantova domandi perdono della disubidienza e della chiamata de' Franzesi, e riconoscendo l'errore commesso; e dall'altro canto che S. M.tà non prometta né assicuri il possesso de' stati al duca (ancorché insinuasse, ma senza impegno, che gli si lasciaria), che gli faria gratia e concederia perdono delli errori commessi in modo che si conosceria l'affetto di S. M.tà, e che fusse stato giovevole al duca l'intercessione del re di Francia (con termine però che 'l parlar di S. E. si potria verificar quando anche una parte de' stati gli fusse concessa); e finalmente che quanto a' passi della Retia si metteria in negotio e si sentiriano le parti interessate, accennando del vescovo di Coira, e che li passi siano di quella chiesa, e che N. S.re doverà haver caro che più tosto a quella che ad eretici restino in potere; aggiungendo che a casa d'Austria molto più importi non lasciar questi passi che di levar Francia da quello di Susa. Se ben viddi le cose mettersi in termini così duri, procurai nondimeno non troncar affatto il filo del trattato; e quanto al possesso dissi che, molto cessavano li timori dell'affetto, pareva che S. M.tà per sua libera volontà, come cessando le cagioni che lo mossero al sequestro, e non per sodisfar ad altri, potrebbe lasciare che non s'innovasse circa 'l possesso contro la volontà delle parti. Quanto al perdono, che questa formalità e la confessione del duca si potria considerar pregiuditiale alla solida reputatione del duca e della sua successione, nella quale vi era indelebilmente la mistura del sangue Austriaco, anzi alla dignità di S. M.tà, essendo molto più che questa non fusse stata offesa, che offesa havesse concesso il perdono; e però che la bontà e generosità di S. M.tà havria largo campo di esercitarsi senza pregiudicar al duca e molto meno a' nepoti e pronepoti, senza dubbio innocenti. Quanto al punto de' passi insinuai che si potria trattar di pigliare per temperamento che sino alla decisione della causa restasse S. M.tà in Grisoni e Francia in Susa, et aggiustato il resto si trovarebbe ripiego anco a questo. Havendo riferito a monsignor arcivescovo di Strigonia quello che havevo passato co 'l principe, restò con ugual confusione e disgusto, e mi affermò più e più volte passar il negotio come egli haveva detto a me et io havevo scritto; e tanto monsignore come il palatino, esaggerando il pericolosissimo stato di quel regno e dicendo che tra poche settimane vedremo l'incendio dalle nostre finestre (il che so che hanno detto in pieno consiglio), mi dissero non poter penetrare il motivo né il fondamento di sì strana risolutione d'impegnarsi tanto senza necessità nelle guerre d'Italia, mentre li proprii regni e stati hereditarii si trovano in tanto pericolo e necessità che non può aspettar se non di esser preda dell'invasore, mancandogli ogni assistenza et ogni aiuto, senza che restino fuori di questo pericolo le fortezze medesime, senza munitioni di guerra, senza viveri e quasi senza soldati, ritrovandosi quei pochi che vi sono senza paghe da anni in qua et in estrema necessità e quasi disperatione; non trovandosi quieto l'imperio, e le cose di Fiandra nel pessimo stato che si vede. Dal discorso del principe e da altri non leggieri rincontri vedo che si reputano punti troppo importanti alla casa d'Austria il ritener li passi della Retia e 'l far che resti mortificato e danneggiato il duca di Nivers, acciò non resti in Italia esempio di commodo, ma del contrario, con l'aiuto de' Franzesi. Monsignor arcivescovo di Strigonia ha detto al padre Lamermain che se lui fusse confessore dell'imperatore non l'assolverebbe, mentre non desistesse da questa guerra d'Italia. Ad un altro padre, che per lo più confessa il principe, ha detto il medesimo e di più altri concetti simili, incaricandoli che lo dicesse al principe medesimo. Di questo non so anche quello che habbia fatto.
