The sheet breaks off in mid-word; the despatch continues on R307. --- Last week I made effective representations to Prince Eggenberg, and to His Excellency himself, for the settlement of Italian affairs, as I wrote in other letters of mine, suggesting, as speculative talk and without committing not only the masters but not even the parties, that the difficulty did not lie in the point of reputation, as they seemed to think, since on this side it is believed that much advantage would be given to the Emperor's; but in the suspicions and misgivings that the interested parties conceive, and, as they claim, not without grounds, about the substance: namely that, once the French have withdrawn, the aim is to have the deposit again; that the decision of the case is to turn not on the point of the succession but rather on the devolution, because of the alleged disobedience and the calling-in of the French, so as to have the free disposal of those states, unless Nevers consents to the exchange, the garrison or the demolition to satisfy the Spaniards, and to give up to Savoy, Lorraine and Guastalla as much of the states as will content them, weaken the Duke and make French help harmful to him; and finally that the aim is not then to leave the passes of the Rhaetia free. And since they always profess the very opposite of these ideas, I had room to press that, this being so, the settlement would perhaps become easy, which they likewise declare they desire. Meanwhile the Palatine of Hungary and the Archbishop of Esztergom arrived to deal with the affairs of that kingdom, which they found in the greatest danger, as much with Bethlen Gabor alive as with his death; and both made most effective representations for the settlement of Italian affairs, as necessary in order to be able to meet the needs and prevent the ruin of that kingdom. Prince Eggenberg told Monsignore that he had talked with me at length and had made certain arrangements; but when I told Monsignore what had passed and what I thought necessary to reach some conclusion, he went back to the Prince the same day and at once reported to me the views and arrangements made with His Excellency. In accordance with them I drafted a letter to give an account of it by express courier to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, and showed it the next day to the said Monsignore; since he approved it from the first to the last word, and particularly in the substantial points as agreeing with what Your Most Illustrious Lordship had arranged with His Excellency, I almost believed I had concluded the business, since, having discreetly sounded the Bishop of Mantua and the Venetian resident here, I did not find them far off. But when I then went to the Prince and read him that paper, I found His Excellency's views very different: in effect, that the King of France should write to His Imperial Majesty and at the same time withdraw his arms not only from Montferrat but from Susa too; that the Duke of Mantua should ask pardon for the disobedience and for calling in the French, acknowledging the error committed; and on the other side that His Majesty should neither promise nor assure the Duke the possession of the states (though he hinted, without commitment, that they would be left to him), but would grant him grace and pardon for the errors committed in such a way that His Majesty's goodwill would be seen, and that the King of France's intercession had been of use to the Duke (on the understanding, however, that His Excellency's words could come true even if only part of the states were granted to him); and finally that as to the passes of the Rhaetia it would be put in negotiation and the interested parties heard, mentioning the Bishop of Chur, and that the passes belong to that church, and that Our Lord ought to be glad that they should remain in its power rather than in heretics'; adding that it matters far more to the House of Austria not to give up these passes than to remove France from that of Susa. Although I saw things set on such hard terms, I nevertheless tried not to cut the thread of the negotiation altogether. As to the possession, I said that, since the fears of partiality were much lessened, it seemed that His Majesty, of his own free will, as the reasons that moved him to the sequestration were ceasing, and not to satisfy others, could allow that nothing be changed about the possession against the will of the parties. As to the pardon, that this formality and the Duke's confession could be considered prejudicial to the solid reputation of the Duke and of his succession, in which Austrian blood was indelibly mixed, and even to His Majesty's dignity, it being much more that it had not been offended than that, offended, it had granted pardon; and that therefore His Majesty's goodness and generosity would have ample field to exercise itself without prejudice to the Duke, and much less to his grandsons and great-grandsons, who are without doubt innocent. On the point of the passes I suggested that one could negotiate taking as an expedient that until the decision of the case His Majesty should remain in the Grisons and France in Susa, and once the rest was settled a remedy would be found for this too. When I reported to the Archbishop of Esztergom what I had discussed with the Prince, he was equally confused and displeased, and assured me again and again that the business stood as he had told me and I had written; and both Monsignore and the Palatine, stressing the most dangerous state of that kingdom and saying that within a few weeks we shall see the fire from our windows (which I know they said in full council), told me they could not grasp the motive or the ground of so strange a decision to engage so deeply without necessity in the wars of Italy, while His Majesty's own kingdoms and hereditary states are in such danger and need that they can expect nothing but to be the invader's prey, lacking all assistance and all help, without even the fortresses being out of this danger, without munitions of war, without victuals and almost without soldiers, the few who are there having gone unpaid for years and being in extreme need and almost despair; the Empire not being quiet, and the affairs of Flanders in the very bad state that is seen. From the Prince's talk and from other weighty indications I see that they consider it points of great importance to the House of Austria to keep the passes of the Rhaetia and to see that the Duke of Nevers is humbled and damaged, so that no example of advantage, but of the contrary, should remain in Italy from French help. There are those who believe it is also thought necessary to humble and weaken, if it cannot be destroyed, the power of Venice, and that they consider it an opportune moment that the Emperor, powerful in the number and quality of his soldiery, and Spain, through the quality of the leader commanding its arms and the effort in men and money they are putting together with Savoy, Florence, Parma and Modena, are now united; the Pope is neutral, Mantua destroyed; France, they expect to divert it, or that its forces will not arrive in time, or at least will not suffice for the help needed and to overcome at the same time the obstacles on Savoy's side, of whom it is presumed that, to reassure the Spaniards further, he will give them the posts of Avigliana, Pinerolo and the others to guard; and finally Venice, that it will not be able to resist force from several sides and the secret understandings and leanings towards the Empire claimed to exist in their principal cities, above all with Collalto leading the army; I have heard these designs about him from a serious person, and from another, that he has at other times let it be understood that if the Emperor made war on the Venetians, and in earnest, and he led it, he too would hope to attain the title of Highness. The Archbishop of Esztergom told Father Lamormaini that if he were the Emperor's confessor he would not absolve him unless he gave up this Italian war. To another father, who usually hears the Prince's confession, he said the same and other similar things besides, charging him to tell the Prince himself. Of this I do not yet know what he has done. M.tà" (checked on the scan). --- ‹Del padre Lamermain so che la mattina della natività della Madonna par›lò liberissimamente et efficacissimamente con S. M.tà in questa materia, et alla M.tà S., che si scaricava con li consiglieri, replicò chiaramente che S. M.tà non doveva deferir ad un solo, ma al tale e tale, nominando quattro o cinque altri; e se bene comunemente non si sanno questi particolari, si sa però universalmente che detto padre contradice a questa guerra; ma che hanno assicurata la coscienza all'imperator co 'l parer d'altri, e l'hanno impresso che più tosto deve di nuovo lasciare in contingenza tutto 'l resto, che lasciar la sua dignità et autorità disprezzata in Italia. Con tutto questo, se i Franzesi si mostraranno pronti a tempo con forze et applicatione bastanti, non par credibile che i Spagnuoli siano per lasciar di usare della solita loro prudenza, mentre in Italia hanno tanto che perdere, in Fiandra stanno ricevendo sì gran ruine, le forze dell'imperatore dependono da tanti e sì gravi accidenti, che paiono non remoti, e per tant'e tant'altre ragioni che da essi saranno ben considerate, e molto più alla prudenza singolare di V. S. Ill.ma saranno presenti. In questo punto mi vien detto che da un consigliero secreto si è saputo che in un consiglio fatto questa mattina in Heberstorf, con intervento del Stralendorf, per le cose d'Italia, durato dalle sette sino alle undici, cioè sino ad un'hora avanti mezzo giorno, si è trattato gagliardamente dell'accomodamento di esse per gli ufficii efficacissimi fatti dal padre Lamermain con S. M.tà e con li consiglieri, et haver soggiunto detto consigliero che egli spera che debba seguire, vedendovisi S. M.tà inclinatissima. Piaccia a Dio che se ne veda l'effetto. Mentre li sopranominati Ungheri erano qua, vennero lettere di Transilvania con avviso che quei paesi erano in termine fra due settimane di dichiararsi uniti con i Turchi contro S. M.tà, poiché Giorgio Racocci, principal Transilvano et eretico, pretendendo succeder al Gabor così nel principato come ne' sette contadi, per tutto fa pratiche con li baroni e paesani, e già per lui s'erano dichiarati li aiduchi e grandi, anzi la maggior parte del paese, e che in una dieta che si era fatta a pena si erano opposti alla general risolutione di ribellarsi alcuni pochi cattolici, li quali erano stati rispinti fuori ad urtoni, e 'l Racocci, abboccatosi co 'l bassà d'Agria, era in punto. Potrà però questo moto ricever impedimento, perché hieri mi disse monsignor cancelliere d'Ungheria che Gabor si trovasse con qualche miglioramento della sua indispositione. Il palatino d'Ungheria mi confirmò lo scritto altre volte circa la conversione della principessa di Transilvania alla fede cattolica, e che ne teneva tre lettere scrittagli da quella di suo pugno; e che, essendo stato penetrato dal marito e dalli principali del paese, che per la maggior parte sono eretici, havevano preteso che essa si dichiarasse, et havendo risposto non esser obligata a farlo, l'havevano costretta a dar riversali che lo farà quando venga il caso della successione al principato, del quale essa ha l'investitura dal Turco, e da non molto tempo lo scettro et altri segni del principato medesimo procuratigli dal Gabor suo marito. Ma si crede che, dichiarandosi cattolica, sarà facile al Racocci l'escluderla co 'l favore de' paesani, mentre non habbia una grand'assistenza da S. M.tà. Rendo humilissime gratie a V. S. Ill.ma di quello che mi avvertisce e comanda con occasione del viglietto scritto a S. M.tà circa la deputatione di plenipotentiario, e per quanto porta la mia poca capacità procurarò eseguirlo puntualmente nell'avvenire. Non lasciando però di dirli che uno de' motivi per far riformar qua la risposta data la prima volta, de' quali mi valsi con più energia, fu il dirgli che redarguissero la mia proposta se in alcuna cosa li offendeva, e se questo non era, non esser né anche ragione che pungesse la risposta. Circa le propositioni di accordo col padre Magno scrissi con le mie sussequenti, et haverà veduto che 'l principe d'Echembergh non persiste nell'appuntato. Da che presero questi interessati tanto più occasione di sospettar del padre, la cui stessa trattatione con quest'ambasciadore di Toscana, senza uscir a dire quel che tratti, né anche piace, sapendosi che 'l granduca va affatto unito con Spagna. Nel negotio della Carolina non si è per ancora presa risolutione. Ho fatto gran sforzo con alcuno de' deputati che, supposto che le scritture date dal padre Valeriano nella specificatione di alcuni particolari contro li padri Giesuiti mostrino qualche passione, dalla quale è aliena la sacra congregatione, e però non haverà gusto di quelle, nondimeno convien riguardar la sostanza, che risguarda l'autorità e giurisditione universale della sede apostolica, e particolarmente sopra la detta università. Delle quali ho anche informato opportunamente, ancorché come di negotio che non mi appartenga, et insinuato che la confirmatione della transatione non si concederà mai, e rimostrato che per ogni ragione e motivo toccante a S. M.tà, al regno, alla città et a' signori così secolari come ecclesiastici di quel regno, conviene che detta università sia veramente universale a similitudine di quelle di Coimbra, Salamanca e simili, delle quali ho esortato a far venir li statuti e modi di governarsi, e credo non haver parlato affatto infruttuosamente. Nel resto toccante alla persona del padre mi regolerò secondo il comandamento di V. S. Ill.ma, alla quale il medesimo padre scriverà quello che ha passato nell'ultima audienza che gli ha data, per quanto dice, molto grata S. M.tà. It continues R306. --- ‹Of Father Lamormaini I know that on the morning of the Nativity of Our Lady he› spoke most freely and most effectively with His Majesty on this matter, and when His Majesty unburdened himself on his councillors, he answered plainly that His Majesty ought not to defer to one man alone, but to such and such, naming four or five others; and though these particulars are not commonly known, it is known everywhere that the said father opposes this war; but that they have reassured the Emperor's conscience with the opinion of others, and have impressed on him that he must rather again leave all the rest at risk than leave his dignity and authority despised in Italy. For all that, if the French show themselves ready in time with sufficient forces and application, it does not seem credible that the Spaniards will give up using their usual prudence, since in Italy they have so much to lose, in Flanders they are suffering such great ruin, and the Emperor's forces depend on so many and such grave accidents, which do not seem remote; and for many other reasons that they will consider well, and that will be much more present to Your Most Illustrious Lordship's singular prudence. At this moment I am told that it has been learned from a privy councillor that in a council held this morning at Ebersdorf, with Stralendorf present, on the affairs of Italy, lasting from seven to eleven, that is to one hour before noon, the settlement of them was vigorously discussed, because of the most effective representations made by Father Lamormaini to His Majesty and to the councillors; and that the said councillor added that he hopes it will follow, His Majesty being seen to be most inclined to it. May God grant that the effect be seen. While the above-named Hungarians were here, letters came from Transylvania with news that those lands were on the point of declaring themselves united with the Turks against His Majesty within two weeks, because György Rákóczi, a leading Transylvanian and a heretic, claiming to succeed Bethlen Gabor both in the principality and in the seven counties, is intriguing everywhere with the barons and country people, and the Haiduks and great men, indeed most of the country, had already declared for him; and that in a diet that had been held a few Catholics had barely opposed the general resolution to rebel, and had been pushed out by force; and Rákóczi, having met the pasha of Eger, was ready. This movement may however be checked, because yesterday the Chancellor of Hungary told me that Gabor was somewhat better in his illness. The Palatine of Hungary confirmed to me what I wrote at other times about the conversion of the Princess of Transylvania to the Catholic faith, and that he had three letters written to him by her in her own hand; and that, it having been discovered by her husband and the leading men of the country, who are mostly heretics, they had demanded that she declare herself, and when she answered that she was not obliged to do so they had forced her to give an undertaking that she will do it when the case of the succession to the principality arises, of which she has the investiture from the Turk, and not long ago the sceptre and other insignia of that principality, obtained for her by Gabor her husband. But it is believed that if she declares herself Catholic it will be easy for Rákóczi to exclude her with the support of the country people, unless she has great assistance from His Majesty. I give most humble thanks to Your Most Illustrious Lordship for what you warn and command me on the occasion of the note written to His Majesty about the appointment of a plenipotentiary, and as far as my small capacity allows I shall try to carry it out punctually in future. Not omitting, however, to tell you that one of the arguments for having the answer given the first time reworded here, which I used with most energy, was to tell them that they should refute my proposal if it offended them in anything, and if it did not, there was no reason either that the answer should sting. On the proposals for an agreement with Father Magni, I wrote in my subsequent letters, and you will have seen that Prince Eggenberg does not hold to what was arranged. From this these interested parties took all the more occasion to suspect the father, whose very dealings with the Tuscan ambassador here, without his coming out to say what he is negotiating, are not liked either, since it is known that the Grand Duke is entirely united with Spain. In the business of the Carolina no decision has yet been taken. I have made a great effort with some of the deputies that, supposing the papers given by Father Valeriano in specifying certain particulars against the Jesuit fathers show some passion, from which the Sacred Congregation is far removed, and it will therefore not like them, one must nevertheless look to the substance, which concerns the universal authority and jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, and particularly over the said university. I have also informed them of this at the right moment, although as of a business that does not concern me, and suggested that the confirmation of the transaction will never be granted, and pointed out that for every reason and motive touching His Majesty, the kingdom, the city and the lords both secular and ecclesiastical of that kingdom, it is fitting that the said university be truly universal, like those of Coimbra, Salamanca and the like, whose statutes and ways of governing themselves I have urged them to send for; and I believe I have not spoken altogether fruitlessly. For the rest touching the person of the father I shall follow Your Most Illustrious Lordship's command; the father himself will write to you what passed in the last audience His Majesty gave him, a very gracious one, as he says. Read from the figures and the clear words on the sheet; Kiewning (1897) Nr. 177 has only a German summary of this despatch. --- They have not been satisfied here with the decision about the matter of the visitor in the diocese of [?Aquileia]; they have, however, reserved giving me an answer until it has been discussed in council. It has been said in recent days that the [?Patriarch] had died; it is true that he has been gravely ill, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship will no doubt have heard. I do not know whether they will want to wait to hear what becomes of him before giving an answer. I have heard that on the occasion of the said [?illness] they have [?talked] of handing the free election over to the [?chapter], as the other churches that are principalities of the Empire have it. I do not doubt that His Holiness's supreme prudence will not be taken unawares. The man they had appointed to come and negotiate this business there has died at Trieste, his home town, while, having been dispatched from here, he had gone there to prepare for his departure for that court. On the point of the visitor I shall not fail to tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship that they show much feeling here that a foreigner is to be deputed, who, not having the language, will not understand nor be understood; and it will be a burden on the people because of the expense, which would be avoided if someone otherwise [?suitable] in the country were deputed; who, however, […] does not claim that it is at his nomination, nor that the discretion and will of Our Lord be restricted; to the [?alienation] of which it seems they rather attribute this, what they call the usual difficulties and [?hardness] when His Majesty's pleasure is in question. Your Most Illustrious Lordship with His Holiness will take the decision you judge most opportune with your most singular prudence. The clear text and the cipher runs are read on the sheet; the middle of paragraph 3 agrees with the Roman decipherment printed by Kiewning (1897), Nr. 178. --- By the last ordinary post I understand that His Majesty wrote to Our Lord and to Signor [596: Prince Savelli] about the church of Verden in [...] of Count Adam Schwarzenberg; and from what I know of having hinted at in other letters of mine on this matter, this request will not have reached Our Lord as news. To one [207: privy councillor] I gave a hint, as of something that had leaked out here, that it had [?already] been promised to Tilly for a relative of his. [?Werdenberg] showed much feeling, since His Majesty has much committed himself in this business, and moreover [said] that Tilly's relative is unfit for this church, being [425: ?a Fleming], and on other counts. I have managed to obtain copies of the letters written by His Majesty in this matter, which I send enclosed; and although I am willing to believe that by the arrival of this one Our Lord will have received the one addressed to His Holiness, nevertheless the contrary is not impossible, and in any case he ought not to be displeased to see the one addressed to the Prince, especially since two quite important points are found in it: the one, His Majesty's nomination, and the other, that of the possession to be given before the apostolic provision, or rather confirmation, as they call it. I point out to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, however, that it would be prejudicial to the person who got me the copies, and consequently to Your Most Illustrious Lordship's service, if it leaked out there that I have them, and especially if they were shown [?outside] of [...] of them. If it is possible to grant what is asked, it will be most expedient, both for the [?feeling] mentioned and for the fruit that may be hoped for through Count Adam, as I have indicated in other letters. In the manner [of granting it] some caution will be needed, so that no prejudice is suffered on the point of the nomination, which will become greater because they will probably state him to be provided on His Majesty's nomination in the despatches they issue here for the grant of the temporal regalia and investitures by right of the principality; and therefore it will perhaps be necessary not only to state the reasons why it belongs to the free provision of the Apostolic See as devolved, but to see to it that the imperial despatches do not say the contrary, and likewise that no act of possession is done before it is done by virtue of the apostolic bulls; and perhaps both points will be provided for if, before it is known that the grace has been made, I can tell the Count that it will be done for him on the said conditions: not to meddle in the spiritual and temporal until he has the apostolic bulls, and not to accept an imperial despatch that does not conform to the same bulls; and to take from him a declaration and obligation in writing. It is true, on the other hand, that [?Tilly] has deserved so well of the Catholic religion and of the Emperor that it seems very fitting that the Apostolic See should show him this gratitude, and that the Emperor should not hinder it for him, especially since he himself [46] by his valour and industry recovered the said city and bishopric of Verden individually, and his garrison is actually inside it. I have not wished to go into these or other similar ideas [?without orders] and without knowing the mind of Our Lord and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship. Kiewning's German regest confirms the sense of each paragraph but supplies no words. `[?word]` partly carried, `[…]` unread, `[nnn]` a group not identified, `[word]` a word the figures lack. --- Ho ricevuta in questa settimana dal Fortiguerra, vicario generale dell'esercito cesareo et assai caro al generale, perché scrive le sue historie, e molto più per haverlo in concetto di gran astrologo, la lettera, della quale mando l'aggiunta copia; e come lo stringer il partito che si propone per l'aggiustamento delle cose d'Italia non sia in mia mano, anzi vi si possano incontrar gravi difficoltà per il punto del deposito, e dall'altro canto escluderlo mi paresse molto inconveniente, presi per [404: ?espediente] rispondergli nella forma che vedrà dalla copia, che parimente mando con questa. Ho altri rincontri che il duca sia alienissimo dal passar in Italia, principalmente per creder, secondo l'astrologia, alla quale è addictissimo, che le succederebbe infelicemente; e però si [649]ar che non passerà se non forzato, e come chi va alla giustitia, e con simili termini esagerati. Si accresce questo senso hora maggiormente per il timore che il Sueco sia per passar nell'Imperio, hora che si suppone conclusa la [347] con Polonia, e che prima d'ogn'altra cosa sia per tentar la ricuperatione dello stato [di] Michelburgh per gli antichi padroni; alla quale impresa non si dubita che alle proprie forze del Sueco sia per concorrere la propensione di que' sudditi, non solo per l'interesse della religione, ma per l'antichissima possessione di quella casa, che senza esempio in Europa numera sopra mille anni di continuata successione legitima masculina in quei stati; e come Gustavo per il valore, vigilanza et ogni altra dote di gran capitano sia nemico da farsene stima, la farà tanto maggiore il generale per principii parimente di astrologia. Questi ministri han continuato a parlar di pace et a dir che si farà senz'altro, senza specificar […]. Ho rincontro che un c[orriero] di Spagna habbia portato questa settimana concetti di pace e forse qualche partito; ma non ho potuto penetrar la risolutione presane qua, essendo stati fuori [203: i consiglieri] appresso S. M.tà, et havendo io sotto altri pretesti lasciato di andarvi, eccetto che nella precisa funtione di […] dell'anello, al che mi hanno [?invitato], per fuggir l'occasione di trovarmi col signor duca di Neoburgh in luoghi terzi, essendomi chiarito domenica a otto [?passata] che egli pretende avanzarsi meco; ma sì come col tener il mi[o] luogo procurai [?non] pregiudicarmi, così sol[…] [?nelle] occasioni non necessarie stimo conveniente non cimentarmi, ma più tosto lasciar far alli [232: ambasciatori di Spagna], a' quali destramente h[o] cercato insinuar in questa materia quello che conviene, et han [?detto] di vo[ler] far alcune diligenze, et io star a vedere; perché se [900] aggiustano per sé, a fortiori resta aggiustato per il nuntio. Ma tornando al proposito, ho non leggieri con[g]etture che con queste voci di pace e forse con qualche partito con Francia hanno la mira di addormentare Franzesi particolarmente, e, restando a cavallo nel fosso, veder se gli riesce far qualche acquisto considerabile, non lasciar di tentarlo, e quando ve[…] l'inimico potente, all'hora stringer partiti […]mente; e che però non si concluderà qua cosa alcuna circa alcun partito sino che dal [603: ?Spinola] e Colalto si senta in che stato si trovino o pensino potersi [?metter] le cose. Dal marchese d'Aitona ho sentito che hora si può far la pace, che 'l suo re e l'imperatore sono con tante forze in Italia che l'accettar mezzi di pace non può attribuirsi ad altro che a desiderio della publica tranquillità; dal conte di Castro poi ho cavato che si persiste tuttavia nella pretensione della permuta o altro che gli assicuri dalla gelosia di Casale e gli ristori la riputatione in questa parte, sì come che si dia sodisfattione a Guastalla. E si può temere che, se Francia si lascia addormentare, li suoi […] faranno [266]i sogni. Parlai fin della settimana passata a S. M.tà circa li particolari che vanno espressi nella copia del viglietto datone a S. M.tà, che lo domandò e dimostrò ottima dispositione, ma ancora non ne ho havuta risposta; la quale però solleciterò con tanto maggior premura, quanto che ho saputo da buonissimo luogo potersi con molto fondamento temere che 'l Palatinato sia restituito al Palatino, inclinandovi Spagnuoli per concluder la pace col re d'Inghilterra, e che già l'hanno fatto insinuare a Baviera da [?Bruneo], che li giorni passati, come scrissi, con occasione o pretesto di congratularsi col nuovo elettore di Magonza, passò per quest'effetto da S. A.; sì che succederebbe di questo come de' beni ecclesiastici del regno e stati del re di Danimarca. Del duca di Baviera so haver risposto che di questo particolare è necessario trattare et aggiustarsi con l'Imperatore, poiché, tenendo S. A. quella parte del Palatinato per essergli stata data da S. M.tà in pagamento de' suoi crediti in luogo dell'Austria Superiore datagli prima in pegno, ogni volta che S. M.tà o li paghi quello che gli deve o gli restituisca l'Austria Superiore, S. A. sarà pronta a lasciar la detta parte del Palatinato. S. M.tà poi non solo non inclina a questo, ma pretende che i Spagnuoli diano in mano sua il Palatinato Inferiore, che essi possiedono, e per questo negotio anderà un gentilhuomo, ancorché forse sotto altro pretesto, correndo fino a hora tutte queste cose in gran secreto. Nondimeno prevagliono in questa corte tanto li sensi et interessi di Spagna, che si può creder che si farà sempre quello che là efficacemente si vorrà e sarà accomodato a loro interessi. Dal signor D. [955] non ho mai havuto risposta della [479] scrittale verso il fine di luglio, [né] dal medesimo mi è stato scritto cosa alcuna, o almeno non mi è giunta fin hora, dopo l'arrivo del corriero speditogli di ce[200] sotto nome del signor [353] suo padre; che nel principio di questo mese ho aviso che, passato per il campo [329]ereo, […]se il generale in Alberstat, pensando che quivi si [?trovasse], [649] era inviato verso Amburgo, dove s'intende si trovi ancora convalescente del suo male. Nel particolare […] uffitii nel[la] S. Orsola farò [?quanto] mi [?comanda]; ma supplico […] condonare al[l'] […] mia divotione, e non attribuirlo né ad importunità né a soverchio ardire, se mi fo lecito di [659]sti[445]carle che sono appunto queste le materie dove, supponendo il lor desiderio pio, più tosto de[gne] di ringratiamento che di repulsa, et allegando esempi di uffitii pratic[346]i concessi per santi men insigni et ad […] inferiori a quello di una se[…]ma, [potria] pigliare campo il […] poco bene affetto di esagerarle soliti concetti di poco [?buona] volontà. The stretches printed by Kiewning (1897), Nr. 182 follow the Roman decipherment; the rest is read from the figures. --- This week I received from Fortiguerra, vicar general of the imperial army and very dear to the General because he writes his histories, and much more because he holds him to be a great astrologer, the letter of which I send the enclosed copy. And since pressing the proposal being made for settling the affairs of Italy is not in my hands, and indeed grave difficulties could be met over the point of the deposit, while on the other hand excluding it seemed to me most unsuitable, I took it as [404: ?the expedient] to answer him in the form you will see from the copy, which I likewise send with this. I have other indications that the Duke is utterly averse to going into Italy, chiefly because he believes, according to astrology, to which he is much addicted, that it would turn out unhappily for him; and therefore [649] that he will not go unless forced, and like one who goes to execution, and with similar exaggerated terms. This feeling grows now all the more from the fear that the Swede will come into the Empire, now that the [347] with Poland is supposed concluded, and that before anything else he will attempt to recover the state [of] Mecklenburg for its old masters. In that enterprise no one doubts that the inclination of those subjects will join the Swede's own forces, not only for the interest of religion but for the very ancient possession of that house, which, without example in Europe, counts over a thousand years of continuous legitimate male succession in those states; and as Gustavus, for his valour, vigilance and every other gift of a great captain, is an enemy to be reckoned with, the General will reckon with him all the more, on principles of astrology as well. These ministers have continued to speak of peace and to say that it will be made without fail, without specifying [...]. I have an indication that a c[ourier] from Spain has brought this week ideas of peace and perhaps some proposal; but I have not been able to learn the resolution taken on it here, since [203: the councillors] were away with His Majesty, and I, under other pretexts, had omitted to go there, except for the particular ceremony of [...] of the ring, to which they [?invited] me, so as to avoid the occasion of meeting the Duke of Neuburg in third places, having made sure on Sunday week [?last] that he means to take precedence over me. But just as by keeping my own place I tried [?not] to prejudice myself, so [...] on occasions that are not necessary I think it fitting not to put myself to the test, but rather to let the [232: Spanish ambassadors] act, to whom I have adroitly tried to suggest in this matter what is fitting, and they have [?said] they will make some efforts, and I shall stand and watch; for if [900] settle it for themselves, it is all the more settled for the nuncio. But to return to the point: I have no slight conjectures that with these rumours of peace, and perhaps with some proposal to France, they aim to lull the French in particular and, staying astride the ditch, to see whether they can make some considerable gain, and not to omit trying it, and when they [...] the enemy strong, then to close on terms [...]; and that therefore nothing will be concluded here about any proposal until it is heard from [603: ?Spinola] and Collalto in what state things are or where they think they can [?put] them. From the Marquis of Aitona I have heard that peace can be made now, since his king and the Emperor are in Italy with such forces that accepting means of peace cannot be put down to anything but a wish for public tranquillity; from the Count of Castro I then drew that they still persist in the claim to the exchange, or something else that would secure them from the jealousy of Casale and restore their reputation in this respect, and likewise that satisfaction be given to Guastalla. And it may be feared that, if France lets itself be lulled to sleep, its [...] will have [266] dreams. At the end of last week I spoke to His Majesty about the particulars set out in the copy of the note given to His Majesty, who asked for it and showed the best disposition, but I have not yet had an answer; I shall press for it with all the more urgency because I have learnt from a very good source that it may be feared with much foundation that the Palatinate will be restored to the Palatine, the Spaniards inclining to it so as to conclude peace with the King of England, and that they have already had it suggested to Bavaria by [?Bruneau], who the other day, as I wrote, on the occasion or pretext of congratulating the new Elector of Mainz, went to His Highness for this purpose; so that it would go with this as with the church property of the kingdom and states of the King of Denmark. Of the Duke of Bavaria I know that he answered that on this particular it is necessary to negotiate and come to terms with the Emperor, since His Highness holds that part of the Palatinate because it was given him by His Majesty in payment of his credits in place of Upper Austria, given him first in pledge; whenever His Majesty either pays him what he owes him or gives him back Upper Austria, His Highness will be ready to give up the said part of the Palatinate. His Majesty, then, not only does not incline to this, but claims that the Spaniards should put into his hands the Lower Palatinate, which they hold, and a gentleman will go for this business, though perhaps under another pretext, all these things running so far in great secrecy. Nevertheless the views and interests of Spain prevail so much in this court that one may believe that whatever is effectively wanted there and suits their interests will always be done. From Signor D. [955] I have never had an answer to the [479] written to him towards the end of July, [nor] has anything been written to me by him, or at least none has reached me so far, since the arrival of the courier sent him from [200] under the name of Signor [353] his father; for at the beginning of this month I had word that, having passed through the [?imperial] camp, [...] the General at Halberstadt, thinking that he [?was] there, [649] was sent towards Hamburg, where he is understood still to be convalescing from his illness. In the matter of [...] offices for St Ursula I shall do [?as] you [?command]; but I beg [...] to forgive my [...] devotion, and not to put it down either to importunity or to excessive boldness, if I make bold to [...] you that these are precisely the matters where, supposing their wish to be pious, they are worthy rather of thanks than of refusal, and, by citing examples of offices [...] granted for less eminent saints and at [...] lower than that of one [...], the [...] who is not well disposed [could] take occasion to exaggerate to her the usual ideas of little [?good] will. The sheet ends in mid-word ("interes-", the end of the cipher) with the catchword "per"; R312 continues "giustificate in tutto o in parte". `[ati]` is supplied from the print. --- Trattai col signor principe d'Echembergh mercordì circa 'l negotio d'Italia, prendendo occasione della lettera scritta da S. M.tà a N. S.re, e dissi come S. S.tà, havendo passati co'l Christianissimo caldissimi uffitii per mezzo di monsignor nuntio colà residente e del signor di Bettunes, ambasciador di quella M.tà presso la S.tà S., conforme al desiderio di Cesare, haveva trovate diverse difficoltà, le quali haveva communicate al signor principe Savelli, acciò si trovasse qualche via da superarle; e che per il medesimo effetto si erano ordinate nuove publiche et universali orationi in cotesta città; e che 'l zelo e desiderio ardente che ha S. B.ne della pace della christianità cattolica l'haveva portato non solo ad insinuare al detto signor principe che, quando sia certo di conseguirla, si muoverà in persona e verrà a Bologna o Ferrara per dar motivo a S. M.tà di piegare la sua pia volontà alla quiete d'Italia, ma l'haveva scritto anche a me, acciò lo rappresenti a S. M.tà medesima, facendole ogni più viva espressione del molto che stimerà S. S.tà tutto ciò che S. M.tà giudicherà di poter fare per l'effetto sudetto, e come darà per ben impiegato tutto l'incommodo e travaglio che perciò potrà ricevere nella persona propria la S.tà S. Dichiarò S. E. esser da S. M.tà stato sommamente stimato il zelo grande di N. S.re. In ristretto però non cavai altro, se non che persista ne' concetti altre volte accennati: che 'l re di Francia si contenti di haver operato quello che da principio dichiarò di haver preteso con la mossa delle sue armi, cioè la liberatione di Casale, ritiri le sue armi da' feudi imperiali, e se vorrà amichevolmente e senza minaccie intercedere per il signor duca di Nivers, vedrà che la M.tà dell'imperatore stima quanto conviene gli uffitii di un tanto re e suo nipote. In quel giorno non potei parlare a S. M.tà, perché haveva appuntata una caccia, ma mi fece dire che, havendone una assai bella per il giorno seguente, m'invitava ad intervenirvi, e che mi havria anche sentito. Vi fui perciò il giorno seguente, et havendo con S. M.tà passato in sostanza lo scritto uffitio nel miglior modo che seppi, dopo haver S. M.tà mostrato una gran stima della volontà e dispositione di N. S.re, dichiarò la sua al solito desiderosissima di pace e dispostissima a tutto quello a che possa condescendere senza offesa della dignità et autorità non sua, ma dell'imperio, che per giuramento è obligato a conservare. Risposi che la conservatione della riputatione e dignità della M.tà S. non solo è giusta, ma è interesse della religione cattolica e della sede apostolica, e che N. S.re non desiderava dalla M.tà S. se non quello a che giudichi poter condescendere salva la sua riputatione. Uscì S. M.tà a dolersi del re di Francia, che habbi voluto metter per terra la dignità Cesarea in Italia, habbi mandato a fare uffitii con minaccie, che con trattati in tutte le parti habbia macchinato contro l'imperio e casa d'Austria, et hora habbia di nuovo mandato Mr. di Marcheville co'l pretesto di rallegrarsi con l'arcivescovo di Magonza della sua elettione, a sollecitarlo con offerte di assistenza per liberarli dalle oppressioni di S. M.tà Ces.a, et ad esplorar la sua volontà se concorrerà che le armi della fede cattolica assistino S. M.tà Ces.a nelle cose d'Italia; e che il medesimo andava dalli altri elettori ancora. Risposi a qualsivoglia mancamento che si potesse pretender contro il re di Francia e suoi ministri dover preponderare presso la singolar pietà della M.tà S. il merito e l'interesse della religione cattolica e della publica quiete; et insinuai che queste medesime cose potevano esser motivo a S. M.tà di comporre tanto più volentieri gli affari d'Italia, mentre con questo cessaria qualche stimolo che forsi pigli il Christianissimo di divertire, e S. M.tà, restando libera con le sue armi e con quelle del Re Cattolico, potria non solo resistere, ma opprimere chiunque volesse molestarla. Aggiunsi con riverente affettionatissima preghiera che si compiacesse di considerare la presente opportunità di far cessare queste turbolenze con grandissima riputatione e gloria non meno delle sue armi e potenza che della sua singolar pietà, mentre al trovarsi così potente in Italia con le proprie e con le armi del Cattolico, e pe'l contrario quelle di Francia sì deboli, si aggiungesse la mossa di un Papa da Roma sino a' confini del suo stato, quasi trecento miglia distanti. Hebbi chiari rincontri, e dalle parole e dalla maniera di proferirle, che questo e simili altri concetti fecero qualche impressione nell'animo di S. M.tà, la quale mi disse che 'l giorno seguente ne haveria trattato e presa risolutione in consiglio; onde ne parlai anche con alcuni de' consiglieri secreti che si trovavano fuori, e la sera, subito tornato, ne parlai lungamente co'l baron Verda. Hoggi è venuto da me il baron di Questembergh a dirmi in nome di S. M.tà che la dispositione della M.tà S. alla pace è cresciuta grandemente per li paterni e zelanti uffitii di N. S.re, e particolarmente per l'affettuosa offerta che ha fatta, la quale S. M.tà con affetto et ossequio filiale stima e gradisce; e che 'l solo obligo di conservar la dignità e giurisditione imperiale potrà fare che non condescenda a tutto ciò che le sia ricercato; haver mostrato quanto desideri far cessar le armi, havendo prima fatto il decreto del sequestro per questo fine, poi dato luogo alle trattationi di molti temperamenti, e finalmente propostone uno S. M.tà medesima; il proporne altri, massime non sapendo che debbino essere accettati, non par conveniente, e però quando gli venghino proposti li ascolterà con dispositione di ammetterli, quando non siano, come si è detto, pregiudiciali alla dignità e giurisditione imperiale, parendo anche inconveniente o lasciar questa da parte o pigliarvi compagno. Ho risposto in sostanza, oltre a' concetti spiegati già a S. M.tà, che N. S.re ha passato con ogni maggior efficacia gli uffitii desiderati da S. M.tà, et haver significate le risposte che haveva riportate e le difficoltà che ha ritrovate, acciò S. M.tà si compiaccia considerarle e condescender benignamente fino a quel segno che lo giudica conveniente; che quando a S. M.tà non paia, per il rispetto accennato, dichiararsi con le parti in alcun temperamento, ancorché l'habbia fatto un'altra volta, potrà considerar se quello cessi quando confidentemente comunichi il senso suo a N. S.re, promettendosi dell'affetto e prudenza di S. S.tà che lo porterà col riguardo che conviene; della cui intentione quanto sia aliena dalli inconvenienti accennati della diminutione o compagnia della dignità e giurisditione imperiale, quando cessassero tanti altri evidenti testimonii, poteva bastar quello che ne rendeva l'esibitione di sì gran mossa e 'l non qualificar le pretensioni de gl'interess[ati] per Translation R311_en.md # R311 — Pallotto to Barberini, Vienna, 29 September 1629 (despatch "A", first part): English translation Translation of `R311_reading.md` (22 Oct 2026, Claude Opus 5.5). The text follows the Roman decipherment printed by Kiewning (1897), Nr. 184, which the figures on the sheet match; the despatch continues on R312. --- On Wednesday I dealt with the Lord Prince of Eggenberg about the affair of Italy, taking occasion of the letter written by His Majesty to Our Lord, and I said how His Holiness, having made most pressing representations to the Most Christian King through the nuncio resident there and through Monsieur de Béthune, that Majesty's ambassador to His Holiness, in accordance with the Emperor's wish, had found various difficulties, which he had communicated to Prince Savelli so that some way might be found to overcome them; and that for the same purpose new public and general prayers had been ordered in Rome; and that the zeal and ardent desire His Beatitude has for the peace of Catholic Christendom had led him not only to suggest to the said Prince that, when he is certain of obtaining it, he will move in person and come to Bologna or Ferrara to give His Majesty a motive to bend his pious will to the quiet of Italy, but had also written it to me, so that I should represent it to His Majesty himself, giving him every most lively expression of how highly His Holiness will value all that His Majesty judges he can do to that end, and how he will consider well spent all the inconvenience and toil he may suffer in his own person for it. His Excellency declared that His Majesty had valued Our Lord's great zeal most highly. In short, however, I drew nothing more from him than that he persists in the ideas indicated at other times: that the King of France should be content with having achieved what he declared from the start he aimed at by the movement of his arms, that is, the liberation of Casale, should withdraw his arms from the imperial fiefs, and if he will intercede for the Duke of Nevers amicably and without threats, he will see that His Imperial Majesty values as is fitting the good offices of so great a king and his nephew. That day I could not speak to His Majesty, because he had fixed a hunt, but he had me told that, having a very fine one for the next day, he invited me to take part and would also hear me. So I went the next day, and having gone through with His Majesty in substance the written representation as best I could, after His Majesty had shown great esteem for Our Lord's will and disposition, he declared his own to be, as usual, most desirous of peace and most ready for everything he can agree to without offence to the dignity and authority, not his own, but of the Empire, which he is bound by oath to preserve. I answered that the preservation of His Majesty's reputation and dignity is not only just but in the interest of the Catholic religion and of the Apostolic See, and that Our Lord desired from His Majesty only what he judges he can agree to without loss of his reputation. His Majesty broke out in complaints of the King of France: that he had tried to throw the imperial dignity to the ground in Italy, had sent to make representations with threats, had plotted everywhere by treaties against the Empire and the House of Austria, and had now again sent Monsieur de Marcheville, on the pretext of congratulating the Archbishop of Mainz on his election, to urge him with offers of help to free them from His Imperial Majesty's oppressions and to sound his will whether he would agree that the arms of the Catholic faith should assist His Imperial Majesty in the affairs of Italy; and that the same man was going to the other electors as well. I answered that, against any failing that might be alleged against the King of France and his ministers, the merit and interest of the Catholic religion and of public quiet ought to weigh more with His Majesty's singular piety; and I suggested that these same things could be a motive for His Majesty to settle the affairs of Italy all the more willingly, since this would remove any spur the Most Christian King may feel to make a diversion, and His Majesty, remaining free with his own arms and with those of the Catholic King, could not only resist but crush anyone who wished to trouble him. I added, with a reverent and most affectionate entreaty, that he be pleased to consider the present opportunity of ending these troubles with very great reputation and glory, no less for his arms and power than for his singular piety, since to his finding himself so powerful in Italy with his own arms and those of the Catholic King, and the French arms on the contrary so weak, would be added the journey of a Pope from Rome to the borders of his state, almost three hundred miles away. I had clear signs, both from the words and from the manner of uttering them, that this and other similar ideas made some impression on His Majesty's mind; he told me that the next day he would deal with it and take a resolution in council; so I spoke of it also with some of the privy councillors who were out there, and in the evening, as soon as I returned, I spoke of it at length with Baron Verda. Today Baron Questenberg came to me to tell me in His Majesty's name that His Majesty's disposition towards peace has grown greatly through Our Lord's fatherly and zealous offices, and particularly through the affectionate offer he has made, which His Majesty values and welcomes with filial affection and deference; and that only the obligation to preserve the imperial dignity and jurisdiction could keep him from agreeing to all that is asked of him; that he has shown how much he wishes to stop the fighting, having first issued the decree of sequestration for this purpose, then given room to negotiations on many compromises, and finally proposed one himself; to propose others, especially not knowing whether they would be accepted, does not seem fitting, and therefore when they are proposed to him he will listen to them with a disposition to admit them, provided they are not, as has been said, prejudicial to the imperial dignity and jurisdiction, it seeming improper either to set that aside or to take a partner in it. I answered in substance, besides the ideas already explained to His Majesty, that Our Lord has made with the greatest efficacy the representations His Majesty desired, and has made known the answers he received and the difficulties he found, so that His Majesty might be pleased to consider them and kindly yield as far as he judges fitting; that if His Majesty does not think fit, for the reason mentioned, to declare himself to the parties on any compromise, although he did so once before, he might consider whether that objection ceases when he confidentially communicates his mind to Our Lord, trusting to the affection and prudence of His Holiness to carry it with due regard; and how far His Holiness's intention is from the drawbacks mentioned, of diminishing the imperial dignity and jurisdiction or taking a partner in it, would be shown, if so many other evident testimonies were lacking, by the offer of so great a journey and by his not qualifying the claims of the interested parties as justified [continued on R312] R312, BAV, Barb.lat. 6960, pp. 181-183 (DigiVatLib pagination), 29 Sept 1629, Kiewning Nr. 184 (end) The Spanish ambassadors and Casale; the Empress; Spinola; Flanders and the Dutch. Dal parlar di questi ambasciadori di Spagna non so cavar dispositione alla pace, se loro non restano con Casale o in un modo o in un altro per sicurezza e riputatione, e se Savoia e Guastalla non restano contenti. Supposto questo, non è maraviglia che Echembergh, addictissimo a Spagnuoli, tien saldo ne' punti di sempre, non senza sentimento della maggior parte de' consiglieri, li quali non possono o non ardiscono andar contro il parer di lui. M.tà, parlando con l'imperatrice si aprì con qualche senso perciò verso il principe, e che procurino renderla sospetta in questo negotio e far che né meno debba parlarne; che perciò, non si trattenendo a parlare in secreto tutto quello che haveria voluto, per non dar sospetto che si discorresse di questi affari, mi disse che pigliaria l'occasione di parlarne più lungamente, e che diria di haver parlato all'hora meco del negotio di questo convento di Sant'Agostino e dell'offitio di Sant'Orsola. Le quali particolarità ho voluto accennare a V. S. Ill.ma, acciò possa con la sua singolar prudenza inferire ciò che può sperarsi in questo negotio, massime se fusse ben fondato il discorso di una persona, che 'l marchese Spinola, per non tornare in Fiandra, dove si suppone habbia ordine di andare aggiustate le cose d'Italia, vedendo le cose di quella provincia in tanta rovina, sia più tosto per dar calore alla guerra d'Italia, o almeno per portarne avanti l'accomodamento. Del partito proposto dal re di Francia in Spagna e dato da' signori nuntii, da' quali mi è stato mandato, non trovo qua rincontro alcuno, né appresso li ambasciadori di Spagna né appresso li ministri dell'imperatore; et o sia che di là non l'habbino comunicato, o qua voglino tenerlo secreto, l'uno e l'altro è contrasegno che non si vuole accettare, ma si voglia dar pastura per tener addormentate e sospese le risolutioni di Francia e di altri interessati, sinché gli riesca di far qualche colpo in cotesta provincia; e non pare che per altro che per questo fine siano da un pezzo in qua andati suscitando trattationi e speranze di aggiustamento, come ho significato di mano in mano; et in questa settimana di nuovo havevano messo in sugo monsignor vescovo di Mantova, sì che pareva che volessero accomodare il negotio con una semplice lettera di complimento del re di Francia; ma quando si è venuto al ristretto, ha trovato le solite forme di negotiare. Hieri parlando meco il conte di Castro si allargò grandemente, essaggerando che la republica di Venetia potria dare la pace all'Italia se si mantenesse neutrale, come fa N. S.re, e gli si daria sicurezza di non ricever pregiuditio di sorte alcuna con la parola dell'imperatore e del re Cattolico; anzi si faria che la desse anche per questo S. B.ne, facendomi molta instanza se S. S.tà la daria, assicurato dall'imperatore e dal re. Al che, se bene potevo risponder sufficientemente con dire non so, nondimeno potendo dubitare che non fusse affatto suo senso, e parendomi bene che restassero tronche, per quanto è possibile, simili trattationi, oltre al dire di non sapere né poter sapere il senso di N. S.re in simil materia, aggiunsi che per mio parere gravissime difficoltà potria ritrovar S. S.tà, ma quando cessassero tutte l'altre, potria bastar quella di metter in contingenza il sommo rispetto dovutole con quella republica, della quale si potria più che probabilmente credere che in materia dove è tanto impegnata, e dove si tratta di sì gravi interessi di stato, non saria per deferire o appoggiarsi alla parola di S. B.ne. Se la lentezza di Francia non dà campo alle armi Cesaree e cattoliche di far qualche considerabil acquisto, si può non senza fondamento sperare che s'inducano le volontà de' ministri di Spagna e di qua a piegare con gli accidenti di Fiandra, donde, oltre alla caduta di Bolduch, vengono avvisi che titubi tutto il restante, così pe'l mancamento di danari, di gente e di capi, come per l'alienatione d'animo de' paesani da Spagnuoli, oltre a quello più particolare delli eretici, e che però nelle piazze più principali si scoprivano ogni giorno nuove intelligenze e pericoli; sì come anche con quello che può qua temersi del re di Suetia dopo la tregua conclusa co'l Polacco, scrivendosi che detto re passi con potente essercito verso il ducato di Michelburgh con l'assistenza di gente e danari di Francia, Inghilterra, Danimarca, Venetiani et Olandesi, e che perciò il generale Valestain se ne tornava verso detto ducato per difenderlo; il che mi viene anche confirmato con lettere de' 17 del corrente da Alberstat, dove tuttavia si tratteneva detto generale. Mando copia della lettera scritta da' Svizzeri a S. M.tà, havuta in confidenza di buon luogo, et ho rincontro di queste istanze dal signor principe d'Echembergh, dal quale mi fu detto di più essergli scritto da personaggio principale di quella natione che i Franzesi e Venetia vi procuravano impegnarli contro l'imperatore e divertir dall'Italia le armi imperiali sopra di loro, ma che non gli riuscirà. Mando parimente copia di una scrittura che contiene l'espositione fatta dal signor di Sabran in Genova in nome del Christianissimo. In questo punto mi vien detto da persona confidente, in conformità di quello che si può cavare dal negotiato del Questembergh, haver sentito da un consigliero che, se N. S.re s'impiegherà per l'aggiustamento di queste controversie e proporrà qualche partito o temperamento, ne haverà ogni sodisfattione e ne resterà con honore. Ho detto a questo medesimo, al quale posso dubitare sia stata fatta quest'apertura perché la riferisca a me, che preghi questo signore che si contenti accennarne qualch'uno, acciò si possa insinuare a me, perché lo partecipi a N. S.re; e la medesima instanza ho fatta ancor io al Questembergh, che voglia applicar il pensiero a temperamento che possa ricever questo negotio e comunicarmelo confidentemente, poiché N. S.re non può far altro che rappresentare a ciascuna delle parti la pretensione dell'altra e pregar da ogni banda a calar, quanto si può pattuir a concordia; ma che il qualificare o temperar le pretensioni lo lascia alle parti medesime, per non rendersi sospetto et inhabilitarsi ad esser mediatore per la pace. Di Vienna 29 7mbre 1629. The text follows the Roman decipherment printed by Kiewning (1897), Nr. 184, which the figures on the sheet match; it continues R311. --- [as] justified in whole or in part, but leaving the judgement and decision on them entirely free to His Majesty. From the talk of these Spanish ambassadors I cannot draw any disposition towards peace unless they remain with Casale in one way or another for security and reputation, and unless Savoy and Guastalla are left content. This supposed, it is no wonder that Eggenberg, utterly devoted to the Spaniards, holds firm on the usual points, not without the agreement of most of the councillors, who cannot or dare not go against his opinion. And on the day I was at the hunt, being in the pavilion with His Majesty, the Empress, talking with me, opened herself with some feeling about this towards the Prince, saying that they try to make her suspect in this business and to see that she should not even speak of it; and therefore, not staying to speak in secret all that she would have wished, so as not to give rise to suspicion that these affairs were being discussed, she told me that she would take the occasion to speak of it at greater length, and that she would say she had then spoken with me about the business of this convent of St Augustine and of the office of St Ursula. These particulars I wished to indicate to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, so that with your singular prudence you may infer what can be hoped for in this business; especially if a person's report were well founded, that the Marquis Spinola, so as not to return to Flanders, where he is supposed to have orders to go once the affairs of Italy are settled, seeing the affairs of that province in such ruin, is rather inclined to stoke the war in Italy, or at least to drag out the settlement. Of the proposal made by the King of France in Spain and passed on by the lord nuncios, by whom it was sent to me, I find no trace here, either with the Spanish ambassadors or with the Emperor's ministers; and whether they have not communicated it from there, or want to keep it secret here, either is a sign that it is not meant to be accepted, but that they want to give fodder to keep the resolutions of France and the other interested parties asleep and in suspense until they manage to strike some blow in that province; and it seems that for no other purpose than this they have for some time now been stirring up negotiations and hopes of a settlement, as I have reported from time to time; and this week they had again set the Bishop of Mantua going, so that it seemed they wanted to settle the business with a simple letter of compliment from the King of France; but when it came to the point, he found the usual ways of negotiating. Yesterday the Count of Castro, speaking with me, opened himself at length, urging that the Republic of Venice could give peace to Italy if it remained neutral, as Our Lord does, and that it would be given security of suffering no prejudice of any kind on the word of the Emperor and the Catholic King; indeed, that His Beatitude would be made to give it too, and he pressed me hard on whether His Holiness would give it, being assured by the Emperor and the King. Although I could have answered sufficiently by saying I did not know, nevertheless, since I could suspect that this was not entirely his own view, and since it seemed good to me that such negotiations be cut short as far as possible, besides saying that I did not and could not know Our Lord's mind on such a matter, I added that in my opinion His Holiness might find very grave difficulties, but if all the others ceased, that of putting at risk the supreme respect owed to him by that Republic would suffice; of which one could more than probably believe that, in a matter in which it is so engaged and where such grave interests of state are at stake, it would not defer to or rely on the word of His Beatitude. If the slowness of France gives the imperial and Catholic arms no room to make some considerable gain, it may be hoped, not without foundation, that the will of the Spanish ministers and of those here will be brought to yield by the misfortunes of Flanders, from where, besides the fall of 's-Hertogenbosch, news comes that all the rest is tottering, both for lack of money, men and leaders and for the alienation of the inhabitants from the Spaniards, besides the more particular one of the heretics; and that therefore in the principal strongholds new plots and dangers were discovered every day; and likewise by what may be feared here from the King of Sweden after the truce concluded with the Pole, it being written that the said King is moving with a powerful army towards the duchy of Mecklenburg, with the help of men and money from France, England, Denmark, the Venetians and the Dutch, and that therefore General Wallenstein was returning towards the said duchy to defend it; which is also confirmed to me by letters of the 17th of this month from Halberstadt, where the said General was still staying. I send a copy of the letter written by the Swiss to His Majesty, obtained in confidence from a good source, and I have confirmation of these requests from the Lord Prince of Eggenberg, who told me further that he had been written to by a leading personage of that nation that the French and Venice were trying to commit them against the Emperor and to divert the imperial arms from Italy onto them, but that they would not succeed. I likewise send a copy of a paper containing the statement made by Monsieur de Sabran in Genoa in the name of the Most Christian King. At this moment I am told by a confidential person, in keeping with what can be drawn from Questenberg's negotiation, that he heard from a councillor that, if Our Lord exerts himself for the settlement of these disputes and proposes some plan or compromise, he will have every satisfaction from it and will come out of it with honour. I told this same person, to whom I can suspect this opening was made so that he would report it to me, to ask this gentleman to be pleased to indicate one, so that it could be suggested to me and I could pass it on to Our Lord; and I made the same request myself to Questenberg, that he apply his mind to a compromise this business could admit and communicate it to me in confidence, since Our Lord can do no more than represent to each party the claim of the other and beg on every side to come down as far as possible to agree on terms; but the qualifying or tempering of the claims he leaves to the parties themselves, so as not to make himself suspect and disqualify himself from being mediator for the peace. Vienna, 29 September 1629. The same [203: councillor] suggested that by admitting a foreign visitor His Majesty would be entering into new difficulties, confirming what I indicated under the fifteenth about paying the visitor's expenses; which would cease if [?Our Lord] deputed one of the bishops of the country, whichever pleased him most; and if not [...]. It was sent on with a covering letter of 8 August 1729. Where Huntington Library, William Blathwayt papers addenda, mssBLA 191, p. 5 (Huntington Digital Library p15150coll7 id 61005). Not on DECODE. The cipher A one-part French code of numbers from 1 to about 1370. Letters, syllables, words and names are listed in alphabetical order, so 580 is je, 581 ie and 585 ig. How it was read 942 code/gloss pairs were copied from five sibling letters in the same file, which were deciphered between the lines in 1729. That gives 364 values. Fifteen more groups were filled from the sense, bracketed by their alphabetical neighbours. What it says The agent complains that Mr Keene, the British envoy at Madrid, has left him without orders for weeks during the accommodation with Spain: "Mandez-moi donc quelque ordre pour ma conduite." Still open Seven groups: 6, 274, 254, 937, 1052, 726 and 836.

J'y ai répondu ce six de mars à la première adresse. Quand vous me ferez sçavoir, comme je dis, [il s']agit après le départ du [274]. Car Monsieur Keene ne m'avoit [rien], mais il [254] a aucun ordre des semaines pour moi [937] dans l'affaire passée. Je lui ai fait trouver bon [1052] ce, sans qu'il m'ait jamais dit ce [726] je pouvois faire pour le mieux à l'accommodement. [836]es je ignore vos intentions, et je serai inutile dans l'ignorance. Mandez-moi donc quelque ordre pour ma conduite … English: The obligation I owe you, my Lord, is very great for your letter of the [?]. I answered it this sixth of March at the first address. When you let me know, as I say, it concerns [what follows] the departure of [?]. For Mr Keene had [told] me nothing, and there has been no order for me for weeks in the past affair. I got him to approve this, without his ever telling me what I could do for the best towards the accommodation. I do not know your intentions, and I shall be useless in ignorance. Send me then some order for my conduct … The "accommodement" is the settlement between Britain and Spain that was being negotiated in the summer of 1729 and ended in the Treaty of Seville (9 November 1729). Benjamin Keene was the British envoy at Madrid. The page breaks off after the last group with a row of dots.

The page was transcribed from the HDL image: 141 groups, 102 of them distinct. The sibling letters were transcribed group by group with their glosses, giving 942 pairs and 379 distinct values ( pairs_A.tsv , pairs_B.tsv ). Applying the table directly read 116 of the 141 groups, and the result already formed French sentences. Because the code is alphabetical, an unknown group can be bracketed by its neighbours. 585 lies between 581 ie and 588 il, and gives ig-no-re and ig-no-ra-n-ce. 1210 lies between 1209 cinq and 1211 sept, so it is six. 222 lies between 218 conclure and 224 confidence, so it is conduite. On the same reasoning 275 is dans, 816 ordre, 666 lu, 1118 trouver, 689 m (de m-ar-s), 460 fe (fe-re-z), 84 apres, 1152 vos and 805 obligation. Groups 1240–1370 appear under dashes in the glosses. 1250 is taken here as a separator.

Readings by grade: 116 groups have the value glossed in the siblings (H). Six have variant glosses (C). Twelve were inferred from context and alphabetical order (M). Seven are unread (I): 6 : a number, the date of Newcastle's letter. The code's numbers run 8 vingt and 11 cinquante. 274 : a d- word or a name, after "le départ du". 254 , 937 (qu-), 1052 (s-), 726 (m-), 836 (p-): none of these is glossed in any sibling. The agent's other coded pieces in the file (mssBLA 184 and 186) carry no glosses. More of the series may hold the missing values but has not been digitised.
