Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (56% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription) and Brice Dudout (verification) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) · Also credited · Gustav Adolph Bergenroth (key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (56% of the cipher) The letter Rodrigo González de Puebla, Ferdinand’s ambassador in England, to Miguel Pérez de Almazán, secretary of the King, from London, 21 April 1506. One page of clear Spanish with cipher passages in lines 11–29, signed by Puebla, and an address leaf. Where Archivo General de Simancas, Patronato Real, legajo 54, doc. 78 (foliation 179), on PARES as description 2208120. Catalogue entry 617. The cipher One sign for each letter, with a second sign for a, i and u/v, run on without word division; one code word of Puebla’s Great Roman Numeral code (DCCCLXXXVIII, “el Rey de Inglaterra”) occurs three times. How it was deciphered With Satoshi Tomokiyo’s reconstruction of Puebla’s First Cipher (Bergenroth’s key no. 6), applied unchanged. Under an Early Modern Spanish language model the decode scores −1.69 per letter; 1,000 shuffled keys score at best −4.73. What it says People around the Princess of Wales had her write the letters Puebla encloses, for their own interest; he sees her household “tan bien ataviados que mas no pense ver”; and the greed of certain persons is such that even the treasure of the King of England would not content them. Still open The clear text around the cipher, read only in part at the size PARES serves; the fragments of ll. 11–17, which do not yet build sentences; three unread signs; the C-count of the code word. Credit Transcription, decipherment and controls by WAINUT (pull request #101, 27 October 2026), done with AI language-model agents and re-read by a second agent. The key is Satoshi Tomokiyo’s reconstruction of Puebla’s First Cipher (cryptiana, “Spanish ciphers”), after Bergenroth’s key no. 6; the code word is from the contemporary key in AGS Patronato Real leg. 52 doc. 33.

The unit has four images on PARES: the letter (image 1), two blank pages, and the address leaf (image 4). The address reads Al muy noble señor el señor Miguell Perez dalmaçan secretario y del consejo del Rey nuestro señor ; the endorsement, written across the leaf, gives del doctor de la puebla … xxj … abril 1506 , and the date line on the letter itself is de Londres a xxj de abril . The image carries the archive’s watermark PTR,LEG,54,78, a pencilled “PR54-78” and the foliation 179. The PARES id is the one Tomokiyo gives for this letter; the catalogue first had 2208061, which is Puebla’s letter of 15 April 1507. Philip and Juana, King and Queen of Castile since Isabella’s death, were driven ashore in England in January 1506 on their way from Flanders to Spain, and stayed until late April, when they sailed from Falmouth ( Falamua in the Spanish of the time) to La Coruña. The clear opening of the letter says that Puebla had written at length to the King and to Almazán by way of Martín Sánchez de Zamudio, the Bilbao shipowner, and that the King and Queen were waiting for the weather at Falmouth. Those clear readings are uncertain at the size PARES serves and are not part of the reading files.

Tomokiyo calls it Puebla’s First Cipher and identifies it with Bergenroth’s key no. 6. He reconstructed the table from the letters of 1496–1507 before finding the original, and lists this letter among those that use it, without a reading. The table gives one sign for most letters and two for a, i and u/v: a is written q or M , i is b or a 5-like sign, u and v share a small o with the b of b(v) . Several letters are written with the shape of another letter ( e for l, g for f, f for g, a for h, R for t), and r is the figure-like sign 46 . The transcription names each sign by a short ASCII label ( key_first_cipher.tsv ), and the decoder works on those labels. Words that the Great Roman Numeral code holds were written as code words instead. Only one occurs here, three times: DCCCLXXXVIII, “el Rey de Inglaterra” on key image 51 of the contemporary code book (AGS Patronato Real leg. 52 doc. 33). The scribe writes CC and CCC as ligatures distinguished by a small mark, and the mark was not checked on this letter, so the value stays doubtful at every occurrence. The letters run on without word division. Doubled letters are written twice. One sign in l. 13 (in ra?on ) is not in Tomokiyo’s table, and the table has no z: in l. 12 a hooked form of the o-sign seems to stand for it ( plazer ).

WAINUT transcribed the cipher passages of lines 11–29 from three-times enlarged crops of the PARES image, 370 signs and three code words, and decoded them with the table unchanged ( decode.py ). A second agent then re-read lines 14–20, 24–26 and 29 on fresh crops in its own sign labels and reproduced every reading letter by letter, with three corrections: abra quien , not abra bien , in l. 16; a single c in inclusas ; and the words va a at the start of the passage in l. 29. The controls ask whether the table could produce Spanish from these signs by chance. Language model (the project’s shared es-golden-age model, Spanish 1490–1650, five-letter context, no spaces): the decode of lines 14–29 scores −1.69 per letter. 1,000 keys made by shuffling the table’s values among its signs score at best −4.73 (median −6.12); the true key on 1,000 texts with the signs shuffled within each line scores at best −4.26 (median −4.77). On the word-divided reading, the language check ranks Spanish first (−1.62), ahead of Catalan (−1.95) and Portuguese (−2.09). Word list: a short list of common Spanish words, without the rare content words, covers 0.61 of the decoded letters; shuffled keys cover at most 0.29 and shuffled texts at most 0.26. The decode is therefore not an artefact of the table or of the transcription; what limits the reading is the clear text around it.

Lines 18–29, with word division and punctuation added. Clear words of the letter are in plain type where they were transcribed; […] is clear text not transcribed, [?word] a doubtful word and { } the code word. […] por aquella gente hazia, por su propio interese, que la princesa me escriviese estas cartas que aqui van inclusas . […] Los de la señora princesa veo tan bien ataviados que mas no pense ver. Por la codicia de algunas personas [?] [?] es tal que con [?el] tesoro de {el Rey de Inglaterra?}, dudo que se [?contentasen] […] […] va a beneficio de natura con este […] […] those people brought it about, for their own interest, that the princess wrote me these letters, which go enclosed here. […] I see the lady princess’s people so finely dressed that I did not think to see more. [?For] the greed of certain persons [?] [?] is such that, even with [?the] treasure of {the King of England?}, I doubt they would be [?content] […] is going along at the mercy of chance with this […] “A beneficio de natura” is a set phrase of the period, “left to nature”, that is to chance: Cisneros’s secretaries write in 1516 that something “no se ha de dexar a beneficio de natura”. The day after this letter, Katharine wrote to her father from Richmond that her people were ready to ask alms and that she herself was all but naked (CSP Spain I no. 459, 22 April 1506). Puebla tells the King’s secretary in cipher that her household is finely dressed beyond what he expected, and that the letters she writes are prompted by people around her for their own interest. The two letters belong to the long quarrel over Katharine’s maintenance and her dowry after Prince Arthur’s death.

The earlier cipher lines decode as well, but between them are clear words that could not be read, so they do not build sentences. Secure words are y de la partida , de todo el [?aresto] , con mucha [?razon] , señora princesa , conviene , bien y acrecentamiento , de {el Rey de Inglaterra?} y del principe and abra quien le [?pedir] que ningun malcontentamiento . The departure and the “arrest” may be Philip and Juana’s detention in England and their sailing, and the prince is presumably the Prince of Wales, Henry; with the clear words missing, neither can be confirmed. The decode of these lines is shown in the full texts below as decoded, not read. The first words, y de la partida , are also in a note Tomokiyo left in the source of his “Spanish ciphers” page next to his entry for this letter (an HTML comment, not shown on the page). He had begun to decipher it and published nothing further.

No printed text of this letter was found. The searches, all on 27 October 2026: Bergenroth, Calendar of State Papers, Spain , vol. I (1862), April 1506, pp. 385–386: nos. 458–460, none from Puebla; and the 1868 Supplement, 1506 section: none. G. Gómez de Fuensalida, Correspondencia (1907), Rodríguez Villa, La reina doña Juana la Loca (1892), which prints Puebla’s letters of 1507 only, and the Colección de documentos inéditos vol. 8 (1846), which prints Philip I’s letters from England in 1506: their OCR texts were searched for the distinctive words of the reading ( ataviados , inclusas , codicia de alg- , beneficio de natura , propio interese , malcontentamiento ) and for Puebla’s letters of April 1506. None matched. A. Paz y Meliá, Series de los más importantes documentos del archivo y biblioteca del Duque de Medinaceli , vols. 1–2 (1915–1922): no Puebla letter, no match. G. Mattingly, “The reputation of Doctor De Puebla”, English Historical Review 55 (1940), pp. 27–46: no use of this letter. The Internet Archive’s full-text search across its Spanish holdings, which include the whole Colección de documentos inéditos , for the phrases of the reading: no hit outside unrelated texts (the phrase a beneficio de natura occurs widely, never with Puebla). Not searched: Mattingly’s Catherine of Aragon (1941), which is not available in full text, and HathiTrust, whose full-text search could not be reached. The claim of novelty is limited to the prints above.

The clear text of the letter, about twenty lines in Puebla’s cursive: read only in part. At 1017 × 1413 pixels, the largest size PARES serves, many words cannot be read with confidence; a better scan from Simancas would allow it. Lines 11–17: the fragments do not build sentences, because the clear words between them are not read and descenders from the lines above run through ll. 11–13; l. 12 ( [?desto] [?stares] … [?aresto] ) divides uncertainly. Graded C (conjectural) as a whole. Unread signs: one in l. 13 ( ra?on , presumably z, not in the table) and two after personas in l. 25. Doubtful readings: pedir for the decoded pedri (l. 16, C); contentasen across the line end (ll. 26–27, M); the article el before tesoro (l. 26, clear, M); plazer with the hooked sign (l. 12, C). The code word DCCCLXXXVIII, “el Rey de Inglaterra”: its value fits each of the three places, but the ligature mark that fixes its C-count was not checked on this letter (M). A parallel reading: Brice Dudout read the same letter the same day, independently, with the same table, and published it on Europe chiffrée ; his files are in the repository folder ( dudout/ ). The two decipherments agree word for word on most passages, and he adopted two readings from this one (“a beneficio de natura” and “por aquella gente hazia”). Where this page has a doubt, he reads z in razón (l. 13), de la for da la , and pedrique (from pedricar ) for pedri (l. 16), and he does not count the two signs after personas . He also transcribes the clear text of ll. 11–17. None of this is taken here yet: it needs a look at the image, which PARES refused on 27 October 2026.

Translation translation.md # English translation By Martín Sánchez de Zamudio I wrote at length to the King our lord, and the same to Your Grace. […] Doña María de Rojas […]. What I wish to say in this one is that the King of England […] so fair a wind that […] tomorrow […] he will embark. And he also says […] Doña María de Rojas […]. […] when he pleases; and the departure […] and all the rest greatly please the King of England, and with much reason. […] that, on the part of my lady the Princess, […] is well fitting, as is the increase and {respect} of the King of England and of the Prince; and there will be no one to preach any discontent to her. Those people, for their own interest, were making the Princess write me these letters, which go enclosed herewith. […] My lady the Princess’s people I see so well attired that I never thought to see better; but the greed of certain persons is such that even with the treasure of the King of England I doubt they would be content. I trust in the prudence of Your Grace and of the King our lord, who will not allow […]. And because […] is left at the mercy of chance with this one (?). I say no more […] [may Our Lord] increase and prosper the life and estate of Your Grace as you desire. From London, 21 April 1506. Key: key_first_cipher.tsv

DECODE R1862 is four images of a despatch at ASVe, Busta 27 f. 354, dated 29 April 1628 and placed at Rome. The record carries no transcription, no sender and no receiver, and the archive’s images are not in the public domain, so nothing of them is reproduced here. Cipher and clear text alternate on the page: page 1 and page 2 are almost entirely in figures, page 3 runs clear for eleven lines and then ciphers again, page 4 opens in the clear, then runs cipher, clear and cipher again. The way in was a sibling. DECODE R1874 (ASVe Busta 30 f. 174) is a despatch of Alvise Mocenigo from Madrid, 26 October 1628, in the same cipher; its sixteen images hold the ciphered despatch, a second enciphered copy of it, and, on images 8955–8959, the chancery’s own decipherment , paragraph by numbered paragraph. An earlier attempt on R1874 had transcribed that decipherment but had not used it to recover the key.

The decipherment of R1874’s paragraphs 5 to 16 was transcribed here, about 4,800 letters of plaintext. DECODE’s transcription of R1874’s cipher was then split into five stretches matching those paragraphs (the ratio is a steady 1.84 letters per group), and each stretch was aligned to its plaintext by EM over the possible divisions of the plaintext into group values, sharpened each round until every group settled on one value. The solver was checked first on a synthetic syllabic cipher built over the same text, which it recovered exactly (97 of 97 groups). The first run on the real data collapsed, because a group was allowed to stand for nothing and the frequent groups went null; capping values at four letters and forbidding nulls fixed it. One detail decided the shape of the answer. DECODE’s transcriber wrote the figure 5 in two forms, as “13” and as “21”. Folding both to a single 5 gave a muddled key; keeping them apart made the table regular at once, because they are two different rows of it (51 and 53 in R1862’s clearer hand).

The cipher is a syllabary laid out as a grid . The prefix gives the vowel and the last two digits the consonant: vowels: 6 = a, 51 = e, 62 = i, 53 = o, 64 = u (61 is a second i/e row) consonants: 07 b, 08 c, 09 l, 10 d, 11 f, 13 g, 14 gn, 17 gr, 19 l, 20 m, 21 n, 22 p, 23 pr, 24 qu, 26 ss, 27 r, 28 s, 31 st, 33 t, 34 tr, 37 v, 38 z; so 6210 di , 5133 te , 5333 to , 6433 tu , 5308 co , 6220 mi single letters: 680 a, 6280 e, 6480 i, 5190 o, 6490 u, 692 n, 6292 r, 6482 l, 5390 s word codes: 670 che , 672 con , 6270 in , 6249 il , 5102 del , 5302 nel , 5124 and 5387 quel , 5384 qual ( che ), 5374 per , 5142 duca , 6440 sua , 6442 suo , 6240 ave , 5373 part , 6477 poc , 6287 non , 5347 papa , 6247 Cesare paragraph marks: 698, 5198, 5199 stand at the edges of the ciphered passages, as 6499 does in R1874 The word band is alphabetical. Above column 39 the codes of each prefix row run in alphabetical blocks — row 53 gives papa 47, part 73, per 74, piu 77, qual 84, quel 87, ques 88; row 64 gives signor 39, sua 40, suo 42. That brackets every code that is still open, and it is how several were identified: 6274 falls just after in and is “molto” (“star molto oculati et avvertiti”), 5140 falls just below duca and is “dov” (“dovrian star”). It also caught three values inherited from the R1874 alignment that were wrong: 628 is sa , not “n” (“non sarian giamai”, “fatto sapere”); 6439 is signor , not “mini” (“Sua Signoria Illustrissima”, “il Signor Cardinal Barberino”); 6481 is a second i . The grid cells that R1874’s decipherment never reached were filled by the structure itself (a cell’s value is its column’s consonant plus its row’s vowel), and the word codes were identified from context in this letter: 5384 by “cavar anche qualche intimo particolare”, 5347 by “a fin che il Papa deliberasse”, 6240 by “ ave ndomi ricercato”.

It opens in the clear and turns to cipher in the middle of the first line: Opportunissima occ.ne ho io havuta hieri col Cardinal Barberino di parlargli di quel negotio che lei mi si è commesso con cotesto Eccelso Conseglio, et di cavar anche qualche intimo particolare desiderato da lei… What the ambassador had been asked to find out, and what the Cardinal had asked him, are the heart of it. Twice the Cardinal had wanted to know …perché due volte nelle capele [papali] e avendomi ricercato con [più] instanza se Palma sarà ben fortificata, quanto presidio aveva, se il passo della Pontebba si era ben assicurato… (“…because twice in the papal chapels, and having asked me with [more] insistence whether Palma will be well fortified, how large a garrison it had, whether the pass of the Pontebba had been well secured…”) Two words in it were supplied on 30 September 2026, both grade I. The code 5349 has no value from R1874, but the word band is alphabetical and 5349 stands just after 5347 papa and before 5373 part : after nelle capele that gives papali , the papal chapels where the ambassadors met the Cardinal (or the stem papal , with the next group’s e as its ending). Before instanza the clerk wrote 6202, which is bi (as in du·bi·tando on page 2) and gives no word; read as one of his one-digit slips for 6222, pi , it gives con pi[ù] instanza . A slip for an unknown word code 6242 (between ave and Cesare , so a b - or ca - word such as calda ) cannot be excluded. That is, whether the Republic’s great fortress of Palmanova and the Alpine pass above Venice were ready. Hearing from other quarters that “Imperiali uniti con Spagna parlavano con molto sprezzo” of the Republic, the ambassador answered by asking, “con intiera confidenza”, whether the questions had been put “a qualche fine”, and begged that anything of the kind be told him, so that the Serenissima might know in time “perché da lei fossero trovati i rimedii oportuni”, but without naming “quelli che trattassero simili” matters. The rest of page 2 is the substance of the audience, and it turns on secrecy: such dealings “non sarian giamai […] palesi, ma ben sotto profondissima segretezza”, and the Cardinal spoke “aprendosi in strettissima confidenza”. He had “havuto particolar notitia de pensieri vasti”; he had heard of the disgusto di Aquileia , the Venetian–Imperial quarrel over the Patriarchate; and of arms and men “che si trovavano in piedi nella Germania”, which left him “dubitando avessero qualche pensiero di molestare la Republica dalla parte del Friuli in particolare”; and he told the Cardinal that “quelli Signori dovrian star molto oculati et avvertiti”, so that he “non potei far di meno di non dimandarle” more. The Cardinal “interrogavami per dir il vero”, and the ambassador “mi sono andato certificando” that even if Spaniards and Imperialists had set “l’animo contro la Republica”, they “non sono in tu[tto]… effettuar i loro… disegni”. The clear paragraph at the foot of page 2 and the top of page 3 carries the Cardinal’s argument that Venice need not fear an imperial descent: the Emperor ha pur troppo che fare in casa propria , having to watch the King of Denmark, Bethlen Gabor, the Dutch and perhaps the Turk; Wallenstein would not come into Italy without his whole army, and quartering it would take gran summa d’oro, di che l’Imp.re n’ha gran carestia . The ciphered part of page 3 reports the Cardinal on the imperial aulic council , “nel qual, se ben la maggior parte de’ consiglieri sia aderente al Re di Spagna”, and that he shows himself “più tosto amorevole che difidente”. It ends with the Cardinal offering “un particolare da esserne gran ri[f]lesso” and asking, in the line that had been missed out of the transcription altogether, “la prego non nominarme” : do not name me as the source. Page 4, in the clear, lays the attempt on Genoa at the Duke of Savoy’s door, and argues that Spaniards and Imperialists, ill satisfied with him, will trust him less. Then, in cipher, the ambassador’s own move: …ringratiai il cardinale di co[sì] confidenti communicatione, et sopra […] l’ultimo del Duca di Sivoia presi ocasione di caricar la mano a fin che il Papa deliberasse mandar la sua persona legato […] per acomodar gli interessi di Mantova e di Savoia insieme… He pressed “la facilità che già si averia trovata nel Duca di Savoia di ridursi”, and the glory for His Holiness of “questa opportunità di dar pace”. The last ciphered lines return to the Cardinal, who “have dato il sudetto aviso… di Genova”. All of this is late April 1628: Vincenzo II Gonzaga was dead, Nevers was in Mantua, Spain and Savoy had agreed to partition Monferrato, and Urban VIII’s nephew was running a papal policy of professed neutrality.

The record has no transcription, so the 1,280 code groups were transcribed from the images here and then checked, line by line, with the key in hand: a line that does not decipher into Italian is a line to look at again. Five such passes were run at first. Two traps in this hand mattered: a final n-shape is a 2 , not a 1, and a 7 is a “>” with a long open tail while an 8 is a hook plus a closed loop. Page 2’s lines bow by up to 35 px, and two of its transcribed rows turned out to have been blended from the head of one physical line and the tail of another, with a third row belonging to no line at all; tracking the baselines and re-splitting fixed the alignment, and the join it produced across two lines, “andavo dubitando avessero qualche pi | nsiero”, confirms it. Sixteen passes of that kind were run in all, and two of them changed the shape of the text: one manuscript line on page 3 had never been transcribed at all (it reads “la prego non nominarme” — I beg you not to name me ), and the lines slope enough that a fixed horizontal band picks up the neighbour’s ink on the right-hand side, which is what produced the blends. The clerk miscodes as well as misspells , always by one digit, and reading him means reading through both. His spelling slips stand in the plain text — sivoia for Savoia, germinia for Germania, dovore for dovere, partcolar , soto , conunicarla . His encipherment slips are recorded separately (the transcription keeps the digits he wrote, and the key file lists the group he meant): 6220 for 6223 in esprimersi , 632 for 672 in confidenza , 5337 for 5137 in altrove , 5388 for 5308 in così , 68 for 637 in Mantova , 537 for 627 in considerati , 6480 for 6490 in più , 6222 for 622 in preparati . What remains: twelve group tokens (0.9%) have no value: 6443, 6279 and 6478 twice each, and 5349, 5370, 51708, 5378, 5379, 6241 once each (5349 now has the conjectural value papali from its alphabetical place, section 04). All of them sit in the word and name band, the part R1874’s decipherment does not cover, so only another letter in this cipher would settle them: none is digitised on DECODE, and the Venetian key registers that are (the Codice Amadi, ASVe Inquisitori di Stato reg. 1269, and the Busta 4 registers) are all of the previous century. One line, P2 L22, is image-true after four independent readings and still gives no sense; every group in it is a structural grid value, so it turns on one of the clerk’s slips or on a word outside the corpus. The ambassador himself is still anonymous: he does not name himself, and the Calendar of State Papers Venetian, which calendars only the England-related despatches, has nothing from Rome for 29 April 1628. The extent was measured. Each line’s decipherment is scored against an Italian character model of the period, calibrated on genuine Italian of the same length taken from R1874’s decipherment (real text of this length falls below −2.25 per character only 5% of the time), and scored with the edges of its neighbours so that a word split across a line end is not counted against it. By that measure 0.95 of the code groups stand in lines that give sense ; a stricter 25-character sliding window gives 0.92 and a hand audit token by token gives 0.96, the spread being the clerk’s own spelling. That meets this project’s threshold for a complete decipherment (95% of tokens giving sense, no gap untried, only scattered codes open).

The opening of the War of the Mantuan Succession. Perche due volte nelle capele [5349] e avendomi ricercato con bi instanza se Palma sara ben fortificata, quanto presidio aveva, se il passo della Ponleba si era ben asicurato, io presi ocasione di dirgli che, avendomi dimandato cose di questa natura, udendo io da qualche altra parte ancora che imperiali uniti con Spa[gna] parlavano con molto sprezzo delle cose [?hapude] [5370]i di esse et in partcolare della repubblica, ricercavo con intiera confidenza Sua Signoria Illustrisima se le instanze predete mi avesse [?sallafate] a qualche fine, et se altra cose intorno a cio di recondito ne sapesse, mi facesse gratia di conunicarla, sicura che avevo trovavo modo ben si che la serenissima repubblica risipesse vo[51708]lari di poco momento, perche da lei fossero trovati i rimedi oportuni; et [?celepa], ma certo che da qual part vonisse notitia tale, et meno i nomi di quelli che tramassero simili insidie, non sarian giamai [6443] palesi, ma ben [?setolti] soto profondissima segretezza. Il cardinale, aprendosi in co[n] instretissima confidenza, mi disse: [?vora] [6279] signor fatore, io avendo havuto partcolar notitia de pensieri vasti et [?silatide] gli inperiali et de Sp[agnuo]li uniti, o massime a quelli il disgusto di Aquileia, considerati la piu preparati tro di armi che si trovatino in piedi nella germinia, et l'oasione delle [?troi] comotione, in qua andavo dubitando avessero qualche pinsiero di molestare la repubblica della parte del Friuli in partcolare; onde mi mossi a ha esprimersi con molto i et qua et altrove che queli signori dovrian star molto oculati et avortiti. Et ⟨a Vostra Paternità⟩ ancora non potei far di meno di non dimandarle [5378] le vidi […] intero [?gavami] per dir il voro: ogni [?maoro] mi sono andato certificando che [5379] ben Sp[agnuo]li et inperiali avessero come [?edoche] lo [6279] casi sono l'animo contro la repubblica, non sono in [?tuli] efetuar i loro [?cheli] i disegni. ⟨E perche l'Imperatore ha pur troppo che fare in casa propria, dovendosi guardare molto bene dal Re di Danimarca, che par che ritorni, da Gabor, dai Stati d'Holanda, e forse anche dal Turco; tanto piu che per far l'impresa che disegnano, e contro la Francia, nesso nel e nel tener i Svizzeri in dovere, quando volesse mandar esserciti in Italia, vi bisognerebbe altre forze che quelle che ha hora in piedi. Aggiungesi a questo che, non volendo Spagna [?] tener gente qui in Italia del Volestein, questo ricusa di venirvi quando viene con tutta la sua gente; et di passar per venirvi in gli Stati, sia per i Stati degli amici o degli inimici, converria pagar i viveri e gl'alloggi, et a gl'effetto bisognando gran summa d'oro, di che l'Imperatore n'ha gran carestia; perche dir pecunia, il Volestein medesimo nel [?tramischiar] i … quella gente sopra le sue spese et a dispendio della propria borsa, che ben sa non lo potria fare. Concludo io dunque,⟩ disse il cardinale, tro [6478] e con ragione ben da me avorti queste considerate, non esservi [a]lcun dubio, et di poco male esser bene pevo che ei stia avortita, che si mostra piu tosto amorevole che difidente del consiglio aulico del Cesare, nel quale, se ben la magior parte di consiglieri sia aderente al re di Sp[agna], [6478] a volta vie qualche [?dustodi] buona et retamente che puo introdur confidenza con suoi buoni uficivoglio anco [?sogiu]. Se il cardina[le] [?dedir] ⟨a Vostra Paternità⟩ un partcolare da essene gran rilesso, in la prego non nominarme che glielo have fatto sapere; et e ⟨che con fondamento altri l'huomo s'e venuto in chiaro, que machinationi della congiura … tentato di Genova esser stata tramata dal Duca di Savoia, onde da questo male si potrà cavare questo bene, che Spagnoli et Imperiali, mal sodisfatti della parte operata d'esso Serenissimo Duca, che non meno non si potranno più fidar di lui in conto alcuno; potriano però attender gl'i legami d'unioni d'esso, et il medesimo Duca, col pensar bene a' fatti suoi, e trovando di non stare bene, nè con Francia, nè con Spagnoli, nè con Imperiali, ma d'i tutti esser diffidente molto, forse potria risolver d'acquietarsi, et accommodar i fatti suoi col Duca di Mantova.⟩ Ringratiai il cardinale di cosi confidenti conunicatione, et sopra quanta [?o] ultimo del duca di Sivoia presi ocasione di caricar la mano a fin che il papa deliberisse mandar la sua persona legato mi [6241] per acomodar gli interes di Mantova et di Sivoia insieme; et mi fesi forte a persuaderlo [?incis] per la facilita che gi si averia trovata nel duca di Sivoia di ridursi alle cose del dovore, onde si rebe [6443] a Sua Signoria di quant [g]loria questa oportunita di dar pace al [?sionome] ⟨che, tenendoci abbondantemente nell'Eccellentissimo Senato, non aggiungerò maggior particolari, per non apportar molestia à cotesto Eccellentissimo Consiglio; ben supplicherò l'Eccellenze Vostre à non communicarli⟩ che il signor cardinal Barbarino have dato il sudeto aviso delo cose di Genoa, perche se a caso risisse che non gli avessi … Translation R1862_en.md <!-- English translation of tx/R1862_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), the reading of the project's decipherment (tx/plain.txt). ⟨ ⟩ = written in clear in the letter; [5349] etc. = code with no value; […] = the unread line P2 L22; [?word] = doubtful word kept as in the Italian where it cannot be translated. Where the clerk's Italian is garbled the English follows it closely rather than guessing. --> # R1862, the Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 (ASVe Busta 27 f. 354): English translation ⟨Most Serene Prince.⟩ ⟨I had a most opportune occasion yesterday⟩ with Cardinal Barberini to speak to him of that business which was committed to me by that most excellent Council, and also to draw out some intimate particular that you desired. Because twice in the [5349] chapels he had asked me, with [?more] insistence, whether Palma would be well fortified, what garrison it had, and whether the pass of the Pontebba had been well secured, I took the occasion to tell him that, since he had asked me things of this nature, and since I heard from some other quarter as well that the Imperialists, united with Spain, spoke with much contempt of the affairs [?hapude] [5370] of them, and in particular of the Republic, I asked His Most Illustrious Lordship in entire confidence whether he had made the aforesaid inquiries of me to some end, and, if he knew anything else hidden about this, to do me the favour of communicating it, being sure that I had found a way so that the Most Serene Republic should learn [51708] of little moment, so that she might find the fitting remedies; and [?celepa], but certain that from whatever quarter such news came, and still less the names of those who were plotting such snares, they would never be [6443] disclosed, but well [?buried] under the deepest secrecy. The Cardinal, opening himself to me in the strictest confidence, said to me: [?vora] [6279] signor fatore, having had particular notice of the vast designs and [?silatide] of the Imperialists and the Spaniards united, or above all to them the displeasure over Aquileia, considering the most prepared [?troops] of arms that are on foot in Germany, and the occasion of the [?troi] commotions, I went on suspecting that they had some thought of molesting the Republic, from the side of Friuli in particular; whence I was moved to [?have him] express himself, with much [?i], both here and elsewhere, that those lords ought to stay very watchful and on their guard. And ⟨to Your Paternity⟩ I could not refrain, either, from asking [5378] [?le vidi] […] entire [?gavami] to tell the truth: every [?maoro] I have been ascertaining that [5379], though the Spaniards and the Imperialists had as [?edoche] the [6279] cases their intent against the Republic, they are not [?in tuli] to carry out their [?cheli] designs. ⟨And because the Emperor has only too much to do in his own house, having to guard himself very well against the King of Denmark, who seems to be returning, against Gabor, against the States of Holland, and perhaps also against the Turk; all the more since, to make the enterprise that they are planning, and against France, [?nesso nel] and in keeping the Swiss to their duty, should he wish to send armies into Italy, other forces would be needed than those he has now on foot. Add to this that, Spain not wishing [?] to keep Wallenstein's men here in Italy, he refuses to come here unless he comes with all his men; and to pass through the States to get here, whether the States of friends or of enemies, he would have to pay for provisions and quarters, and for that a great sum of gold would be needed, of which the Emperor has a great dearth; for, as to money, Wallenstein himself, in [?mixing] the … those men at his own expense and to the cost of his own purse, which he well knows he could not do. I conclude therefore,⟩ said the Cardinal, [6478] and with reason, well [?warned] by me of these considerations, that there is no doubt, and that it is good, of little harm, [?pevo] that she should stay on her guard; that he shows himself rather well-disposed than mistrustful of the Emperor's Aulic Council, in which, although the greater part of the councillors adhere to the King of Spain, [6478] at times [?vie] some good [?dustodi] and rightly, that can bring in confidence with his good offices; I wish also [?sogiu]. If the Cardinal [?dedir] ⟨to Your Paternity⟩ a particular to be of great importance, I beg you not to name me as the one who made it known to him; and it is ⟨that others have come to light with foundation, that the machinations of the conspiracy … attempted at Genoa were plotted by the Duke of Savoy; whence from this evil this good may be drawn, that the Spaniards and Imperialists, ill satisfied with the part played by the said Most Serene Duke, will no less be unable to trust him any more on any account; they might however attend to the ties of union with him, and the Duke himself, thinking well about his own affairs and finding that he stands well neither with France, nor with the Spaniards, nor with the Imperialists, but is much mistrusted by all, might perhaps resolve to quiet himself and settle his affairs with the Duke of Mantua.⟩ I thanked the Cardinal for so confidential a communication, and on the last [?move] of the Duke of Savoy I took the occasion to press hard so that the Pope should resolve to send his person as legate [6241] to settle the interests of Mantua and Savoy together; and I made a strong effort to persuade him [?incis] by the ease that would now be found in the Duke of Savoy to bring himself back to his duty, whence [6443] would be to His Lordship how much [g]lory [in] this opportunity to give peace to the [?sionome] ⟨which, as I am keeping the Most Excellent Senate abundantly informed, I will not add more particulars, so as not to trouble that Most Excellent Council; I will indeed beg Your Excellencies not to communicate them⟩ that the Lord Cardinal Barberini has given the aforesaid notice of the affairs of Genoa, because if by chance it came out that I had not … Key: key.tsv , key_over.json

Four letters to the French ambassador at the imperial court in the Bishop of Rennes’ cipher, with no contemporary decipherment and none found in print: Catherine’s of 31 July 1563 (BnF fr. 3181 f. 55), whose cipher La Ferrière printed as an empty bracket, a 1564 order to leave the precedence quarrel, Bourdin’s of December 1562 on the leaked marriage overture, and a note to be deciphered by Rennes himself and burned. Tomokiyo’s reconstructed key was applied, with each secretary’s letter forms fixed on glossed letters in the same hand and a language model choosing among ambiguous values. Between 70% and 83% of each letter is measured as sense, 79% overall. ‎q̄q̄ · < · z λ d θ · ꝛa ᷅ ʒ … ᵃ ℬᵃʒ ℬaʒʒᵃʒ que · vous · a v e z · d e s … « sceu ce que vous avez descouvert » the French court → the imperial court · homophonic cipher with word-signs and clear-word nulls · December 1562 – 1564 Catherine de Médicis and the bishop of Rennes: four cipher letters, 1562–1564 from Catherine de' Medici Go to the full text ↓ BnF français 3181 f. 55 and Cinq cents Colbert 390 pp. 139, 357 and 392 p. 231 · catalogue item 11, class B F. 55 was printed in 1885 with the cipher left blank; Tomokiyo lists all four items as having no contemporary decipherment, and no later one was found. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 20 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) · On the map Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) · WAINUT (transcription) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · none (key obtained, text not read) The letters Four letters sent to Bernardin Bochetel, bishop of Rennes and Charles IX’s ambassador to the Emperor: Catherine de Médicis (31 July 1563), a 1564 order on precedence, Bourdin (December 1562), and a note to be deciphered by Rennes himself and burned. Where BnF français 3181 f. 55; Colbert 390 pp. 357–358 and p. 139; Colbert 392 p. 231. None had a contemporary decipherment; La Ferrière (1885) printed f. 55 with the thirteen cipher lines as an empty bracket. The cipher The Bishop of Rennes’ cipher, reconstructed by S. Tomokiyo: homophonic, with about thirty word-signs and nulls that include clear-looking French words. How it was read The key was known; the work was transcription. Each secretary’s sign forms were fixed on glossed letters in the same hand, then a language model chose among candidate values. 79% of the 2,308 signs measure as sense, 15% probable. What it says f. 55 concerns the Council of Trent and the Habsburg marriage; the 1564 letter orders Rennes to drop the precedence quarrel; Bourdin reports the secret marriage overture was « known at once in Spain ». Still open Signs that occur in no glossed passage, on the September 2026 hand estimates: about 9% of f. 55, 1% of pp. 357–358, 15–20% of p. 231 and about 35% of the faint p. 139 (strict 5 October measure: 6% unread over all four, 15% probable). Credit S. Tomokiyo reconstructed the cipher.

Bochetel had written on 18 June. Catherine, at the camp before Le Havre while the English garrison embarked, replied on the last day of July. La Ferrière prints her text from this very folio (« Orig. Bibl. nat. fonds français, n° 3181, f° 55 r° et v° »), and it runs: Monsieur de Rennes, je n’ay receu vostre lettre du xviii e de juing que depuis sept ou huit jours, c’est pour [ ] — footnote: Partie chiffrée. Au demeurant, je veulx bien vous advertir que, après avoir essayé tous moyens de faire départir la royne d’Angleterre de la place du Havre-de-Grâce qu’elle avoit occupée durant ces troubles… That bracket is the thirteen lines. Everything after it (the siege, the plague among the English, the artillery and ships left behind, the hope that the French and the English « n’auront plus que faire ensemble ») Catherine sent in clear. BnF français 3181, f. 55: the clear address and first sentence, thirteen lines of cipher, then the clear Au demourant . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3181 f. 55, via Gallica (btv1b9059845t, view 36).

This is the Bishop of Rennes’ cipher, in use between 1561 and 1564 for the embassy to the Emperor. It is homophonic: two to eight invented signs for each letter, an overbar to tell close shapes apart, about thirty word-signs ( que , vous , nous , vostre , qui , mais , par , la , le , lettre , bien , faire , faict , and signs of their own for l’Empereur and Roy de Boheme ), and a set of nulls. Besides meaningless squiggles, the key allows ordinary French words written out in clear as nulls : que , est , pour , plus , xix , vre , do , fo . They are scattered through the cipher so that a reader glancing at the page sees what looks like ordinary writing interrupted by symbols, and a codebreaker who takes them for cleartext is misled. On f. 55 the last line ends with a run of five of them before the clear text resumes. S. Tomokiyo’s reconstruction of the cipher, built from the letters of Cinq cents Colbert 390 and BnF français 3158 f. 1 that carry decipherments. The bottom rows are the word-signs and the nulls. Image: S. Tomokiyo, Cryptiana (his reconstruction of the Bishop of Rennes’ cipher, 1561–1564).

A key drawn as a table of shapes does not settle how a given scribe forms each sign. Several of this scribe’s forms are near-identical (the s-shapes that serve r and s, the c-shapes that serve o, h and t, the loops that serve e and l), and the table does not say which is which in his hand. This was settled by f. 57 , the letter of 13 August 1563, two views on in the same volume. Its ciphered passage carries a decipherment written down the left margin, phrase by phrase, line for line. Aligning the margin with the cipher gives an exact crib. The first ciphered line of f. 57 glosses as que les princes , and the signs are q̄q̄ · l · e · s · p · r · i · n · c · e · s: seven signs for « princes », which fix p, r, i, n, c, e and s. The margin runs on: moien de se passer par Ferrare les enfans dudict Roy des Romains allans en Espaigne, pour eviter l’incomodité de la mer et le dangier que les temps aigres peult porter a ceste occasion… Every phrase of it is another handful of confirmed shapes. The crib: f. 57 (13 August 1563), the same cipher with a contemporary decipherment written down the margin, phrase by phrase against the line. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3181 f. 57, via Gallica (btv1b9059845t, view 38).

The first decryption, made from a single transcription and a direct table lookup, secured about three fifths of the passage. A second transcription from native-resolution crops, decrypted with a language model (section 09), and a full alignment of the margin decipherments of f. 57 and f. 58 (same scribe, same cipher) now put about 91% of the signs into French: some 80% secure and 11% probable. The glosses settled the looped d-like sign that had been taken as e, s or u: in all of its twenty-odd glossed occurrences it is e . They also gave ʃʃ = le , an underlined dagger = con , an underlined u = pour . One correction to the record: the f. 57 margin reads « par France », not « par Ferrare ». [c’est pour] … vous avez descouvert. … vous par … la [matière] du mariage, et vostre advis sur la conduicte d’iceulx en … mon intention se trouve toute conforme, et ayt tenu ce chemin, dont … ce qui pourra sortir. J’ay aussi entendu ce que l[e …] vous mist en avant, qui l’avoit délibéré faire pour le bien de la Chrestienté et avancer le concile, à ce que je veoy chacun faict … par[t], et monstrer b[onne et] fructueuse … de ce concile. Mais nous sommes à voir l’utilité qui en sortira, mesmes ce qui se promect des sessions de Decembre, desquelz vous avez oy parler, vous estant dernierement à … Trante. In English: … you have discovered … about the marriage, and your opinion on how to handle them … my intention is entirely in accord, and [I hope] he has kept to this course … what may come of it. I have also heard what [someone] put to you, who had resolved to do it for the good of Christendom and to advance the council, so that, as I see, everyone does his part and shows a good and fruitful [outcome] of this council. But we have yet to see what good will come of it, and what is promised from the December sessions, of which you have heard, having lately been at … Trent. f. 55, lines 4–6: « …ayt tenu ce chemin… », « …entendu ce que le… », « vous mist en avant, qui l’avoit… ». Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3181 f. 55, via Gallica (btv1b9059845t, view 36).

The subject is the Council of Trent and the marriage negotiation with the house of Austria: the two things Catherine had reason not to send in clear through the empire in the summer of 1563, and the two things she left out of the open part of the letter. The Havre had just fallen and Charles IX’s majority was about to be declared: those were things to be published. What went under the cipher was the ecclesiastical and dynastic bargaining the crown was conducting at Trent and Vienna at the same moment. The council closed on 4 December 1563, the « sessions de Decembre » of the last line.

An undated letter to Rennes in Cinq cents Colbert 390, pp. 357–358 (views 180–181), signed by Catherine and countersigned by de l’Aubespine. The upper third of p. 357 is clear: the secretary Charron has arrived, and with him the Emperor’s reply on the dispute over la précédence . Fifteen lines of cipher follow, and ten more at the head of p. 358 before the clear « Le S r de Lanssac n’est point encore arrivé ». Tomokiyo lists the page as having no contemporary decipherment, and La Ferrière does not print it. The printed letters on the same quarrel (27 June and 18 August 1564, the latter ordering Rennes to attend Ferdinand I’s obsequies and « n’y rien cedder ») place it in the late summer of 1564. About 99% of its signs were decrypted on the hand estimate of September 2026 (88% secure, 11% probable); the strict measurement of 5 October 2026 (section 10) gives 82% (p. 357) and 76% (p. 358) read as sense: il fauldra prandre autre pretexte que celuy porté par la depesche du s[ieu]r Charon, dont vous avez beau subject, estant l’ennuieux, ce me plest de franchir clairement les a[utres] …, et s’en revenir, que de riens dissimuler, [re]mectant l’amendement de cela au temps et aux ocasions qui se pourront offrir cy après, et sans avoir [à] opérer l’effect de[s] deffiés, que ny autres d’en aucun maniement ny ouverte negociation de vostre part. Bien pourrez, ainsi que porte ma dernière depesche, laisser là quelque secretaire ou aucun des vostres, advisés soubz couleur d’aucuns voz affaires particuliers, de deniers qu’avez envoyé querir ou autres choses que vous attendez, qui puisse faire sçavoir toutes nouvelles de ce qui s’o[ffr]ira, principalement de ce qui se peult esperer de l’[ajour]nement de la diète et de ce qui se preparera à y decider, de quoy vous pourrez paraventure [avoir] toute lumière avant vostre dit partement; que je remects à vous de disposer, à propos, mouvement, avancement ou retardation d’iceluy ne face prejudice à la reputation du Roy ny à l’amitié que je desire estre conservée entre ces deux princes. The order of 18 August is reversed. Rennes is to find another pretext than the one Charron carried and withdraw without conceding anything: no open negotiation, the remedy left to time. He is to leave a secretary or one of his own people at the imperial court under cover of private business (money he has sent for, things he is waiting on) to report all news, above all on the Diet; and the timing of his own departure is left to him, so long as neither haste nor delay harms the King’s reputation or the friendship between the two princes. Not decrypted: six signs on p. 358 before toute lumière ([avoir] is restored from the sense), and whether the Diet’s word is ajournement or gouvernement . Cinq cents Colbert 390 p. 357: the clear « en la dispute de la précédence, » and the cipher that begins il fauldra prandre autre pretexte . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cinq cents Colbert 390 p. 357, via Gallica (btv1b10033942k, view 180).

A letter of about twenty-five cipher lines under the salutation « Monsieur », in Cinq cents Colbert 392, p. 231 (view 112). Its clear ending is on the next page (view 113): « De Paris le …e jour de decembre 1562 », signed by the secretary of state Jacques Bourdin. The letter Bourdin encloses is Catherine’s to Rennes of 15 December 1562 (La Ferrière I, 448–451), whose marriage paragraphs La Ferrière printed from the decipherment joined to it: the overture for one of the Emperor’s daughters made through the archbishop of Trier. The cipher is in a third secretary’s hand, with its own forms (a tailed 2 for p, a looped ʒ for r, + for f, a double dagger for et , ‖ for the word plus ). About 85% is decrypted: Monsieur, je vous envoye la lettre que [Madame] la Royne escript [à vous] sur le faict dont vous m’avez donné advis. Dernierement pour advise[r] que l’en ne luy parle de la secrete, qu’elle a en vous, en moindres paroles et termes que de luy dire, ne l’asseurer, qu’elle la trouve telle que de sa propre personne; de sorte que si le[dit] … Roy n’y est retenu en ce que l’on desire d’aultre occasion que celle-là, il n’y [a] plus … devera plus faire de difficulté. Au demeurant [je] vous advise que ce que je vous mande, que … sçavoit incontinant en Espaigne. Tous les pro… que [luy?] teniez secret … ne fut pas s[a]ns occasion, [et] nous eusmes advis que [s]a femme nous [a]voit [fait?] triumphe de la premiere ouverture que vous luy feistes de [ce] mariage. Je croy bien que de nous il y aura à peu changer d’advis [et] conseil, me semble, que … en donne assez, com[me] en grande occasion. Dieu veuille que toutes [choses] se conduise[nt] et succede[nt] au commun desir et contentement de [leurs] Majestés, et avec un tel et si ferme establissement d’amitié et alliance que … nous tous en ressentions, tant d’une part que d’aultre, le bien et l’utilité, à l’honneur de Dieu et [au] repos de la chrestienté. The secret of the overture has leaked: what Rennes reports was « known at once in Spain », and « his wife » (most likely Maria, Queen of the Romans and Philip II’s sister) made a triumph of the first opening Rennes made of the marriage. Bourdin’s own clear continuation on p. 232 (« faire changer d’opinion ») echoes the cipher’s « changer d’advis et conseil ». Cinq cents Colbert 392 p. 231: « Monsieur » and the opening, je vous envoye la lettre que … la Royne escript . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cinq cents Colbert 392 p. 231, via Gallica (btv1b100339594, view 112).

Decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026): lines 1–7 build sentences, lines 8–14 are mostly unread runs and code words. A small sheet bound as p. 139 of Cinq cents Colbert 390 (view 70), fourteen faint lines of cipher under three clear-looking words, and beneath them a clear instruction: « Deschiffrez vous mesmes ceste cy et ne vous en fiez en clerc ny secretaire que vous ayez, et la mettez au feu si tost que vous l’aurez veue. » Tomokiyo noted that it uses nulls not only at the ends but between words and inside them. The facing p. 138, in the same secretary’s hand, carries a ciphered paragraph with its decipherment in the margin (« Et pource qu’il m’a semblé que je ne sçaurois trouver ung plus digne et suffisant personnage pour faire parler à mons[ieu]r mon [beau] frere du mariage… »), which gave this hand’s forms; other glossed pages in the volume (pp. 189/199, 221–231) added more. Two first attempts that let the language model choose nulls freely produced fluent nonsense and were discarded. A fresh transcription from contrast-enhanced crops gave about 37% secure and 28% probable decryption. The partial reading of 23 October 2026 ( c390_p139_reading.md ), in the secretary’s spelling, with [?word] for a word the signs carry only in part: Que ie vous tienne pour trop aduise et affectione [?et] loyal [?seruiteur] du roy mon fils pour vous en dormir bien en chose qui est […] et en son seruice, [?ie] ne laisseray […] vous dire qu’il [?fault] bien que vous [ayez] les yeux [?ouuerts] pour obseruer come totes [?choses] passeront en ce [?voyaige] de mon cousin […] [?que les] […] ses actions, encores que ie n’en visse aucunement a doubter, afin [?de me] [?donner] aduis [?et] tout ce que vous congnoistre le meriter […] [?l’envoyez] […] beau frere [?se separe] de vostre […] […] bien. The three [CODE] places are signs of the form ẟ with a small letter above it. The full decipherment of p. 117 on pp. 120–121 shows this form is a code word: ẟ with a raised a stands for Allemaigne , and on p. 347 ∂ with a raised l stands for Metz . The one before « ses actions » names a person Rennes is to watch (the Emperor fits), and the one after « des » is a plural. Neither occurs in any decipherment found, so both stay undecrypted. Catherine (the « roy mon fils » fixes the writer) tells Rennes she holds him too wise and loyal a servant to need telling, but that he must keep his eyes open and watch the doings of « mon cousin » and send her everything he learns. The decrypted text does not name the cousin. The sheet sits among the copies of her 1562 letters to Condé that she sent to Rennes; the Cardinal of Lorraine, whom she calls « mon cousin » in the letters of 1563, is the other candidate. A control re-run with the values from the glossed pages withdrew four earlier decryptions of this sheet (among them passeront and fault ) and added four. Two re-readings, 23 October 2026. All 184 views of Colbert 390 were contact-sheeted: there is no clear copy or decipherment of this note. The volume does hold an unused key source, Catherine’s letter of 15 December 1562 (pp. 115–127), whose cipher (pp. 117–118, 125–126) has its cursive decipherment on pp. 119–121, printed by La Ferrière (I, 449–451). Pages 117–118 were transcribed sign by sign (949 signs) and aligned with the print: ∂ = m , ẟ = r , ā = g , ℒ = dict , ∂ with a raised a = Allemaigne , and a sign for le roy des Romains . With them fils is carried, and line 8 can be proposed as “passeront en ce [?voyaige] de mon cousin”, the Cardinal of Lorraine’s journey. But none of this sheet’s open signs and code words occurs in the 1562 letter, so lines 8–14 stay mostly unread and the note stays decoded, not read: the blocker is now that no key material for those signs is known.

Images by IIIF region request from Gallica at native resolution (8720 px for français 3181, about 6300–7600 px for the Colbert volumes); in français 3181 the folio number is the Gallica view plus nineteen. Each cipher line was transcribed glyph by glyph from crops at native or double resolution, with contrast enhancement for the faint p. 139. Every sign was then given its candidate values (usually one; two where the hand leaves a homophone ambiguous; a null option only for known null shapes), and for each line a French n-gram language model of sixteenth-century despatches chose the most probable combination of those candidates ( targets/rennes1563/lattice.py , the shared lang/ model fr-1530-despatches ). Letting the model choose among many nulls produced fluent nonsense on p. 139; with the candidates held narrow it cannot invent text. The calibration also used every full decipherment found in Colbert 390 (p. 317 against p. 313, p. 117 against pp. 120–121, p. 189 against the slip on p. 199) and the margin-glossed letters of 1561 (pp. 49–69) and 1564 (pp. 339–349). The sister volumes Colbert 391, 394 and 395 contain no deciphered passage in this cipher. The key is Tomokiyo’s, but each of the four letters is in a different secretary’s hand, and the hands form the same signs differently. The values for each hand were fixed on letters in that hand carrying contemporary decipherments: f. 57 and f. 58 for f. 55; p. 138 and the glossed pages 189/199 and 221–231 of Colbert 390 for p. 139 and the Bourdin letter. The glossed pages 241–305 of Colbert 390 are in the hand of français 3181 f. 52, not of f. 55, and added little. La Ferrière’s two volumes were searched for parallels; none of the four passages is printed there.

The duc de Nevers’ letters of August–October 1593 to the secretary of state Revol, copied in BnF fr. 3985 and 3986, are in the Court’s symbol cipher, Tomokiyo’s no. 60. The key was transcribed in full and corrected from a reader’s issue; it gives three words of the 21 August letter and anchors on the 7 October one, but the copyist’s cursive forms block the rest. Where BnF Français 3985 ff. 88, 115, 176 and Français 3986 ff. 146v, 157v, 198, via Gallica; the key in Français 3995 ff. 108–111. Part of catalogue entry 21. The cipher The Court’s symbol cipher, given to Nevers at Montereau in August 1593: four or five symbols for each letter, a syllabary, Roman numerals for names and places, word signs and nulls. How it was tried Both key tables transcribed from the images, checked on two pages the office deciphered between the lines, and corrected from a reader’s issue; then applied to the transcribed passages. What it says On the 21 August letter: … de absolution , le Roy , qu’il . Elsewhere only anchors. Still open Almost all of it: the three passages tried (ff. 88r, 146v, 157v) are decoded, not read, and three more are not yet transcribed. A re-reading on 23 October 2026 found no interlinear decipherment on ff. 88, 146v and 157v (canvas 287 checked at full resolution) and no Nevers–Revol letter of 1593 in the Mémoires de Nevers ii (pp. 324, 425, 453, 513); f. 146v re-read at native resolution keeps its anchors (“de l’absolution”, “Mr de Mercure”) with nothing readable between them. The next step is a glyph atlas of the copyist’s forms from the interlined Instruction of 31 August. Credit Key identified by Satoshi Tomokiyo; corrections and the f. 88 transcription by Robert Węglarek (issue #32). Nevers’s two letters to the marquis de Pisany of the same autumn are in his numerical cipher no. 46 and have their own page, Nevers to Pisany, 1593 : a different cipher, with its own page. The two were written up together until 14 October 2026.

The letters to Revol are in the Court’s symbol cipher, Tomokiyo’s no. 60, endorsed “Chiffre baillé à Monsieur de Nevers, Montereau, aoust 1593”. Its enciphering sheet (fr. 3995 f. 109) gives four or five symbols for each letter, a syllabary ba … vu , word signs, Roman numerals for provinces, towns and persons ( iiij xx for 80), and a row of nulls; Nevers’s secretary added a deciphering table sorted by the shape of the symbols (ff. 110v–111). Both tables were transcribed from the full-resolution images on 17 September 2026 and are transcribed in key60.txt ; the deciphering table is complete and legible, and it settles the values Tomokiyo found doubtful (the y-shaped sign is s , the closed 4-shaped sign is x , the crossed η is the doubling sign). The deciphering table, fr. 3995 f. 110v: Roman numerals, Arabic figures, letter-shapes. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3995 f. 110v, via Gallica (btv1b525085665).

The cursive forms the copyist uses in the letters differ from the Court hand of the table, so the values were checked on Henri IV’s letter to Nevers of 7 October 1593 (fr. 3986 f. 151), a page in the same cipher with the office’s interlinear decipherment: plusieurs , contre , de la , promesse , respondre , Bellièvre , Villeroy , Zamet fix thirty of the commonest signs. The Instruction of 31 August is the richer crib: part 2 of the Mémoires de Nevers is on Gallica after all (ark bpt6k64451005, reached through the catalogue notice rather than search), and its pp. 492–499 print the Instruction in clear, and the cipher pages of the manuscript Instruction itself (fr. 3985, canvases 264–268) carry the office’s interlinear decipherment in the same copyist’s hand as the Revol letters, matching the print word for word. That gives three full pages of symbol–plaintext pairs in the target hand, on top of the King’s letter of 7 October. The crib: Henri IV to Nevers, Chartres, 7 October 1593, with the decipherment between the lines. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3986 f. 151, via Gallica (btv1b9060631k). The second crib: the Instruction of 31 August 1593 (fr. 3985), interlined by the office; the same text is printed in the Mémoires de Nevers , ii, 492–499. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3985, Instruction of 31 August 1593, via Gallica (btv1b90606498, canvases 264–268).

Where the cipher sits in the copies, from the full-resolution pages: 21 August, fr. 3985 f. 88–88v, six lines; 27 August, f. 115, one line (the earlier pages of that letter are in clear); 2 September, f. 176, about ten lines with the sign lxxix for Rome; 7 October, fr. 3986 f. 146v, nine lines; 9 October, f. 157v, four lines; 23 October, f. 198, five lines. The f. 146v and f. 157v passages are transcribed symbol by symbol ( ct_3986_f146v.txt , ct_3986_f157v.txt ) and run through the decoder; a second pass at higher magnification then showed that both pages, like the interlined Instruction, mix short cipher stretches into faded clear cursive, so those transcriptions take some clear strokes for cipher and carry a revision note. Tomokiyo’s three decrypted words on f. 146v come straight out of the table, l’absolution (λ 14 ꝑ ſ+ 20 xx ‡ π ⊥ = la·b·so·l·u·t·i·o·n; the l is the sheet’s ſ+, first transcribed as 4), à la vérité and intérêt , with qu’il , bien , et , que , nous , si around them; but between the anchors the output is still not French, because the copyist runs the small symbols together ( ue , ur , ıı , v ) and the same stroke stands for two or three table entries. The next pass is a glyph-level alignment of the copyist’s forms against the crib page in the same hand, then the other four letters. Corrections from issue #32. On 12 October 2026 Robert Węglarek (GitHub tunarob ) sent corrections to the transcribed key no. 60 and a first transcription of the 21 August letter (fr. 3985 f. 88). His work was LLM-assisted, and we checked each point on the full-resolution images. Ten of his twelve key corrections hold and are now in key60.txt : chiefly, b’s first homophone is o– (a ring with a tail), which the old tags confused with tu (–o–); the 4-shaped signs are four different signs (ſ+ = l , open 4+ = i , closed 4 = x , 2+ = u or i ); and c, i, m, o and u each had one homophone wrong or missing. With the corrected b, line 5 of f. 88r deciphers as … de absolution (g ∂ o– Ⱡ ſ+ 20 8 ++ π ⊥). No shuffled arrangement of the same 86 symbols out of 5000 produced a word that long. Line 6 has the signs for le Roy and qu’il . The rest of f. 88 and the 2 September and 23 October passages are not yet deciphered here. fr. 3986 f. 146v, the block of cipher in the letter from Vese, 7 October 1593. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 23 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) Contributed by Michael Brackx (solution) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter François d’Espinay de Saint-Luc, governor of Brouage, to Henri III, “De Brouage, ce … de Juing 1586”: two pages almost wholly in cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 15572, f. 260r–v (Gallica, canvases 268–269). Not in the catalogue and not on DECODE as far as found. The cipher Letter substitution with some homophones, word signs ( je, le, que, la, pour ), name codes and nulls: Tomokiyo’s “St. Luc’s Cipher”. How it was decoded Michael Brackx corrected Tomokiyo’s table on the margin decipherments of another Saint-Luc letter, f. 245r–v, transcribed f. 260 sign by sign and decoded it with a French language model. What it says Rochelais galliots at Oléron, ships loaded with stone against the harbour palisade, an unpaid garrison, and a plea against letting the tax-farmers buy salt at La Rochelle. Still open Many transcription labels still stand for two to four letters; they must be split by shape on the images before the text can count as deciphered. Credit Michael Brackx (issue #90), with Claude Code; key table by Satoshi Tomokiyo.

Français 15572 gathers despatches of 1586 to Henri III and Villeroy. (The January-to-July range and the description of the writers as the King’s commanders in the west are not from the sources and were not checked here.) Saint-Luc held Brouage, the salt port facing Huguenot La Rochelle. (That he was Henri III’s former favourite is background not from the sources and was not checked here.) Folio 260 (older foliation 274, struck through) carries 26 lines of cipher on the recto and 29 on the verso, closed in clear “De Brouage, ce … de Juing 1586” and signed St. Luc. Folio 245 is another Saint-Luc letter in the same table, and it was deciphered at the time. Its verso has a clear letter and then a 12-line cipher block, with the decipherment in the margin. Its recto has two cipher passages with margin decipherments. These two margins are the cribs ( texts/f245_cribs.md ). The f. 245v margin reads in part: “Si comme l’on dict l’armée de Mons.r du Mayne doibt travailler à Castillon, il s’approchera fort de Royan”. Saint-Luc’s letter of 30 January 1586 at f. 43 uses a different table: a different cipher, with its own page (George Lasry’s key).

Satoshi Tomokiyo publishes the table as “St. Luc’s Cipher” on his cryptiana page on Henri III’s ciphers and reads the opening line of f. 260. Brackx encoded it as transcription labels with values and corrected it on the f. 245 cribs, keeping a change only when a crib or at least two contexts supported it and the sign shape checked on the image. His main changes: Δo = Monsieur du Mayne and ʞ = pour (crib 1); ⊔ = la Rochelle , listed as a null before; a small hooked ɣ = ss (19 contexts, and asseurer in crib 2); ɑ with a raised stroke = la ; Ↄ = rr ; ʒ with a crossed tail = h ; plain 3 = m ; and a sign for x (crib 2, extrême ). With the corrected key the decode agrees with the f. 245v margin on 89.3% of letters and with f. 245r on 83.2%. On f. 260, 79.2% and 80.7% of decoded letters fall in French words, against 27–46% and 31–49% when each label’s set of values is moved at random to another label. The key is in brackx2026/key_r3.json .

Brackx’s reading keeps the writer’s spelling (one sign each for u/v and i/j). [?] is one unread word or group, [?word] a doubtful word. The opening, f. 260r ll. 1–5: arriua [?hier] en Olleron, et a ce matin [?est] [?venu] en son [?] [?] [?], ou il a eu le [?plaisir] de uoir batre nos chalupes auec ses galliotes, et de quelques canonades de nostre fort. Ie croy il n’y fera pas gran [?] seiour sans retourner a [?] la Rochelle. “[He] arrived [?yesterday] at Oléron, and this morning [?came] to his [?] [?] [?], where he had the [?pleasure] of seeing our shallops beaten by his galliots, and some cannon-shots from our fort. I believe he will not make a long stay without returning to La Rochelle.” The recto goes on to the Rochelais attempt to block the harbour with ships loaded with stone, one of “six uingts [?toneaux]”, work timed by the tide, and a ship taken. The verso turns to the garrison, unpaid and murmuring, with no word from the King since his letters of April; to La Rochelle’s plan to keep the sea and sell passports to its captains; and to “une chose … de tres grande importance”: the council has allowed the farmers of the grand parti to take salt at La Rochelle. Saint-Luc asks that French merchants be forbidden to take salt there “a peine de confiscation de corps et de biens”. The full reading and English of both pages are under Full texts.

Measured on the reading, 76.1% of the words of f. 260r and 85.1% of f. 260v read as sense. But many transcription labels still stand for two to four letters: z for u, v, h or m ; 9 for n, m or g ; S for m, s, g or mm ; f for c or s ; p for i or r ; and others. The decoder picks among them with a model of French. Letters on such labels are 39.4% of f. 260r and 33.8% of f. 260v, far over the 3% this project allows for look-alike signs. The f. 245 margins confirm these values as part of the key, but not each choice on f. 260. So both pages are decoded, not read, whatever their share of words. Where Brackx’s reading departs from the decoder, it always takes another value of the same label (22 letters in all). The several values could have been different sign shapes merged in transcription, so Brackx checked every multi-valued label on the full-size images, token by token. Two do split: S is a pair of S-curves (§§) for mm and a long s for s , which turns dosame into dommage ; and d has a hooked arch for l beside the ∂ for c . The other eight (z, 9, 6, p, f, t, pi, y) show one shape for all their values. What remains needs a contemporary decipherment of this letter or another in the same key.

Splitting the multi-valued labels by shape on the full-size images, then decoding again. Unread runs: on the recto ll. 1–2 (the places after “en son”), 5–11, 13–14, 17 and 19–24; on the verso l. 3 (the day of the King’s April letters), 4, 8–9, 12–18, 23 and 27. The sign Π, taken as a null, stands where affaire(s) needs ff (verso ll. 25 and 27); two signs after n’oze in crib 2 are not aligned. The transcription has not been checked against the images by a second person.

Where Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, AKM 21 plik 30/1 (DECODE R7486–R7500), catalogued on DECODE as from “NN z Drezna (jezuita?)”, with no decipherment. The cipher Clear German with single words and phrases in a homophonic letter table (a = 7, 8, 9; b = 10, 11, 12; … three numbers to a letter in alphabetical order), three-digit code numbers for people and things, and dotted letter signs. How it was deciphered A free solver gave nothing; a search that kept the table in alphabetical blocks and moved only the block boundaries found it from the ciphertext alone. The recipient’s own glosses agree with it and give three words of the code: der , von , der Kayser . Words of the code’s alphabetical 500s and a few persons were then fixed from context. What it says Court news from Vienna in the year of Ramillies and Turin, the Saxon king's affairs at the imperial court, rivalries for a post, the Malcontents in Hungary: “dieser glaubet sey kein guttes omen”. Still open Ten letters (R7486, R7488, R7489, R7490, R7492, R7493, R7496, R7497, R7498, R7500) break in most lines on open person codes, dotted signs and, in R7493, water damage: decoded, not read. R7487, R7491, R7494, R7495 and R7499 build sentences (22–23 October 2026) but read at 90.1%, 92.5%, 86.7%, 92.4% and 91.7% of their words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. 65 of the 77 three-digit codes, nearly all persons (187, 181, 166, 190 …): their roles are clear, their names are not, and no key survives. Also eight short runs and about ninety small word signs. On DECODE these fifteen letters were catalogued with eighteen letters to Hetman Adam Mikołaj Sieniawski under one range of records (R7468–R7500, catalogue entry 333). Those are other correspondents in four other keys, each with its own page (a different cipher in each): Brâncoveanu and Cantacuzino , news from Bender, 1709 , an adviser, c. 1707 and Chomentowski at the Porte .

DECODE R7486–R7500, Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, AKM 21 plik 30/1, items 1–15, uploaded in September 2023 with status N/A, cipher type “unknown” and no key or decryption file. DECODE gives the sender as “NN z Drezna (jezuita?)” and the receiver as “Schenck (Szench) szambelan Augusta II”. The neighbouring records R7460–R7467 and R7501–R7507 belong to other collections and correspondents and give no key for these.

The address leaf of the letter of 27 March reads A Monsieur / Mons.r Le Baron de Schenck / Chambell. de Sa Majesté / Le Roy de Pologne / à Cracovie . Every letter is dated from Vienna (“W. d. 12. Maj 1706”), not Dresden; the writer numbers them (N. 15 on 27 March, N. 47 on 14 July, so more than one a week), closes “Votre tres humble et tres obeiss. Serviteur” and signs with a name read “Sidon” or “Sadon”, probably a cover name. The receipt dockets say “Recept. d. 18 May 1706 in Cracau”, “d. 7. Junÿ 1706 in Lublin”; a later archive hand wrote “Seligman” and “Lehman” on two address leaves. Seven runs that a single slip spoils still read ( introduc[t]ion , punc[t]en , d[i]mission , be[m]ühen ); eight do not: “gutswor”, “sollwiglaufeenden” (perhaps zuwiderlauffenden , with the recipient's a u f over it), “lceth”, “ditlan”, “datmseyihm” and three of one or two letters (“iwzo” is ijzo , the writer’s spelling of itzo ). Their digits were checked twice on the images. Which letters read. A number given a value is not a reading, and the reading audit of 22 October 2026 judged each letter as text. On the same day every doubtful word of the letters then unread was re-read on the 32 DECODE images (about 170 corrections, mostly a hard hand rather than lost ink), and readings with English were written for every letter. Five letters build German sentences with the person codes left as numbers: R7487, R7491, R7494, R7495 and R7499 . In the other ten the sentences break on the open person codes and dotted signs (R7486, R7488, R7489, R7490, R7492, R7496, and on 23 October R7497, R7498 and R7500, which fall just under the bar once their running readings are written out), and in R7493 on water damage to the lower halves of its pages. Those ten are decoded, not read ; their partial readings stay in the repository. The share of the cipher in letters that read is about a quarter (estimated). Measured word by word on 24 October 2026, with the open codes and doubtful words as holes, those five build coherent sentences but read at 86.7–92.5% of their words (R7487 90.1%, R7491 92.5%, R7494 86.7%, R7495 92.4%, R7499 91.7%), under the 95% a complete reading needs.

Three layers sit beside the letter table: three-digit numbers for persons, courts and words (77 distinct, 502 occurrences), a few two- and one-digit numbers (83, “5”, “3.”, “2.”), and dotted letters before codes and runs (o., b., L., d., e., f., g., c., m., p., oo, ooo; 134 occurrences). The recipient settled the last two layers himself in N. 32: he wrote der over “o.” and von Kayser over “5 83”. The dotted letters are therefore a code for small words, not nulls. Code n Value Grade Evidence o. 34 der C the recipient’s gloss; “Es hat 189 o. 187 heute … schreiben wollen”, where the writer first wrote der and struck it 5, 83 3, 9 von, der Kayser C the recipient’s gloss; “83 ist wegen 204 also zu timide”, “f. 83 gar sehr wohl angesehen” L., f., b. 11, 13, 18 und, bey, von dem M, M, I “b. 154 L. 166 zugleich unterschrieben”; “ob 189 f. 254 reussire”; “b. 187 bin ersuchet worden” 189 56 Baron Schenck, the addressee M “einem diplomate vor 189”, “das diploma des 189”, the genealogy of “der Schenckisch-Nideggischen familie”; “des 189 zugestossenen Unpäßlichkeit” 150 42 King Augustus II M “in favorem 150”; “dass 150 nichts von Schweden zu erwarten habe”; “Ministres 3. 150” 100 9 the imperial court M “das interieur von 100”; “bei 100 mächtige grosse desordre” 204 5 Sweden M “83 ist wegen 204 also zu timide”; “Resolutionen, so etwann 204 eine jalousie verursachen könnten” 509, 513, 515, 519, 524 17 Friede, Ordre, Progressen, Reise, Urlaub M “in pto des 509, worauf nunmehro gedacht werden will”; “die 513 du cabinet”; “weiter glückliche 515”; “seine 519 auf morgen oder übermorgen festgestellet”; “beÿ 100 524 nehmen” 502, 518, 521 9 Abreise, Recommendation, Resolution I bounded by the alphabetical order of the 500s, which rise from F (509) through O, P, R to U (524), and fitting their sentences The persons are the gap. Their roles are clear from a second reading of every sentence that holds a code: 187 (102 times) is the writer’s principal in Vienna, in the King’s service and paid by bill of exchange; 181 (67) is the King’s man at the imperial court, with a secretary, couriers to 150 and rheumatism in his arm; 166 a minister at the King’s side; 190 an imperial minister who “nec superiorem, nec parem aut inferiorem vertragen kann” and wants “ein monopolium der affairen” (not Charles XII, who is named in clear in the same letter); 132 and 193 rivals for one post. The 100s and 200s do not follow the alphabet (204 Sweden breaks it), so position bounds nothing, and none of the names written in clear (Wackerbarth, Senfft, Plessen, Heinisch) can be tied to a code.

Pulled the metadata of R7460–R7507 through the DECODE API and the images with a logged-in session; no record carries a key or decipherment. Two transcription passes over the 52 images of the Schenck letters: clear text as far as legible, every cipher number, superscript and docket. A free homophonic solver (any number to any letter, German n-grams of the 1720s–60s) gave no sense on the 642 numbers then in hand. The runs end in 19 43, 21 45, 20 44, 19 55, and the frequent numbers cluster. If the homophones are consecutive numbers in alphabetical order, the key is only 23 boundaries. Annealing those boundaries alone against the same model gave blocks of three from a = 7–9 in the best restart (−913 against −1,212 to −1,496 for the others) and, at once, de Baron Kleinburg alhier and correspondenz . Every run was transcribed again at full resolution against the key: 24 lines corrected, most of them the writer's 31 taken for 21 and his delta-shaped 6 for 0 or 8. A second pass re-read every sentence that holds a code or a dotted sign (about 90 crops) and the recipient's glosses; the code was then tested for alphabetical order, which holds for the 500s and not for the persons. Outside help was sought for the names: printed editions, the lists of Saxon envoys at Vienna (Wackerbarth to 1706, Vesnich 1706–08), and the Wiener Diarium of 1706 for dated cribs, which the Austrian National Library serves only behind a bot check. None gave a key or a name. The keys of the Sieniawski letters once filed with these (Kaczka’s key A, the R7475 table) were scored on the runs and do not fit (−5.6 and −7.0 per character against −2.8 for the block key).

65 of the 77 three-digit codes, 363 occurrences, nearly all persons: 187, 181, 166, 190, 254, 258, 132, 193, 186 and the singletons. No key is filed with the letters, on DECODE or in print, and the clear text gives roles, not names; the Saxon cipher keys of the period would be in the Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden. About ninety small word signs (d., e., g., c., m., p., oo, ooo, “3.”, “2.”): articles or pronouns, but no single value fits every occurrence. Eight runs (44 numbers) with no sense, listed above; their digits were checked twice, and each occurs once. Grades: o., 5 and 83 C (the recipient's gloss); 189, 150, 100, 204, L., f. and five words of the 500s M; b., 502, 518, 521 I. The clear text is transcribed only in part ([?] where water damage or the hand defeat it). Who “Sidon” was, and which Schenck: neither is identified. DECODE's “NN z Drezna (jezuita?)” does not fit letters dated from Vienna.

Where BnF espagnol 336, no. 99, ff. 196r–198r (Gallica views 336–340, cipher on 337–338). Tomokiyo lists it as the remaining letter in the volume with no known decipherment. The cipher A homophonic substitution with 35 sign classes, two nulls and one sign for ll ; 125 cipher tokens. How it was read A Spanish homophonic solver produced Spanish only after joined signs were split. The segmentation was then fixed from the images. No outside key or plaintext was used, so the decipherment has internal support only. What it says A councillor reports a meeting on the comet: dizen que el mundo se acabará o morirá el rey por setiembre . The shorter passage concerns Ponte or Aponte and Escudero.
