The five written pages discuss money, services, court business, military news and marriage negotiations. The last page gives Madrid, 8 August 1596, and Matheo de Segura's signature. The cipher occupies only brief passages on f. 196v and f. 197r. The clear pages provide context; none supplies a decipherment of the encrypted words. Direct Gallica access failed during this attempt. Full-resolution Wikimedia Commons mirrors supplied the images. The often-repeated locator “view 280” is not this letter: it shows folio 164. The correct image sequence is 336 = 196r, 337 = 196v, 338 = 197r, 339 = 197v and 340 = 198r.

Bold words were encrypted. Spaces, accents and punctuation are editorial; the surrounding clear Spanish is lightly normalized. …que no quieren hazer gracia sino mera justicia, con que estaría yo contento si se guarda. A Ponte creo cierto se le deve amistad, y no sé si se conforman conforman él y Escudero , ni si ay razón de encuentro entre ellos, que si la huviesse a entrambos les costaría su dinero… F. 196v, view 337. The shorter passage: A Ponte/Aponte, friendship, and Escudero. BnF, via Wikimedia Commons. The decrypted letters run apon / tecreocierto / conformanelyes / cudero . “A Ponte” and “Aponte” are alternative segmentations; no first name is established. The clear se conforman followed by cipher conforman is awkward and is kept as written. In sense, Segura discusses friendship owed to Ponte/Aponte, whether he and Escudero agree, and the financial consequences of a quarrel. The clear text that follows says Segura does not want the Constable's money diminished by it and will return to Toledo to finish these matters.

Un consejero muy grave me ha dicho que han hecho aquí junta sobre la cometa que ha avido estos días, y dizen que el mundo se acabará o morirá el rey por setiembre. Él bien cerca dello paresce que anda. Creo en Dios. “A very weighty councillor has told me that they have held a meeting here about the comet that has appeared these days, and they say the world will end or the king will die around September. He seems to be very close to it. I believe in God.” F. 197r, view 338. The first two cipher signs, which decrypt as di , stand at the end of the introductory line. BnF, via Wikimedia Commons. The four decrypted lines are dizenqueelmundoseacabara / omoriraelreyporsetiem / breelbiencercadellopa / rescequeandacreoendios . The line break inside setiembre helps resolve an overwritten sign at the end of the second line. The final creo en Dios is kept; its punctuation and tone are interpretive. Segura is reporting a councillor's account. It does not establish an official council decision, and the comet has not been identified astronomically.

The first transcription had 114 tokens and wrongly treated several joined pairs as single signs. A Python homophonic solver failed; a guessed crib, pronostico , also failed and was discarded. A faster C# solver (simulated annealing) then tested three transcription variants, 250 restarts each, against the repository's Spanish Golden Age five-gram model. Only the variant that split the joined signs and temporarily merged dotted with undotted forms produced connected Spanish: dizen que el mundo , el rey , paresce que anda and Escudero . The final segmentation was then fixed from the images, using the solver output only as a guide. Joined forms separate into qu , el and es ; two signs attached to the clear introduction begin dizen . A final loop differs from the n-sign, and square and hooked c-like forms have different values. The final transcription keeps the dot distinctions and has 125 tokens in 35 sign classes. The key is a homophonic substitution with two nulls and one special sign for ll . Published Descovar, Fuentes–Pimentel, Ibarra–Doria, Ibarra–Zúñiga and Cg.13 inventories were compared without finding a match. The full Devos 1950 tables were unavailable, so that comparison is still to be made. No external plaintext was used. The decoder and saved key reproduce the decipherment and generate the sign-by-sign display above.

There are no unassigned tokens, but six singleton values are grade M, depending on context. All other token values are grade I, inferred. None is graded H or C because no original key or independent plaintext was obtained. The 95.2% figure counts the proposed values after excluding the M grades; it is not a probability of correctness. This measures the proposal, not independent proof of its correctness. ## A — f. 196v, view 337 …que no quieren hazer gracia sino mera justicia, con que estaría yo contento si se guarda. **A Ponte creo cierto** se le deve amistad, y no sé si se conforman **conforman él y Escudero**, ni si ay razón de encuentro entre ellos, que si la huviesse a entrambos les costaría su dinero; el de V.Ex. no querría que menguase por esta causa, y los demás cada uno le ayude su suerte, y así yo me bolveré a Toledo a dar mate a estas cosas, y avisaré de lo que huviere. Literal decrypted runs: ``` apon tecreocierto conformanelyes cudero ``` The first name may be segmented **A Ponte** or **Aponte**; the signs alone do not decide. No first name is established for this person or for Escudero. The apparent clear/cipher repetition *se conforman / conforman* is retained. Its awkwardness must not be hidden by silently replacing cipher text with a different name or verb. In sense, Segura discusses friendship owed to Ponte/Aponte, agreement between him and Escudero, and the financial consequences of a quarrel. ## B — f. 197r, view 338 Un consejero muy grave me ha dicho que han hecho aquí junta sobre la cometa que ha avido estos días, y **dizen que el mundo se acabará o morirá el rey por setiembre. Él bien cerca dello paresce que anda. Creo en Dios.** Literal decrypted lines (the first begins with the two cipher signs at the end of the introductory line): ``` dizenqueelmundoseacabara omoriraelreyporsetiem breelbiencercadellopa rescequeandacreoendios ``` English: “A very weighty councillor has told me that they have held a meeting here about the comet that has appeared these days, and they say the world will end or the king will die around September. He seems to be very close to it. I believe in God.” This reports what a councillor told Segura. It does not establish an official council decision or the astronomical identity of the comet. The punctuation and tone of the final pious formula remain editorial. ## Other pages 196r: money, expenses, debts and payments involving the Council of Italy; concern for services and reputation. 196v: royal help and consultation with Don Alonso Idiáquez, followed by passage A. 197r: passage B, truce and military news, Carmona, the adelantado and Cebiaur, ships and men, Lisbon/Portalegre, and the sale of Don Blasco's estate. 197v–198r: marriage negotiations involving García de Alvarado, the Duke of Alba's sister, Jerónimo de Salamanca, Gaspar Bullón and Haro; dowry and vocation; the Cortes' grant of thirty million over six years. The last page supplies Madrid, 8 August 1596, and Matheo de Segura's signature, with a postscript about infantry for the expedition. These are contextual summaries, not additional recovered ciphertext. ## Doubtful assignments | Token | Proposed value | Occurrence | Grade and reason | |---|---|---|---| | Hd | null | A, run 1 | M: underdotted sign, deletion inferred from the name/context | | rd | null | A, run 2 | M: underdotted sign, deletion inferred from *creo* | | openC | t | A, run 2 | M: singleton in *cierto* | | Q | n | A, run 3 | M: singleton in *conforman* | | X | m | B, line 2 | M: overwritten end-of-line sign in *setiem-bre* | | ud | ll | B, line 3 | M: dotted singleton in *dello* | The other 119 token readings are I, inferred from the substitution and Spanish context. Twenty-five DECODE records from Sloane MS 3188, catalogued as ciphertexts with no decipherment, are a 17th-century reader’s notes on John Dee’s spirit diaries and writings. They are in English stroke shorthand with names and dates in longhand. Not a cipher; the shorthand system is not yet identified. 1582 … E.T. … Uriel … Reuchlin · Reconciliatio Kelliana longhand names inside shorthand strokes Sloane MS 3188 · notes on John Dee's actions with spirits · English shorthand · 17th century (leaves dated to 1595) Shippen's shorthand notes on Dee British Library, Sloane MS 3188 ff. 109–169 · DECODE R8506–R8530, catalogued as 25 ciphertexts with no decipherment on record, "unknown sender to unknown recipient" The leaves are a reader's notes on Dee's spirit diaries and on his writings, in a stroke shorthand. They contain no cipher, so there is nothing to decipher; the shorthand itself was not transcribed. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: not a cipher closed At a glance Not a cipher The document DECODE records R8506–R8530 (25 leaves, ff. 109–169) of notes on John Dee’s spirit conferences, listed as “Non-decrypted” with no sender, recipient or language. Three were viewed. Where British Library, Sloane MS 3188 ff. 109–169, which the Library describes as notes in cipher by William Shippen; DECODE catalogue items 138 and 139. The cipher None: the running text is a 17th-century English stroke shorthand, with vowels marked by dots and small letters. Angel names, Latin phrases, titles and years are in longhand. What it says f. 109 indexes Dee’s Actions; f. 155 lists Dee’s writings year by year; f. 137 is a note on Kelley, Pucci and Prague dated 1595. Still open The shorthand system is not identified and the notes are not transcribed; the writer is given as Shippen by the Library, not checked. A DECODE correction is queued for all 25 records. f. 109r, the chronology column: years in the margin, shorthand strokes with vowel marks, and longhand E.T., Uriel and Reuchlin. Image: British Library, Sloane MS 3188 f. 109r, via DECODE R8506.

Each DECODE record is one leaf, or a pair of conjugate leaves, of ff. 109–169 (R8506 = f. 109, … R8530 = f. 169). DECODE dates only two of them, R8509 (f. 137, 1595) and R8520 (f. 155, 1594). Those two became a separate catalogue entry (138), and the rest became entry 139. They are one set of notes in one hand. f. 109r (R8506). An index to Dee's Actions. The left column runs "Actio 1 … Saulina p. 3, 4", "Actio 2", "Actio 3", "Actio 4 p. 10 Uriel als Nariel", "Actio 5 … 13", with "Salamian", "Raphael", "Michael" and "Sigillum Dei" in longhand. The right column is a chronology from 1569 to 1583, with "E.T." (Edward Talbot, Kelley's alias at Dee's house), "Uriel", "Reuchlin", "p. 67", "p. 181", "Reconciliatio Kelliana" and "E.K. March 22 1583". f. 137 (R8509). Four lines about "E.K.", Dee (Δ), "Puccius" (Francesco Pucci), "fortissima foemina", "Prage" and "1000 fl.", dated at the foot "1595 Δ". f. 155 (R8520). A list of Dee's writings with the years in the margin, 1547–1592. The titles are in longhand, among them Mercurius coelestis lib. 24 (1549), Monas Hieroglyphica ad Maximilianum (1564), the Math. praeface to Euclide (1570) and Parallaticae commentationis praxeosque nucleus quidam (1573). "M. Casaub." is cited at the head.

The script is a small set of connected strokes. A dot, a comma or a tiny letter placed above, beside or below a stroke gives the vowel, and many words are a single mark. That is the mechanism of the English "character" shorthands of the 17th century: Shelton's Tachygraphy , Rich's system and their relatives, the family Pepys wrote his diary in. It fits William Shippen (1635–1693). The writer switches to longhand wherever a proper name, a Latin title or a number would be hard to recover from strokes. A cipher hides a fixed message behind a key. These strokes write the sounds of English in an abbreviated way. Transcribing them means identifying the system and learning its signs. The notes are also secondary. They index and summarise Dee's diaries, which Whitby edited in 1982 and Casaubon printed in part in 1659, and they list Dee's own writings. Nothing is concealed that is not available in those texts.

The shorthand system. Not identified. The first step would be to compare the stroke inventory of f. 109r with Shelton's alphabet (1641 and later editions) and with Rich's. A transcription. Not attempted beyond the longhand. Once the system is known, the Actio index can be transcribed and checked against Whitby's edition, and the p. references checked against Casaubon's True & Faithful Relation (1659). The writer. Shippen, per the BL catalogue. Some descriptions give Ashmole. Not checked against either hand. DECODE. A correction is queued for all 25 records: shorthand notes on Dee's Actions, English, not cipher correspondence.

A long cipher letter to the King from a member of Henrietta Maria’s household at Paris (TNA SP 106/10 ff. 235–236, DECODE R924), against Sir Henry Compton’s embassy and on Prince Charles’s marriage. George Lasry reconstructed the key (SP106-8) and deciphered it on DECODE in 2020; his key, applied here group by group, gives back his text. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · George Lasry (key or decipherment used) · Sofia Pettersson (transcription) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter A writer in Henrietta Maria’s household at Paris to Charles I, January [1646]. Signed with the number 385. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 235–236; DECODE R924. It was part of catalogue item 59, which grouped six letters in four different keys. The cipher One- and two-digit numbers for letters, up to four for a vowel, and a numbered word list from 100 up, roughly in alphabetical order (100 all , 108 and , 141 for ). How it was deciphered George Lasry reconstructed the key (“TNA SP106-8”) and deciphered the letter on DECODE in October 2020. His plaintext was not in this repository on 22 October 2026, so the reading audit of that day counted the letter as decoded, not read; on 24 October he gave permission and it is now saved verbatim as lasry/R924_decryption.txt, credited to him. On 23 October his files were fetched and the letter decoded afresh; with four code values set by sense it builds most sentences, but counting those as holes it reads at 89% of its words, just under the 95% bar: read in part. Applied here group by group, his key gives his text on every line that can be compared. What it says The writer argues against sending Sir H. Compton as ambassador and against the treaty for Prince Charles’s marriage with Portugal. He reports on Montreuil’s mission and on levies of five or six thousand men. Still open 58 three-digit numbers not in Lasry’s word list and 11 low figures with no value in the key: 162 groups in all. Other keys The five other letters once filed with it are in different ciphers: R785, R790, R923 (TNA SP 106), R787 (SP106-2), R929 (SP106-5).

Catalogue item 59 grouped six cipher letters of SP 106/10 from Henrietta Maria’s household in France to Charles I. George Lasry reconstructed four keys for the run, and on 14 October 2026 the entry was split so that each page presents one key. This letter is the only one of the six in his “SP106-8” key, dated January 1646. In his files the same key also covers the next record, R925 (ff. 238–240), a letter of the Queen on the same marriage. The writer is not the Queen (“the Queen sends …”, “the Queen desires your Majesty …”) and signs with the number 385. Lasry dates the letter from its content: Montreuil’s mission, and a frost also mentioned in the Hague letter of January on ff. 245–246. He prefers 1646 to 1645. DECODE’s date of 26 June 1646 does not fit the letter’s own “Paris Jan”; the correction is queued for DECODE. The key has one- and two-digit homophones (A 5, 15, 23, 25; E 2, 11, 22, 26) and a numbered word list starting at 100: 100 all , 101 are , 102 as , 103 at , 108 and , 109 be , 141 for , 173 I , 174 in , 176 -ing . Lasry’s file says the key has no nulls. F. 235, the head of the letter (written sideways on the leaf; shown turned). Line 1, 76:53:14:13:26:39:30:236 , begins Lasry’s “PARIS JAN …”; the second line is almost all word-list numbers (141, 107, 227, 240 …). Image: The National Archives, SP 106/10 f. 235, via DECODE R924.

The plaintext is Lasry’s and is on the DECODE record, quoted here with punctuation added: PARIS JAN … IT PLEAS YOUR MAJESTY, YOU HAVE SO MUCH <797> <320> HANDS THAT I WILL NOT BEGIN ANOTHER WITH YOU BUT I LAY IT DOWN … FIRST THOUGH YOUR MAJESTY SHALL KNOW YOU ARE OBEYED AND SR H COMPTON IS <487>D … THE TREATY OF MARRIAGE, WHICH IS A THING OF IMPORTANCE ENOUGH WHEN IT SHALL BE <307> <142> TO BE SET AFOOT WITH PORTUGALL … … FOR WE KNOW NOW THAT MONTREUL HAS BEEN WITH YOU … THE LEVIES NOW IN HAND IN SO GOOD AN ADVANCE THAT WE HAVE GOOD BRING TO HOLD THAT WE SHALL PASSE A BODY OF AOR [5 OR] 6 THOUSAND MEN AS GOOD AS ARE ANY <330> TO BE FOUND … I AM YOUR MAJESTY’S <219> OBEDIENT <SERVANT> <385>

Lasry’s interlinear file pairs each line of Sofia Pettersson’s transcription with his plaintext. His key was applied group by group to the cipher lines, without his plaintext. Of 2012 groups, 1850 (91.9%) get a value. On 11 lines his plaintext line has a different number of words from the cipher line, so the columns shift and those lines are not compared; on all the others (1604 groups) the key gives exactly his text. The 162 groups with no value are 58 three-digit numbers (85 occurrences; 324 and 428 four times each) and 11 low figures (77 occurrences; 21 alone 24 times), which Lasry writes as “_”. The replay in section 02 shows the first 120 groups of that run.

The three-digit numbers that are not in Lasry’s word list, left in brackets in his plaintext. Some are probably words of the list, others names. The low figures 21, 30, 42, 50, 16 and a few others, which have no value in the key. The re-reading of 23 October 2026 (below) treats them as nulls between words, although Lasry’s key file says there are none. Who 385 is. The letter speaks for the Queen’s council at Paris and does not name its writer, but Eric Sams deciphered this letter and the Queen’s (R925) in 1976 for Ian Roy ( Archivaria 21, 1985–86, pp. 89–90): the writer is Henry Jermyn , at Paris on 26 January 1646, the day of his letter to Nicholas referring him to the King’s letters on the Portugal embassy. Sams’s solution was never printed; it is said to be in the Bodleian with Roy’s papers. Re-reading, 23 October 2026. Lasry’s files were fetched with the project’s DECODE login and the letter decoded afresh from Pettersson’s rows ( R924_reading.md , English R924_en.md ). The unvalued low figures are nulls between words; “Ian. 26” and “5 or 6 thousand” are numerals in clear; four codes were valued by sense at every occurrence: 168 hope (Lasry hold ), 116 can (Lasry brought ), 334 what , 227 new . Counted as holes, those four and the 85 open code tokens leave the letter just under the reading bar: decoded, not read. Sams’s decipherment would settle them.

A DECODE record with an unknown recipient is Stafford’s holograph despatch to Walsingham of 19 September 1586, in clear English with four short cipher runs, each deciphered between the lines at the time. The runs were transcribed sign by sign and checked against the glosses: a warning that Guise’s guards were sworn to kill Navarre and Condé. DECODE lists it as a letter of Sir Edward Stafford to an unknown recipient, partially decrypted. It is his holograph despatch to Walsingham in clear English, with four short cipher runs on f. 74v. Each run was deciphered between the lines when the letter arrived. Every sign of the runs was transcribed and checked against that decipherment, which also gives the letter values of the key. DECODE catalogued it as a two-page cipher letter to an unknown recipient, dated London. Where British Library, Harley MS 1582 ff. 74–75; DECODE R8503, four images. The cipher Only four short runs on f. 74v (28 signs in all) are in cipher: letter signs with homophones, a sign 6 (first taken as a null; see section 03), and two-digit name codes. How it was read A contemporary hand wrote the decipherment above each run: “villequier”, “K. Navar”, “Kyll him and ye P. of Condé”, “D. Guise”. The glosses were checked sign by sign; run 1 spells villequier if the four 6 signs are dropped (the correction of 22 September 2026 in the project notes instead reads 6 as e; see section 03). What it says Men of the Duke of Guise’s guard had sworn to kill the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé. 47, 59 and 74 are name codes. Still open Nothing in the cipher. The letter is not in the Calendar of State Papers, Foreign .

DECODE R8503 has four images: f. 74r, f. 74v, f. 75r (blank) and f. 75v (address leaf). The address, written upside down, reads “To the right honorable Sir Francis Walsingham knight, her Majesty’s principal secretary”, and the endorsement reads “19 Sept. 1586. From S r Edw: Stafford”. So DECODE’s “unknown recipient” is Walsingham. Its “London” is where the manuscript is kept: the letter was written in Paris, where Stafford was ambassador. The despatch is Stafford’s news of the court, a month after the Babington plot was uncovered (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.). F. 74r covers the stir in England over a false report, the King of France and the Queen of Scots, Mendoza, and “that vile traitor Charles Paget”, who went to the Capuchins to speak with the King. F. 74v covers the copy of a letter about Épernon, a plot against Navarre, and the Queen Mother’s new powers to treat with the King of Navarre on the point of religion.

Navar “I have made the King of Navarre be advertised of it” 3 (l. 12) M x ◇ h 6 47 ω ʒ ϖ 59 Kyll him and y e P. of Condé “dispatched to kill him and the Prince of Condé ” 4 (l. 13) 74 D. Guise “some of them of the guard of the Duke of Guise , who assure themselves to bring it to pass” The glosses are in a darker ink than the letter and are written in a different hand, which suggests Walsingham’s secretariat. The words between the runs are Stafford’s clear text as it reads on the page. They are quoted to show the sense and not transcribed letter for letter. F. 74v, runs 2–4: 47 glossed “K. Navar”, the run glossed “Kyll him and ye P. of Condé”, and 74 glossed “D. Image: British Library, Harley MS 1582 f. 74v, via DECODE R8503.

Stafford mixed an alphabet of letter forms and graphic signs with two-digit codes for persons. The glosses give these values: Letters, with homophones: v = D; i/y = x, ⊕; l = ◇, h; e = Δ, ꟷ; q = Ɗ; u = X; r = ʃ; k = M. 6 : first taken as a null, because dropping its four occurrences from run 1 leaves exactly v-i-l-l-e-q-u-i-e-r , with the line break after the second ◇, and it also follows kyll in run 3. A correction of 22 September 2026 in the project notes, from the sibling letters R8501 and R8502 (Harley 1582, where 6 = e), says instead that 6 is the letter e and that the readings are unchanged. With 6 = e the four 6 signs in run 1 as copied here do not obviously spell villequier , so the two accounts are not reconciled. ⊗ closes run 1, as a final s (“Villequier’s”) or a stop. · is a separator. ω ʒ ϖ = “and”. It could be three letters or one word sign; we did not split it. Codes: 47 = the King of Navarre, 59 = the Prince of Condé, 74 = the Duke of Guise. Run 3 confirms the values from run 1 independently: the same x and ◇ stand for the y and l of kyll , and 47 recurs there as “him”, meaning Navarre. No key sheet for Stafford’s cipher with Walsingham has been found. S. Tomokiyo’s survey of Elizabethan ciphers ( Cryptiana ) notes only that Stafford used different ciphers with Walsingham and with Burghley, and that he sent Walsingham names to add to his.

Nothing in the cipher. All 28 signs are accounted for. The only value taken from the gloss without a check at letter level is ω ʒ ϖ = “and” (grade C: it fits the sense and the gloss, but no other occurrence confirms it). The clear text of the despatch was consulted for context but not transcribed in full.

A Latin “encrypted letter” in the Szembek papers at Kórnik, catalogued as an 18th-century letter to the Szembeks, is the postscript of a letter from the Wallachian court written after the death of Prince Şerban Cantacuzino in October 1688. Every two-digit cipher run was glossed at the time; the key rebuilt from the glosses (22 numbers, no conflicts) reproduces them. It denounces the imperial Jesuit envoy Antide Dunod as the man who misled the late prince. 43 12 51 13 43 · 25 23 46 51 42 46 25 46 → Dunod · Principi a = 17 · c = 42 · d = 43 · e = 14 · i = 46 · n = 51 · o = 13 · p = 25 · r = 23 · u = 12 Wallachia → a Reverend Father · two-digit letter substitution inside clear Latin · after October 1688 · deciphered at the time A Wallachian postscript against Antide Dunod, after 1688 Go to the full text ↓ A Latin cipher postscript in the Szembek papers blames the Jesuit envoy Antide Dunod for misleading the late Prince Şerban Cantacuzino; its contemporary decipherment was checked against a key rebuilt here. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 28 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter The postscript (“P. S.”) of a letter to a “Most Reverend Father”, written by someone in the service of a “Celsissimus Princeps” after the death of Şerban Cantacuzino, Prince of Wallachia, on 29 October 1688. Three pages, unsigned and undated; the main letter is not with it. Where PAN Biblioteka Kórnicka, BK 1560 (a volume partly from the archive of Jan Szembek), item “List zaszyfrowany” (“encrypted letter”), Wielkopolska Digital Library edition 343124. Our catalogue had it as an early-18th-century letter from an unknown sender to the Szembek family. The cipher Single letters replaced by two-digit numbers from 12 to 51 in a mixed order, one number per letter, with a separate number for the ae diphthong. It is used for single words inside clear Latin, often with the ending left in clear. Two three-digit code groups occur. How it was deciphered A second hand wrote the plain word above every cipher run but one. The key was rebuilt from those glosses (22 numbers, no conflicts). Deciphering each run with the key alone reproduces the gloss, apart from the writer’s own slips. What it says The writer protests that his side has kept faith while “some Christians” broke their promises. He calls Dunod an “impostor and detractor” who led the late Prince Şerban astray, and reports that a certain Gegenbey was killed and his head sent as a gift. Still open One code group, 202, which has no gloss, and the clear word before it. The writer’s prince and the recipient are not named.

BK 1560 is a 150-leaf miscellany of papers from 1694 to 1731, partly from the archive of Jan Szembek, Crown Chancellor of Poland. The Wielkopolska Digital Library has split it into about a hundred items. One of them, “List zaszyfrowany”, is three pages foliated 40–41 in an old hand. It sits among letters to Szembek of 1730–31, which is probably why it was taken for an 18th-century Szembek letter. The text begins “P. S.” and ends at the foot of the third page without a signature. The letter it belongs to is not in the item. The postscript is in clear Latin, but about seventy words are written in numbers and struck through with a line. Above each run a second hand, in lighter brown ink, wrote what it means. The opening: “P. S. Ip[sis] Literis scripta grato animo, tam Celsissimus Princeps …”. The glosses “Celsissimus Princeps”, “qui” and “ego” stand above the struck-through numbers. Image: PAN Biblioteka Kórnicka, BK 1560, image 065 (f. 40r), via the Wielkopolska Digital Library.

Each letter has one two-digit number. The table is not in alphabetical order (a = 17, b = 29, c = 42, d = 43, e = 14), so it was mixed on purpose. There are no homophones and no nulls. The writer spells ae as a separate number, 15, and e as 14. He leaves y in clear and often writes the end of a word in clear letters, so “25 er 40 46 43 13” is perfido and “42 13 50 25 er 20 17” is comperta . a b c d e ae f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u/v x 17 29 42 43 14 15 40 41 44 46 48 49 50 51 13 25 24 23 21 20 12 19 Two groups have three digits. 203 , followed by the clear ending -is , is glossed Literis , so the key had a short code list for words. 202 has no gloss. In all there are 436 two-digit cipher numbers in 70 runs, plus the two code groups and one heavily struck single digit.

Words in cipher in the original are in italics. The reading is the contemporary gloss, confirmed number by number with the rebuilt key; where the two differ, the note under section 05 says which is right. “impostor et Detractor ille et sine conscientia Burgundus Antidius Dunod ”: 43 12 51 13 43 = D-u-n-o-d. The marginal cross is on the line with the unglossed code group 202. Image: PAN Biblioteka Kórnicka, BK 1560, image 066, via the Wielkopolska Digital Library. P. S. Ip[sis] Literis scripta grato animo, tam Celsissimus Princeps ( qui R[everendi]ssimam D[omi]nationem debita veneratur salutatione) quam ego et alii , quibus convenit , amplexi sumus. Et sicut hactenus syncere in omnibus processimus , ita et nunc secundum rectam Christianam conscientiam procedimus et procedemus , quamvis aliqui Christiani non ita se gerant et nobiscum procedant , uti pro miserant , et multis modis nos solicitaverant . Sed hoc remitti mus ad divinam Justitiam et Providentiam, quae omnia scit et videt. Oh! D[omi]ne mi R[everendi]ssime Pater, si audiret quanta et qualia, ac quibus modis impostor et Detractor ille et sine conscientia Burgundus Antidius Dunod , importunitate et garrulitate in mundo nemini secundus, cum addicto suo socio, perfido ac proditore , Damis(?) sub [202], nobis et isti afflictae patriae causavit, ac illum piae memoriae de functum Principem Serbanum seduxit : quorum mendaciis et deceptionibus , pulchris verbis obvolutis , credens , et consilia omnium aliorum respuens , in grandes nos et istam miseram patriam intricavit difficultates . O si intelligeretis promissiones quas ab illa aula defuncto Principi adducebant, et hinc ducebant, quae nunc propter illorum iniquas delationes plura falsa sunt comperta . Profecto quaedam ad risum moverent, quaedam admirationem causarent, quaedam vero prae pudore silentio obvolvi deberent. Deus iustissimus secundum opera et conscientiam illorum de ipsis vindictam sumat . De Gegenbeio sciat, quod per fraudes unius sui falsi amici ab aliquo iam tempore occisus , eiusque caput in vim honorarii missum. Sed ipsius Gegenbeii socius, nomine Gityk , plus quam ille de facto in oriente operatur . Translation. P.S. The letter written in your own hand was received with a grateful heart, both by His Highness the Prince (who salutes Your Most Reverend Lordship with due veneration) and by me and the others whom it concerned. As we have so far proceeded sincerely in everything, so now too we proceed, and will proceed, according to a right Christian conscience. Some Christians, however, do not behave so and do not proceed with us as they had promised and as they had urged us in many ways. But this we leave to divine Justice and Providence, which knows and sees all things. Oh, my Lord, Most Reverend Father, if you heard how great and what kind of things, and by what means, that impostor and detractor did to us and to this afflicted country: the Burgundian Antidius Dunod, without conscience, second to none in the world for importunity and chatter, with his devoted companion, a perfidious traitor […]. He led astray that Prince of pious memory, the late Şerban, who believed their lies and deceptions wrapped in fine words, rejected the counsel of all others, and entangled us and this wretched country in great difficulties. O if you understood the promises they brought from that court to the late Prince and carried back from here! Through their wicked reports, most of them have now been found false. Truly, some would move one to laughter, some would cause wonder, and some ought to be wrapped in silence for shame. May God most just take vengeance on them according to their works and their conscience. Of Gegenbey, know that some time ago he was killed through the treachery of a false friend of his, and his head was sent as a gift. But this Gegenbey’s companion, named Gityk, is in fact more active in the East than he was. The last lines, on Gegenbey and Gityk. The glosser wrote “Gergenbeio”, but the numbers 41 14 41 14 51 29 e 46 13 spell Gegenbeio . Image: PAN Biblioteka Kórnicka, BK 1560, image 067 (f. 41r), via the Wielkopolska Digital Library.

“Burgundus Antidius Dunod” is Antide Dunod, a Jesuit from Franche-Comté (the County of Burgundy). With Count László Csáky he was Emperor Leopold I’s envoy to Bucharest in 1687–1688, pressing Şerban Cantacuzino to break with the Ottomans and join the Holy League. “Defunctum Principem Serbanum” is Şerban himself, who died on 29 October 1688, so the postscript was written after that date. “Illa aula”, the court whose promises proved false, is then Vienna. The letter does not name the living “Celsissimus Princeps”. Speaking of “this wretched country” after Şerban’s death points to his successor in Wallachia, Constantin Brâncoveanu (1688–1714), but that is an inference, as is any date closer than “after October 1688”. Gegenbey, Gityk and the “Most Reverend Father” were not identified. How the paper reached the Szembek archive in Poland is not known.

The item was found in the WBC structure of BK 1560. Its three DjVu pages were downloaded and decoded with the DjVu.js library. Every run and its gloss was transcribed from full-resolution crops ( runs.tsv ). A script aligned each run with its gloss where the lengths agree and collected the number–letter pairs: 22 numbers, each with a single letter. It then deciphered every run with that key alone. 61 of the 70 runs match their gloss letter for letter. The nine others: 203 is : the code group, glossed Literis . gerant , solicitaverant , Gegenbeio , Gegenbeii : the numbers spell these; the glosser wrote gerent , sollicitaverant , Gergenbeio , Gergenbeii . de- functsm : the writer put 21 (s) for 12 (u). pricipem : the writer left out 51 (n) in Principem . defunct : the final o of defuncto is not written. audi?et : a heavily struck digit (20 or 23) stands where the gloss has the r of audiret . None of these is a key conflict: the key and the contemporary gloss give the same text.

202 : a code group with no gloss. It follows a clear word read here as “Damis” (the first letter is D or P), which is itself uncertain; the phrase probably names Dunod’s companion or the damage he did. A cross in the margin marks the line. Open. The struck digit in audi?et : its value is r by the gloss and the sense (H). The final letter of the blotted run in intricavit (12 or 27) reads v by the key and the gloss (H). The identification of the writer’s prince as Brâncoveanu (M), and the persons Gegenbey and Gityk (unidentified).

Sed hoc remitti*mus* ad divinam Justitiam et Providentiam, quae omnia scit et videt. *Oh!* D[omi]ne mi R[everendi]ssime Pater, si *audiret* quanta et qualia, ac quibus modis ## f. 66 (WBC 066) impostor et *Detractor* ille et sine conscientia *Burgundus Antidius Dunod*, importunitate et garrulitate in mundo nemini secundus, cum addicto suo socio, *perfido ac proditore*, Damis(?) sub [202], *nobis et isti* afflictae *patriae* causavit, ac illum *piae memoriae* de*functum Principem Serbanum seduxit*: quorum mendaciis et *deceptionibus*, pulchris verbis *obvolutis*, *credens*, et *consilia* omnium aliorum *respuens*, in grandes *nos* et istam *miseram patriam intricavit difficultates*. O si *intelligeretis* ## f. 67 (WBC 067) *promissiones* quas ab illa *aula defuncto Principi* adducebant, et *hinc* ducebant, quae nunc propter illorum iniquas *delationes* plura *falsa* sunt *comperta*. Profecto quaedam ad risum moverent, quaedam admirationem causarent, quaedam vero prae pudore silentio obvolvi deberent. Deus iustissimus secundum opera et conscientiam illorum de ipsis *vindictam sumat*. De *Gegenbeio* sciat, quod per fraudes unius sui falsi amici ab aliquo iam tempore *occisus*, eiusque *caput* in vim *honorarii* missum. Sed ipsius *Gegenbeii* socius, nomine *Gityk*, plus quam ille de facto in *oriente operatur*. (The text breaks off here: the leaf is the end of the item in the WBC edition; no signature, date or address.) ## Translation P.S. The letter written in your own hand was received with a grateful heart, both by His Highness the Prince (who salutes Your Most Reverend Lordship with due veneration) and by me and the others whom it concerned. And as we have so far proceeded sincerely in everything, so now too we proceed, and will proceed, according to a right Christian conscience, although some Christians do not behave so and do not proceed with us as they had promised and had urged us in many ways. But this we leave to divine Justice and Providence, which knows and sees all things. Oh! my Lord, Most Reverend Father, if you heard how great and what kind of things, and by what means, that impostor and detractor, the Burgundian Antide Dunod, without conscience, second to none in the world for importunity and chatter, together with his devoted companion, a perfidious traitor, [...] under [202], caused to us and to this afflicted country; and how he led astray that Prince of pious memory, the late Şerban, who, believing their lies and deceptions wrapped in fine words and rejecting the counsel of all others, entangled us and this wretched country in great difficulties. O if you understood the promises that they brought from that court to the late Prince and carried back from here, which now, through their wicked reports, have been found for the most part false! Truly, some would move one to laughter, some would cause wonder, and some ought to be wrapped in silence for shame. May God most just take vengeance on them according to their works and their conscience. Of Gegenbey, know that some time ago he was killed through the treachery of a false friend of his, and his head sent as a gift. But the companion of this same Gegenbey, named Gityk, is in fact more active than he was, in the East. ## Notes on the reading - *Antidius Dunod*: Antide Dunod SJ, a Jesuit from Franche-Comté ("Burgundus"), Emperor Leopold I's envoy who, with Count László Csáky, pressed Şerban Cantacuzino of Wallachia (prince 1678-1688) in 1687-1688 to join the Holy League. - *defunctum Principem Serbanum*: Şerban Cantacuzino, who died on 29 October 1688. The letter is therefore later than that date. "Celsissimus Princeps", the writer's living master, is then most likely his successor Constantin Brâncoveanu (1688-1714), and "illa aula" the imperial court in Vienna. This identification is inferred from the text, not stated in it. - *Gegenbeio / Gegenbeii*: the cipher spells Gegenbe(i)-, the glosser wrote "Gergenbeio" and "Gergenbeii". Not identified (perhaps a "bey"). *Gityk*: not identified. - "Damis(?)": the clear word before "sub 202" is a capital D or P + "amis"; not resolved. The marginal "+" on this line in the same ink suggests a contemporary reader also stopped here. The duplicate of the viceroy of Sicily’s despatch of 16 July 1565, written during the Great Siege of Malta, with the sensitive words in two-digit figures. The key, a homophonic alphabet on the figures 12–43 in alphabetical order, was recovered from two cribs in the adjacent cleartext, and all 1,930 groups were decrypted. The letter reports that the Piccolo Soccorso reached the Borgo and that La Valette’s fire-signals turned a second relief back. The covering note written the same day, no. 249, deciphers with the key unchanged, every one of its 150 cipher tokens. 3538 4229 · 2938183812 3618243616241829 373036 3630271713173136 1929 3725193514 · 36 = s Messina → Philip II · homophonic cipher in two-digit figures, alphabetical order · 16 July 1565 García de Toledo to Philip II, Messina, 16 July 1565 from García de Toledo → to Philip II Go to the full text ↓ AGS Estado leg. 1394 no. 247, the duplicado of a ciphered despatch from the viceroy of Sicily two months into the Great Siege of Malta · four pages of Spanish with every sensitive word in two-digit figures · no decipherment on the leaf or in the catalogue The key was recovered from two cribs in the cleartext around the figures. It is the alphabet in order on the figures 12–43, so once eleven letters were fixed the rest followed; most of the work was transcribing and decrypting the 1,930 figure groups, all of which give sense. Tomokiyo lists the Malta cipher letters of 1565 as having no contemporary decipherment; whether anyone held this key before is unknown. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: complete · On the map adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · complete The letter Don García de Toledo, viceroy of Sicily, to Philip II, Messina, 16 July 1565, with news from besieged Malta; plus a short covering letter of the same day (no. 249). Where Archivo General de Simancas, Estado, legajo 1394, no. 247, on PARES: the duplicado , in clear Spanish with names, numbers and intelligence replaced by runs of two-digit figures. Nothing on the leaf says what they mean. The cipher A homophonic substitution: figures 12 to 43 run through the alphabet in order, three figures for each vowel and one for each consonant, with no nulls and no code words. How it was read Two runs beside clear words, seiscientos soldados and en tiera , gave eleven letters; the order of the table predicted the rest. No. 249 was deciphered on 2 October 2026 with the key unchanged: all 150 cipher tokens give sense. What it says The 600 soldiers Don Juan de Cardona landed entraron en el burgo a saluamento , and a second run of galleys turned back at La Valette’s fire signals. The rest is money and fortification. Still open A handful of words are doubtful in sense, none in their figures. The original despatch, which could carry a contemporary decipherment, has not been found.

The Archivo General de Simancas, Estado, legajo 1394, no. 247, is catalogued on PARES as Duplicado de carta cifrada de García de Toledo, capitán general del Mar, a Felipe II, rey de España , 16 July 1565. It is two leaves: four pages of text (ff. 1r–2v) and an address leaf, sealed and inscribed En manos del señor Franco de Erasso , for the King’s secretary Francisco de Eraso. The first page is docketed Dupp.do in the upper left. A duplicate was a second copy sent by another route in case the first was lost, and this one is a clerk’s copy: it carries copying slips that the original presumably does not ( quesido for querido , puddo for puedo , lonze for onze ). PARES serves the six images (four text pages and the address leaf twice) as plain JPEGs about 915 pixels wide. That is the largest size the viewer gives; asking for any zoom other than the default returns a smaller image. At that size the figures are legible when a line is cropped and enlarged two and a half to five times, which is how every figure here was transcribed. F. 1r, lines 1–3: Llevo tan [ ruyn ] . [ nueua ] a V. Mag. el correo passado que no me ha parescido detener este para que [ en parte ] la mejore. los [ seiscientos / soldados ] que don Juan de Cardona puso [ en tiera ] fue . The run after los and the run after puso are the two cribs that gave the first key values. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1394 no. 247 f. 1r, via PARES (image 1). The letter is written in running Spanish, and the figures stand in the line wherever a word was thought sensitive: the relief, the Grand Master, the galleys, the signals, sums of money, place names, the enemy. Figure runs are written without word breaks, so a run such as 3618243616241829 is one or several words run together.

A homophonic substitution on two-digit figures, in which the values 12 to 43 are assigned to the letters in alphabetical order. The five vowels and u/v have three figures each, every consonant one: letter figures letter figures letter figures a 12 13 14 i 24 25 26 r 35 b 15 l 27 s 36 c 16 m 28 t 37 d 17 n 29 u / v 38 39 40 e 18 19 20 o 30 31 32 x 41 f 21 p 33 y 42 g 22 q 34 z 43 h 23 The alphabet has no j , k or w , and u and v are one letter, as in the clear hand. The table uses exactly the thirty-two values from 12 to 43, and no figure outside that range occurs in the letter: no nulls, and no code groups for names or words. Names are spelt out letter by letter, Caragoca (Syracuse), Augusta , Cabo Bono , Argel , Maltta , Mecina , Mosiur de Lenni . The homophones are not used evenly. Of the three a figures, 13 occurs about 140 times, 14 about 95 and 12 about 50; of the e figures, 19 is used twice as often as 18 and nearly four times as often as 20; of the o figures, 31 about a hundred times against 40 for 30 and 13 for 32. The clerk had favourites. The overall letter frequencies are ordinary Spanish: a and e first, then s , r and o . Four features of the hand affect the decryption. ñ is written nn ( sennales , Espanna , campanna ). Double letters are sometimes written single ( en tiera ) and sometimes doubled where the word has one ( spantaado , quinta[a]les ). The duplicado has its own copying slips, listed above. And the confusable pairs in this hand are 17/19 , 35/36 , 35/38 (a long-tailed 3 against a dotted 8) and 13/14 .

Two cribs from the clear text. The second line of f. 1r has los followed by the run 36 18 24 36 16 24 18 29 37 30 36 and, on the next line, 36 30 27 17 13 17 31 36 . Eleven figures with the first repeated at the fourth and eleventh places, standing after an article, fit seiscientos , and the next run then reads soldados . A few words on, the run after don Juan de Cardona puso is 19 29 37 25 19 35 14 , en tiera , “put ashore”, spelt with one r . Together these fix a c d e i l n o r s t , with two figures each for a , e , i and o . The alphabetical order gives the rest. Set out by value, the recovered figures were in alphabetical order: 13 14 a , 16 c , 17 d , 18 19 e , 24 25 i , 27 l , 29 n , 30 31 o , 35 r , 36 s , 37 t . The remaining values could each be predicted from its position and then checked on a word: 21 f , 41 x , 42 y and 43 z were filled that way and confirmed on 18212118373136 effetos , 15124119271836 baxeles , 42151329 yban and 332712431935 plazer . Transcribe, decode, correct. The whole letter was then transcribed digit for digit with the clear text around the runs, and decoded by script. Nonsense in the output points to a misread figure, almost always one of the confusable pairs above; every correction to the transcription was found that way. The audit. All 1,930 figure groups fall inside 12–43; all thirty-two values occur; no run has an odd number of digits. An out-of-range value or an odd run would be the mark of a transcription error, and none is left.

A key built from the clear text could in principle only reproduce what the clear text already implies. The check is a name the clear text does not contain. On f. 1v, after the Grand Master’s signal not to enter, the clear hand writes y ansi lo dize and then the run 2830362539 35 1719 271929 2925 , which decodes to Mosiur de Lenni : Monsieur de Leinì, taken here to be Andrea Provana di Leinì, the Savoyard commander whose galleys sailed in the relief squadron, and exactly the man who would report whether the signals were made (the identification and the squadron are from memory, not from a cited source, and were not checked here). Nothing in the clear text points to him. F. 1v: millas del [ puerto ]. el [ maestre ] les hizo [ las senna / les ] del [ fuego clarissimas ] para que no [ entrassen ] / y ansi lo dize [ Mosiur de Lenni ] y todos los demas y dentro de . The run after dize is the check on the key. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1394 no. 247 f. 1v, via PARES (image 2). The rest of the ciphered matter is consistent in the same way: Don Juan de Cardona’s 600 soldiers, the pilot Don Juan Çanoguera , and the fortification of Syracuse and Augusta. (The Conde de Módica serving at his own cost is in the clear postscript, and Juan Andrea’s name stands in the clear too, with only the surrounding phrases such as hazer poco in figures.)

Clear text roman, figures in italic ; spelling of the leaf kept ( nn = ñ, u / v as written); word division inside a figure run is editorial, since the cipher writes none; square brackets are editorial f. 1r Llevo tan ruyn nueua a V. Mag. el correo passado que no me ha parescido detener este para que en parte la mejore. Los seiscientos soldados que don Juan de Cardona puso en tiera fue Dios servido de guiallos tanbien que todos entraron en el burgo a saluamento . Dizeme este que ha salido que fue tan grande la alegria del maestre , abracando la gente sin podello hablar, que lloraua de plazer ; y tanbien dize que otro dia salio la misma gente a dar en los Turcos y que mataron mas de dozientos, aunque estas salidas en ningun caso queria que las hiziese , y por muchas letras se lo tengo scripto con mucho encarescimiento. Del maestre no tengo carta , que estoy spantado [ms. spantaado ] dello, pero no tengo por mala seña olvidarse de mi, aunque no creo que tardara a dos o tres dias a venir; y conforme a lo que scriuiere uere de proueer lo mas que por el se pudiere . El estar sin galeras me destruye , porque se po- f. 1v -drian hazer algunos effetos en baxeles suyos que van y vienen, pero trayendo las que aca ay ocupadas en iuntar la gente no se puede proueer a todo . Si [u]iniessen las de Spanna me darian mucha ayuda . Las galeras que yban a entrar por el puerto llegaron a quatro millas del, con muy buena orden y gran determinacion , y aquella noche , que sera lunes , vna hora antes que amaneciesse , viniendo el martes , entro a saluamento la uarqueta que yo hauia embiado para auisar al maestre de las sennales , con la qual tuuo auiso de lo que hauia de hazer ; y tornando las galeras el martes en la noche a otras quatro millas del puerto , el maestre les hizo las sennales del fuego clarissimas para que no entrassen , y ansi lo dize Mosiur de Lenni y todos los demas; y dentro de la hora sennalada las continuo la segunda vez, y las galeras se tornaron a meter a la mar por no ser descubiertas , y han llegado aqui esta mannana . El don Juan Çanoguera, que es el que las guiaua , lo hizo muy bien , y todos los demas. Y este no sabe que[r]ido [ms. quesido ] el maestre aceptar estas galeras ; aunque podria ser por parescelle la entrada muy dificultosa , no dexo de tenella por buena senal . Dizen todos los nuestros que, en acabando de hazer el maestre las sennales , vieron y oyeron vna gran cantidad de arcabuzeria, y que juzgauan ellos que sera salua para mostrarnos que nuestra gente sera dentro . Este ombre que es venido salio del burgo el mismo lunes a los diez y nueue, y no trae nueua de la uarqueta que entro , porque no sera aun llegada ; la qual puso el que yo embie a do le mande, y de alli f. 2r hauia de yr a nado hasta el burgo , y ansi llego saluo , como a la clara se ve por las sennales ; y la ciudad hizo el mismo fuego , que tanbien es indicio que llego el que por aquella parte embie con el duplicado . Los tiempos son tales y las necessidades tan grandes, que aunque se tuuiesse mucho dinero no osaria deshazerme de vn rreal para pagar deudas ; y aunque es justissimo lo que V. Mag. manda de Juan Andrea, se podra hazer poco con el, pero lo que se pudiera no se dexara de hazer como V. Mag. lo manda, que cierto yo desseo dalle toda satisfacion, y el solo sera en este tiempo el que de mi cobrara alguna quantidad. Es necessario poner luego mano en comencar a fortificar , por todo lo que podria suceder , la fruente que Caragoca tiene en tierra firme , y en leuantar vn cavallero en la mar que corresponde —çierto es secanos donde podria ser assaltada . Tanbien es necessario comencar al fin de octubre la fortificacion de Augusta , por que la ocasion no mostrasse a los enemigos el segundo salto. Para estas casas es menester dinero , y en este reyno no ay si no infinitas deudas . V. Mag. mande echar quenta de los ytalianos que se han de leuantar , y de los spannoles que se han de pagar, y del sueldo de las naues, que cada mes importa quarenta mil escudos sin dos mesadas que se les deuen; y vease tanbien el uizcocho que de nueuo es menester hazer, que aunque despues se desquente a las galeras su parte, todavia este dinero sale del que V. Mag. me ha embiado. Hanse comprado quinientos quintales de artilleria de peso f. 2v de Espanna , mucha xarcia y madera para las yaretas [jaretas]; y aunque esta xarcia y madera puede seruir para las galeras que se huuieren de hazer, y lo del metal es dinero que no se pierde , todavia cuesta buen pedaço. Tanbien se haze armamento para las ocho galeras que vienen de Espanna , y otros gastos de botas, barriles, murriones y coracinas que no se pueden escusar. Y si se quenta esto, y se añade el sueldo de la ynfanteria , contando tanbien el gasto de [l]onze galeras que se arman de nueuo, vera V. Mag. que la prouision echa no basta para tantas casas, ni yo pu[e]do [ms. puddo ] sustentar con ella los gastos que V. Mag. apunta en su carta , tanto mas si esto se fuesse nada alargando . Y los quarenta y ocho mil ducados que venieron para las galeras ya estaua comido la mitad , y otra buena parte se deue a la gente. Y considerado esto, suplico a V. Mag. mande proueer como mas se paresciere que conuiene a su seruicio, y en el gastallos se terna el miramiento que V. Mag. manda. Dize este que ha salido que todos los turcos que estan en tierra , demas de los bastiones a do tienen sus baterias , estan todos circundados de trincheas siete, ocho y diez palmos altas , assi a la parte de los nuestros como a la parte de la campanna ; y que quando el partio no hauia otros que no las tuuiessen si no mil y quinientos turcos que estauan al agua . Confirma que hauian perdido mucha gente , y que en el campo corrian dolencias de que morian . Por essos auisos vera V. Mag. los nauios que hallo sobre Cabo Bono el baxel que yua con uino a la Goleta . Tengo por cierto que son los de Argel que se uienen a iuntar con la armada ; y esto creo por no saber que de Maltta aya salido cantidad dellos , porque dize este que del armada no se hauia desmandado nauio ninguno quando el partio , ni tan poco lo escriue el gouernador de la ciudad , como vera V. Mag. por su carta original que yra con esta. Cuya vida guarde Nuestro Señor por tan largos años como sus criados y vassallos desseamos y la christiandad ha menester. De Mecina , a XVJ. de Julio 1565. Postscript (entirely in the clear) Ya tengo scripto a V. Mag. por otras quan bien le sirue el conde de Modica, y a su costa; y hauiendole agora scripto el almirante su padre la muerte de la duquesa su madre, y llamandole que vaya a España, no obstante que esto le ymporte mucho, no ha querido hazello ni yrse deste reyno hasta ver el sucesso de las cosas de aca. Hame parescido muy justo auisar dello a V. Mag., para que tenga entendido su voluntad y el seruicio que haze en ello a V. Mag. English García writes from Messina on 16 July 1565, about two months into the siege and some days after the relief known as the Piccolo Soccorso reached the Borgo (Birgu) at the start of July. Everything below that is in italics in the Spanish was in figures. The relief got in. He had sent the King bad news by the last courier and writes now to soften it: the six hundred soldiers Don Juan de Cardona put ashore all entered the Borgo safely. A man just out of the Borgo says the Grand Master embraced them, unable to speak, and wept for joy; and that the next day the same men sortied against the Turks and killed more than two hundred, though García had written many times that there were to be no sorties. He has no letter from the Grand Master himself and expects one within two or three days. A second run turned back. The galleys meant to enter the harbour came within four miles of it, in good order. That night, an hour before dawn on Tuesday, the barqueta he had sent ahead to arrange the signals with the Grand Master got in. On Tuesday night the galleys came again to four miles off, and the Grand Master made the fire-signals, very clear, that they were not to enter, and repeated them within the appointed hour, as Monsieur de Leinì and all the others report. The galleys put back out to sea so as not to be seen, and reached Messina this morning. Çanoguera, who guided them, did it very well. Nobody knows why the Grand Master would not take the galleys in; perhaps the entry looked too hard, but García takes it for a good sign. As the signals ended the galleys heard a great volley of arquebus fire, which they judged a salute to show that the men were inside. The messengers. The man who left the Borgo that Monday has no news of the barqueta , which had not arrived when he left. The barqueta landed García’s messenger where it was ordered, and from there he was to swim to the Borgo; the signals show he arrived. La ciudad , Mdina, made the same fire, a sign that the man sent by that route with the duplicate had arrived too. Money. Even with money in hand he would not dare part with a real to pay debts. He will do what he can for Gian Andrea Doria, as ordered, and Doria will be the only one paid anything. He asks the King to reckon the Italians to be raised, the Spaniards to be paid, and the ships, which cost forty thousand escudos a month with two months’ pay already owed; biscuit to be baked; five hundred quintals of artillery by Spanish weight, cordage and timber for the jaretas ; fitting out the eight galleys coming from Spain and eleven more being armed; casks, barrels, morions and cuirasses; and the infantry’s pay. The provision sent does not cover it: half the 48,000 ducados sent for the galleys is already spent and much of the rest is owed to the men. “Being without galleys ruins me.” Fortification. Work should begin at once on the landward front of Syracuse and on a cavalier facing the sea, where the ground would let it be stormed; and on the fortification of Augusta at the end of October, so that the occasion should not show the enemy “the second leap”. For this money is needed, and in this kingdom there is nothing but infinite debts. The besiegers. The man from the Borgo says all the Turks ashore, besides the bastions where they have their batteries, are ringed with trenches seven, eight and ten palms high, facing both the Christians and the open country; when he left, only fifteen hundred Turks at the water were without them. The Turks have lost many men, and sickness is killing men in their camp. At sea. The ships that a vessel carrying wine to La Goleta found off Cape Bon, García is sure, are the Algiers squadron coming to join the fleet. No ship had left the fleet at Malta when his man came away, and the governor of la ciudad says none either, as his original letter, sent with this one, will show. Postscript, in clear. The Conde de Módica serves well and at his own cost; summoned to Spain by his father the Admiral after his mother’s death, he will not leave Sicily until he sees how things end here. The letter was written during the worst of the siege, while García was still gathering the force that landed on Malta as the Gran Soccorso in September; the siege was raised days later (the 7 September date and the interval are not from the sources and were not checked here). In July he had few galleys to spare, and this letter shows what they could do: put small parties into the Borgo by night and watch for the Grand Master’s fires.

Estado leg. 1394 no. 249 (PARES record 3576586) is the duplicado of a one-page letter García wrote to the King the same day, 16 July 1565, docketed Dupp.do and addressed on its fourth image En manos del señor Fran.co de Erasso ; images 2 and 3 are a blank verso and a blank leaf. The courier carrying no. 247 was already on board when La Valette’s latest letters reached Messina, and this is the note sent with them. It has 25 figure runs, 150 cipher tokens: 147 figures, two of a barred θ for ll , and one overlined M-like sign for r , neither of which occurs in no. 247. With no. 247’s table unchanged, all 150 tokens give sense ; the word-divided decrypt scores −1.67 per character under the es-golden-age model, against −5.89 for the same letters shuffled. No. 249, lines 4–8: Sauiendole [ entrado el socorro ] … y deuia de ser [ la llegada de los ] Nauios que comparescieron a [ Cabo Bono ]. que cre cierto son los de [ Argel ] / y si huuiera embido [ las galeras ] con la [ gente a la ]. The barred sign in the third line is θ = ll . Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1394 no. 249, image 1, via PARES (record 3576586). Clear text roman, figures in italic ; word division and punctuation editorial S. C. R. M. Estando embarcado el correo con este despacho, he rescebido essas cartas del Maestre, las quales embio a V. M. para que pueda ver muy particularmente todo lo que scriue, que es harto mas apretado de lo que yo pense, sauiendole entrado el socorro . Este que ha traido estas ultimas cartas dize que oyo salua de artilleria de las galeras del Armada, y deuia de ser la llegada de los nauios que comparescieron a Cabo Bono , que creo cierto son los de Argel . Y si huuiera embiado las galeras con la gente a la Goleta , huuiera llegado a mal tienpo . [H]elas detenido hasta agora sperando respuesta del Maestre , porque si me scriuiera que hauia forma de ponelle mas gente por tierra, no quedara por falta dellas; pero el pide mas de la que yo agora le puedo dar, y ansi partiran las galeras mannana . N. S. guarde la vida de V. M. por tan largos años como sus criados desseamos y la Christiandad ha menester. De Micina, a 16 de Jullio 1565. Criado y vasallo de V. M. que sus reales pies y manos besa, don Garcia de Toledo [autograph]. English. As the courier was embarking, García received fresh letters from the Grand Master and forwards them, so that the King can see how much worse things are than he had thought, even with the relief got in. The bearer heard an artillery salute from the galleys of the Turkish fleet, which must mark the arrival of the ships sighted off Cape Bon, surely the Algiers squadron. Had he sent the galleys with the troops to La Goletta they would have arrived at a bad moment. He has held them back waiting for La Valette’s answer: had the Grand Master written that there was a way to put more men in by land, the galleys would not have been lacking; but he asks for more men than García can now give him, so the galleys leave tomorrow. The figures carry exactly the military matter: the relief, the Algerian arrival, the galleys and troops for La Goletta, the wait for La Valette’s reply, the reinforcement and the departure. It is the same news as no. 247 in a short covering note, and it reads with the same key: a second text, not used to build the key, that the key deciphers in full.

yaretas (f. 2v, line 1): the figures are unambiguous, 42 12 35 20 37 14 36 . It is taken as jaretas , the netting rigged over a galley’s deck; with the 41/42 confusion it could be xaretas , the same word. secanos (f. 2r): “çierto es secanos donde podria ser assaltada ” is taken as shoals or dry ground that would let the sea-facing cavalier be stormed. The figures are certain; the sense is a guess. “salio del burgo el mismo lunes a los diez y nueue”: taken as the hour, not the day of the month, since 19 July is after the letter’s date. Which duplicate went by way of Mdina (f. 2r, el que por aquella parte embie con el duplicado ) is not said; it is presumably a second copy of García’s own message to the Grand Master. No. 249: the last group of entrado is written 17·0 , with a small mark between 7 and 0, and is taken as 17 30 ( -do ); PARES serves no image larger than about 970 × 1390 pixels, which does not resolve the mark, and any other reading turns the run odd. The overlined M-like sign (once, at the start of respuesta ) is taken as r , and the barred θ (twice) ll ; neither occurs in no. 247, and no key sheet or third letter in this key has been found to confirm them. The originals of nos. 247 and 249, of which these are the duplicates, and the Mdina governor’s letter that went with them have not been found on PARES; a text search for the ciphered Toledo letters of 1565 returns only these two items. Estado leg. 1395 has not been searched. The original could carry a contemporary decipherment in the secretariat’s hand, and that would be the independent check on this decryption. Until it is found, the check is internal: the self-consistency of the table, the audit, and the names. No published text of the letter was found in web searches for the document and for editions of the Simancas Malta correspondence (18 September 2026). That is not the same as a search of the printed literature on the siege, and an edition may exist that the searches missed. The key table was rebuilt here from two cribs in the cleartext, not taken from a published source. The alphabetical key is easy to recover and the letter is on no list of open ciphers, so the key may have been known before, to Tomokiyo or from other material. The contribution is the transcription and decryption of this letter; no first break of the cipher is claimed.

Six images on PARES (catalogue id 3576569, dbCode 27138924); ff. 1r–2v text, address leaf signed *En manos del señor Franco de Erasso* under the seal. The letter is written in Spanish with every militarily sensitive word replaced by two-digit figures — 1,930 figure groups in all. *Words in italics below stand for figures in the manuscript*; roman text is in the clear as the scribe wrote it. Spelling is the manuscript's own (*hauia*, *sennales* = señales, *u*/*v* undifferentiated); word division inside a figure run is editorial, since the cipher writes none. Square brackets are mine. --- ## f. 1r Llevo tan *ruyn* *nueua* a V. Mag. el correo passado que no me ha parescido detener este para que *en parte* la mejore. Los *seiscientos soldados* que don Juan de Cardona puso *en tiera* fue Dios servido *de guiallos* tanbien que todos *entraron en el burgo a saluamento*. Dizeme este que ha salido que fue tan grande la alegria del *maestre*, *abracando* la gente sin *podello* hablar, que *lloraua de plazer*; y tanbien dize que otro dia salio la misma gente a dar en los Turcos y que *mataron* mas de dozientos, aunque *estas salidas* en ningun *caso queria* que las *hiziese*, y por *muchas letras* se lo tengo *scripto* con mucho encarescimiento. Del *maestre* no tengo *carta*, que estoy *spantado* [ms. *spantaado*] dello, pero no *tengo* por *mala* seña olvidarse de mi, aunque no creo que tardara a *dos o tres dias* a venir; y conforme a lo que *scriuiere uere de proueer* lo mas *que* por el se *pudiere*. El estar sin *galeras* me *destruye*, porque se po- ## f. 1v -drian *hazer* algunos *effetos* en *baxeles* suyos que van y vienen, pero trayendo *las* que aca ay *ocupadas* en *iuntar* la gente *no se* puede *proueer a todo*. Si *[u]iniessen las de Spanna* me darian *mucha ayuda*. Las galeras *que yban a entrar por* el puerto *llegaron a quatro* millas del, con *muy* buena *orden* y gran *determinacion*, y aquella *noche*, que sera *lunes*, vna *hora* antes que *amaneciesse*, viniendo el *martes*, *entro a* saluamento la *uarqueta* que yo *hauia* embiado para *auisar* al *maestre* de las *sennales*, con la qual tuuo *auiso* de lo que hauia *de hazer*; y tornando *las galeras* el *martes* en la noche a otras *quatro* millas del *puerto*, el *maestre* les hizo *las sennales* del *fuego* *clarissimas* para que no *entrassen*, y ansi lo dize *Mosiur de Lenni* y todos los demas; y dentro de la *hora sennalada las* continuo la *segunda* vez, y las *galeras* se *tornaron* a meter a la *mar* por *no* ser *descubiertas*, y han *llegado* aqui esta *mannana*. El don Juan Çanoguera, que es el que *las guiaua*, lo *hizo* muy *bien*, y todos los demas. Y este no sabe *que[r]ido* [ms. *quesido*] el *maestre* aceptar *estas galeras*; aunque podria ser por *parescelle* la *entrada* muy *dificultosa*, no dexo de tenella por buena *senal*. Dizen todos los *nuestros* que, en acabando de hazer el *maestre* las *sennales*, vieron y *oyeron* vna *gran cantidad* de arcabuzeria, y que juzgauan *ellos* que sera *salua* para *mostrarnos* que *nuestra* gente sera *dentro*. Este ombre que es venido *salio del burgo* el mismo lunes a los diez y nueue, y no *trae* nueua de *la uarqueta* que *entro*, porque no sera aun *llegada*; la qual puso el *que* yo *embie* a do le mande, y de alli ## f. 2r hauia de yr *a nado* hasta *el burgo*, y ansi *llego saluo*, como a la clara se ve por *las sennales*; y la *ciudad* hizo el *mismo fuego*, que tanbien es *indicio* que *llego* el que por aquella *parte embie* con el *duplicado*. Los *tiempos* son tales y las *necessidades* tan grandes, que aunque *se tuuiesse* mucho dinero no *osaria deshazerme* de vn *rreal* para pagar *deudas*; y aunque es justissimo lo que V. Mag. manda de Juan Andrea, se podra *hazer poco* con el, pero lo que se *pudiera* no se *dexara* de hazer como V. Mag. lo manda, que cierto yo desseo dalle toda satisfacion, y el solo sera en este tiempo el que *de mi cobrara* alguna quantidad. Es necessario *poner* luego mano en *comencar a fortificar*, por todo lo que *podria suceder*, la *fruente* que *Caragoca* tiene en *tierra firme*, y en *leuantar* vn cavallero *en la mar* que *corresponde* —çierto es *secanos* donde *podria* ser *assaltada*. Tanbien es necessario *comencar* al fin de *octubre la fortificacion de Augusta*, por que la *ocasion* no mostrasse *a los enemigos* el segundo salto. Para estas casas es menester *dinero*, y en *este* reyno *no ay* si no *infinitas deudas*. V. Mag. mande echar quenta de los *ytalianos* que se han de *leuantar*, y de los *spannoles* que se han de pagar, y del sueldo *de las naues, que cada mes importa quarenta mil escudos* sin dos *mesadas* que se les deuen; y vease tanbien el *uizcocho* que de nueuo es *menester* hazer, que aunque despues se desquente a las galeras su parte, todavia este *dinero* sale del que V. Mag. me ha embiado. Hanse comprado *quinientos quintales* de artilleria de peso ## f. 2v *de Espanna*, mucha *xarcia y madera* para las *yaretas* [jaretas]; y aunque esta *xarcia y madera* puede seruir para *las galeras* que se huuieren de hazer, y lo del *metal es dinero* que no se *pierde*, todavia cuesta buen pedaço. Tanbien se haze *armamento* para las *ocho galeras* que vienen de *Espanna*, y otros gastos de *botas, barriles, murriones y coracinas* que no se pueden escusar. Y si se quenta esto, y se añade el *sueldo* de la *ynfanteria*, contando tanbien el gasto de *[l]onze galeras* que se *arman* de nueuo, vera V. Mag. que la prouision echa *no basta* para *tantas* casas, ni yo *pu[e]do* [ms. *puddo*] *sustentar* con ella los *gastos* que V. Mag. apunta en *su carta*, tanto mas *si esto* se fuesse nada *alargando*. Y los *quarenta y ocho mil ducados* que venieron para las *galeras* ya estaua *comido la mitad*, y otra buena parte *se deue a* la gente. Y *considerado* esto, suplico a V. Mag. mande *proueer* como mas se paresciere que conuiene a su seruicio, y en el *gastallos* se terna el miramiento que V. Mag. manda. Dize este que ha *salido* que todos los *turcos* que estan en *tierra*, demas de los *bastiones* a do tienen sus *baterias*, estan todos *circundados* de *trincheas* siete, ocho y diez *palmos altas*, assi a la parte de los *nuestros* como a la *parte* de la *campanna*; y que quando el *partio* no hauia *otros* que no las tuuiessen si no *mil y quinientos turcos* que estauan *al agua*. Confirma que *hauian* perdido *mucha gente*, y que en el *campo corrian dolencias* de que *morian*. Por essos *auisos* vera V. Mag. *los nauios* que hallo sobre *Cabo Bono* el *baxel* que *yua* con *uino* a la *Goleta*. Tengo por cierto que *son los de Argel* que se *uienen a iuntar con la armada*; y esto creo por no saber que de *Maltta* aya *salido* cantidad *dellos*, porque *dize* este que *del armada* no se hauia *desmandado nauio* ninguno quando *el partio*, ni tan poco lo *escriue el gouernador* de la *ciudad*, como vera V. Mag. por su carta original que yra con esta. Cuya vida guarde Nuestro Señor por tan largos años como sus criados y vassallos desseamos y la christiandad ha menester. *De Mecina*, a XVJ. de Julio 1565. ## Postscript (entirely in the clear) Ya tengo scripto a V. Mag. por otras quan bien le sirue el conde de Modica, y a su costa; y hauiendole agora scripto el almirante su padre la muerte de la duquesa su madre, y llamandole que vaya a España, no obstante que esto le ymporte mucho, no ha querido hazello ni yrse deste reyno hasta ver el sucesso de las cosas de aca. Hame parescido muy justo auisar dello a V. Mag., para que tenga entendido su voluntad y el seruicio que haze en ello a V. Mag. --- ## What the letter says (English) Written from Messina on 16 July 1565, about two months into the siege of Malta (begun 18 May) and about a week after the *Piccolo Soccorso* reached Malta. Every proper name, number and item of intelligence is in cipher. 1. **The relief got in.** The 600 soldiers Don Juan de Cardona put ashore all entered Il Borgo safely. A man just out of the Borgo reports the Grand Master (La Valette) embraced the men and wept for joy, unable to speak; the garrison sortied next day and killed more than 200 Turks — sorties García had repeatedly written to forbid. 2. **A failed second run into the harbour.** The galleys came within four miles of the port, meaning to enter; the *barqueta* sent ahead to arrange fire-signals got in safely before dawn on Tuesday; but the Grand Master made the fire-signals unmistakably *not* to enter, repeated them within the appointed hour, and the galleys stood out to sea to avoid being spotted, reaching Messina that morning. Don Juan Çanoguera, who piloted them, "did it very well". The man the *barqueta* landed swam the last stretch to the Borgo, and the signals show he arrived; a second man, sent by the other side with a *duplicado* of García's message, evidently reached Mdina, which lit the same fire. 3. **Money and materiel.** Without galleys "me destruye". Blocked on more material in the same key (Estado leg. 1395 siblings, not checked). - The barred θ = *ll*: two occurrences, both certain from context (*la llegada*, *ponelle*); also absent from no. 247, which spells *ll* as 27 27. It is probably one of the extra signs of the full key sheet, which has not been found.
