C. R. M. The courier being already embarked with this despatch, I have received these letters of the Grand Master, which I send to Your Majesty so that you can see in great detail all that he writes, which is much more pressed than I thought, knowing *the relief had entered*. This man who has brought these last letters says that he heard an artillery salute from the galleys of the Armada, and it must have been *the arrival of the* ships that appeared off *Cape Bon*, which I believe for certain are those of *Algiers*. And if I had sent *the galleys with the men to La Goleta*, they would have arrived *at a bad time*. *I have* held *them* until now, waiting for *the Grand Master's answer*, because if he had written to me that there was *a way to put more men into it by* land, it would not have stayed for *want* of them; but he *asks for more than* I *can now give him*, and so the galleys *will leave tomorrow*. May Our Lord keep Your Majesty's life for as many years as your servants desire and Christendom needs. From Messina, 16 July 1565. Your Majesty's servant and vassal, who kisses your royal feet and hands, don García de Toledo. Key: key.json

Archivo General de Simancas, Estado, leg. 1394, no. 247, Duplicado de carta cifrada de García de Toledo … a Felipe II , 16 July 1565: PARES, description 3576569 , images 1–6. The same, leg. 1394, no. 249, the companion letter of 16 July 1565 ( duplicado ): PARES record 3576586, images 1–4. S. Tomokiyo, cryptiana , which marks the Malta cipher letters of 1565 as undeciphered. In Tomokiyo’s usage that means there is no interlinear decipherment or nearby deciphered copy. It does not mean unsolved; unsolved material from cryptiana is listed on its unsolved page (G. Lasry, personal communication, 21 September 2026). The key may therefore already be known from other material. Context: the Great Siege of Malta (18 May – September 1565), the Piccolo Soccorso of late June and early July and the Gran Soccorso of September, in the standard accounts of the siege. The digit-for-digit transcription ( transcription.txt ), the key ( key.json ), the decode and render scripts, the raw and edited readings and the notes are in the repository ( targets/toledo1565/ ), with the six PARES images in targets/toledo1565/img/ ; no. 249 is in transcription_249.txt and read_249.md .

Hungarian cipher letters among the papers of Ferenc Bethlen of Keresd, Rákóczi envoy to Poland, with no decryption on DECODE. A reciprocal letter alphabet shared by four of them was recovered from the ciphertext alone; the 1646 letter to the Hofmeister and Zsigmond Rákóczi’s two of 1648 give sentences with it. R4939, in a second alphabet and another hand, was broken separately: the Rákóczi brothers tell the envoys their father is dying and bind them to Zsigmond’s Polish candidacy. The 1645 points for the Warsaw mission decode but rest on look-alike letters the scan cannot separate. pmwxwh oncckdzwnw xyhyiq xyzznq czasar dipplomaia serent semmit c = p · p = c · g = u · q = t Transylvania → Ferenc Bethlen of Keresd · Hungarian letter substitution, two alphabets · 1645–1648 · key recovered from the ciphertext alone, partial Keresdi Bethlen cipher letters, 1645–1648 Go to the full text ↓ Hungarian cipher letters to the Rákóczi envoy Ferenc Bethlen, with no decryption on DECODE, deciphered from the ciphertext alone in two separate alphabets; four give sentences and one more decodes in fragments. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 23 October 2026 · updated 8 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (58% of the cipher) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (58% of the cipher) The letters Six records of the Keresdi Bethlen papers, 1645–1648: numbered points for Bethlen's Warsaw mission (1645), a letter to the Hofmeister (1646), a clear letter with three cipher spans (1647), and three of 1648, two of them from Zsigmond Rákóczi and one from the Rákóczi brothers to Bethlen and Andrew Klobusiczky, envoys to the Polish diet. Where Romanian National Archives, Cluj (not Sibiu), Keresdi Bethlen 14–15; DECODE R4936–R4940 and R4942, all listed N/A with no decryption. The cipher Letter-for-letter substitution of Hungarian, written without word breaks, in reciprocal pairs (c = p, g = u, q = t ...). R4939 uses a second paired alphabet in another hand. How it was deciphered The family alphabet was found by annealing against a Hungarian quadgram model on R4936 (23 Sept 2026) and applied unchanged to the others; R4939 was broken the same way from its own 1,631 letters (23 Oct 2026). A blind second transcription of six R4939 lines agrees on 93.9% of letters. What it says Hiring musketeers and dragoons in Poland (1645), distrust of the Emperor's diploma for the Protestants (1646), and in 1648 the Polish crown: the brothers write that their father, György I Rákóczi, is dying and bind the envoys to push Zsigmond's candidacy. Still open R4936 (1,956 letters) decodes but 130 of the reading’s 1,932 letters (6.7%) sit on g/q look-alikes the scan cannot separate; R4938's three spans are fragments; about twelve words of R4939 and two runs of R4937 are illegible. R4939 is to become a target of its own. R4937, 1646: the cipher runs on without word breaks; the writer left some words in clear, among them Cum satisfactione Evangelicorum in line 2. Image: Romanian National Archives, Cluj, Keresdi Bethlen 15 (1646), via DECODE R4937.

DECODE holds ten cipher records from two Transylvanian collections in Cluj under R4933–R4942. They were first grouped by number and split by cipher on 14 Oct 2026: R4941 is a different substitution ( r4941 ) and R4933–R4935 are the Kemény collection of 1628 ( kemeny1628 ). This page covers the six from Keresdi Bethlen 14–15: R4936 (Keresdi Bethlen 14, 1645): numbered points in the prince's “we” for Bethlen's mission to Warsaw, both pages almost wholly in cipher. Decoded, not counted (see section 04). R4937 (15-01, 1646): one long page to “edes Hokmester”, sender not named. Deciphered. R4938 (15-02, 24 Apr 1647): a clear letter with three short cipher spans, 54 letters. Decoded in fragments. R4939 (15-03, 1648): two pages of cipher in another hand, addressed in clear to “Magnificis Francisco Betthlen de Keresd ... ac Andreae Klobusiczki ... ad moderna comitia Reipub. Poloniae legatis”. Deciphered in its own alphabet. R4940 (15-04, Munkács, 2 Aug 1648): Zsigmond Rákóczi to Bethlen, clear with two cipher spans of 23 letters. Deciphered. R4942 (15-06, 1648): Zsigmond Rákóczi, a cipher block of 252 letters; DECODE's image 3 is a clear slip of the same block in his name. Deciphered. No decipherment of any of them was found in print: Lukinich's edition of Bethlen's correspondence (1907) and his biography (1908), Szilágyi's documents on the peace of Linz (1885) and Erdély és az északkeleti háború I were searched; the last prints the envoys' reports of October 1648, not these letters.

The writers spell Hungarian letter by letter in a substitution whose letters are swapped in pairs, so that the same table enciphers and deciphers: c and p, g and u, q and t, among others ( shared-key-hypothesis.json in the folder). A first statistical key on R4936 had c = u, g = t and q = p; the error was in the hand transcription, which had confused those letter shapes, and once the transcription was corrected the pairs fell into place. The opening of R4937 shows it: pmwxwh oncckdzwnw is czasar dipplomaia , “the Emperor's diploma”. The alphabet was recovered on 23 Sept 2026 by simulated annealing against the shared Hungarian quadgram model, with no crib, on R4936. On 23 Oct 2026 R4936 was re-transcribed from the images (215 label changes) and R4937 and R4942 were transcribed in full; all three were decoded with the alphabet unchanged and aligned letter by letter with the figures. In R4937, 839 of 847 letters of the reading stand on the cipher letter's own value.

R4937, 1646, to the Hofmeister The letter opens in cipher and keeps clear words between the runs (in italics in the reading). From R4937_reading.md : czasar dipplomaia serent semmit nem sem akar efectualni Cum satisfactione Evangelicorum ; ... az clerus elbirta czasart ... “According to the Emperor's diploma he wants to effect nothing at all cum satisfactione Evangelicorum ... The clergy has prevailed over the Emperor.” The writer urges Bethlen to keep the plan from the King of Poland and, if the Emperor's armies move, to hire four thousand good foot with their officers and dragoons, or at the least a thousand foot and five hundred dragoons. A run after megsegni in line 3 and the end of line 13 decode to letter strings that are not words. R4940 and R4942, Zsigmond Rákóczi, 1648 R4940 is a clear letter from Munkács of 2 August 1648 with two cipher spans: votumiok and niert dolog volna , “if their votes were as Your Grace writes, it would be a won matter”. R4942's cipher block speaks of using the intermediaries and of the plenipotentiary power his brother has given him; its clear slip on image 3 carries the same text and confirms the decipherment.

R4939, p. 1: another hand and another alphabet. The family key gives nothing here. Image: Romanian National Archives, Cluj, Keresdi Bethlen 15 (1648), via DECODE R4939. R4939 is in a different simple substitution: 23 cipher letters, each standing for one plain letter, with ten reciprocal pairs (a–m, b–i, c–p, d–u, e–g, f–v, h–l, o–y, r–z, s–t). It was transcribed (1,631 letters) and broken from its own ciphertext by annealing on 23 Oct 2026; 50 look-alike labels were then corrected on 3× crops ( R4939_key.md , R4939_corrections.tsv ). An independent second reader transcribed six randomly drawn lines blind: 200 of 213 letters agree (93.9%), and eight words of 36 were not carried by the blind decode at first, three after re-cropping. Under the project's one-key rule it should be a target of its own; it is described here until it is split. The brothers write to Bethlen and Klobusiczky that their father is dying ( az doctor itileti szerent is eletehez ... semmi ... ninc , “by the doctor's judgement there is no [hope] for his life”), that he did not want the Polish crown for himself, that seeking the principality for Zsigmond now would put the country in danger, and they bind the envoys to further oeczem uram promotioiat , “my younger brother's promotion”, with money to be spent on it. Lines 3–9 keep about twelve words that decode to non-words with every look-alike pair tried.

R4936 (1645, 1,956 letters). It decodes into numbered points on the Warsaw mission (three thousand musketeers and a thousand dragoons to be hired, money at Danzig, Bregy and Croissy), but 130 of the reading’s 1,932 letters (6.7%) sit on the other member of a look-alike pair, mostly t written on g-shaped letters; at the scan's 1,704-pixel width the hand's g and q do not separate, and no contemporary or printed text settles the choice. Counted as decoded, not read; blocker: illegible (a sharper image of Keresdi Bethlen 14 would settle it). R4937 : a run on line 3 and the end of line 13 (illegible at 2.2×). R4938 : three spans of 54 letters decoded with the family key ( az Rakoczi Sigmon , az nekunk [...] volna , mi [?nevunkre] forogion ); one word, ailunkker , occurs once and is too short to settle. The clear letter around them is not transcribed. R4939 : about twelve words in lines 3–9 (illegible on the scan). The family alphabet's statistical validation on R4940 alone is “too short” (23 letters); the checks that carry it are the R4942 clear slip, the alignments and the sense of the longer letters. Measured on the transcriptions: R4937 869, R4942 252, R4940 23 and R4939 1,631 cipher letters are in letters that give sentences, 2,775 of 4,785 (0.58). The modern Hungarian word list cannot score 17th-century spelling (it gives 0.07 on printed letters of 1645), so the sentences were judged by reading; the explicit-hole share of the readings is 0.90–1.00. Measured word by word on 24 October 2026, R4937 builds coherent sentences but reads at 93.3% of its words, R4939 at 89.6% and R4940’s two spans at 88.7%, under the 95% a complete reading needs.

We would have wished to be able to write happier news from God to Your Lordships: on our gracious lord our father [?his health ...] God's great visitation is upon us; [?it has grown very much worse], so that by the doctor's judgement there is no [?further] [hope] for his life ... taking it to mind, His Highness ordered that Your Lordships should conduct yourselves ... knowing ... His Highness did not want the election for himself but meant it for us ... As for our own state, we certainly do not want it, for we do not want to throw this poor country ... into a more dangerous condition; Your Lordships know how things stand with the Porte. For good security ... may God preserve him ... after His Highness's death we must think, and not leave this country without a head [?in danger]. If we wanted to win the principality for my younger brother it would take a long time, and meanwhile ... the state would be in great danger, and [...] an uncertain matter. Therefore we bind Your Lordships, by the duty you owe to our gracious lord and father and after His Highness to us, to employ our grace with every means where it is needed in my younger brother's promotion; Your Lordships, being there, are to work on everyone, since His Lordship's fortune ... assuring those whom it concerns, and it must be known that as his father, who was ready to lay down his life for him, so we will strive to further him with all our means. May God preserve him; we will inform Your Lordships of His Highness's death too, if God has so ordained, which we do not wish to live to see. We will use our money so that by spending it ... it may be turned to his promotion. May God preserve him; if His Highness should happen to die, we will send letters, if needed, so that Your Lordships can deliver them to those whom it concerns, and further the business of my younger brother in the best way. 28 July 1585, Nonsuch (R4838; CSP no. 40) Walsingham is sorry to hear of a move in Scotland to ask for an English duchy for the King: it would offend the Queen and breed jealousy against the league. Wotton should dissuade it through Gray. On the slip of f. 126: 13 is “affected to 19” and Wotton should deal warily with 13 in anything that concerns Arran. 7 August 1585, the Court (R4839; CSP no. 65) After the killing of Lord Russell on the Border, the Russells’ friends are incensed against Farnihurst (24) and Arran (19). Wotton is to insist that the King do justice and not set Arran at liberty. 21 August 1585, the Court (R4840) “39 dothe complayne in a late letter wrytten to his frende here … of the alteration of your countenaunce towardes him.” Gray offers to prove himself if 28 and 29 come down to the Borders to join with 20 (Maxwell); without that, he fears that “10 wyll be carried awaye from 36, the party of 11 increasing”. Walsingham trusts none of them: “The best is to deale warely with them all.” He advises Wotton to tell Gray of the suspicion without naming its author. The Queen wants Farnihurst (24) imprisoned. Wotton’s draft answer of 30 August is on the companion page . The opening, re-read on the image for the quotation list (30 Sept 2026; bracketed words are grade M readings of hard places in the secretary hand): “Sir, 39 dothe complayne in a late letter wrytten to his frende here, whom you knowe, of the alteration of your countenaunce towardes him, with the [courage] to procure the practice of 27 and 40, which as he professeth dothe greatly [abuse] you, being altogether bent to [ruin] 11 course; and for himself he voweth to be altogether at 3 devotion, whereof he offereth to make a most manifest proofe” (spelling restored on the images on 23 October 2026). The earlier transcription had “overthrow 11”; the manuscript has a short word and course after the number (“11 course”, as in Wotton’s answer of 30 August: “I could never perceive cause to suspect them in the 11 course”). 3 here is Gray’s object of devotion, so the Queen or England (M); Wotton’s draft of 25 August has “divert him from 3” but also “convey him towards 3 … into France”, so the number is not settled. The glosses of 28, 29 and 36 could not be checked again against CSP Scotland viii on 30 September (the HathiTrust text view now sits behind a bot check and the Internet Archive copy is lending-only); they stay grade M. 10 September 1585, the Court (R4844) Decoded, not read. The sign words and the open name codes fall in nearly every sentence of this letter, so it counts as decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026); the 21 August letter reads. Wotton’s letters of 1 September have bred “some better lykinge of the [signs] set downe by 39”. This is Gray’s plan to seize the King. The 28 and 29 “wyll be [signs]”; 13 “wyll in no sorte neyther be [signs] nor otherwyse make [signs] [signs] a partye”. Wotton is to confer with the King so as to be “[signs] at the [signs]”, but must “warde your [signs]” and avoid [signs]. In the postscript Walsingham sends on a letter and reports that [23] “is the principal dealer in [37] between 10 and the Jesuites”. The working transcriptions of both uncalendared letters ( reading_R4840.txt , reading_R4844_r2.txt , with the gaps read on the images merged into the second on 22 October 2026) keep the secretary’s spelling, re-read on the DECODE images on 23 October.

The sign words are a second cipher, unrelated to the name code, and are counted on their own: about 23 words, none read. The name code alone reads at 34 of its 46 occurrences. About fourteen words, some 120 signs in all, are written in an alphabet of geometric and letter-like signs: squares, triangles, =, ≠, ÷, a crossed 4, ω, and borrowed letters f, d, c, k, R. They also carry dots and dashes that look like nulls. The same signs (square, triangle, ≠) open many words, which suggests homophones. Over every sign word Wotton, or his secretary, wrote the decipherment and later scribbled it out in loops. Nothing of it can be read on the scan. No key was found. DECODE has no key record for Wotton or Walsingham’s Scottish correspondence, and Tomokiyo’s survey of Elizabethan ciphers has none for 1585 (his “Wotton” cipher is Nicholas Wotton’s of 1548). Wotton’s drafts in the same volume use the numbers but no signs, so they give no crib. A homophonic alphabet with nulls cannot be recovered from the ciphertext alone when it has only 120 signs. The words are copied as far as they can be in targets/walsingham1585/NOTES.md .

The fourteen sign words of 10 September (R4844), without a key. They would yield to Wotton’s cipher key or to any other letter in this alphabet with its decipherment, most likely among the sent despatches in TNA SP 52/37–38. Numbers 13, 14, 23, 30, 37 , unidentified; 27, 28, 29, 36 possible only. The transcriptions of 21 August and 10 September are working texts with gaps, not editions.

The cipher There is no letter cipher: a small nomenclator of one- and two-digit numbers stands in place of names (“39. came to me yesterday”). How it was read No cipher had to be broken. The drafts were transcribed and eleven code numbers collected from context, seven of them identified from the drafts themselves; the Calendar of State Papers, Scotland vol. 8 later confirmed 19 and 39, gave 40 as the Justice Clerk, and 24 as Ferniehirst, not Huntly. What it says The plot that ended in the fall of Arran at Stirling in November 1585. Certain: 19 Arran, 39 the Master of Gray, 10 King James VI. Still open 27, 32 and 36 are unidentified; 9, 20 and 3 are probable only. Credit Later glosses: Calendar of State Papers, Scotland, vol. 8 (1914). Add MS 32657 f. 167: the draft of 25 August opens “Sir, 39.”, with “came to me” struck and “sayed to me” written above, “yesterday”; further down, “to disgrace 19 with 10”. Image: British Library, Add MS 32657 f. 167, via DECODE R4841.

Add MS 32657 is a volume of Walsingham’s Scottish correspondence (DECODE gives the span of the volume, 1547–1590, as the records’ date). DECODE imaged four pages each of three items: R4841 , ff. 167–168: “To Mr Secretary the 25th August”. The top of f. 167 carries the end of an earlier draft and jotted notes (“Maxwel”, “1000”, “Sterling”). R4842 , ff. 173–174: “To Mr Secretary the 30th of August 1585”. R4843 , ff. 175–176: “To Mr Secretary the first of September”. All three are working drafts in Wotton’s hand, with deletions and interlinear additions. The code numbers are written inline, usually followed by a point, where a name would stand. The drafts also write “the K.” and “her M tie ” in clear in places, so the code was applied unevenly.

Read on the full transcription (22 October 2026); every occurrence fits, but on sense only. 27 unidentified I One of Gray’s associates at court (39, 40 and 27 cannot “live safely” at court); “[27] was greatly hers, and is a great favorer of the Hameltons” (Mary’s). Candidate: Secretary Maitland (the Justice Clerk Bellenden is 40, per the calendar). 40 Sir Lewis Bellenden, the Justice Clerk (CSP Scotland viii) H Another of Gray’s associates at court. 32 unidentified I A place, probably a castle, into which Arran might “convey himself”. 36 unidentified I The source of money for 39’s hundred men (“money out of [36]”); perhaps the Queen’s treasure.

25 August 1585 (R4841) The King is hunting in a land of the Duke of Lennox. Gray (39) came to Wotton “yesterday”: although he had written that he would forbear to deal further until he heard that the Queen was satisfied with his doings, he judged delay dangerous. His discourse: he and the rest have run a wrong course “in seeking to disgrace 19 with 10”, whose love toward Arran is so extreme that he will not suffer a hair of his head to fall; as long as Arran continues in favour it is impossible to bring home the banished lords, and the league “cannot be sure”. Arran will be able to divert the King from England and toward France (3). To obviate this, the Queen should furnish the lords to take Arran and seize the King’s person. There are rumours that Arran and 24 are agreed, and that 24 may carry the King to France. 30 August 1585 (R4842) Wotton answers Walsingham’s letter of the 21st about Gray’s complaint to “his friend in England”. Gray, 40 and 27 cannot live safely at court while Arran may return; 27 “was greatly hers, and is a great favorer of the Hameltons”. Arran still remains at Kinneil under guard. Bothwell has come to court, “to the great grief of the Arranistes”. The Jesuits Hay and Dury are in the country, and the King has charged Gray to take them. 1 September 1585 (R4843) The device of Gray and the Prior of Blantyre: the lords are to join with 20 under colour of his feud with Johnstone, and send 500 men to seize the King and Arran. Gray asks for money to keep a hundred men and hold the King’s house; the commissioners are to meet on the Borders. This is the plan that became the return of the banished lords and the fall of Arran at Stirling in November 1585.

The twelve images were fetched from DECODE with a logged-in session and transcribed directly; there was no cipher to break, only a hand to read. Each code number was identified by collecting every sentence it occurs in across the three drafts and matching it to the persons and events of August 1585 (Arran’s warding after the Russell affair, Gray’s intrigue with England, the Maxwell–Johnstone feud, the Jesuit mission). A number counts as certain (H) where two or more independent contexts fit only one person; probable (C) where one context points to one person or to a small set.

27, 40 : two of Gray’s associates at court. The calendar gives 40 as Bellenden (below); 27 is untested, with Maitland a candidate. 32 : a place of refuge for Arran. 36 : a source of money. 9, 20, 3 : probable only (grade C); for 20 and 24 see the calendar below. 3 was first read as France; on the full transcription it is the Queen of England, on sense only. 11 : open; and a few interlineations and struck-over phrases in the drafts of 30 August (p. 2 ll. 5–9, on embarking the Scots) and 1 September (p. 2 ll. 10–17, the commissioners), read only in their legible last state. Prior identification, checked later the same day. CSP Scotland vol. 8 (1914) was consulted afterwards through the HathiTrust text view for the companion page on Walsingham’s side of this correspondence . The calendar glosses the numbers in Wotton’s sent despatches: Arran [“19”], the Master of Gray [“39”], the Justice Clerk [“40”] and Farnyhurst [“24”] . So 40 is Sir Lewis Bellenden, and 24 is Sir Thomas Kerr of Ferniehirst, not Huntly. Its no. 106 calendars the despatch of 1 September with “Morton” for 20 (Lord Maxwell, styled Earl of Morton).

To Mr Secretary, the 25th of August. The King being at hunting in an yland of the Duk of Lennox. Sir, {39 = the Master of Gray} sayed to me yesterday that, notwithstanding he had written to your Honour that he would forbeare to deale any more in the course undertaken by him til he hearde out of England that her Majesty did rest fully satisfied of his doinges, yet considering with himself that in matters of importance protraction of tyme is dangerous, he thought good to imparte unto me his opinion touching the state of matters heere, to the end that your Honour, being therof advertised by me, might acquainte her Majesty with it. His discourse tendeth to this end: that he now findeth how he and [the] rest of his party have runne al this while a wrong course in seeking to disgrace {19 = Arran} with {10 = the King}, whose love towarde him is so extreeme as [he] wil not suffer one hair of his head to fall to the ground if he may helpe it; that as long as {19 = Arran} shal continew in favour with {10 = the King}, it will be a thing impossible to bring home the Lords; that unles they may be restored the league cannot be sure, nor {39 = the Master of Gray} and the rest in safety. For {19 = Arran}, receaving the King presently, then wil he with his credit be able to ruine them and diverte {10 = the King} from {3 = the Queen of England}; or if, that finding the King constantly [in] affection towarde {3 = the Queen of England} [?immoveable], [?stick], he wil not fail to convey him into France. To obviate therfore al thees inconveniences, his advise is that her Majesty, having so good occasion ministred unto her by the death of my Lord Russel, [should] take the matter very highly and hold [the King] from concluding the league for this time; that she lette slippe the Lords, who, if they may have from her some supporte of money, wil by their frendes heere and suche as they may levy for money be able to take {19 = Arran} and possesse [and] seize {10 = the King's} persone; wherunto they shal have the best helpe he can give them by himself and his faction. If he may perceive that this overture be liked of, he wil direct a spetial frend of his and theirs into England very shortly, who shal conferre with the Lords particularly about the execution of this plotte. This was the effect of his whole speeche, saving that in the end he saied, in answeare of an objection which I made, that he would undertake (this thing being once done) to bring the league to a perfect conclusion, and that the King shal notwithstanding al this be wrought to assente unto it with a [..] heart, as wel as to confirme it with his hand and oath. It is suspected that {19 = Arran} and {24 = Ferniehirst} be secretly agreed, and some heere feare lest {24 = Ferniehirst} by consent of the other take the King and convey him into France. It is now very constantly reported that {24 = Ferniehirst} payeth his men with crownes of the sun, and that the greatest parte of the six thousand [crowns] which the Jesuites brought fell to his share; which, if it be true, is a shrewd token. Postscript. Article: if her Majesty shal like of the Master's overture, I could wishe the matter so handled that {10 = the King} might first waxe colde in the matter of the league [and] refuse the league, which I suppose might easely be compassed if her Majesty do meet with that article which is proposed touching the King's title; she would inserte another for the home comming of the Lords. [Endorsed:] Copie. To Mr Secretarye, 25 Auguste. The King is out hunting on an island belonging to the Duke of Lennox. Sir, {39 = the Master of Gray} told me yesterday that, although he had written to you that he would stop dealing in the course he had taken up until he heard from England that the Queen was fully satisfied with what he had done, he had concluded that in important matters delay is dangerous, and so decided to give me his view of affairs here, so that you, informed by me, could pass it on to the Queen. The gist of what he said is this. He now sees that he and the rest of his party have all along been going the wrong way about it in trying to bring {19 = Arran} into disgrace with {10 = the King}, whose love for him is so extreme that he will not let a hair of his head fall to the ground if he can help it. As long as {19 = Arran} stays in favour with {10 = the King} it will be impossible to bring the Lords home; unless they are restored the league cannot be relied on, and {39 = the Master of Gray} and the rest will not be safe. For {19 = Arran}, once he has the King again, will use his credit to ruin them and to turn {10 = the King} away from {3 = the Queen of England}; or, if he finds the King's affection for {3 = the Queen of England} [?unshakeable], he will not fail to carry him off to France. To head off all these dangers, his advice is that the Queen, given so good an occasion by the death of Lord Russell, should take the matter very seriously and hold the King back from concluding the league for now, and let the Lords loose. If they can have some money from her, they will be able, with their friends here and the men they can hire, to take {19 = Arran} and seize the person of {10 = the King}; and he will give them all the help he can, himself and his faction. If he sees that this proposal is liked, he will very shortly send a special friend of his and of theirs to England to confer with the Lords in detail about carrying out the plan. That was the substance of his whole speech, except that at the end, answering an objection of mine, he said he would undertake, once this was done, to bring the league to a full conclusion, and that the King would nonetheless be brought to agree to it with a [..] heart, and to confirm it with his signature and his oath. It is suspected that {19 = Arran} and {24 = Ferniehirst} have come to a secret understanding, and some here fear that {24 = Ferniehirst}, with the other's consent, may seize the King and carry him to France. It is now firmly reported that {24 = Ferniehirst} is paying his men in French gold crowns, and that most of the six thousand crowns the Jesuits brought went to him, which, if true, is a telling sign. Postscript. If the Queen likes the Master's proposal, I would wish it handled so that {10 = the King} first cools towards the league and refuses it. I think that could easily be managed if the Queen answers the article proposed about the King's title by inserting another one for the return of the Lords. [Endorsed:] Copy. To Mr Secretary, the 30th of August 1585. Your Honour's of the 21st came to my handes the 26th of the same, by which I perceive that {39 = the Master of Gray} hath complayned of the alteration of my countenance towarde him. My answeare thereunto is that I never, what cause soever he gave me to the contrary, altered my countenance, but used him alwaies with as great familiaritie and curtesy as I did [..]. Mary, the trouth is that after he had spoken to {10 = the King} for the enlargement of {19 = Arran} without the knowlege of {40 = the Justice Clerk}, [27] or myself, he then for three or four dayes abstained from his wonted manner of visiting me, so that the alteration of countenance was on his parte and not on myne. This proceeding in that matter I wil now interprete in the best parte, seeing he hath so wel taken up himself, and [..] again. For [27] and {40 = the Justice Clerk}, I never sawe cause to suspect them to be in the [11] course, neither doo I suppose that {39 = the Master of Gray} in his conscience is so perswaded of them. Yet can it not be denied, as your Honour wryteth, [but] [27] was greatly hers, and is a great favorer of the Hameltons, and as yet no ernest frend to the Lords; [?howbeit] in all matters concerning my negotiation wherein I have had to deale with him I have found him fully as forwarde as any of the other two. Neverthelesse I meane to folow your Honour's grave advice in dealing warely with him and all others. For by that litle experience I have of this contry men, I thinke it dangerous to trust any of all their [..] further than it shal stande with his owne particulars, as they terme it heer. So that in my simple judgement, if her Majesty wil procure herself fast frendes in this contrey, she must both have a consideration to their particulers and so embark them in her course [..] that necessity [..] [..]. [Men that] are bounde wil quickly for greater gain free themselfes. To feed them with money is good, but to no great purpose unles you do so embarke them as [they] may not hope to leape ashore without [?drowning]. {19 = Arran} yet remayneth at Kinneil, where, under a colour [or] pretense of feare to be suddenly assaulted by his [enemies], he is, as I heare, very wel accompanied. To kepe him from the courte longer than the meeting of the commissioners, unles he bee found by them gilty of the [?late] breache on the Borders, will be, as I suppose, very harde. If he recover the King's presence, I cannot see how {39 = the Master of Gray}, {40 = the Justice Clerk} [and] [27] can live safely in the courte; and if {19 = Arran}, being there alone do fac totum, we may easely coniecture what successe matters are like to have. For my owne part, I am to yong to find out a remedy for this mischeef, and therfore leave it to the consideration of her Majesty whether she wil harken to the {39 = the Master of Gray's} offer or no. [I] expect daily her Majesty's resolution touching the overture made by {39 = the Master of Gray}. This morning I saw a letter written to the Prior of Blantire from the Laird of [?Jamington's] brother, by which it seemeth that {20 = Lord Maxwell} [is] very desirous to make his peace with the King by the means of {19 = Arran}, with whom I suspect he is secretly alreadye contracted; and therfore I wil doo what I can to hinder his reconciliation with {10 = the King}. Erle Bothwel is by the Master's means newly come to the courte, to the great grief of the Arranistes. It is very certain that Hay and Dury are in this contrey. The King seemeth very desirous of their apprehension, and hath laied that charge on {39 = the Master of Gray}, who hath promised to performe it. I cannot perceive any change in the King, but that he seemeth stil as desirous of the {9 = English} frendshippe as ever he was. Ticket to my Lord of L[eicester]. This morning Sir William Steward told his Majesty that Cutberd Armorer is now [..], [and] his brother was advertised that her Majesty is resolved to banishe the distressed Lords out of England for a few dayes, [and] that her meaning is to send them shortly into this contrey to shuffle the cardes. Whether there be any suche meaning or no, your Honour best knoweth. But in the meane season this companion plaieth his parte very kindly. I wishe therfore some order might be taken that no Englishman without espetial licence passe into this contrey. I wishe some order might be taken to stay his repaire into this contrey. [Endorsed:] Copie. To Mr Secretarye, 30 Auguste. Your letter of the 21st reached me on the 26th. From it I see that {39 = the Master of Gray} has complained that my manner towards him has changed. My answer is that, whatever cause he gave me, I never changed my manner, but always treated him with as much familiarity and courtesy as I did [..]. The truth is that after he had spoken to {10 = the King} for the release of {19 = Arran} without the knowledge of {40 = the Justice Clerk}, [27] or myself, he stopped his usual visits to me for three or four days, so that the change of manner was on his side, not mine. I will now take that proceeding in the best sense, seeing he has corrected himself so well, and [..] again. As for [27] and {40 = the Justice Clerk}, I have never seen cause to suspect them of being in the [11] course, nor do I think {39 = the Master of Gray} really believes it of them. Still, it cannot be denied, as you write, that [27] was much hers, is a great supporter of the Hamiltons, and is so far no earnest friend of the Lords; [?yet] in every matter of my negotiation I have had to handle with him I have found him fully as forward as either of the other two. Even so, I mean to follow your wise advice and deal warily with him and with everyone. From the little experience I have of the people of this country, I think it dangerous to trust any of them further than suits his own interests, as they call it here. So in my simple judgement, if the Queen wants to win reliable friends in this country, she must both take account of their interests and so commit them to her course [..] that necessity [..] [..]. Men who are only bound will quickly free themselves for a greater gain. Feeding them with money is good, but serves little purpose unless you commit them so far that they cannot hope to jump ashore without [?drowning]. {19 = Arran} is still at Kinneil, where, under colour of fearing a sudden attack by his [enemies], he is said to be very well guarded. Keeping him from the court beyond the meeting of the commissioners will, I think, be very hard, unless they find him guilty of the [?recent] breach on the Borders. If he regains access to the King, I cannot see how {39 = the Master of Gray}, {40 = the Justice Clerk} and [27] can live safely at court; and if {19 = Arran} is there alone as the man who does everything, we can easily guess how things will go. For my part I am too inexperienced to find a remedy for this mischief, and so leave it to the Queen to consider whether she will listen to {39 = the Master of Gray}'s offer or not. I expect her decision on the proposal made by {39 = the Master of Gray} any day. This morning I saw a letter written to the Prior of Blantyre by the brother of the Laird of [?Jamington], from which it appears that {20 = Lord Maxwell} is very eager to make his peace with the King through {19 = Arran}, with whom I suspect he already has a secret agreement; so I will do what I can to block his reconciliation with {10 = the King}. The Earl of Bothwell has, through the Master's efforts, just come to court, to the great dismay of Arran's party. It is quite certain that Hay and Dury are in the country. The King seems very keen to have them caught and has given the task to {39 = the Master of Gray}, who has promised to do it. I can see no change in the King, except that he seems as eager as ever for {9 = English} friendship. Note for the Earl of L[eicester]. This morning Sir William Stewart told the King that Cuthbert Armorer is now [..], and that his brother had been told that the Queen has decided to expel the distressed Lords from England for a few days, and that her real intention is to send them shortly into this country to shuffle the cards. Whether that is really her intention you know best. Meanwhile this fellow is playing his part very nicely. I would therefore wish some order to be made that no Englishman may come into this country without a special licence. I would wish some order to be made to stop his coming into this country. [Endorsed:] Copy. To the Secretary, 30 August. Sir, to carry out the proposal of {39 = the Master of Gray}, of which I have already told you, he and the Prior of Blantyre think it right that the Lords should by all means come to an agreement, quickly and secretly, with {20 = Lord Maxwell}; that {20 = Lord Maxwell} should then make a raid on the Laird of Johnstone, with whom he has a feud; so that, under colour of helping the Laird against {20 = Lord Maxwell}, the L. B., the L. H., S. J. H. and S. can gather their forces and join {20 = Lord Maxwell}, while the Lords send five hundred of their best men as fast as possible to seize {10 = the King} and {19 = Arran}. These five hundred are to be led by the Lord of Arbroath, the Earl [?of Mar] and the Master of G[lamis]. {39 = the Master of Gray} says that if he can quickly have enough money out of [36] to keep a hundred men for a short while, he will guarantee that the Lords are so strong inside {10 = the King}'s house that if {10 = the King}, on hearing that the Lords are coming into the country, tries to cross the water into Fife or to take refuge in [32], he will stop him by force and hand him over to them. You can well judge how necessary it is to have a friend inside the court who can (should the surprise attack of the five hundred fail) keep {10 = the King} from slipping away until the Lords' whole force arrives. So in my judgement it would be no bad thing to grant {39 = the Master of Gray}'s request. He is now so far committed that, unless this succeeds, I consider him utterly ruined; and so he can be trusted all the more. {39 = the Master of Gray} has had long talks with the Prior of Blantyre about this, and asks you to tell the Lords from him that whatever the Prior says to them when they come to the Borders, they should believe it, for he will certainly carry it out. I have held back from telling the King the part of your letter about postponing the commissioners' meeting to a later day, [..] [..] until such a day, having been told by the Secretary that his commissioners cannot be ready so soon. They want one of the commissioners to be an earl, one of the men of highest rank. I made a show of disliking his proposal, but told him I would report it, and asked that his commissioners should have full power and authority to do and conclude whatever the purpose of the meeting requires, which he says they will have. If the violent course is decided on, it cannot be consistent with {3 = the Queen's} honour for me to be in this country at that time. I beg you therefore to ask the Queen to recall me quickly, for I am in great danger; though I am unfit to be her ambassador, I may still live to serve her some other way. My sword cuts as well as any man's, and I have some friends in the part of the country where I live. Note. The matter proposed by {39 = the Master of Gray} is being kept from {40 = the Justice Clerk} and [27], because we here think {40 = the Justice Clerk} would reveal it to [27], whom we do not take for any great friend of the Lords. I beg that the matter be handled so that {39 = the Master of Gray} can be sure the Queen places great trust in him; otherwise he may out of spite reveal the whole thing and wreck it. As long as I stay in this country, people [?will] imagine that the Queen wants the league to go ahead and does not mean to support the Lords; that belief may do much harm and make their friends here hesitate. [Endorsed:] Copy. To the Secretary, 1 September. Key: key.md

Four Saxon despatches (DECODE R5005–R5008); the 1841 one was transcribed in full, 3,969 unseparated digits. Traces of an erased contemporary pencil decipherment give seven values and show a two-digit table of letters and syllables. No key survives on DECODE, and ciphertext-only solvers checked on a control produced no French; not solved. … 67 11 70 82 34 29 40 20 62 … … la pre m i er e …: the one phrase the erased pencil still gives Dresden → St Petersburg · two-digit syllabary · 1841–1843 Zeschau to Seebach, 1841–1843 Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden, 10731 Sächsische Gesandtschaft in Russland, Nr. 12, DECODE R5005–R5008: four despatches from the Saxon foreign minister to his minister resident in St Petersburg, one wholly in figures and three with cipher passages inside clear French or German. The despatch of 18 January 1841 was transcribed in full and attacked from the ciphertext alone. The type of cipher, a two-digit table of letters and syllables, and seven of its values were recovered from the traces of an erased contemporary pencil decipherment. No key was recovered and the letters have not been deciphered. Where Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden, 10731 Sächsische Gesandtschaft in Russland Nr. 12; DECODE R5005–R5008, “partially decrypted”. The cipher Unseparated digits forming a two-digit table of letters and syllables, not the homophonic letter cipher DECODE records. How it was tried Rubbed-out pencil words, brought back by background-subtracted crops, give la première over 11 70 82 34 29 40 and que over 46. Annealing solvers for homophonic and syllabic keys produce no French. Why it resists DECODE has no Dresden key later than 1806, and none filed with fonds 10731. Still open The key, UV or multispectral imaging of the erased pencil, or a transcription of the three sibling letters would finish it.

R5005, the despatch of 18 January 1841, image P5 (right-hand page): the middle line is 0064029740671170823429402062… , and the rubbed pencil above 11 70 82 34 29 40 reads “la pre m i er e”. Image: Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden, 10731 Sächsische Gesandtschaft in Russland Nr. 12, image P5, via DECODE R5005. DECODE Date Language Cipher R5005 18 Jan 1841 French the whole despatch, 70 lines, 3,969 digits R5006 6 Apr 1842, No. 13 French clear opening (“J’accuse la réception de vos rapports … nº 17 du 22 Mars”), then 8 + 3 lines R5007 13 Jun 1842, No. 18 German about ten lines between clear paragraphs (DECODE’s title has 1846) R5008 26 Oct 1843, No. 17 German five lines inside a sentence: “Indem ich nach dem Eingang Ihrer Berichte NN. 21 und 22 … bekenne, [cipher] habe ich die Ehre”

The figures are written without separation. Divided into pairs, the digits use 96 of the 100 possible groups. About a third of the lines have an odd number of digits, so a group can run over a line break. Where each line’s pairs begin was fixed by choosing the division with the strongest pair statistics. Long repeats such as 7778948206 (five times) and 06777818711001 (three times) should be names or set phrases. The erased decipherment settles the unit size. Seven values are legible in it: group 11 70 82 34 29 40 46 value la pre m i er e que So the table mixes single letters with syllables ( pre , er , que , la ). Elsewhere the pencil gives stray words (“pour”, “ce”, “ne”) that cannot be tied to a group with any confidence. Show-through from the reverse side adds false strokes.

Keys and print. Every Dresden key record on DECODE was listed. The latest dates from 1799–1806, and none belongs to fonds 10731. No edition of the Zeschau–Seebach correspondence was found. Structure. Tested single-digit nulls (every set of one to three digits), a prefix code (the first digit fixes a group length of 1, 2 or 3) and pairs in both phases. Only plain pairs are consistent with the glosses. Letter solver. A homophonic solver (simulated annealing) scored with a French 4-gram model deciphers a synthetic 1,800-letter homophonic control (score −2.18 per letter). On R5005 it reaches −3.05 to −3.17 under every division into units, which is not French. Syllable solvers. A solver (simulated annealing) choosing each group’s value from letters plus about 150 common French syllables, with the seven gloss values fixed, was run in three variants: free, one cell per syllable, and length-neutral scoring. All three drift to fluent-looking nonsense.

The key, or Seebach’s deciphered copies, in the legation papers (HStAD 10731, other numbers) or Seebach’s own papers. UV or multispectral imaging of R5005. The pencil decipherment was once complete, and a rubbed graphite trace often survives under raking or UV light. Transcribing R5006–R5008, which add text in the same table, with clear frames on either side of each cipher passage.
